IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_general_2_Body: Registration is open for evening courses in first aid, home repair and basic computing. Space is limited.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_medical_1_Body: Additional clinical coverage is needed this week. Reply with your certification and the hours you can work.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_medical_2_Body: The infection control refresher has been moved to the main conference room. Attendance will be recorded.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_outdoors_1_Body: Recent rain has damaged several access roads. Use the north trail and report fallen trees when you return.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_outdoors_2_Body: Line, seed, gloves and water purification tablets are discounted for registered field workers this week.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_police_1_Body: Several patrol shifts still need coverage. Confirm your availability with the desk before this afternoon's briefing.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_police_2_Body: The revised evidence intake sheet is now in use. Old forms will not be accepted after Friday.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_trades_1_Body: Three maintenance calls remain unassigned. Check the work board for locations and required parts.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_trades_2_Body: Wire, fasteners and replacement blades arrived this morning. Professional account holders may reserve stock by phone.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_veteran_1_Body: Your regional services office has opened additional appointment times. Call before Friday to reserve a slot.
IGUI_ComputerMod_SP_Mail_veteran_2_Body: The monthly post meeting begins at 1900. Volunteers are also needed to organize the storage room beforehand.

IGUI_KBW_GuideAboutBody: <H2> A passion project for builders <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> I have always wanted Project Zomboid to offer a building experience where a large collection stays organized, choices are easy to understand, and an entire base can be planned before spending the first plank. That idea began with my Building Menu for Build 41. <LINE> <LINE> Build 42 changed construction and introduced a new vanilla Building Menu, but the planning tools, grouped choices, detailed recipe information, flexible presentation, and multiplayer controls I wanted were still outside what the vanilla menu offered. Rather than leave those ideas behind, I started again and built Knox Buildworks around them. <LINE> <LINE> This mod is my attempt to make building feel like a complete part of the game: browse naturally, understand what a recipe will do, design large projects, share them with friends, and give server communities meaningful control without losing the fun of construction. <LINE> <LINE> <PUSHRGB:0.88,0.78,0.40> <SPACE> Knox Buildworks is made for the community and continues to grow through player feedback. <POPRGB> <SPACE> If you enjoy the mod and would like to support the time that goes into it, the button below opens my Ko-fi page. Support is always optional, and playing, reporting problems, and sharing the mod are appreciated too.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminAddonsBody: <H2> Core and Vanilla Expanded <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Knox Buildworks provides the system and its converted core construction. The included Vanilla Expanded add-on is optional and adds a much larger organized collection of walls, roofs, doors, windows, floors, fences, containers, furniture, decorations, vegetation, road pieces, and survival structures. <LINE> <LINE> Other compatible add-ons can place their buildables into the same catalog and reuse its categories. Enable only the collections wanted by the server, but remember that removing one also removes its recipes from searches, plans, and rule choices. <LINE> <LINE> For multiplayer, add each chosen construction add-on to both the server mod list and Workshop list, then ensure every player downloads the same version.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminAuthorityBody: <H2> Rules are shared by the server <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> When an administrator saves a valid ruleset, connected players receive the new revision. The server then checks availability, requirements, placement, blueprint access, item use, XP, and the finished construction whenever somebody builds. A client preference cannot bypass those checks. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Keep the mod list consistent <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Enable the same Knox Buildworks version and construction add-ons for the server and every player. If an add-on is removed, review rules and presets that used its categories or buildables. Ask players to reconnect after changing the server mod list or applying a major update. <LINE> <LINE> Keep exported presets as backups before a large rules change, and test with a normal player rather than only an administrator account.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminPresetsBody: <H2> Starting points <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Current Server Rules reloads the rules players are using now. Definition Defaults returns the draft to the normal Knox recipes. Disable All is useful when you want to begin with a tightly restricted server and enable only selected groups. Loading any source changes only your draft. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Share and reuse a ruleset <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Give the preset a clear name and export it to your client. Another administrator can copy that preset into their own preset folder, select Import to refresh the list, and load it as a draft on another server. <LINE> <LINE> <BHC> Loading is not the same as applying. <RGB:0.92,0.91,0.88> <SPACE> Review the effective rules, select Validate and Save, and wait for the new server revision. Warnings usually mean that the preset expects buildables or add-ons that are not enabled here.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminRecipesBody: <H2> Change only what your server needs <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Each build stage can have its own material and tool requirements, minimum skills, XP rewards, required learned recipes, and construction time. Turn on an override only for the part you want to replace; everything else continues to use the normal buildable recipe. <LINE> <LINE> Requirement rows let you choose valid items or tags, how many are needed, and whether they are consumed, kept, drained by uses, or destroyed. Use alternatives when several items should satisfy the same requirement. <LINE> <LINE> Select Validate and Save when finished. The editor will point out unknown items, recipes, skills, duplicates, and invalid values before anything is applied to players. Some special Build 42 objects keep protected native requirements, but their availability, XP, and build time can still be adjusted.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminRulesBody: <H2> Safe draft workflow <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Authorized administrators open Build Rules from the ElyonLib dock. The editor copies the synchronized server document into a private draft; browsing, loading a preset, and changing controls do not affect players. Validate and Save must succeed before the server publishes a new revision. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Editor layout <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Select a category, subcategory, or buildable on the left, then select a stage and tab on the right. Availability, inputs, finishes, skills and XP, recipe knowledge, and time are separate controls. The Finishes tab can waive plaster, paint, or wallpaper materials for every wall, while selected walls can explicitly inherit, require, or waive each cost. Non-wall paintable objects keep their normal requirements. Reload discards the draft and requests current server data. Reset Selected removes that buildable's overrides. <LINE> <LINE> Concurrent saves use revision checks. If another admin saves first, reload the newer revision before applying your changes.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminSandboxBody: <H2> Menu and planning <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Replace vanilla Build Menu decides whether the sidebar Build button opens Knox Buildworks directly. Enable Planning Mode controls blueprint UI availability. Max planned buildables limits ghosts per blueprint, while Blueprint radius limits the square area around its first anchor. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Construction and water <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Build XP multiplier scales Knox construction awards. Water well supply selects infinite or limited-and-refilling behavior; limited mode also uses capacity, initial fill, groundwater-per-hour, and rain-refill settings. <LINE> <LINE> Sandbox options are separate from Build Rules. Use sandbox controls for global systems and limits; use Build Rules for category, subcategory, buildable, and stage policy.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminScopesBody: <H2> Category to buildable <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Availability is checked from category, to subcategory, to individual buildable. Inherit means that level follows the broader setting. A more specific choice can create an exception. <LINE> <LINE> <INDENT:18> Disable a whole category when it does not fit the server. <LINE> Re-enable one useful subcategory inside it. <LINE> Disable or re-enable a single buildable for a final exception. <INDENT:0> <LINE> <LINE> The Effective Status line shows what players will actually receive. Use the broadest sensible rule first, then add only the exceptions you need.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminToolsBody: <H2> Test Runner <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Use the Test Runner when an add-on or update introduces many buildables and you want a quick health check. Its filters help you find entries with missing sprites, incomplete stages, bad requirements, or unsupported special objects. Select a result to focus on the affected buildable. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Tile Browser <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> The Tile Browser lets you search the loaded tile library and inspect a sprite's visible properties. It is useful when a placed object behaves differently from its preview, when checking storage capacity, or when identifying the correct face of a multi-direction object. <LINE> <LINE> These tools help locate problems; always finish by placing and using the object in the actual world.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAdminWorkflowBody: <H2> A safe way to change server rules <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> <INDENT:18> 1. Reload Current Server Rules before editing. <LINE> 2. Export a named preset so you can return to the current setup. <LINE> 3. Prefer a category or subcategory rule when many related pieces need the same treatment. <LINE> 4. Use individual buildable and stage overrides only for exceptions. <LINE> 5. Review Effective Status and validate every edited section. <LINE> 6. Save and wait for the confirmation that a new revision was synchronized. <LINE> 7. Join as a normal player and try the affected recipes, plans, and permissions. <INDENT:0> <LINE> <LINE> If the result is not what you intended, reload the saved backup preset, review it, and apply it through Validate and Save.
IGUI_KBW_GuideAppearanceBody: <IMAGECENTRE:media/ui/inventoryPanes/Button_Gear.png,28,28> <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Knox UI Appearance <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Choose a theme, high contrast, panel opacity, and checkerboard, light, dark, or custom object-preview backgrounds. A checkerboard makes both very dark and very light objects easier to distinguish. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Readability controls <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Fade unavailable buildable icons is an on/off toggle. Disable it when dimmed objects are hard to recognize; readiness borders and building restrictions remain active. Grid, detailed list, and compact views let you choose between more information and less screen coverage. <LINE> <LINE> If you use a larger game font, widen or raise the panel when you want more details, or use compact mode for a smaller footprint. Drag the resize corner after changing modes. Appearance choices are personal and do not affect other players.
IGUI_KBW_GuideBuildingBody: <H2> Using the construction cursor <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Select Build, move the preview to the desired square, rotate or change its face when available, and confirm on a valid location. Many compatible buildables stay on the cursor so you can place several in a row while you still have the required materials. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> If the preview is invalid <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Look for occupied tiles, missing support, the wrong side of a wall, a required floor or frame, poor light, distance, or something blocking part of a multi-tile footprint. Stairs, gates, large furniture, and irregular objects need every tile in their footprint to be valid. <LINE> <LINE> When the timed action finishes, the recipe uses its materials, keeps or wears its tools as described, awards its XP, and creates the finished object.
IGUI_KBW_GuideCatalogBody: <H2> Search and filters <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Search can look through buildable names, requirements, or everything at once. Combine it with category pages and the type, material, and skill filters to narrow a very large collection. Clear a filter or return to All when something expected is not visible. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Fast navigation <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> <INDENT:18> Favorites keeps hand-picked recipes together. <LINE> Recent returns to recipes used lately. <LINE> Sorting changes the order without changing availability. <LINE> Category arrows reveal additional category pages. <INDENT:0> <LINE> <LINE> <IMAGE:media/ui/inventoryPanes/FavouriteYes.png,20,20> The star changes only your personal favorite list. A server-disabled buildable remains unavailable even when it is a favorite.
IGUI_KBW_GuideChoicesBody: <H2> Families instead of duplicate recipes <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Related pieces are often gathered into one buildable family. Use the arrows to move between roof shapes, wall pieces, furniture models, directions, or construction qualities instead of searching for a separate entry for every sprite. <LINE> <LINE> Material, colour, model, and finish selectors appear when that family supports them. The preview and requirements follow your selection, and the same choice is remembered when you place a plan. <LINE> <LINE> <PUSHRGB:0.88,0.78,0.40> Check the preview before placing. <POPRGB> <SPACE> Members of one family may have different dimensions or may need a wall, floor, frame, or open space.
IGUI_KBW_GuideDetailsBody: <H2> Reading the inspector <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> The right-hand inspector shows the selected name, description, preview, useful properties, dimensions, readiness, skills, and materials. Dimensions appear as width x depth x height beneath the preview, so you can judge the space needed before starting placement. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Storage capacity <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Storage is shown for one usable face instead of repeating the same information for every rotation. <INDENT:18> <LINE> Multi-tile objects list every tile that provides storage on that face. <LINE> A two-tile dumpster can therefore show two separate capacities. <LINE> Multiple compartments on one tile, such as Fridge and Freezer, are listed separately. <INDENT:0> <LINE> <LINE> <PUSHRGB:0.88,0.78,0.40> Important: <POPRGB> <SPACE> previewed capacity describes the finished object. A blueprint ghost cannot hold items.
IGUI_KBW_GuideFinishesBody: <H2> Before and after construction <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> A material or finish selector changes the planned construction variant. Supported world actions can later apply plaster, paint, signs, or other finishes to a finished target. Each action still checks its normal tools, resources, skills, and target type. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Paintable objects <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Paintable furniture uses the object's custom color, matching the vanilla painting approach. White military crates are the neutral color base; green and gray military crates are also recognized by the Knox painting system. <LINE> <LINE> <PUSHRGB:0.88,0.78,0.40> Painting changes appearance only. <POPRGB> <SPACE> It does not alter container capacity, construction XP, recipe requirements, collision, or ownership.
IGUI_KBW_GuideFunctionalBody: <H2> More than decoration <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Storage furniture, fridges and freezers, doors, windows, lights, work surfaces, appliances, wells, and other supported objects keep the gameplay functions appropriate to them after construction. Multi-tile storage can provide a container on more than one tile, while one appliance tile can have separate compartments such as Fridge and Freezer. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Water wells <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Depending on the server settings, built wells either provide an unlimited source of clean water or hold a limited supply that slowly returns through groundwater and rain. If a limited well is empty, give it time or wait for rainfall. <LINE> <LINE> Read the inspector before building to see dimensions, storage capacity, and other useful properties of the selected object.
IGUI_KBW_GuideMultiplayerBody: <H2> When one player cannot build <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Check that character's materials, tools, skills, learned recipes, light, distance, and blueprint access. Select the buildable again to read the missing requirement, then try the placement cursor on a suitable square. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> When everyone has the same problem <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Ask an administrator whether the buildable or its category was disabled and whether Planning Mode is allowed. Everyone should use the same versions of Knox Buildworks and its enabled add-ons. After a server or mod update, reconnect before testing again. <LINE> <LINE> <BHC> The server makes the final decision. <RGB:0.92,0.91,0.88> <SPACE> It checks the recipe, position, permissions, item use, XP, and finished object so every player sees the same result.
IGUI_KBW_GuidePinnedBody: <IMAGECENTRE:media/ui/inventoryPanes/Button_Pin.png,28,28> <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Keep requirements visible <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Select the pin on a buildable to keep its recipe visible after the catalog closes. The pinned panel updates readiness, materials, tools, skills, and learned-recipe knowledge as the character and inventory change. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Pinned panel options <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Collapse individual recipes, move the panel when manual positioning is selected, and use its gear menu for alignment, position mode, opacity, accent bar, and icon or text presentation. <LINE> <LINE> Pinned recipes are a client convenience. They do not reserve items, start a queue, or change the server recipe.
IGUI_KBW_GuidePlanningBody: <H2> Plans are editable ghosts <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Place Plan adds a ghost to the active blueprint instead of building immediately. Planning Mode can create, duplicate, rename, delete, activate, and move blueprints, subject to access rights and server limits. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Layout tools <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> <INDENT:18> Place individual buildables on the chosen level. <LINE> Draw, update, and erase room layouts. <LINE> Change levels for multi-storey planning. <LINE> Move the blueprint origin or erase incorrect placements. <INDENT:0> <LINE> <LINE> <BHC> Ghosts provide no collision, storage, water, light, or protection until constructed. <RGB:0.92,0.91,0.88> <SPACE> The server can disable Planning Mode or limit placements and blueprint radius.
IGUI_KBW_GuideQueueBody: <H2> Gather area <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Contributors can mark an area used to search supported containers and vehicles for construction resources. The area belongs to the blueprint and can be moved or cleared. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Building a plan <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Build Selected targets one planned placement. Build All queues valid ghosts and works through them in order; Stop Queue cancels the remaining queue. Each construction still performs readiness, reach, placement, permission, and server validation. <LINE> <LINE> <PUSHRGB:0.88,0.78,0.40> <SPACE> The queue does not create missing resources or bypass locked recipes. <POPRGB> <SPACE> If it stops, inspect the next ghost, character inventory, gather area, path, and current permissions.
IGUI_KBW_GuideReadinessBody: <IMAGE:media/ui/craftingMenus/BuildProperty_Book_16.png,20,20> <SPACE> <IMAGE:media/ui/craftingMenus/BuildProperty_Light_16.png,20,20> <SPACE> <IMAGE:media/ui/craftingMenus/BuildProperty_Clock_16.png,20,20> <LINE> <LINE> <H2> What Ready checks <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Materials, retained tools, drained uses, skills, learned recipes, light, reach, stage rules, and server availability can all affect readiness. Counts show available versus required amounts. Alternatives are grouped so any permitted item or tag can satisfy that input. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Requirement types <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> <INDENT:18> Consumed items disappear when used. <LINE> Retained tools must be present but are normally kept. <LINE> Drainable inputs remove uses rather than the entire item. <LINE> Destroyed inputs are deliberately removed by the recipe. <INDENT:0> <LINE> <LINE> <BHC> Ready in the catalog is guidance, not a promise that every world square is valid. <RGB:0.92,0.91,0.88> <SPACE> Placement performs the final world and server checks. Fading unavailable icons can be turned off in Knox UI Appearance without changing any rule.
IGUI_KBW_GuideSharingBody: <H2> Building together <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> A blueprint owner can keep a plan private or give access to everyone, a faction, or individual players. View access lets someone see the plan. Build access lets them construct its ghosts. Contribute access also lets them edit placements, rooms, and the gather area. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Taking a plan elsewhere <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> You can write a selected plan onto a supported in-game blueprint item and import a carried blueprint later. Planning Mode also provides local export and import controls for sharing a plan outside the game. An imported plan appears near the importing player so it can be moved into position. <LINE> <LINE> Access and ownership are not carried over as free permissions. The destination world or server still decides what the player may see, edit, and build.
IGUI_KBW_GuideViewsBody: <IMAGE:media/ui/craftingMenus/Icon_Grid.png,24,24> <SPACE> <IMAGE:media/ui/craftingMenus/Icon_List.png,24,24> <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Choose the view that suits you <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Grid view gives each buildable a large visual card. Detailed list view shows more names, categories, and status information at once. Compact mode uses a side list of subcategories and a dense icon grid, making it useful when you want a quick overview or a smaller window. <LINE> <LINE> Selecting an icon in compact mode still gives you the available group, quality, model, material, and finish choices at the bottom. Hover over an icon to read its name and requirements. <LINE> <LINE> <PUSHRGB:0.88,0.78,0.40> Tip: <POPRGB> <SPACE> drag the bottom-right corner to find a comfortable size. The layout adapts to the current font size and available space.
IGUI_KBW_GuideWelcomeBody: <H2> Welcome to Knox Buildworks <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> Knox Buildworks gives you one organized place to discover, preview, plan, and construct buildings and objects. Open it from the building sidebar or with the configurable catalog key, which is F7 by default. It can live beside the vanilla Building Menu, or a server can make Knox the primary building action. <LINE> <LINE> <H2> Build something <TEXT> <LINE> <LINE> <INDENT:18> 1. Browse or search for what you want. <LINE> 2. Choose its quality, model, material, colour, or finish when those choices are available. <LINE> 3. Check what it needs and whether the current character is ready. <LINE> 4. Select Build to construct now, or Place Plan to leave a blueprint ghost for later. <INDENT:0> <LINE> <LINE> <GHC> Ready means your character passes the recipe checks shown in the catalog. <RGB:0.92,0.91,0.88> <SPACE> The placement cursor will then check the chosen location.

IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Better Aiming <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forget everything you've seen on television. Hollywood actors hold guns as if they were toys, shoot without looking, and drop villains a hundred meters away firing with one hand. In real life, if you do that, the recoil will break your nose and you will miss every shot. <LINE> <LINE> Accurate shooting is not a divine gift; it's biomechanics, physics, and emotional control. It's the art of aligning pieces of metal with your eyes while controlling your own breathing. <LINE> <LINE> Whether you bought your first revolver for home defense or a hunting rifle, don't put ammunition in it just yet. Sit down, read this manual, and learn the respect that gunpowder demands.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Flinch (Anticipating Recoil) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The human body is smart and hates explosions near its face. The 'Flinch' is the involuntary reflex of closing your eyes tightly, locking your shoulders, and pushing your hands down a millisecond before the shot. It is the worst enemy of accuracy. <LINE> <LINE> If you are shooting a large revolver (.357 Magnum) and your shots are hitting the dirt a meter before the target, you are suffering from a flinch. <LINE> <LINE> To cure this, practice Dry Firing. Unload the gun. Triple-check that it is empty. Point it at a safe wall and pull the trigger. The hammer will drop (Click!). Did the barrel of your gun move an inch downward at the moment of the click? If so, you are anticipating the kick. Dry fire until the barrel doesn't move a single millimeter during the 'click'.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Respiratory Pause <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your chest rises and falls all day long. If you try to hold the gun perfectly still while you are panting, your sights will swing up and down violently following the expansion of your lungs. <LINE> <LINE> Precision shooting occurs during the 'Natural Respiratory Pause'. Breathe in normally, exhale most of the air, and stop. When your lungs empty, there is a natural pause of two to three seconds before you feel the urge to breathe in again. <LINE> <LINE> It is during these three seconds of absolute pulmonary silence that your torso is static as stone. That's when you squeeze the trigger and let the shot break.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Follow-Through <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In golf and baseball, the club or bat continues its motion after hitting the ball. In sport and defensive shooting, we use Follow-Through. <LINE> <LINE> The amateur pulls the trigger, hears the noise, and immediately lowers the gun and raises their head to see where it hit on the paper. Doing this is terrible. The brain anticipates the movement and begins to lower the gun before the bullet even leaves the barrel. <LINE> <LINE> The professional shooter fires, absorbs the recoil, and keeps the sights locked on the target and their finger holding the trigger back for a full second AFTER the explosion. You only relax after you see the sights return on their own to the center of the target. Never be in a hurry to see your score.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Myth of the Giant Caliber <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don't learn to drive in an eighteen-wheeler. You shouldn't learn to shoot with a 12-gauge shotgun or a .44 Magnum revolver. <LINE> <LINE> Massive calibers generate a deafening report and real pain in the hands, which creates an uncontrollable fear reflex (Flinch) in the novice on their first afternoon at the shooting range. <LINE> <LINE> True mastery of sight mechanics is built with .22 Long Rifle (.22LR) ammunition. It's cheap, quiet, and has almost no recoil. Practice hundreds of shots and put them all in the same coin-sized hole at fifteen meters using the humble .22. Only after the fundamentals are carved into your muscle memory do you advance to combat calibers like 9mm and .38 Special.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Maintenance is Accuracy <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your stance may be perfect and your breathing static, but if the inside of your rifle's barrel is coated in melted lead, unburnt powder, and rust, the bullet will come bouncing out of there and fly aimlessly. <LINE> <LINE> Clean your guns. The rifling of the barrel, those spiral lines inside the metal, are designed to make the bullet spin like a top, giving it gyroscopic stability. <LINE> <LINE> If the grooves are clogged with dirt, the barrel becomes smooth, the bullet doesn't spin, and your hunting rifle loses its accuracy at fifty meters. Buy a kit of copper brushes, solvent, and gunsmith oil. The shooter takes care of the iron before taking care of themselves.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Foundation is Ready <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We have concluded the first stage. You've stopped holding your gun as if it were going to bite your hand and learned that the key to accuracy is not in the barrel, it's in your cold mind and your smooth finger. Focus on the front sight. Surprise trigger break. Pause in breathing. <LINE> <LINE> But in this volume, you shot against a piece of paper that doesn't shoot back. You had all day to align your eye, in a quiet environment, standing and motionless. <LINE> <LINE> The real world demands urgency. In Volume Two, 'Drawing and Shooting', we will level up. You will learn how to draw the gun from the holster under stress, shoot with speed without losing sight alignment, how to clear clothing, and prepare so the gun doesn't get caught when the threat is two meters away. Practice dry firing and we'll see you there.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Four Universal Laws <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before we talk about how to hit the target, you need to learn how to not accidentally kill your neighbor. <LINE> <LINE> 1. Every gun is ALWAYS loaded. Even if you just checked it. <LINE> 2. Never point the muzzle at anything you are not willing to destroy completely. <LINE> 3. Keep your finger straight and OUT of the trigger guard (away from the trigger) until the exact second your sights are on the target and you have decided to shoot. <LINE> 4. Be absolutely sure of your target and what lies behind it. Bullets tear through drywall as if it were paper.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Stance: Your Foundation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Shooting is like boxing. If your feet are wrong, you'll be knocked down by the first punch. In the case of guns, that punch is the recoil. <LINE> <LINE> Forget that sideways, twisted stance as if you were in an Old West duel. Police departments adopted the Weaver and Isosceles stances for a reason. Face the target. Place your feet shoulder-width apart. Take a small step back with your dominant foot (the side of your shooting hand). <LINE> <LINE> Lean your torso slightly forward, shifting your weight to the balls of your feet. You must be the wall that absorbs the gun's kick, not a rigid post that falls backward with every shot.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Grip (Handguns) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The way you hold the pistol defines where the bullet goes. The most common novice mistake is the famous 'Teacup Grip', where the support hand sits relaxed underneath the gun's butt. This is useless. <LINE> <LINE> Your dominant hand should grip the gun as high as possible on the back strap, close to the slide. The higher your hand is, the less the gun will jump upward (Muzzle Flip). <LINE> <LINE> Your support hand (your weak hand) should firmly wrap around the fingers of your strong hand, with both thumbs pointing forward, parallel to the barrel. It's the support hand that does 70%% of the work, squeezing the gun to stabilize it, while the trigger hand remains relaxed just to shoot.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Mounting the Rifle <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you are using a rifle or a shotgun, the grip extends to your shoulder. The stock of the long gun must be pulled firmly into the 'pocket' formed in your shoulder when you raise your arm. <LINE> <LINE> If you leave the stock loose, floating millimeters in front of your body, when the shot happens, the gun will gain momentum and deliver a violent punch to your collarbone, leaving a giant purple bruise. <LINE> <LINE> Pull the rifle into your body as if it were part of your skeleton. The closer the metal is to your shoulder and your cheek is to the stock (Cheek Weld), the more your body will absorb the recoil as a single, unified piece.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sight Alignment <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Look at the top of your gun. You have the Rear Sight (close to your eye, looking like the letter 'U') and the Front Sight (the post at the tip of the barrel). <LINE> <LINE> Perfect alignment happens when you place the front post exactly in the middle of the rear 'U'. The post must have the same amount of empty space on both the right and left sides, and the top of the post must be perfectly level with the top of the 'U'. <LINE> <LINE> If the front post is even a millimeter higher than the rear sight, your bullet will pass three spans above the target's head at twenty meters. The alignment of the metal pieces is sacred.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Eye Focus (The Secret) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Here is the secret that separates elite shooters from frustrated amateurs. The human eye cannot focus perfectly on three different distances at the same time (the rear sight, the front sight, and the target far away). <LINE> <LINE> The novice tries to look at the target in the background. The gun's sights blur and they miss the shot. <LINE> <LINE> Your eye must be focused SOLELY and EXCLUSIVELY on the Front Sight. Yes, your paper target in the background will be blurry, and the rear sight close to your nose will also be a bit blurry. But the front post of the gun must be sharp, clear, and razor-sharp. Focus on the front sight, always.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Trigger Control <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The trigger is not a button that you slap or pull quickly. We use the word 'squeeze'. <LINE> <LINE> Place only the tip of your index finger on the trigger (the first phalanx). If you shove your entire finger in up to the knuckle, you will pull the gun to the side when firing. <LINE> <LINE> Pressure must be applied continuously and incredibly smoothly, pulling the trigger in a straight line perfectly to the rear. If you give it a sudden jerk because you got anxious to hear the bang, the barrel of the gun will dip downward or to the side in the exact fraction of a second before the bullet leaves. The shot isn't pulled; it's earned smoothly.
IGUI_BookAiming1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Surprise Break <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the gun fires, you shouldn't know the exact moment the bullet is going to leave. This is called a 'Surprise Break'. <LINE> <LINE> You just keep increasing the pressure on the trigger, milligram by milligram, with the sights aligned, until 'BANG!'. The gun fires and startles you slightly. <LINE> <LINE> If you 'decide' to shoot and jerk it all at once ('Now!'), your brain will make your arms push the gun forward to compensate for the recoil before the shot even happens. Let the shot surprise you. It's the only way to ensure your body didn't ruin the aim in anticipation of the recoil.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Drawing and Shooting <LINE> Chapter 1: The World Outside the Firing Line <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first volume, you learned to shoot at a paper target, standing still, in a quiet environment where nobody was trying to kill you. Congratulations, you master the basics of physics. Now, let's step into the real world. <LINE> <LINE> Shooting in a defense or crisis situation is 90%% psychology and 10%% mechanics. Your heart will race to 160 beats per minute. Your tunnel vision will close in. Your hands will shake and your fine motor skills will disappear. <LINE> <LINE> This volume is about the transition from the gun in the holster to the gun on the target. If you can't draw your gun and place an accurate shot in less than two seconds, you don't have a defense tool; you have an expensive and dangerous paperweight on your belt.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ammunition and Reliability <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your weapon is a complex machine with springs and moving parts. If you use ammunition reloaded at home by an amateur or old ammo that has been stored in moisture for five years, a malfunction (misfire) is only a matter of time. <LINE> <LINE> Learn 'Tap, Rack, Bang'. If the gun goes click instead of bang, don't try to investigate why. Deliver a firm slap to the bottom of the magazine (Tap), pull the slide completely back to eject the faulty round (Rack), and release the slide to chamber a new bullet (Bang). You do this in less than a second, without even thinking.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Use of Cover and Concealment <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Concealment is something that hides you. Cover is something that stops a bullet from killing you. A wooden door or a drywall partition is just a hiding place; a bullet cuts through it like paper. An engine block, a concrete pillar, or a truck tire is cover. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When shooting from behind cover, never rest the weapon against the object. The weapon will vibrate and your accuracy will be nil. And never expose your face and weapon together on the same side. Change angles. Your weapon must be protected, and you must be the smallest target possible.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Sound of the Shot <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Firing inside a closed room or a narrow hallway is one of the most common mistakes made by those without training. The roar of the shot in a confined environment is so loud that it can rupture your eardrums instantly and cause severe labyrinthine disorientation. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You will lose your balance and have a constant ringing that will prevent you from hearing the footsteps of a second threat coming from behind. If you can avoid shooting indoors without hearing protection, avoid it. If you can't, open your mouth slightly when firing; this helps equalize internal ear pressure and reduces the risk of a ruptured eardrum.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Emergency Draw on the Ground <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You've been knocked down. You are on the ground, on your back, looking up, and the threat is coming your way. Most people panic and try to get up. Wrong. You are a bigger and slower target trying to stand up. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> On the ground, you have stability. Roll on your own body, use your legs to maintain distance, and draw the weapon keeping the barrel pointed at the threat while moving. The ground is your shield. Learn to shoot from your back, your side, and your knees. The battlefield rarely offers a nice, flat floor.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Target Identification Under Tension <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The light is low, adrenaline is exploding, your heart is beating in your neck, and you see a figure running towards you. Is it an attacker or a frightened civilian? Your brain under stress will trick you and create 'targets' that do not exist. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The amateur shooter shoots first and asks questions later. The professional shooter has a mental brake: 'Positive Identification'. You need an extra millisecond to see the person's hand. Are they armed? Are they attacking? Don't trust your instinct. Trust your vision. Shooting an innocent person is a mistake you will never forgive yourself for, even if you live a thousand years.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Practice to Exhaustion <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We have closed Volume Two. You learned to draw, move, control your breathing in panic, and understand that your brain is your greatest enemy on the firing range. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Defensive shooting is not about 'shot group size', it's about 'speed of delivering a solution'. Practice your draw in the mirror until it is boring. Practice dry firing until your finger is independent of your mind. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> But you are still dealing with targets that are too close. In Volume Three, 'Leading Moving Targets', things will get tough. We'll talk about trajectory physics, how to calculate the speed of targets crossing in front of you, the use of optics, and how to compensate for bullet flight time. Prepare your eyes and continue training.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Draw <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The most common mistake is trying to be too fast and ending up fumbling. Speed in shooting comes from efficiency of movement, not brute force. A correct draw is divided into four steps. <LINE> <LINE> Step 1: Dominant hand grips the weapon's handle and the thumb unlocks the holster. Step 2: You pull the weapon straight up until it completely clears the holster, keeping your elbow tucked against your ribs. Step 3: Your support hand joins the weapon at the center of your chest. Step 4: You push the weapon toward the target, aligning the sights as the barrel rises. <LINE> <LINE> Practice this a thousand times without ammunition. The movement must be fluid, like a choreography. If you stumble on any of these steps, you will fumble the draw in a panic situation.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Clothing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your holster might be the best in the world, but if you are wearing a baggy jacket, a heavy sweater, or an untucked shirt, you have just created a deadly barrier between you and your safety. <LINE> <LINE> It's common to see novices draw their weapon and catch their finger on the jacket fabric or, worse, snag the front sight on the shirt hem. In a real situation, you don't have time to ask the attacker to wait for you to 'adjust your clothes'. <LINE> <LINE> If you carry a gun, your attire is part of your equipment. Your shirt hem should be tucked or cleared to allow full access. Train drawing with the same clothes you wear every day. Drawing in shorts and a t-shirt is one thing; drawing from under a winter coat is an art that requires practice.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tunnel Vision (The Effect of Stress) <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the threat arises, your brain enters survival mode. It blocks your peripheral vision to focus 100%% on the threat. You will lose track of time, sound, and even your weapon's sights. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you don't train your draw until it becomes a core reflex (muscle memory), you will draw the weapon, but your eyes will refuse to focus on the front sight post, because your brain only wants to look at the danger ahead. <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This is why you train: so that, even under the tunnel effect, your body raises the weapon at the correct angle and the front sight enters your line of vision automatically, even if you aren't 'looking' for it.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Point Shooting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> At close range — say, three meters or less — you don't have time to bring the weapon up to eye level and look for the metal sights. The threat is too close and moving fast. <LINE> <LINE> Point Shooting is the ability to place the weapon in front of your face, keeping your head up and both eyes open, and fire using the silhouette of the weapon as a reference. <LINE> <LINE> It's like pointing your finger at an object across the room. You don't 'aim' your finger; you just point. Your brain instinctively knows where the gun is pointing if you train enough. At this distance, the focus is not surgical accuracy of a centimeter, it's the speed of putting the bullet into the target's center of mass before they reach you.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Breath Control in Panic <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first thing panic does is make you hold your breath, which is a fatal mistake. Holding your breath with a tense body deprives your brain of oxygen and makes your muscles shake. <LINE> <LINE> The professional's technique under fire is not to 'stop' breathing, but to control breathing so that it doesn't interfere with the shot. Inhale, let a little out to stabilize your chest, and pull the trigger in the interval between your racing heartbeats. Yes, you can feel your heartbeat in your chest when you are under stress. It is during those beats that you must learn to fire.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Movement and Shooting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A stationary target is a dead target. If you draw your weapon and stand planted like a statue waiting to shoot, you are an easy target. Shooting on the move is what separates the range shooter from the combatant. <LINE> <LINE> The basic technique is the 'glide'. Keep your torso stable, with your shoulders locked, and move with your knees slightly bent, as if walking on thin ice. You should never stamp your heel on the ground; walk by rolling the sole of your foot, from heel to toe, keeping your head height constant. If your head bounces, the gun bounces.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Verbalizing and Firing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> It sounds silly, but opening your mouth to shout commands like 'STOP!' or 'DROP IT!' is a tactical tool. When you shout, you are forced to exhale air. This forced exhalation helps stabilize your torso and empty your lungs for the shot. <LINE> <LINE> Furthermore, the verbal command can, in a fraction of a second, cause a hesitation in the threat that will give you the advantage of time. Never fire in absolute silence if you can avoid it. The verbal order establishes your dominance and prepares your own respiratory system for the dirty work.
IGUI_BookAiming2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Support Hand Problem <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Many inexperienced shooters, when drawing their weapon, forget that the support hand is also a weapon. In a stress situation, your weak hand must always be ready. <LINE> <LINE> If you are in a dark area, your support hand should be holding a flashlight. If you are in a hostile area, it must be ready to block, push, or open doors. <LINE> <LINE> The support hand is not dead weight. Learn to draw and shoot using only your dominant hand, while your support hand does all the work of manipulating the environment. Shooting with one hand is less accurate, but it is an urban survival requirement.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Leading Moving Targets <LINE> Chapter 1: The Target Has Legs <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first two manuals, we dealt with shooter stress, breathing, and the mechanics of drawing the weapon. But there was a comforting constant in all of it: the paper target was nailed to a piece of wood. It didn't run away. <LINE> <LINE> Welcome to advanced physics. In the real world of hunting or combat, targets run, jump, dodge, and duck. If you aim exactly at the chest of a deer running at full speed fifty meters away and pull the trigger, your bullet will hit the dust three meters behind it. <LINE> <LINE> This book is about 'Leading'. It is the unnatural and counter-intuitive art of shooting at empty air and trusting that the target will meet your bullet.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dirty Training: The Old Tire <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You can't train at a municipal range because running is forbidden there. If you have a piece of land in the country, do this: take an old car tire and tie a piece of firm cardboard into the middle hole. <LINE> <LINE> Have a friend hide safely at the top of a small hill or embankment and roll the tire down the hill, crossing transversely across your line of fire (from right to left). <LINE> <LINE> The tire will bounce, accelerate, and swerve on rocks, mimicking an escaping animal almost perfectly. Try to put a shot in the cardboard while it's rolling at maximum speed. You will be shocked by how bad you are for the first twenty shots.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Second Shot Discipline <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Shooting on the move breeds errors. It's inevitable. If your first bolt-action rifle shot misses the running target, your initial reaction will be panic and a rush to cycle the second shot. <LINE> <LINE> Haste destroys the weapon's cycle. The novice shooter pulls the bolt with such anger that they jam the cartridge in the magazine, completely locking the weapon (Double Feed). <LINE> <LINE> Operate the machine coldly. Missed? The target is still running. You chamber the bolt or release the trigger of your pistol with deliberate force, not desperation. You re-evaluate the lead – if you missed behind, you need more lead. Breathe. One calculated second shot is worth more than ten shots fired in a shower of panic.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Balance and Unorthodox Positions <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Volume One taught you to stand perfectly. In the field, you don't have time for a textbook stance. The target appeared jumping the fence and you need to shoot fast. <LINE> <LINE> If you try to shoot on the move with stiff legs, the uneven ground will make your sights jump. You have to absorb the terrain with your legs, lowering your center of gravity. <LINE> <LINE> And don't be ashamed to use the environment. Resting your back, your arm (never the gun barrel) against a tree, wall, or the side of your truck stabilizes your body immediately, allowing your eyes to track the target's run smoothly, like a camera with a tripod.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ethics of a Heavy Trigger <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hunting is sustainability, not cruelty. In the doctrine of culling, we have non-negotiable rules. If you shoot at a moving target that is too fast or at an angle where you have only a 30%% chance of a clean hit, you are a terrible shooter. <LINE> <LINE> An irresponsible shot in the animal's hind legs or lower abdomen (Gut Shot) won't drop it instantly. It will run for miles bleeding, escape you, and die hours later, alone and in agony, with its meat spoiled by the fever of infection. <LINE> <LINE> The mature shooter is the one who knows when to lower the weapon. If its run left you behind, lower the barrel and accept defeat. Let the threat or the quarry go.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Post-Shot Photographic Memory <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the exact millisecond you pull the trigger, your mind must take a mental snapshot of that scene. <LINE> <LINE> If you shot and the target kept running until it vanished into the brush, your 'mental photo' will tell you where your sight was when the gun fired. Was it too low? Was the post unfocused? <LINE> <LINE> We call this 'Calling the Shot'. Before even seeing the hole, the experienced shooter says: 'I hit the ground behind'. This is fundamental in tracking. If the mental photo says your sight was perfect on the chest at the moment of the roar, the animal didn't go far. You just sit down, smoke a cigarette for twenty minutes (to let it lie down and pass out in the brush), and only then start looking for the blood trail.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hunter's Axis <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> End of lesson three. You already know how to shoot on paper, draw from under a jacket, and intercept a deer (or a fleeing car) with the mathematics of visual lead. Your mechanics as a civilian and police shooter are robust and formed. <LINE> <LINE> But there is a frontier where the thick iron sights of pistols and shotguns lose their utility. It is the frontier of silence, crosswinds, and camouflage. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Four, 'Long Range Sniping Tactics', I will transfer your knowledge to the use of Optics. Telescopic scopes, MOA (Minute of Angle), gravitational bullet drop, and the silent tactics of snipers. When distance increases, physics is no longer an ally; it becomes your greatest opponent.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Flight Time (The Laser Illusion) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hollywood has convinced the world that bullets travel at the speed of light, like sci-fi laser beams. That is a lie that costs missed shots every day. <LINE> <LINE> Bullets are fast, yes, but they are not instantaneous. A .308 caliber projectile from a hunting rifle travels at about 800 meters per second. This means it takes a fraction of a second to cross an open field. <LINE> <LINE> In that fraction of a second, a target running laterally has already moved forward. Your job as a shooter is not to focus on where the animal is now; your job is to mathematically calculate where it will be the moment your bullet crosses that exact distance.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Angle of Incidence <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before calculating speed, you need to read the geometry of the movement. The lead you give in your aim depends on where the target is going. <LINE> <LINE> If a man or an animal is running directly towards you (or running in a straight line away from you), the lateral lead is ZERO. You shoot straight into the target's center of mass, because the target isn't leaving your line of sight, just changing size. <LINE> <LINE> But if the target is crossing your field of vision laterally, at exactly 90 degrees (running from your left to right, parallel to you), it will require Maximum Lead. Any diagonal angle between these two extremes will require a fraction of that lead.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Technique 1: The Ambush <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> There are two main techniques for hitting moving objects. The first and safest for beginners with rifles is the Ambush Method. <LINE> <LINE> You are tracking a deer running through the field. You don't try to shoot while it moves. Instead, you advance your aim and lock it on a fixed point ahead of it (a specific tree or a bush in its path). <LINE> <LINE> You keep the gun perfectly still and focused on that empty spot. When the animal's snout crosses your sights, you press the trigger. You are letting the target do the work of crossing the line of fire. The disadvantage? It requires absolute timing.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Technique 2: Swing-Through <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The preferred method for duck hunters with shotguns and urban professionals is Swing-Through. Here, your weapon never stops moving. <LINE> <LINE> You raise the gun, point at the rear of the moving target (like the animal's tail), and sweep the sight rapidly through its body, overtaking the head into the empty space ahead. <LINE> <LINE> The exact instant your sight passes the target and reaches the required 'lead' distance in front of it, you fire. The magic of this technique is that your own sweeping motion with your arms cancels out much of the mathematics of the target's speed.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fatal Error: Stopping the Barrel <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you choose the Swing-Through technique, you will fight against the worst instinct of the human brain. When your eyes say 'Now, shoot!', your brain tells your whole body to freeze to stabilize the shot. <LINE> <LINE> If you stop the movement of the gun barrel for a fraction of a millisecond at the exact moment you pull the trigger, the target will keep running while your gun stayed behind in the past. The bullet will hit dust behind the target. <LINE> <LINE> You must keep rotating your torso and following the target's movement AFTER the shot is fired. Follow-through in motion is the only way to ensure the barrel didn't freeze before the hammer struck the bullet.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ammunition and Caliber Effect <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You must memorize the ballistics of what you carry. If you are hunting with a .308 rifle that fires at over 800 meters per second, at a target 100 meters crossing in front of you, your lead will be small, perhaps aiming just at the tip of the animal's nose. <LINE> <LINE> But if you are shooting with a heavy, slow handgun like a .45 ACP or a .22LR rifle, the bullet flies at half that speed. For the same distance and the same target, you will need to aim into the air, a full meter ahead of the animal. Knowing your weapon is not a luxury; it's the math that gets you dinner.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Zig-Zag and Axis Breaking <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> On television, criminals flee in a zig-zag. This may confuse aim, but it cuts forward speed in half. In hunting, rabbits do this naturally. <LINE> <LINE> The tactic against erratic targets is not to swing your gun wildly right and left trying to follow every move. You will get dizzy and hit nothing. <LINE> <LINE> Focus on the center of the target's axis. It runs in a pattern. Instead of shooting while it runs diagonally to the left, wait for the moment of the break (the Pivot). In the millisecond it turns its foot to change direction (to go right), its body slows to almost zero. It is in this static millisecond of the axis break that the professional fires.
IGUI_BookAiming3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> False Speed (Perception) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The further away the target is, the slower it 'seems' to be running. This is an optical illusion of panoramic perspective. A car at a hundred kilometers per hour on the horizon seems to crawl. <LINE> <LINE> But it's still going a hundred. And worse, at that astronomical distance, the flight time of your bullet will be measured in seconds, not fractions. The lead stops being measured in 'fingers' and starts being measured in 'car lengths'. <LINE> <LINE> This is why infantry shooters rarely fire at moving targets in extreme parallel flight. Unless you have advanced optics and a ballistics chart, trying to hit someone crossing a valley 400 meters away is a loud waste of ammunition.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Long Range Sniping Tactics <LINE> Chapter 1: The Mathematics of Death <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Up until now, we've fought up close. At less than twenty meters, physics is your friend and the bullet travels in an illusory straight line. But if you bought a precision rifle, mounted an expensive scope on top of it, and think you're going to hit a target at eight hundred meters just because the crosshair is in the middle of its chest, you're a fool who failed math. <LINE> <LINE> Long-range shooting is not a sight test; it's solving a complex equation under stress. Gravity pulls your bullet down, wind drives it sideways, air temperature alters atmospheric density, and your own heartbeat makes the weapon tremble. Welcome to the world of snipers. Where the trigger is the easiest part of the job.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Trigger Fault Magnified <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We talked about trigger control in Volume One. Let me explain long-range math. If you give an anxious jerk on the trigger that causes your gun barrel to swerve a mere two millimeters, at ten meters, you miss the center by a few centimeters. <LINE> <LINE> But at 500 meters? Those same two millimeters of deviation at the source multiply geometrically. That tiny jolt of anxiety in your index finger will cause your bullet to miss the entire man by more than a meter and a half. Trigger control at long range shouldn't be a squeeze; it should be the weight of a thought. Move your finger so slowly that your brain barely registers the movement.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Respiratory Trance <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The sniper doesn't shoot when they want to; they shoot when their body allows it. When you look through the scope at high magnification, the crosshair will rise and fall rhythmically over the target's chest following your breathing. <LINE> <LINE> You don't lock your breath with lungs full of air, or your muscles will shake from oxygen deprivation within five seconds. You let all the air out naturally. <LINE> <LINE> At the bottom of the exhalation, your body enters a empty pause (Respiratory Deflation). Your heart slows down slightly. The aim stops swinging and freezes. You have between three and five seconds of near-mortal physical lethargy. It is there, in that tiny space between active life and body silence, that you send the bullet flying.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Temperature Effect on Powder <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You zeroed your rifle perfectly at noon in scorching forty-degree summer heat. Months later, you are on a snow-covered roof in the dead of winter, and your long-range shot drops miserably into the ground before the target. The math was right. The chemistry failed. <LINE> <LINE> Gunpowder burns at different speeds depending on the ambient temperature. On a hot day, powder burns fiercely, creating massive pressure and pushing the bullet faster, shooting higher. In extreme sub-zero cold, the powder becomes sluggish, chamber pressure drops, and the bullet leaves slower, sinking into the snow long before. Your logbook must have separate tables for summer and winter.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Spotter (The Real Brain) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Snipers don't work alone in real life; they work in pairs. The most important figure on the team is not the guy with his finger on the trigger; it's the Spotter. <LINE> <LINE> While the shooter is focused on the small scope tube (forced tunnel vision), the Spotter uses a large spotting scope or binoculars to scan peripheral terrain. He calculates wind using mirage, reads the ballistic chart, does the math, and tells the shooter exactly how many 'clicks' to give the sight. <LINE> <LINE> If the shooter misses, the shooter is temporarily blinded by recoil. The Spotter is not. He sees the dust impact kicked up by the miss, says 'Half a meter left' and ensures the second attempt hits flesh.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Psychological Toll <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forget the glamour of the lone sniper. Long-range shooting demands a psychological torture that few can endure. It is the war of unbearable patience. <LINE> <LINE> You will spend days hidden in the cold, in the mud, urinating lying down in your own pants because if you raise your head from the ground to go to the bathroom in the woods, it will reveal your position to the enemy. You are a motionless predator. <LINE> <LINE> The body atrophies, the back aches, and boredom blinds. And then, after thirty hours of torturous statics, the target appears. You have three seconds to perform all the math I taught you, control the breathing that accelerated from adrenaline shock, and take the perfect eight-hundred-meter shot. Most fail because the mind broke hours before.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The End of Calculation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Volume Four concludes here. The precision weapon is not a crutch; it is a surgical tool that punishes mathematical ignorance with resounding failure. You learned to respect the minute of angle, the parabola gravity forces, and the lie the wind tells. <LINE> <LINE> With this, your mechanics as a civilian, police, and tactical shooter are complete. But shooting is just the act of making noise and sending metal through the air. <LINE> <LINE> How do you hide so you aren't killed before your first shot? In Volume Five, the final in the series, 'Secrets From the World's Best Snipers', we will abandon cold math and enter the dark art. Tactical camouflage (Ghillie suits), breaking the human silhouette, choosing a shooting position (Hides), and how to vanish into the environment from even the most trained eye. Keep lenses clean.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Scope Myth (Optics) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The biggest lie you've been told is that a scope makes a gun more accurate. The scope doesn't shoot for you; it merely magnifies the target and, cruelly, also magnifies all your errors. <LINE> <LINE> If you look through a lens with ten times magnification (10x) while standing, without support, you won't see a clear target. You will see the crosshair jumping violently up and down with every beat of your heart. <LINE> <LINE> The scope steals your peripheral vision and leaves you blind to what happens at your sides. Using a powerful lens requires your weapon to be supported like a statue. If you try to shoot at a running target at ten meters using a sniper scope, you will see only a blur crossing the lens and die squeezing the trigger.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Inevitable Drop (Bullet Drop) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the millisecond the bullet leaves the hot barrel, Earth's gravity begins pulling it to the ground. The bullet doesn't fly in a straight line like a beam of light; it travels in a curved trajectory, like a baseball thrown from afar. <LINE> <LINE> If you aim exactly at the center of a target 400 meters away with a standard .308 rifle, your bullet will hit nearly a meter BELOW the point where you aimed. <LINE> <LINE> The long-range shooter needs to compensate for this drop. You don't shoot 'at' the target; you shoot into the empty space ABOVE the target (Holdover), as if casting an arrow, allowing gravity to pull the bullet down in the perfect parabola to the target's chest.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Zeroing the Rifle (The Starting Point) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To know how much your bullet will drop, you need an absolute reference point. That is the weapon's 'Zero'. We usually zero hunting or tactical rifles at 100 yards (or meters). <LINE> <LINE> You go to the range, shoot at 100 meters, and adjust the dials (Turrets) of your scope until the bullet's point of impact coincides exactly with the center of the reticle's crosshair. <LINE> <LINE> From that moment on, you have a pact with your rifle. You know that at 100 meters, the bullet goes exactly where the crosshair is. Any target beyond that distance will require you to turn the elevation turret to 'raise' the aim, according to your paper ballistic chart.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Minute of Angle (MOA) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The turrets on your scope do not turn in 'centimeters' or 'inches'. They use artillery math, based on angles. The most common is the Minute of Angle (MOA). <LINE> <LINE> Imagine a circle around you. It has 360 degrees. Each degree is divided into 60 minutes. An MOA is one of those minutes. In field practice, 1 MOA equals approximately 1 inch (2.5 cm) for every 100 yards of distance. <LINE> <LINE> If your target is at 300 yards and your shot is hitting 3 inches below it, you don't need complex calculations. You are exactly 1 MOA off. Give the corresponding clicks on the scope turret up, and the next shot will be devastatingly accurate. Write down your MOA table and tape it to your rifle stock.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Wind: The Invisible Killer <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Gravity is constant; wind is not. Wind is the shooter's ultimate test, as it changes direction, strength, and speed along the bullet's path. A gentle 15 km/h crosswind will push your bullet incredibly far off target at 500 meters. <LINE> <LINE> How do you read something invisible? You read the symptoms of the environment. <LINE> <LINE> Look at the leaves on the trees, the flags in the distance, and the dust kicking up. The sniper's best friend is the Mirage. Looking through an out-of-focus scope, you will see heat waves rising from the ground undulating like water. The angle at which these heat waves bend tells you exactly the wind speed and direction at the target.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Uphill and Downhill (Angle Shooting) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You are at the top of a mountain or on the roof of a ten-story building, aiming at a target on the street below. Intuition screams at you to aim higher, as the distance down the slope seems long. <LINE> <LINE> Wrong. Whether you shoot at a very steep angle UPHILL (going up the hill) or DOWNHILL (shooting from the roof), gravity acts upon the bullet over a much shorter effective horizontal distance than your actual line of sight. <LINE> <LINE> The golden, counter-intuitive, and irrefutable rule of snipers is: In severe angle shots (up or down), you must always compensate by aiming LOWER than normal. If you don't, your shot will fly right over the target.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Prone Position <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don't take a six-hundred-meter shot standing up. Your rifle needs to be coupled to planet Earth to eliminate human muscle tremor. <LINE> <LINE> The Prone position is the tactical shooter's office. Lie flat on your stomach, spread your legs to the sides to stabilize your pelvis against the ground, keeping the leg on the weapon's side straight parallel to the rifle barrel. <LINE> <LINE> The rifle rests on a bipod in front, and the stock (rear) must be supported on a sandbag squeezed by your support hand. Your dominant hand (the trigger hand) exerts absolutely NO force to hold the weapon's weight; it serves only to squeeze the trigger without shaking.
IGUI_BookAiming4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Parallax: The Crosshair Illusion <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you place the rifle on the table, aim at the target, and move your head from side to side without touching the gun, does the crosshair also move and leave the center of the target? If so, you have a Parallax error. <LINE> <LINE> This happens because the focal plane of the image is not perfectly aligned with the focal plane of the reticle (the crosshair) inside the glass tube. If you shoot with parallax error while your eye is not perfectly centered in the lens, the bullet will swerve miserably. <LINE> <LINE> Modern tactical scopes of this decade possess a magical side parallax adjustment knob. Turn it until the target becomes perfectly sharp and the crosshair becomes unchangeable, even if you move your head slightly.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Secrets From the World's Best Snipers <LINE> Chapter 1: The Shot is the End <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The amateur thinks an elite sniper's job is to shoot. It's a lie. The shot is merely the last and loudest one percent of a mission. The other ninety-nine percent is Fieldcraft. It's crawling into a position unseen, observing the target for three days, and vanishing into the wind before smoke clears the barrel. <LINE> <LINE> In this final volume, I won't teach you to pull the trigger. You already know how to do that. I will teach you to become a ghost. We'll talk about camouflage suits, urban hides, how to break the human silhouette, and how patience is the most lethal weapon you can carry to war.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Golden Rule: The Void (Shoot and Scoot) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> No matter how good your hiding spot is, there is an inevitable moment where you pull the trigger. The barrel unleashes fire, the blast shakes the neighborhood, and a supersonic vacuum snaps in the air. The enemy now knows you exist. <LINE> <LINE> The ultimate rule of survival: Never fire a second shot from the same hole. As soon as the roar echoes, you have seconds before suppressive fire returns against your position or dogs are released. Break down the position, grab your rifle, and retreat using the shadows. Change locations (Shoot and Scoot). You are a spirit: when they look to where the roar came from, they will find only empty dust.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Egress Route (Plan B) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The novice arrives at the empty building, goes straight to the window, mounts the rifle, and looks through the scope. When the shootout goes wrong and he needs to escape, he discovers the stairs behind him are blocked or surrounded. Game over. <LINE> <LINE> You never enter a shooting position without defining, clearing, and memorizing your Egress Route. Before even taking the rifle out of the backpack, unlock the back doors, memorize where the emergency exits are, and create a dark, covered path to vanish unseen. Planning your escape is infinitely more vital than planning your aim.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> False Information (The Decoy) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The enemy sniper (Counter-Sniper) is the most dangerous predator on Earth. He is you, only more patient. To find out where he is hidden, we don't look for his body; we make him act. We use the 'Decoy'. <LINE> <LINE> Place an empty helmet on a broomstick shoved into an old jacket, or use a piece of mirror to flash a fake scope reflection thirty meters from your actual position. When the enemy sniper hunting you takes the bait and shoots the helmet, he just gave away his position with a muzzle flash. You, who were observing from deep shadows the whole time, now fire into the smoke he caused.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Target Has a Name (Priority Selection) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In a real combat operation or in defense of your camp, a crowd approaches. You only have one shot before losing camouflage and revealing your location. Who do you hit? <LINE> <LINE> You don't shoot the easiest target, nor the closest. You eliminate Leadership or the Force Multiplier. You shoot the man with the walkie-talkie on his chest, the man carrying the thick radio transmitter on his back, or the one shouting orders. If you cut off the dog's head (Command and Control) and silence communications, the rest of the squad will fall into absolute chaos, not knowing how to retreat. Cut the leadership, win the war.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mental Cost of Being the Hunter <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I was police, I was a hunter, and I know the burden of the scope. Shooting up close with a revolver in the midst of stress throws you into the haze of instinctive defense. You react. But the long-range sniper acts in pure calm. <LINE> <LINE> You look through the glass of your rifle, see a man standing smoking a cigarette six hundred meters away, take a deep breath, align the math, and intentionally decide to interrupt his breathing before the cigarette burns out. There is something mechanically dark about the distance that protects you from danger, but brings you closer to being a divine machine. Control the rifle, don't let ego control you.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Instructor's Farewell <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We close the classroom door. Here ends the Fifth and final Volume. You started holding a weapon and trembling with closed eyes. Now you are the ghost. You master ballistics, understood the weaknesses of optics, know how to lie in the mud for days, and learned that the true deadly shot is fired by the mind, long before the hand touches steel. <LINE> <LINE> This is not a gentle world. Whether you carry an old thirty-eight revolver under your coat or a bolt-action rifle with long-range optics, the weapon is stupid without you. It doesn't win fights; it is merely the brush in the bloody painting the shooter decides to paint. <LINE> <LINE> Keep your powder dry, don't trust your instinct before seeing the target, always walk in the shadows, don't move fast in the light, and never expose your shoulders in a sun-drenched window. Darkness is your armor, and discipline is your aim.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Alphabet of Vision (The 5 'S's) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The human eye, just like the eye of predators, evolved to detect five things in nature that give away your position. If you don't control the 5 'S's, you are dead. <LINE> <LINE> 1. Shape: The brain instantly recognizes round shoulders, the globe-like head, and straight lines of firearms. <LINE> 2. Shine: Reflection from the scope lens, sweat on the forehead, or polished metal. <LINE> 3. Shadow: The shadow your body casts on the ground betrays you from afar. <LINE> 4. Silhouette: Standing at the top of a hill with the blue sky behind you is suicide. <LINE> 5. Spacing: Nature is chaotic; straight and repetitive patterns (windows, buttons, fences) draw attention.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Ghillie Suit (The Swamp Beast) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Ghillie Suit is not a ready-made Halloween costume. It is constructed. It is an outfit covered in strips of burlap (shredded potato sacks) that hides your worst flaw: your human Shape. <LINE> <LINE> But a base Ghillie suit is just a blank canvas. Before each mission, the sniper must rub the suit in local mud to get the exact scent and color of the earth. Then, he ties dozens of twigs, native grass, and leaves from that specific environment directly into the suit's netting. If you use oak leaves in a pine forest, the trained eye will notice the anomaly in two seconds.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Window of Death (Urban Combat) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Television loves to show the sniper resting their rifle on a window sill, with the gun barrel pointing into the street and their face exposed for the whole city to see. That is a recipe for getting shot in the head within two minutes of combat. <LINE> <LINE> In the real world, the window is the frame of death (Silhouette). The professional sniper never, ever approaches the sill. He steps back into the darkness of the room. He positions a table three or four meters back, in the deepest shadows of the room (where no natural light hits). He shoots from deep inside through the open window. Darkness hides the blast, hides the muzzle flash, and makes you invisible from the street.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Death by Reflection (Glint) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> the curved glass lens of your expensive scope is the perfect mirror. If the sun hits the glass while you spy on the target, a blinding beam of light will be thrown directly into your victim's eyes like a ship's beacon. They call that 'Glint'. <LINE> <LINE> To avoid this in the 90s, we don't have fancy technologies. We use a dirty trick. Steal a piece of your wife's pantyhose. <LINE> <LINE> Stretch the brown or black nylon over the front lens of your scope and tie it with a rubber band or electrical tape. The nylon is porous enough for you to look through without ruining your aim, but it breaks the sun's reflection perfectly. Your glass is now blind to enemies.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Ghost Walk (Stalking) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Entering the shooting position ('The Hide') requires the art of 'Stalking'. The eye is trained to detect rapid lateral movement. If you walk hunched over, you will be seen. <LINE> <LINE> The sniper lies on the ground and crawls moving only their thumbs and toes, flattening their stomach into the dirt (The Sniper Low Crawl). We move with agonizing slowness. To cover a hundred meters of open field crossing the visual line of an observer or alert quarry, you won't take three minutes. It will take you four hours.
