Millimeter movements are processed by the enemy's brain as leaves moving in the wind, not as a threat.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Odor Tracking (The Wind) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you are going to hunt experienced deer or trained humans with dogs, being silent and invisible is not enough. Your scent condemns you. <LINE> <LINE> The city human reeks of floral soap, deodorant, cigarette smoke, and processed sweat. The wind carries this odor hundreds of meters. Before entering the woods, wash your clothes only with water and unscented neutral soap. And most importantly: wind reading (which I taught you for shooting) serves first for odor. You must ALWAYS keep the wind blowing in your face. If the wind hits your back, it is catching your scent and throwing it directly into the face of your target ahead.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Loophole <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Shooting over a wall exposes you. The ultimate concealment tactic is the 'Loophole'. Instead of shooting over the barrier, the sniper finds (or silently digs) a tiny hole through a pile of rubble, an old wooden fence, or a rustic wall. <LINE> <LINE> The hole is just big enough to accommodate the scope lens and the thin rifle barrel. You shoot sitting in the dark on the other side of the wall. When the bullet hits the target, the enemy will focus their search on hilltops, high roofs, and windows; they will never look for a dark barrel hidden in a dirty slit at ground level.
IGUI_BookAiming5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Mental Torture and the Plastic Bottle <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When positioned in 'The Hide', you don't smoke, you don't light stoves to make coffee, and you don't raise your head to stretch your legs. An advanced shooting position requires up to forty-eight hours of absolute immobility and sepulchral silence. <LINE> <LINE> And, to be frank, nature calls. Every sniper carries one or two empty wide-mouth plastic bottles and diapers in their gear. You don't abandon optical surveillance because you need to go to the bathroom. You roll sideways in slow motion, use the bottle silently, cap it, and go back to flattening your eye to the scope. Lack of discipline destroys entire operations.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Elementary Forging Practice <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Welcome to the shop. I am your instructor, and if you follow this elementary manual, you will leave here with useful tools and all of your fingers intact. Blacksmithing is not magic, but it is the oldest art of bending the will of the earth to human will. <LINE> <LINE> Before you start hammering metal like a brute, you must understand that cold steel is stubborn and unyielding. But hot steel, fed by the correct fire, flows like clay in the hands of a master. <LINE> <LINE> Forget the clocks. The metal does not care about your haste. It will tell you when it is ready to be shaped by the color it radiates. Tie your apron and clear your mind. Lesson number one begins now.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Elementary Technique: Drawing Out <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first thing a blacksmith learns is how to turn a thick, short piece of steel into a thin, long piece. This is Drawing Out. <LINE> <LINE> Heat the bar to cherry red. Place it on the flat face of the anvil. Do not strike randomly. Strike with the face of the hammer slightly tilted in sequence, working the piece from the center toward the tip. <LINE> <LINE> Every two or three blows, rotate the bar 90 degrees on the anvil. Hit, hit, turn. Hit, hit, turn. If you do not turn it, the bar will flatten like a pancake. The constant rotation pushes the metal forward, stretching the steel fiber in a cylindrical and homogeneous way. When the metal darkens to a dull red, stop hammering and put it back in the fire.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Elementary Technique: Upsetting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> What if you have a thin bar, but you need its tip to be thick and heavy to make the head of a nail or a rivet? You do the opposite of drawing out: Upsetting. <LINE> <LINE> You heat only the tip of the metal bar in the fire (leaving the rest of the handle cold and hard). Take the bar with gloved hands or tongs and strike the hot tip vertically against the face of the anvil. <LINE> <LINE> Since the rest of the bar is cold and does not yield, all the force of the impact will concentrate on the tip softened by the heat. The glowing metal will have nowhere to escape and will begin to swell like a mushroom, thickening the tip. It is pure thermal manipulation of steel.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hot Knife (The Anvil Cutter) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you cut a one-inch iron bar in half without using a power saw or spending three hours sawing by hand? You cut it using the forge and the Hardy tool (Hot/Cold cutter). <LINE> <LINE> The cutting Hardy is like an upside-down axe head that fits into the square hole of the anvil. You heat the steel bar you want to cut until it turns orange, place it transversely over the blade of the Hardy, and strike it with your forging hammer from above. <LINE> <LINE> The Hardy blade underneath will bite and cut through the hot bar with extreme ease. BUT NEVER cut all the way through with full force, or your hammer will hit the steel blade of the Hardy, destroying both tools. Cut until a thin web of metal remains, and then simply bend it with your hands to break the piece.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Free Fall Rule <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This is a survival concept in the shop. You are holding a heavy bar of steel at a thousand degrees with the tongs. The jaws of the tongs slip, and the glowing bar falls toward the floor, right toward your foot. <LINE> <LINE> The trained primate instinct of someone who drops a pen in the office is to try to catch the object in mid-air, or bring their feet together to cushion the fall. <LINE> <LINE> In the forge, the opposite instinct MUST be cultivated. If a hot piece falls, THROW BOTH HANDS BACK AND JUMP BACK. Spread your legs and let the metal fall freely onto the cement. It is much better to have a burn mark on the workshop's concrete floor than to instinctively try to grab a live coal and char the tendons of your hand forever.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Water: Friend and Foe <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Every blacksmith keeps a large metal bucket (the Slack Tub) filled with water next to the anvil. It serves to cool down tools (like the tips of tongs that got too hot holding the fire) and to cool parts of the metal you do not want to work on. <LINE> <LINE> But plunging hot steel into water abruptly has a lethal chemical effect. Rapid cooling violently contracts the molecules. If you heat a long piece of carbon steel and throw it entirely into the water to cool it down quickly because you want to leave, it will suffer what we call an 'Accidental Quench'. <LINE> <LINE> It will become hard as glass. If you drop it on the floor tomorrow, it will shatter in two. Cool your work slowly by leaving it on top of a brick in the air or buried in ashes, never in freezing water.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of Elementary Education <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your elementary workshop lessons end here. Your homework is to sweep the forge area and stack the hammers properly. <LINE> <LINE> You learned how colors speak, the danger of synthetic clothing, the difference between a hammer's rebound and blind force, and how to manipulate the two raw techniques: thinning a point and thickening a sheet head. <LINE> <LINE> You are no longer an immediate risk to yourself. In Volume Two, 'General Purpose Blacksmithing', we will take off the training wheels. We will leave basic theory behind and focus on general production. We will make nails, hinges, riveting, and begin talking about steel Quenching, which transforms a soft piece of metal into a cutting blade. Put out the fire and go rest.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Clothing Rule (Melted Fabrics) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In woodworking, a mistake gives you a splinter. In the forge, a mistake rips off your skin. The anvil environment is surrounded by sparks flying at eight hundred degrees Celsius. <LINE> <LINE> Golden rule of the shop: Never, under any circumstances, enter the forge wearing synthetic materials (polyester, nylon, or spandex). If a spark lands on your nylon shirt, the fabric will not burn; it will instantly melt into a boiling liquid plastic that will fuse to your flesh. <LINE> <LINE> Wear only thick cotton, heavy wool, or raw leather aprons. Wear leather boots with hard toes. If a three-kilogram hammer slips from your sweaty hand and lands on your running shoe, your foot will be crushed into dozens of pieces.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Forge (The Heart of the Shop) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You cannot shape iron with a lighter. You need a Forge. There are modern and clean gas (propane) forges, but for the novice, I recommend the old mineral coal forge. <LINE> <LINE> The forge consists of a cast iron basin with an air intake at the bottom (the bellows or blower). You do not throw the metal directly on top of the black coal. You light the fire, turn on the air, and wait for the coal to burn until it turns into 'Coke'—grey, hard, smokeless chunks that burn with an intense, focused heat. <LINE> <LINE> It is inside the glowing nest of coke that your metal will rest, not in the open flame. The flame does not heat the iron properly; what melts the metal is the radiating ember.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Anvil (The Sacred Altar) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The anvil is not just a heavy block of iron you found in the scrapyard. A real anvil is forged from hardened high-carbon steel. When you strike it with a hammer, the hammer should 'rebound' back with a crystal-clear bell sound. <LINE> <LINE> Learn the anatomy of your primary tool: The flat surface on top is the 'Face' (where the heavy work is done). The conical tip at the front is the 'Horn' (used for bending and making rings). And the square hole at the back is the 'Hardy' hole, used to fit cutting tools and swages. <LINE> <LINE> Never strike directly onto the face of an empty anvil. The impact of hard steel against hard steel can shatter shards of metal that fly like bullets toward your eyes.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hammer and the Hand <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The novice tries to use force. The master uses gravity and rebound. If you grip the hammer handle squeezing with all the strength of your fingers and use your shoulder to strike, you will have chronic tendinitis in two weeks and ruin your arms forever. <LINE> <LINE> Hold the hammer firmly but with relaxed muscles, as if you were holding a little bird: tight enough so it does not fly away, but loose enough not to crush it. <LINE> <LINE> Lift the hammer and let gravity pull it down. Your arm merely guides the head of the tool. When the hammer strikes the hot steel resting on the hard steel anvil, the shock will cause the hammer to rebound upward on its own. Use this natural momentum to raise the hammer for the next blow. It is a rhythm, not a fight.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Tongs <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you hold a bar of metal at a thousand degrees? With Tongs. But there is no universal tong that fits everything. <LINE> <LINE> If you use round-nosed tongs to try to hold a square sheet of steel, the piece will slip, spin in the air, and land on your incandescent foot. You must choose the tongs whose jaws perfectly match the shape of the metal you are working on (square, flat, round). <LINE> <LINE> And here is the golden warning of blacksmithing: Black Metal Burns. A bar of iron only emits red light when it is above 500°C. Iron at 400°C looks perfectly cold and black, but if you touch it with your bare hand, your skin will cook to the bone instantly. Never trust the color of cold metal. Treat everything in the shop as if it were boiling.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Air Control (Oxygen) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the forge, air is your car's gas pedal. If you turn off the air (the bellows), the fire sleeps. If you pump too much oxygen, the temperature explodes. <LINE> <LINE> The problem with excess oxygen is not just melting your piece; oxygen at high temperatures reacts with the steel and creates 'Scale'. Scale is that black, flaky crust that breaks off hot iron when you strike it. <LINE> <LINE> Scale is literally your steel being corroded and peeled away by the air of the forge. If you leave the piece in the fire with too much oxygen blowing for twenty minutes, half the thickness of your metal will disappear into the air, consumed by severe oxidation. Manage the wind.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading the Colors (Cherry Red) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Metal is a perfect visual communicator. When you put it in the fire, it starts black, then turns a dull red. At this stage, it is still too hard. If you strike it hard now, instead of bending, the crystalline structure will crack and the piece will split in half (Cold cracking). <LINE> <LINE> You must wait for the 'Bright Cherry Red' color, somewhere around 800°C. This is where the steel begins to get 'soft' like modeling clay. It is at this vibrant cherry color that most of the heavy work (bending and drawing out) should be done by the novice blacksmith.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Risk of White Color (The Burn) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you leave the metal in the fire past cherry, it will turn orange, then yellow, and finally, Bright White. Beware! <LINE> <LINE> The glowing white color is the maximum limit before the melting point. Carbon steel begins to burn and destroy itself above this temperature. If you see your piece glowing white and small sparks start leaping violently out of the fire as if they were fireworks (Sparking), pull the piece out immediately! <LINE> <LINE> Those aggressive sparks are the essential carbon being burned and spat out of the steel alloy. The metal will become brittle and useless, like porous pig iron. You have ruined the piece. Always work between cherry red and dark orange.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> General Purpose Blacksmithing <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first volume, I taught you how not to melt your own hand and to understand the basics of how the hammer and anvil converse with the fire. Now, the theory ends. Let's produce. <LINE> <LINE> A blacksmith is not just a maker of fantasy swords; he is the mechanic of the ancient era. Your primary function is to create the pieces that keep the world glued together: nails, hinges, rivets, and chains. <LINE> <LINE> We are going to learn how to weld metal without using electricity and we will enter the most sacred alchemy of the shop: Heat Treatment. The art of making a soft piece of iron hard enough to cut glass. Light the fire.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Step 1: Normalizing (Relieving Stress) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> After hours of taking hammer blows, the steel of your knife is full of internal tensions. It is stressed, tense, and unpredictable. If you try to harden the steel in this state, it will warp and twist like a banana. <LINE> <LINE> Normalizing relaxes the metal. Heat the entire blade evenly to a cherry red (around 800°C), where the steel loses its attraction to magnets. Remove it from the fire and let it cool in the open air, in the shop's oxygen, until it turns black again. <LINE> <LINE> Do this three times. This process reorganizes the microscopic carbon crystals and relaxes the blade, preparing the steel for the violent shock that will come next.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Step 2: Quenching (The Shock) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Quenching is where the steel is born as a tool. Heat the normalized blade again to the perfect, demagnetized cherry red. <LINE> <LINE> Have a tank of mineral oil or clean used motor oil next to you (some steels use water, but oil is safer for novices). Plunge the incandescently red blade vertically into the oil. The oil will boil, explode into smoke, and perhaps catch fire on the surface. Keep the piece in there. <LINE> <LINE> This drastic cooling 'freezes' the steel's carbon crystals into a hyper-dense structure called Martensite. Your soft piece of metal has just become extremely rigid.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of the Quenched Blade <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You took the blade out of the oil. It is hard. In fact, it is too hard. <LINE> <LINE> Newly quenched steel, pure in martensite, has the same hardness and the same brittleness as a window glass. If you drop this blade on the shop's cement floor now, it will shatter into three pieces like a porcelain plate. The internal tension of freezing is monstrous. <LINE> <LINE> Never use an impact tool (like an axe or knife) that just came out of the quench without immediately moving to the last step. The hard blade needs to regain some of its flexibility.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Step 3: Tempering (The Oven) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Tempering is the act of 'baking' the quenched blade to relieve the extreme tension, trading a bit of the exaggerated hardness for flexibility and impact resistance. <LINE> <LINE> Clean all the burnt oil off the blade. You must heat the metal again, but with a very low heat, never in the powerful coal forge. The ideal way is to use your home kitchen oven. <LINE> <LINE> Place the knife in the oven at around 200°C for two hours. This mild heat allows the carbon crystals to relax just a little. The blade will remain hard enough to hold a sharp edge, but now, instead of shattering when hitting a bone, it will absorb the shock and flex slightly.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading Tempering Colors <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If there is no oven, you perform tempering using a hot iron block, paying close attention to the oxidation colors that appear on the clean steel when it heats up slightly. <LINE> <LINE> When the steel reaches around 200°C, the clean silvery surface turns a 'Straw Yellow' color. This is the perfect color for sharp knives. <LINE> <LINE> If heated further (250°C), the color changes to Bronze and then to Purple (great for axes and tools that take a beating). If it reaches 300°C, it turns Blue (good for springs, super flexible). If you mess up and the blade passes blue and turns grey, you have destroyed the quench and the metal has become soft again. You will have to start all over.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Complete Tool <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We close the second phase of your practical training. You do not just shape iron; you dictate its chemistry. Joining two pieces via Forge Welding and controlling the life of a blade with Quenching and Tempering places you above a simple hammer-swinger. You are a toolmaker. <LINE> <LINE> Keep the heat treatment recipe. Make the colors dance from Straw to Blue according to the tool you need to create. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Three, 'Wild West Blacksmiths and Their Secrets', we will take a rustic journey. I will teach you the improvised methods of frontier shops, how to forge horseshoes, repair broken wagon axles, and the artisanal secrets used before the comfort of power tools.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Iron vs. Steel (The Vital Difference) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before making a tool, you need to know what you are holding. Iron and Steel are not the same thing. <LINE> <LINE> Sweet Iron (or wrought iron) is soft. You can bend it easily, but it does not hold a blade's edge. It is perfect for making fences, nails, and chains. <LINE> <LINE> Steel is iron mixed with Carbon. It is the carbon that allows the metal to be hardened in the fire. Making a knife with sweet iron is useless, it will dent on the first wood it cuts. Making a nail with high-carbon steel is dangerous, as the nail head will shatter when the hammer strikes. Choose the right material for the right piece.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Nail Production <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you run out of carpentry nails, you can make them yourself. A hand-forged nail is not round like a factory one; it is square, which makes it grip the wood with much more force. <LINE> <LINE> Heat the tip of a thin rod of sweet iron. Use the drawing out technique (which we learned in volume one) to thin the tip into a pyramid shape (the point of the nail). <LINE> <LINE> Next, cut the hot rod leaving about a centimeter of thick metal remaining above the thin point. Place this piece into a hole the exact size of the rod (a header or die). The thin point goes in, the thick metal stays out. Give two hard strikes on the thick part to flatten it like a mushroom. Done, you have made the nail head.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rivets (The Metal Glue) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You do not need screws to join two heavy steel plates. You use the Rivet. <LINE> <LINE> A rivet is just a thick metal nail, without a sharp point and with a round head. Drill a hole in the two steel plates you want to join, pass the cold rivet through the hole so that the two plates are together and a small tip of the rivet sticks out. <LINE> <LINE> Heat the plates with the rivet until the metal turns red. Place the bottom head resting on the anvil and hammer the hot tip that remained on top. The hot tip will mash, swell, and create a second head, crushing the two plates together forever with an unbreakable force.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Curves and the Anvil Horn <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The flat face of the anvil is used for straight lines. To make hooks and rings, we use the conical part at the front: the Horn. <LINE> <LINE> Never hammer the metal directly from top to bottom on the horn if you want a clean curve. Place the red metal resting on the horn, but let the tip extend into the void. Strike the metal that is in the air, bending it down, around the cone. <LINE> <LINE> By rotating the piece slowly and following the curve of the horn, you can forge a perfect circle without crushing the internal structure of the bar. This is how we make the links of a chain.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Eye and Hinges <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Rustic door hinges begin with an Eye. The eye is the hollow cylinder through which the hinge pin will pass. <LINE> <LINE> Thin the tip of a flat steel bar. Instead of making an open curve like a hook, bend the hot tip completely back, wrapping it around a cold round bar (which will serve as a temporary mold). <LINE> <LINE> With light and precise strikes, shape the hot steel to hug the round mold, creating a perfect tube at the end of the plate. Pull the mold out before the piece cools and shrinks, or it will be stuck in there forever.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Forge Welding (The Ancient Magic) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You do not have an electric welding machine or argon gas in the forest. How do you join two cut bars of iron into one? With Forge Welding. <LINE> <LINE> You do not use electricity; you use fire and pressure. The secret is extreme heat, almost at the melting point (Glinting White). In this state, the surface of the steel turns into an almost liquid paste. <LINE> <LINE> If you take both bars at this incandescent color, overlap one another on the anvil, and deliver a sharp, heavy blow, the atoms of the two pieces of metal mix. They are not glued; they literally become a single and indivisible piece of steel. This requires speed and brutal force.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Miracle of Borax (The Flux) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Trying to make a Forge Weld without preparation will fail ninety percent of the time. Remember 'Scale' (that black crust of oxidation)? If there is a single black crust between the two pieces of metal you want to weld, the iron will not stick. The dirt blocks the fusion. <LINE> <LINE> This is where Borax comes in (a white cleaning powder you find at the supermarket). When the pieces are at a strong cherry red, take them out of the fire and throw a shower of powdered Borax over the parts to be joined. <LINE> <LINE> The borax melts immediately like liquid glass on top of the metal, cleaning the oxidation and creating a sealing film that prevents oxygen from the air from dirtying the iron. When you hit it with the hammer, the liquid borax will squirt out, allowing a perfect and clean weld.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Heat Treatment (The Soul of Steel) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We now enter heavy physics. You forged a hunting knife out of carbon steel. It looks beautiful, but the fire left the metal's crystalline structure a mess and the steel is soft. If you sharpen this knife now, the cutting edge will bend like paper the first time you try to cut wood. <LINE> <LINE> The steel needs a 'Soul'. This is Heat Treatment. It is a process of three mandatory steps: Normalizing, Quenching, and Tempering. Mess up one of these steps and your blade will shatter in the middle of a fight or lose its edge instantly.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wild West Blacksmiths <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first two manuals, I assumed you were in my clean shop, with electricity powering the forge blower and a two-hundred-kilogram English anvil at your disposal. But what if the world stops? What if you have nothing but rusty scrap metal and dirt? <LINE> <LINE> This third volume rescues the secrets of the blacksmiths of the Wild West and the pioneer frontiers. Men who repaired wagon axles and forged weapons under rainstorms, using holes in the dirt as a forge and pieces of scrap metal as an anvil. <LINE> <LINE> True skill is not in the expensive tool you buy, it is in your brain's capacity to improvise. We are going to step back in time to advance your survival. Turn off the machines.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Farrier's Craft (The White Line) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Many believe that shoeing a horse is driving nails into the animal's live bone. The horse's hoof is, in fact, just a giant keratin fingernail. There are no nerves or blood in the outer wall. <LINE> <LINE> The western blacksmith needed to be a farrier. When cleaning the dirty hoof with the hoof knife, you look for the 'White Line'. This is the visible border that separates the dead, painless nail (outer wall) from the live, sensitive tissue (the inner sole). <LINE> <LINE> Any nail you drive inside this white line will pierce the horse's live flesh. The animal will bleed, limp in excruciating pain, and cannot be ridden. Nails go through the edge of the wall, diagonally and always outward.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Hot Fitting (Burning the Horseshoe) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You do not shape the horse's hoof to fit the horseshoe; you shape the hot iron to perfectly fit each horse's specific hoof. <LINE> <LINE> The blacksmith takes the red horseshoe out of the forge and presses it against the horse's trimmed hoof for two seconds. Foul, white smoke rises. This is Hot Fitting. <LINE> <LINE> The heat slightly burns away excess uneven nail and creates a millimetrically perfect, airtight fit between the keratin and the iron. Since the heat only lasts an instant and does not reach the horse's live flesh, it feels no pain, only mild warmth at the bottom of the hoof. The seal prevents rotting mud from getting between the horseshoe and the nail.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tools Making Tools <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you lose your blacksmith's hammer and tongs in the woods, how do you forge others without the necessary tools to hold the hot metal? The true craftsman starts from absolute zero. <LINE> <LINE> You use a thick green branch split down the middle to hold a small piece of iron that will become the head of your first small twisting pliers. <LINE> <LINE> With small rustic pliers, you forge a decent pair of tongs. With decent tongs, you hold a larger billet and forge a heavy hammer using a round piece of stone as an initial striker. The shop is the only place in the world where your profession creates the next generation of your own livelihood.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Impossible Repairs (Cast Iron) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The old kettle or the wood stove fell and the heavy plate of Cast Iron cracked in half. Trying to weld or forge cast iron on the anvil is a waste of time; it has so much carbon that it does not soften, it simply crumbles like flour if you hit it hot. <LINE> <LINE> To save cast iron, the pioneer used Brazing. Instead of trying to fuse the broken piece, we use Brass. <LINE> <LINE> Clean the crack and heat the broken pot slowly in the entire forge. With the piece very hot, rub borax and melt a brass wire along the crack. The liquid brass will penetrate the rough grooves of the iron like hot glue on fabric. When it cools, the golden brass 'bandage' will be stronger than the black pot itself.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Sound of Success (The Anvil Symphony) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When you are isolated in a cabin with no one to instruct you, you use your ears. The steel warns you of what it is suffering through the sound of the hammer. <LINE> <LINE> If you strike the incandescent metal and it makes a dull 'thump' sound, it means the steel is nice and hot, absorbing plastic energy, and changing shape. <LINE> <LINE> If the sound of the hammer strike suddenly becomes high, metallic, and makes your ears ring ('tiiiiing!'), the piece cooled down too fast and stiffened. The hammer is no longer mashing the steel, it is rebounding against a hard stone. If you continue to force strikes on the piece with this ringing bell sound, internal microfissures will appear and you will destroy the tool from the inside out.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rustic Respect <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We end our rustic camp here. You left the city's fluff behind and learned that truck springs are swords waiting to be born, that the chemistry of calcined horn hardens soft iron, and that shoeing a horse requires anatomical patience and fire adjustment. <LINE> <LINE> Scrap is no longer trash to you; it is your gold mine in a sterile world. You mastered improvisation and desperation. <LINE> <LINE> But the evolution of metallurgy did not stop in the old west. In Volume Four, 'Worker's Manual of the Really Hard Steel Co.', we will leave the dust and enter heavy industrial steel. The manual will not forgive shortcuts. Let's talk about modern structural metallurgy, anchor bolts, support beams for buildings, and the mathematics of steel integrity so you do not let the roof collapse on your head.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Earth Forge (The Ground Hole) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Without a cast iron and propane forge, you will have to return to iron age methods. It is perfectly possible to melt steel in a hole in the ground. <LINE> <LINE> Dig a shallow trench in the dry earth. Line the edges with heavy stones or riverbank clay. You need to channel air beneath the coal. If you do not have an iron pipe for the air (tuyere), use a hollow tree branch or mold a mud tunnel hardened in the fire. <LINE> <LINE> To push the oxygen, if the wagon's old leather bellows tore, use whatever you have: a mattress pump, an adapted old hair dryer, or even two thick trash bags tied as manual bellows. The fire does not care about the look of your forge, as long as the wind blows through the embers.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Frontier Fuel (Charcoal) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Mined mineral coal does not grow on trees in your backyard. If you are forced to live off the land, your fuel will be Charcoal. But do not think that throwing ordinary wood into the forge works; wood burns too fast and does not reach the peak of clean temperature. <LINE> <LINE> You must make your own charcoal. Cut hard woods (oak, hickory), place them in a sealed metal drum with only a small vent hole, and make a gigantic bonfire around the drum. <LINE> <LINE> The wood inside will bake without oxygen and carbonize, expelling volatile gases and leaving only blocks of pure, light carbon. This carbon burns absurdly hot in your earth forge, enough to melt any scrap steel.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Improvised Anvil (Railroad Track) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Lost your professional anvil? Do not hit the metal on a stone, it will shatter and shoot shards into your forehead. The best improvised anvil on the American frontier is the old Railroad Track. <LINE> <LINE> Rails are made of extremely dense high-carbon steel, built to withstand the weight of locomotives. If you find a half-meter piece of rail, do not lay it horizontally like amateurs do. <LINE> <LINE> The flat rail has a hollow support base and will vibrate horribly, robbing the force of your hammer blow. You must fix the piece of rail VERTICALLY (standing up), burying its base into a thick tree stump, using the solid top end as the face of your anvil. The solid column of steel will carry the force of the impact straight to the earth.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Scrap as Gold (Leaf Springs) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A pioneer does not go to a store to buy clean bars of carbon steel; he scavenges scrap. But you must know how to recognize treasure in the trash. If you forge a knife using an old tin can or a car hood sheet, it will not hold an edge. <LINE> <LINE> The scrap blacksmith's gold is in the Suspension Springs of old trucks (Leaf Springs). This material is the formidable 5160 Steel. <LINE> <LINE> It is a steel of extremely high carbon content and is exceptionally flexible, perfectly ideal for making giant knives, machetes, heavy axes, and rugged tools. Just make sure to normalize the spring in the fire first (as I taught in Vol. 2), as it already comes curved and stressed from the factory.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Case Hardening (The Carbon Secret) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> What if you only have soft sweet iron and you need a hard tool to dig stone or cut wood? The ancient blacksmith used 'Case Hardening'. We literally force carbon into the iron. <LINE> <LINE> Take pieces of old leather, broken animal bones, and horns. Burn it all until it turns into an animal charcoal powder rich in carbon. <LINE> <LINE> Place your soft iron tool inside a metal pipe, pack this bone and leather powder tightly around the piece, and seal the ends with mud. Throw the entire tube into the bottom of a continuous fire for several hours. The heat will force the carbon from the powder to penetrate and fuse into the skin of the iron tool. The inside remains soft and unbreakable, but the outer shell turns into a terrifyingly hard steel.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wild Quenching (Lard and Brine) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you do not have industrial quenching oil to harden your hot axe, use what the farm offers. Oil is not the only option. <LINE> <LINE> You can quench hard steel pieces using 'Brine'. Mix rainwater with as much cooking salt as the water can dissolve (until the salt stops disappearing at the bottom). Saltwater absorbs heat incredibly faster than pure freshwater, hardening old tools with absurd violence. <LINE> <LINE> For delicate blades that would crack in saltwater, pioneers used a tank filled with hot melted pork lard. The smell of burning meat in the shop will be unbearable, but the thermal shock in animal fat will produce knives of impeccable quality.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rust Protection (Beeswax) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Rust is the cancer of iron. If you forged a useful tool on the rainy and humid frontier, it will turn orange and useless in a week if left out in the elements. Canned chemical products do not exist here. <LINE> <LINE> The frontier anti-corrosion treatment involves baking Beeswax or pure Linseed Oil. Heat your newly forged tool to a very dim red or a hot black (around 300°C). <LINE> <LINE> Rub a block of raw beeswax directly onto the hot metal. The wax will melt, smoke, and penetrate the dilated pores of the steel. Upon cooling, the steel acquires a deep black patina, sealed against water and hard as leather. Boiled linseed oil in the forge causes the same black sealant effect.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Repairing Wagons (Thermal Contraction) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the wagon's wooden wheel dries out in the sun, it shrinks and the iron hoop around it becomes loose. The hoop falls off and the wheel smashes into the ground. How do you secure iron to wood without screws? With the physics of temperature. <LINE> <LINE> The blacksmith lights a circular fire and heats the entire iron hoop until it turns red. The heat causes the iron ring to expand its diameter, becoming considerably larger. <LINE> <LINE> Immediately, with heavy tongs, you drop the hot ring over the wooden wheel and pour buckets of cold water over the iron. The water causes violent contraction of the metal, which shrinks, crushing the wood in an unbreakable embrace, joining the wheel back with the force of a mechanical vice.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Really Hard Steel Co. <LINE> Worker's Manual <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Attention, employee. Welcome to Really Hard Steel Co. If you spent the last few years playing backyard farm blacksmith and hammering crooked horseshoes, forget everything. The jury-rigging is over. <LINE> <LINE> In structural and industrial metallurgy, improvisation is not a virtue; improvisation is what makes a warehouse roof collapse on fifty workers' heads. We do not deal with guesswork based on the 'color of the fire'. We deal with exact degrees Celsius, controlled chemistry, and millimetric tolerances. <LINE> <LINE> This manual dictates standard operating procedures (SOP) for heavy steel work, structuring, and weld integrity. Read carefully. Mistakes here do not just cost a tool; they cost lives and lawsuits.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sheet Metal and the Press Brake <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Modern metallurgy relies not only on melting bars; it requires cold work with smooth sheet metal. If you hammer a thin sheet of cold zinc or aluminum against the anvil, it will deform, stretch, and get wrinkled like candy wrapper. <LINE> <LINE> In the factory, we use the Hydraulic Press Brake and the Guillotine Shear. The sheet is clamped firmly, and the heavy blade descends, applying uniform pressure across the entire length at the same time. You get sharp, clean angles you could never get by free hammering. Respect for the mechanical tool ensures perfect fitment of conduits and gutters.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Annealing (Softening Steel) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Sometimes we receive batches of steel at the factory that are too hard to be cut on band saws or drilled on a drill press without destroying the bits. We need to soften the metal brutally. This is Annealing. <LINE> <LINE> Place the hard steel in the factory's giant furnace at 850°C. Afterward, we turn off the furnace and leave the metal locked inside for TWENTY-FOUR HOURS, cooling at the most miserable and slow speed possible (inside ashes or rock wool if outdoors). <LINE> <LINE> This lethargic cooling dissolves crystalline tensions down to the last atom. The steel comes out so soft you can easily saw it with your hands. Power tools do not cut hardened steel.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cold Work and Work Hardening <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hammering cold iron is a mortal sin in swordsmithing, but it is a real technique in the industry. This is called Work Hardening. <LINE> <LINE> When you bend, twist, or roll an aluminum sheet, copper, or sweet iron at room temperature (without fire), the friction of internal molecules being forced to slide over one another creates deep tension. The metal becomes rigid. <LINE> <LINE> Airplane rivets and warning plates are not quenched in fire; they are hardened on purpose by the stress of cold work. But beware, if you work harden the metal too much, it loses its ability to bend and snaps in the middle. The line between industrial rigidity and shattering is thin.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Raw Foundry (Sand Molds) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When you cannot hammer metal into shape, you melt everything down and use Foundry. This is how we make giant machine lathe bases or engine blocks. <LINE> <LINE> The metal is liquefied in a gigantic crucible at 1500°C. We create a wooden model of the part, bury it in a box filled with special fine sand ('Green Sand', which does not burn), remove the wood, and pour the liquid hell into the hole left in the sand. <LINE> <LINE> The greatest danger here is not temperature, it is Moisture. If there is a single drop of water inside the sand mold, the shock of liquid steel will vaporize the water in a millisecond. The steam will expand and the box will explode like a bomb, shooting molten metal all over the warehouse. Dry mold, always.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tolerance and Calipers <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The artisan works until the piece looks 'pretty'. The industrial worker works until the piece reaches the Mechanical Tolerance stipulated in the project blueprints. <LINE> <LINE> We use Calipers and Micrometers, clean instruments, not dirty sledgehammers. If a locking pin was ordered with a thirty-millimeter diameter and you produced it 30.5 millimeters thick because you messed up the sander, it will not go into the machine bearing and the entire production line of the neighboring city will stop because of you. <LINE> <LINE> Heavy metallurgy is a discipline of microscopic calibration. An imperfect part is not discarded because it is ugly; it is discarded because it ruins a million-dollar project.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of Shift <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The factory bell rings. You completed Volume Four and the standards manual of Really Hard Steel Co. <LINE> <LINE> You left behind rustic stone forges and understood the laws of structural steel and support beams. You do not breathe zinc vapor, do not trust cosmetic cold welds, and understand the mortal danger of hidden water in foundry molds. <LINE> <LINE> Manual labor has limits, and industry takes over when a bridge needs to be erected or a skyscraper requires a skeleton. But what if we want to go back to the root of everything, adding the extreme chemistry of the ancients with the limitless knowledge of modern masters? <LINE> <LINE> Volume Five is not a work manual. It is 'The Complete Encyclopedia of Metallurgy'. Prepare for the supreme alchemy of complex steels.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Structural Steel (Mild Steel) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Amateur blacksmiths are obsessed with high-carbon steel because they want blades that cut stone. In the construction industry, high carbon is our enemy. Very hard steel is brittle steel. If you make a building's support beam out of knife steel, the beam will not dent in an earthquake; it will shatter like glass. <LINE> <LINE> The backbone of the modern world is Structural Steel (Low Carbon, like A36). It has perfect malleability. Under extreme weight, a low-carbon beam will bend, groan, and warn you that the limit has arrived long before it breaks. This elasticity saves lives. Leave high carbon to the bladesmiths.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Structural Profiles (The 'I' Beam) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Shape dictates strength. If you try to support a roof using solid square steel beams, the building will collapse under the weight of its own skeleton. The miracle of civil engineering is the 'I' (or 'H') Profile. <LINE> <LINE> The shape of the letter 'I' concentrates the maximum metallic mass in the upper and lower flanges (the Flanges), where tensile and compressive stress is brutal, and leaves the center thin (the Web), where forces are almost null. This creates a beam that supports tons but weighs a fraction of a solid block. Your job in the factory is to weld and join these beams at angles of exact 90 degrees. 89 degrees is termination with cause.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Metal Fatigue <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Steel has a memory. If you bend a paperclip back and forth dozens of times, it breaks. This is Metal Fatigue. <LINE> <LINE> In heavy machinery or drive shafts, constant vibration creates microfissures invisible to the naked eye in the steel's crystalline structure. The shop operator thinks the shaft is intact because there is no visible rust or cracks, until the day it explodes in motion at three thousand revolutions per minute. <LINE> <LINE> In our factory, parts under cyclic stress are not repaired with welding. They are discarded and replaced. Trying to 'patch holes' in structural fatigue is signing a death warrant.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fundamentals of Galvanization <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Book three told you to put beeswax on iron to protect it from rain. That is ridiculous on an industrial scale. To protect transmission towers and roofing sheets, we use the Hot-Dip Galvanization process. <LINE> <LINE> We submerge steel beams into a gigantic tank of boiling liquid Zinc. The zinc adheres to the steel, creating a sacrificial barrier. If the piece is scratched, oxygen chemistry will devour the zinc (which is more reactive) and ignore the steel underneath. This is the only real protection against acid rain and the saline atmosphere of modernity.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chemical Smoke Control (Metal Fume Fever) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Welding or heating galvanized metals (covered in zinc) requires the use of heavy ventilation masks from the Safety Department. <LINE> <LINE> If you put a galvanized pipe into the forge, the fire will burn the zinc. The greenish-white smoke that rises is highly toxic. Breathing this will cause 'Metal Fume Fever'. You will get violent chills, incapacitating nausea, a forty-degree fever, and your lungs will burn as if they were filled with sand. <LINE> <LINE> The factory requires that all zinc coating be removed with a mechanical grinder before any application of welding heat or forge heat.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chemical and Mechanical Anchor Bolts <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you secure a two-ton steel plate into pure cement? You do not use rustic little nails; you use Industrial Anchor Bolts (Parabolts). <LINE> <LINE> The employee must drill the concrete and insert the expanding steel sleeve. When tightening the brutally heavy nut with a torque wrench, the tip of the anchor bolt expands like a cone inside, biting and crushing the cement walls. The torque (the turning force) must strictly obey the table on the factory wall. An under-tightened anchor will come loose; an over-tightened anchor will crack the concrete base in half.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Shielded Metal Arc Welding <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forget hitting pieces with borax. At Really Hard Steel Co., joining structural steel is done via Arc Welding with a Covered Electrode (SMAW). <LINE> <LINE> We use high-amperage electricity to create a plasma arc hotter than the surface of the sun. This beam melts the base steel and the filler metal rod simultaneously, creating an impenetrable weld pool. <LINE> <LINE> The slag (chemical protective crust left on top of the weld) can only be chipped away with a slag hammer when the piece cools from red to grey. Trying to strike the liquid pool is the best way to shoot liquid iron splatters straight into your own eyes.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Weld Penetration (The Hidden Danger) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> An electric weld that looks fat, beautiful, and rounded on top of the plate is usually garbage. This is called a 'Cold Weld'. It stuck to the surface, but did not penetrate the root of the metal. <LINE> <LINE> If you weld a support pillar with a cold weld, the first heavy truck that hits the platform will make the pillar pop off as if it were glued with spit. <LINE> <LINE> Beveling is mandatory. Before welding thick plates, use a cutting disc to create a 'V' angle on the edges. The electric arc must penetrate to the bottom of that 'V' and melt the metal from the inside out. We perform ultrasound testing; cosmetic welds are detected immediately.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Complete Encyclopedia of Metallurgy <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You survived the elementary shop, learned to forge nails and hinges, improvised with scrap in the mud, and understood the cold equations of the structural industry. But those were just the foundations. <LINE> <LINE> The true master is not a screw-tightener; he is a manipulator of the mineral kingdom. This Encyclopedia is the pinnacle of metallurgy. Here we do not work with junk iron and anchor bolts. Here we manipulate crystalline structures, forge pattern-welded steels, and understand the secret soul of non-ferrous metals. <LINE> <LINE> Prepare your cleanest fire and your sharpest mind. You are about to stop being a sheet-slammer to become an alchemist of steel.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Non-Ferrous Metals (Copper) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Steel dominates strength, but metals that contain no iron (Copper, Bronze, and Brass) possess completely opposite and alien laws in the workshop. <LINE> <LINE> As I taught in previous volumes, if you heat a steel bar and plunge it into freezing water, the steel hardens and turns to glass. With Copper, physics plays in reverse! <LINE> <LINE> Copper deforms and hardens only when it is cold-hammered (work hardening). If the copper gets too hard from all your cold striking and is about to crack, you throw it into the fire until it turns red and, immediately, plunge it into ice water. The thermal shock, instead of hardening, softens the copper, leaving it malleable like clay again. Fire and water cure copper.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Poison of Galvanic Corrosion <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Joining dissimilar metals can create a deadly battery without electricity. This is Galvanic Corrosion, the invisible killer of plumbing and armor. <LINE> <LINE> If you join a sheet of Steel with Copper or Aluminum screws and this structure catches rain or gets damp, the rainwater will act as the electrolyte of a battery. Electrons will migrate from the less noble metal to the more noble one. <LINE> <LINE> In a few months, the aluminum around the steel will not just rust; it will turn to dust and magically disappear from the structure, corroded to its soul. The more noble metal devours the weaker one in the silence of the rain. Never join dissimilar metals if moisture is a factor.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Liquid Salt Baths <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Advanced blacksmiths who need to harden mirrored blades without having the damn coal 'scale' dirty them use Liquid Salt Quenching. <LINE> <LINE> You mix nitrate salts in a tall stainless steel tube and heat until the salt melts, turning into a red, crystalline liquid that boils at a thousand degrees. Since liquid salt is denser than oxygen, no air touches your knife. <LINE> <LINE> You submerge the blade in this infernal cauldron of bright, transparent salt. It reaches the exact temperature, with no carbon burn, no scale, no variation of cold and heat. When you pull it out and cool it, the blade will be clean, immaculate, and hard. It is thermal perfection hidden from amateurs.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cryogenic Treatment (The Ice Forge) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> What if I tell you that the quench of your advanced steel knife does not end in boiling oil, but rather in brutal ice? <LINE> <LINE> Many superalloy steels are stubborn. When you cool them in oil, a portion of the steel does not convert into hard crystals, leaving an unwanted residue (Retained Austenite) that makes the edge sluggish over time. <LINE> <LINE> The only way to force those last lazy atoms to convert into hard crystals is Cryogenics. We remove the knife from the oil and immediately plunge it into a bucket of Liquid Nitrogen (or dry ice if you are in the middle of nowhere in winter). The cold of minus one hundred and ninety degrees crushes the molecular mesh and extracts the last drop of hardness from the metal. Ice forges as much as fire.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mourning of the Deadly 'Ping' <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Reaching this level does not exempt you from failure. The supreme trial of the Master is the long sword or the thin forty-centimeter machete. You forge and hammer the perfectly thin blade for six grueling hours in the heat of the forge. And then you heat it for cooling (quenching) in the oil. <LINE> <LINE> You submerge the red blade and the oil smokes. Suddenly, from deep within the tank, sounds a loud, sharp, and lethal noise: 'PING!' <LINE> <LINE> That sharp bell sound coming from beneath the oil breaks the heart of the experienced blacksmith. It is the sound of molecular stress defeating matter. The blade shattered in half, sliced by the very internal tension of the temperature and the fine geometry you created. The steel refused your heat treatment. Hours of work destroyed in a millisecond of cold. You do not cry; you pick up the black shards from the oil and light the fire again to start over. This is metallurgy.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Last Strike <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The anvil finally goes silent and the fire cools down. This is the end of the Encyclopedia and the conclusion of your training. <LINE> <LINE> The journey began with the fear of burning your own hands in melted clothes. Now, you look at a pile of rusty scrap, clay, and dead bones and see immortal tools, katanas tempered with a Hamon line, infinite layers of Damascus, and the molecular union of case-hardened forge welding. <LINE> <LINE> The steel you shaped will live centuries longer than your flesh. The hammer is no longer a tool to break, it is the baton you use to conduct the orchestra of the deep Earth. Honor the shop, clean the anvil for the next one who comes to try, and may your nails never bend.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Damascus Steel (The Infinite Fold) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The holy grail of artisanal forging is Damascus Steel (Pattern Welding). Legend says it cuts silk in mid-air, but the truth is purely chemical and mechanical. <LINE> <LINE> Modern Damascus is created by stacking alternating sheets of two different steels: one with a high carbon content (which gets very hard and holds the cutting edge) and another with a high nickel content (which is flexible, tough, and does not rust easily). <LINE> <LINE> You heat the billet in a white fire, apply borax, and fuse the sheets with precise hammer strikes (Forge Welding). Then you draw out the fused bar, cut it in half, stack it again, and weld it once more. Ten layers become twenty. Twenty become forty. Forty become three hundred. You are creating a puff pastry of indestructible metal.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Acid and Revelation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forging three hundred layers of carbon steel and nickel together serves no visual purpose if you just polish the knife. It will look like a piece of ordinary steel, shiny and smooth. The secret to Damascus's flowing water pattern lies in Acid. <LINE> <LINE> When the knife is finished, sharp, and mirrored, the master submerges it in a tube with Ferric Chloride (or any diluted strong battery acid). <LINE> <LINE> The acid reacts violently with the high-carbon steel, darkening it and corroding it deeply. But the acid cannot corrode the nickel steel, which remains silvery and intact. After fifteen minutes in the chemical bath, you remove the blade and the brutal contrast between black (carbon) and silver (nickel) reveals the unique fingerprints of your work.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Legendary Crucible Steel (Wootz) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you do not want to fold metal sheets together, you can create your own super steel through Crucible melting. This is the ancient method, lost for centuries and rediscovered. <LINE> <LINE> Instead of striking on the anvil, you place pieces of pure iron and green leaves (organic matter rich in carbon) inside a perfectly sealed clay pot. Place the pot in the maximum fire of the forge and let it bake for hours. <LINE> <LINE> Without oxygen to burn the carbon, the leaves turn to gas and the iron melts, absorbing liquid carbon until it saturates. When the pot cools down slowly over days, it generates a 'Wootz Ingot'—a perfect steel crystal with dendritic patterns in the shape of microscopic stars that form the most lethal edge known to man.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Magic of Differential Quenching <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A universal dilemma: If an entire blade is too hard, it breaks like glass upon hitting a bone. If it is too flexible, it bends and loses its edge. How do you make a sword have the hardness of diamond at the edge but the flexibility of a spring at the spine? <LINE> <LINE> The answer of the Japanese masters is Differential Quenching. Before taking the sword to the fire for extreme cooling, the blacksmith covers the back (spine) of the blade with a thick layer of refractory clay and ashes, leaving the cutting edge bare. <LINE> <LINE> Upon plunging the hot sword into water, the bare edge freezes brutally, turning into hard martensite. But the clay on the back acts as a thermal blanket; the spine cools slowly, remaining sweet and flexible steel. A single piece of metal with two totally different chemistries.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Line of Life (Hamon) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The visual result of this clay-masked quench is the mythical line of 'Hamon'. <LINE> <LINE> If you look closely at the side of a differentially quenched blade after polishing, you will see a misty line waving along the metal. This is not a painting or a scratch; it is the exact border, the atomic limit, where hard crystals (Martensite) meet soft crystals (Pearlite). <LINE> <LINE> The Hamon is the signature of the blacksmith's soul. If your polishing is careful with fine waterstones, the line will shine like frozen fog inside the steel.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chromium, Vanadium, and Tungsten (The Alloy) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Pure iron with carbon is just the base. Advanced metallurgy requires knowledge of alloying elements that give 'superpowers' to your tool. <LINE> <LINE> A handful of Chromium added to the furnace prevents oxygen from rusting the metal, creating Stainless Steel. A pinch of Vanadium refines the blade's crystals, making the steel's texture so tight that a microscope cannot find pores, resulting in surgical strength. And powerful Tungsten bestows a heat resistance so absurd that industrial drill bits do not melt even when drilling through burning rock. Modern blacksmiths mix what the earth offers.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Curse of Stainless Steel <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> As a blacksmith with a coal forge, let me give you the biggest warning of this Encyclopedia: Never try to forge Stainless Steel on an ordinary anvil. <LINE> <LINE> Stainless steel shines because of chromium, but chromium hates the open air. When you heat a stainless steel bar in the coal forge and start striking it with the sledgehammer under the shop's oxygen, the internal structure collapses. The metal does not draw out like carbon steel; it crumbles into hot granular pieces that look like glowing, useless sand. <LINE> <LINE> Stainless steel can only be manipulated by cold machining and strictly controlled atmosphere furnaces. In the forest, stick to dirty, loyal carbon steel.
IGUI_BookBlacksmith5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cutting Edge Geometry <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You do not cut a tree with a shaving razor, and you do not shave with a lumberjack axe. Sharp metallurgy requires the correct Geometry. <LINE> <LINE> The 'Hollow Grind' is hollowed inward, creating an atomic and brutally sharp edge, ideal for shaving or slicing soft meat, but it chips instantly against a bone. <LINE> <LINE> The 'Convex Grind' has sides rounded outward like an apple. It is much harder to sharpen, but it pushes wood to the sides as it penetrates. The metallic mass behind the edge makes it almost indestructible, perfect for machetes and battleaxes. Shape the knife for the victim, not the other way around.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Basic Principles of Butchery <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Come in. Clean your boots. The strong smell of iron in the air is blood, and you are going to have to get used to it. I have owned this butcher shop for thirty years, and the first thing I teach my apprentices is respect. <LINE> <LINE> An animal gave its life so that you and your family could chew and stay standing tomorrow. Taking a dull knife and mutilating the carcass, turning good meat into chewed rags of garbage because you don't know what you are doing, is a sin against the beast and against your own hunger. <LINE> <LINE> In this first volume, I am going to teach you the basics. I won't talk about picanha or window cuts. We are going to talk about how to remove the hide, clean the guts, and not ruin a thousand kilograms of meat on a hot day.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cleaning the Engine Room <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> After removing the stomach, you will find the diaphragm. Cut this membrane to access the 'Engine Room': The Heart and Lungs. <LINE> <LINE> You must rip out the trachea (the windpipe that goes to the neck) by pulling hard, bringing the lungs and heart along with it. The liver, clean kidneys, and heart form what we call 'Offal'. <LINE> <LINE> Modern people are finicky, but these parts contain ten times more nutrients and iron than muscle meat. Wash them immediately in cold water and place them on ice, as they spoil much faster than the hard-boned carcass.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Splitting the Carcass in Half <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The animal without its hide and guts needs to be cooled down quickly, but the whole body traps a lot of heat in the middle of the bone. We split it in half. <LINE> <LINE> You will do this by sawing exactly down the middle of the spine, from the rump to the neck, dividing the carcass into two identical 'Sides'. This is a job for the heavy Meat Saw (or a sharp, broad axe if you have wide shoulders). <LINE> <LINE> Sawing the central spine of a hanging steer requires raw muscle power, but it is essential. The yellow, fatty spinal cord will open up. Clean everything with hot water to remove the bone dust left by the saw, because that dust sours meat quickly.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rigor Mortis and Aging <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The layman cries out for 'fresh meat'. Let me teach you biology: if you kill a cow right now, slice a steak on the spot, and throw it into the pan, you will chew on something tougher than an old boot. <LINE> <LINE> About six to twelve hours after death, the carcass enters Rigor Mortis. The muscles contract like steel, locking the animal into an ice-statue pose. If you cut up the animal during rigor, the meat will be tough forever. <LINE> <LINE> You MUST leave the half-carcass hanging in a cold room (between 2 and 4 degrees Celsius) for several days. Beef requires one to two weeks. Pigs require three days. During this freezing time, the natural enzymes of the muscle itself will 'digest' and break down the tough fibers of the body. This is Aging. It softens the meat and generates true butcher shop flavor.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Waste and Tallow <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the large dumps of commercial slaughterhouses, they throw fat away. In our daily survival, fat is worth as much as gold. <LINE> <LINE> The hard fat around a cow's or pig's kidneys is called Suet or Leaf Lard. Don't throw this to the crows. <LINE> <LINE> You chop these white blocks into small pieces, throw them into a thick iron cauldron over very low heat, and let the fat melt down (Rendering). When it cools in the pots, it will turn into a pure, white paste. It works for frying, it works for making homemade soap mixed with fireplace ash, and it works for waterproofing your leather boots against the snow. Every bit of the beast has a use.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Doctrine of Cold Cleanliness <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If your wooden cutting table (the Chopping Block) is dirty with rotting blood from the day before, having a sharp blade is useless. Cross-contamination will sicken anyone who eats your work. <LINE> <LINE> The butcher's counter is scraped at the end of every day with a steel scraper, then scrubbed with coarse salt and a brush. Salt kills microbes in the wood by deep osmosis and pulls moisture and fat remnants out of the grain. <LINE> <LINE> And remember the temperature. When the carcass is disassembled into large blocks (the Quarters), you do not work under the afternoon sun. You cut in the freezing dawn or in the basement, so the meat remains cold in your hands.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Canvas <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We have wrapped up the basics. The animal is slaughtered, bled, hanging by its back heels, skinned, and eviscerated clean of any dirt. You now have two identical halves of perfectly clean, cold meat aging in the dark. <LINE> <LINE> The dirty and disgusting parts are over. Now, the true art of the cutter begins. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Two, 'From Chuck to Shank', I will teach you where the dotted lines are. How to separate the hind legs, where to cut the tenderloin, where the picanha comes from, and how to break down a thousand pounds of muscle at the joints without breaking your tools. Clean the block, sharpen the knives, and I'll see you there.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Blades of the Trade <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Television makes you think a good butcher uses a giant two-foot cleaver to cut everything. The cleaver is a blunt tool, used only to break heavy bones or stubborn joints. <LINE> <LINE> The real work is done with the Boning Knife. It has a short, thin, rigid (or semi-flexible), and incredibly sharp blade. It doesn't cut the bone; it dances around it, sliding through the joints and separating the meat with the precision of a scalpel. <LINE> <LINE> You will also need a Skinner Knife, which has a rounded tip so as not to accidentally puncture the hide or the guts, and a Meat Saw to open the backbone. Keep the cleaver in the drawer until I tell you to grab it.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of the Dull Knife <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A dull knife doesn't cut meat, it crushes the fibers. And worse: a dull knife requires you to apply force. <LINE> <LINE> When you use too much force trying to cut through pork cartilage with a bad blade, the knife will invariably slip, and all that brutal force will be directed at your other hand or your leg. I've seen young men lose their thumbs that way. <LINE> <LINE> A perfectly sharp knife makes its own weight slide through the meat. You use the Honing Steel every ten minutes of continuous work. The steel doesn't sharpen; it realigns the microscopic edge of the blade that bends when it hits bone. Real sharpening requires a waterstone. Keep the steel shining and it won't bite your hand.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Bleeding (The First Act) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Meat doesn't start on the chopping block; it starts at the slaughter. The biggest novice mistake is to kill the animal and leave it lying on the ground with blood stagnant in its veins. <LINE> <LINE> Blood is a biological magnet for bacteria and rots meat in record time from the inside out, leaving a strong, metallic, and sour taste of scrap iron in the mouth of whoever eats it. <LINE> <LINE> At the exact moment after the animal's death (or stunning), you must perform the Bleeding. Make a clean, deep cut across the jugular and carotid artery in the neck. The heart will still have some reflexes and will pump almost all the blood out of the body. A well-bled animal ensures clean, pale meat that will last for months frozen without spoiling.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Gravity and the Hook <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Trying to skin and clean a two-hundred-kilogram pig lying on the dirt floor is the work of an idiot. Your back will lock up, the dirt from the ground will contaminate the bare meat, and you won't get any leverage to pull the hide. <LINE> <LINE> You need to suspend the animal. We use a Gambrel and a pulley hoist. Make a small cut behind the Achilles tendon in the animal's hind legs and pass the hooks of the gambrel through there. The tendon can hold the weight of an entire steer without tearing. <LINE> <LINE> By hanging the animal upside down, gravity pulls the blood down and, when you open the belly, the very weight of the guts will pull them out and down, making the job immensely easier.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Skinning (Taking off the Coat) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The hide must be removed before opening the belly to prevent hair filled with dust and feces from falling onto the exposed meat. <LINE> <LINE> Make shallow cuts running down the inside of the legs to the chest. Do not stab the knife in as if you were going to assault it; you only want to cut the skin, without injuring the thin membrane of meat underneath (the silverskin). <LINE> <LINE> Once the edge of the hide is loose, you don't need to keep cutting millimetrically. Clear your hand into a fist and punch between the skin and the meat. Pull the hide down hard; it peels off as if it were adhesive tape coming off a box. Keep the knife in the holster whenever you can use the strength of your hands to tear the fat membrane.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Evisceration (The Ticking Time Bomb) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We have arrived at the inexperienced butcher's nightmare. The animal's belly is a giant, tight balloon filled with feces (intestines) and acid (stomach). <LINE> <LINE> If you stick the tip of the knife into the beast's belly to open it and pierce the large intestine or the urinary bladder, the stench will be immediate. The waste or urine will leak directly onto the fillets and tender ribs inside. Contaminated meat cannot be washed and saved; it will take on the taste of sewage and you will have to throw pounds of food in the garbage. <LINE> <LINE> To open the belly, place two fingers inside the initial cut, forming a 'V' to push the guts down, and slide the knife upside-down into the animal with the blade cutting UP toward your chest. Cut like a zipper, always protecting the guts with your fingers.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Pulling the Guts <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With the belly split from top to bottom, the mass of guts will try to pop out. Have a wheelbarrow or a large, clean bin exactly underneath the hanging animal. <LINE> <LINE> You will need to cut around the anus (the bung) and tie it tightly with a string BEFORE pulling the guts down, to ensure that no feces leak from the back while you pull the tubes through the pelvis. <LINE> <LINE> Pull the stomachs and intestines out together. They are connected by membranes. They will drop into the bin in a single, heavy, slippery package. Don't be squeamish. Butchery work requires hands warm with blood and fat.
IGUI_BookButchering1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Green Poison (The Gallbladder) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> While pulling the organs, you will notice a small, emerald-green pouch attached to the liver. This is the Gallbladder (Bile). <LINE> <LINE> That green liquid inside is the most bitter and disgusting thing nature ever invented. If you pop that little sack with your finger or your knife, and the green bile splashes onto the liver or the loin meat... cut that piece of meat away immediately and give it to the dogs. No washing with water, vinegar, or soap removes the bitter taste of gall from beef or pork. <LINE> <LINE> Hold the gallbladder by the tip of the duct and gently slice with the knife to separate it from the liver intact. Throw it into the brush, far away from here.
IGUI_BookButchering2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> From Chuck to Shank <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The animal has been hanging in the cold room for days. The meat is firm, deep in color, and rigor mortis has passed. Now the apprentice games end and the anatomist's work begins. <LINE> <LINE> Many people think a butcher is someone who chops meat with an axe. On the contrary. A good butcher knows the skeleton so well that he separates an entire leg from a steer using only the tip of his knife, without sawing a single bone. <LINE> <LINE> Meat is not a uniform block. It is a bundle of individual muscles wrapped in collagen membranes. If you cut at the right angle, the muscle separates as if it had a zipper. Let's take this apart piece by piece.
IGUI_BookButchering2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Chopping Block <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your cutting table says a lot about the butcher. If you cut meat directly on top of a cold metal table or cheap plastic, you are destroying your edge with every stroke. <LINE> <LINE> The chopping block should be made of hard, end-grain wood (wood fibers standing upright). Soft wood cushions the impact of the knife. When the knife edge enters the wood, the wood fiber yields. If you use plastic, the knife edge hits rigid plastic, dents, and bends. Wood is health. And wash that block with salt every day!
IGUI_BookButchering2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Identifying Cuts <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Learn to read the piece. Dark meat full of gristle? Stew and sauce (slow cooking). Light-colored, tender meat? Grilling and quick steaks. <LINE> <LINE> If you force a quick steak out of chuck meat, you will hate the animal. If you cook a tenderloin for six hours in the cauldron, you will turn the noblest cut of the animal into a piece of dry string. Deboning ends with the correct separation for the type of heat you are going to apply afterward.
IGUI_BookButchering2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Storing Portions <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Now that the carcass has been split into steaks, cubes, and roasts, you can't just throw it all in a bag. Meat must be packed in a way that removes the air. Air burns meat in the freezer (the famous 'freezer burn'). <LINE> <LINE> If you have butcher paper or waxed paper, wrap each cut tight and firm. The paper seals out direct contact with cold air. If you have nothing, try to keep the cuts large and don't slice everything into cubes right away. Meat kept in large blocks retains its original moisture much longer than chopped meat, which dries out in hours.
IGUI_BookButchering2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sharp Tools (Again) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I cannot repeat it enough. If the knife begins to 'pull' the meat instead of sliding, stop. Your cutting edge is gone. <LINE> <LINE> Keep a two-sided sharpening stone (a coarse one to take off the excess, a fine one for finishing) always damp with oil or water. The movement must be steady: a 20-degree tilt, curving as if you were trying to slice a thin layer off the whetstone itself. Do this until the edge glints beneath the lamplight. A clean cut is the mark of a butcher who respects the animal.
IGUI_BookButchering2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Organized Butcher <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A dirty butcher is a dangerous butcher. Have separate buckets: one for meat that will be consumed, one for bones that will make broth, and one for waste that will be buried. <LINE> <LINE> Keep your apron clean. The blood that dries on your clothes turns into an unbearable stench the next day and attracts every insect around. Order on the bench reflects the quality of the meat that goes to your table.
IGUI_BookButchering2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Craft of the Cut <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Now you have the muscles divided, the ribs sawed, the chuck separated for slow cooking, and the shanks reserved for marrow. The animal that was once whole has been transformed into provisions for the group's survival. <LINE> <LINE> You have learned the anatomy of the joints and how to separate the fillet from the spine effortlessly. This is the basic foundation of deboning. <LINE> <LINE> But game is not always a fat farm steer. Sometimes it is an animal harvested in the field, under rain, where time is your enemy. In Volume Three, 'The Hunter's Guide to Deboning', we will deal with wild deboning: how to dismantle a carcass in the middle of the woods, with no counters, no power, and under the risk of predators. Keep your knives sharp and your awareness doubled.
