It is the traffic cop for electrons. <LINE> <LINE> Made of treated silicon, diodes are essential for transforming dangerous Alternating Current into Direct Current (Rectification), allowing sensitive devices to survive plugged into the wall. They are also your defense against human stupidity. <LINE> <LINE> Every well-designed circuit features a reverse diode at the power input. If some idiot inserts the batteries backward, the current tries to enter the wrong way, but the diode blocks the flow instantly, sacrificing itself but saving the rest of the board. Never remove a protection diode thinking it does nothing.
IGUI_BookElectrician4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Resistors and Ohm's Law <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You can’t inject 12 Volts straight into a tiny panel indicator LED, or it will shine with the fury of a shooting star and burn out in half a second. You need to choke the power. We do that with Resistors. <LINE> <LINE> Resistors are like rocks in the middle of your water pipe; they brake the current and turn excess energy into pure heat. Their value is measured in Ohms and indicated by tiny colored bands painted on the component's body. <LINE> <LINE> If a resistor on your motherboard is black and charred, replacing it with an identical one rarely solves the problem. Resistors almost never burn out from their own failure; they burn out because another component shorted and forced the resistor to hold a massive load. Find the cause, or the new resistor will burn in three seconds.
IGUI_BookElectrician4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Art and Smell of Solder <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Residential wiring is joined by heavy pliers. Electronics are joined by an alloy of tin and lead melted at 350 degrees Celsius. Soldering isn't dripping hot metal on top of two cold wires; that creates the infamous 'Cold Joint'—a dull, brittle connection that will fail at the first sign of vibration. <LINE> <LINE> Real soldering requires thermal conduction physics. You touch the iron tip simultaneously to the board's copper pad and the component lead. You heat both metals. Only then do you touch the solder wire to the hot metals, not to the iron. <LINE> <LINE> The acid flux inside the solder wire will melt, cleaning away oxidation instantly, and the solder will flow, covering the connection like shiny water. Do this in a room with the windows open. The vapors from melting lead-core flux are no pleasant incense; they slowly destroy your brain.
IGUI_BookElectrician4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The green boards you see in every piece of equipment aren't magic plastic; they are made of rigid fiberglass overlaid with thin, tiny, fragile flat lines of copper (Traces) that act as the system's wires. <LINE> <LINE> The number one enemy of a printed circuit board isn't fire; it’s the continuous heat from your poor-quality soldering iron. If you hold a hot iron for more than four seconds on top of a solder pad, the phenolic glue binding the copper to the fiberglass boils. <LINE> <LINE> The copper trace lifts off the board, tears, and you have just irremediably destroyed the power path. Board repairs require fast, surgical touches lasting no more than three seconds. Get in, melt the solder, and get out.
IGUI_BookElectrician4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Killer Static (ESD) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You walk in socks across the living room rug, touch the doorknob, and take a little shock. That is Electrostatic Discharge (ESD). That little pop on your finger carries between 3,000 and 10,000 Volts. Your body handles it because the current is almost zero. <LINE> <LINE> But the sensitive microchips on your computer board operate on a microscopic scale. To them, that shock from the rug is a divine lightning bolt striking the city. <LINE> <LINE> If you pick up a complex electronic board by grabbing its metal contacts or chips after walking on carpet, you will punch through the microscopic silicon barriers inside. The chip will die instantly, without sound, smoke, or visible marks. Never touch a board without using a grounding wrist strap connected to the metal of the bench.
IGUI_BookElectrician4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Electrolytic Capacitors <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Capacitors are tiny energy water towers. They store electrons and discharge them violently when the circuit demands a power spike, smoothing out supply fluctuations. Electrolytic models—those that look like tiny jacketed aluminum cylinders—are miniature bombs. <LINE> <LINE> They have strict polarity. If you solder an electrolytic capacitor backward onto the board, the chemical material inside will boil in seconds. The cylinder will swell, the aluminum top will vent along its safety score lines, and it will explode with a revolver-like pop, spraying shredded paper and acid into your eye. <LINE> <LINE> Furthermore, old capacitors leak their corrosive acid onto the board, destroying the surrounding copper traces. If the top of a capacitor is bulged, the equipment's death is imminent. Swap it out immediately.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: You Are the Grid Now <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The streetlights went dark for good and the hum of the transmission towers stopped. Civilization flipped the main breaker. If you made it to this fifth and final volume, it means the comfort of infinite alternating current supplied by the government is over. <LINE> <LINE> You are no longer a consumer installing outlets in the living room. As of today, you are the Power Company. You generate, you regulate, you store, and you consume. <LINE> <LINE> Electricity in a broken world is your most valuable and dangerous resource. It no longer comes from a distant hydroelectric plant; it will bleed from your sweat, from scarce gasoline, and from parts stripped off abandoned carcasses. Adjust your multimeter. The true test of your technical sanity begins here.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Threat from the Sky (Lightning) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You put up makeshift utility poles, raised massive antennas on roofs, and strung open wires across the compound. You just built a gigantic accidental lightning rod. <LINE> <LINE> When a severe storm rolls in, the static electricity built up in the air doesn't need a direct lightning strike to fry everything; the simple electromagnetic pulse from a bolt hitting five hundred yards away can induce thousands of Volts into your clothesline wires. <LINE> <LINE> Physically disconnect your radio antennas and unplug solar lines from the controller during storms. Standard breakers aren't fast enough to clamp a lightning strike. If the storm comes, the only safe switch is an inch of empty air between the cable and the gear.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Electric Fences (The Stupidity) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> It’s inevitable. In a hostile world, some imbecil in your group is going to suggest: 'Let's hook a line from the generator straight to the barbed wire fence to keep intruders out'. <LINE> <LINE> Doing that isn’t defense; it’s suicide by extreme stupidity. If you connect a live hot leg from your 110-Volt grid straight to a fence, the second an animal, a zombie, or wet grass touches the wire, you will create a dead short circuit that will trip your system or melt your generator on the spot. <LINE> <LINE> Electric fences run on High-Voltage Fence Chargers (bula chargers). They fire pulses of 10,000 Volts for a tiny fraction of a second every two seconds. The ultra-high voltage contracts the intruder's muscles painfully, but the near-total absence of continuous current ensures your house lines don't catch fire and the power doesn't trip. Learn the difference.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Medical Risk in Isolation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I need to be morbid for a minute. We used to work following strict codes in the past because lawsuits were expensive. Today, we work following codes because hospitals no longer exist. <LINE> <LINE> In the old days, if you took a 220V shock that threw your body across the room, the ambulance took you in, you had secondary cardiac arrests in the ICU, underwent dialysis for kidneys failing due to deep internal burns, and came home alive three months later with scars. <LINE> <LINE> Today, if current crosses your chest and fibrillates your heart, or if a spark blows up and causes third-degree burns across your arms, there is no ICU, antibiotics, or defibrillator. A minor wiring slip that yesterday would give you three days off work will tomorrow be the cause of a slow, painful, infectious death in your camp cot.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Hidden Hunger (Phantom Loads) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Rationed power requires Spartan discipline. If you have battery banks struggling to make it through the night alive, you cannot feed the electrical vampires living hidden in the shadows. <LINE> <LINE> Inverters consume energy just to remain switched on, even if no bulb is burning on the other side. Radios and old television power supplies draw what are called 'Phantom Loads' simply by staying plugged into an outlet. <LINE> <LINE> Install heavy, ruthless mechanical disconnect switches on the thick output cables of your battery bank. When the sun goes down and patrol ends, don’t just turn off the gear; physically disconnect the batteries using pure metal levers. Every milliamp saved at midnight is the difference between a radio that cries for help the next morning or dead silence.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Light Attracts Attention <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Electricity yields power, but power is not discreet. With gas generators thumping loudly like old tractors in the dead of night and bright incandescent bulbs leaking through the windows of your refuge, you stop being an anonymous survivor and become a beacon of wealth in the dark. <LINE> <LINE> Human beings in the dark instinctively walk toward the light, whether they are friendly or hostile, living or just something crawling in the shadows. Soundproof your machines in pits or bunkers and use low-intensity red bulbs for night lighting; red light doesn’t travel long distances in fog and preserves your eyes' natural night vision. <LINE> <SIZE:medium> The biggest mistake an arrogant tech can make is restoring power to a house and lighting it up like a Christmas tree in the middle of a dead city. Power is a hidden tool, not a neon sign announcing you have supplies.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Inspector's Farewell <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> My jurisdiction ends here. I wrote these five volumes as the nightmare and obsession of a safety inspector who dedicated his life to understanding why buildings catch fire and people die messing with loose outlets. <LINE> <LINE> The clean world of standardized codes and city inspections must be ashes by the time you close this book. Shiny tools will give way to makeshift knives stripping filthy wires by the side of the highway. <LINE> <LINE> But the physics? The physics didn't break, didn't get sick, and didn't change. An electron from a million years ago behaves today exactly as it always has. Respect the immutable mathematical laws, test with your multimeter before surrendering your blind life to hidden wires inside walls, and keep your splices absolutely unbreakable. Stay alive. The inspector is clocking out.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The False Death of Lines <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first lesson of the collapse: NEVER trust that the street grid is dead. Even weeks after a general blackout, treating a hanging pole cable as an inert piece of rubber is an invitation to the morgue. <LINE> <LINE> Why? Because desperate, idiotic survivors exist. Some neighbor five blocks away might have hooked a heavy diesel generator straight into his house outlet to run a fridge. Remember the 'Lethal Backfeeding' I taught you in Volume II? <LINE> <LINE> Power from that idiot's generator will climb up the pole, pass through the street transformer, step up to thousands of Volts, and energize the downed cable lying in your yard. Physically isolate your house from the street grid by cutting and taping the lines from your main meter. Be an island.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cannibalizing Alternators <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Without powerful generators, your best power-producing friend is under the hood of the millions of dead cars sitting on the highways: The Alternator. <LINE> <LINE> A car alternator isn't a standard DC generator; it’s a primitive three-phase generator that houses an internal diode bridge to output 12 or 24 Volts DC. It is brutal, efficient, and nearly indestructible. <LINE> <LINE> You can rip an alternator out of an abandoned truck, mount a pulley to it, and hook it up to the chain of an exercise bike, a wooden windmill, or a waterwheel in the river. As long as you spin it to at least 1,500 RPM and apply a small excitation voltage to the regulator wire, it will pump out enough juice to charge an entire battery bank.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Lead Graveyard <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Generated power needs to be saved, and the old world left behind twelve-Volt lead-acid batteries in droves. But understand the brutality of chemistry: standard car starter batteries are engineered to give a massive burst of juice for three seconds and get immediately topped off by the engine. <LINE> <LINE> If you take the battery from your sedan and use it to run lights until it drains completely, the thin lead plates inside will sulfate. Within ten deep cycles, the battery will die forever. <LINE> <LINE> You need to hunt down Deep-Cycle Batteries, used in forklifts, heavy tractors, or marine setups. They feature thick, heavy plates of solid lead that endure being drained nearly to empty and recharged hundreds of times. Weight is a sign of quality.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Inverters and the False Wave <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You have battery banks full of 12 Volts DC, but your tube television and ham radio demand 110 Volts AC. The piece that pulls off this magic is the Power Inverter. It electronically chops up the battery power and tries to mimic the swing of the grid. <LINE> <LINE> The danger here is that cheap inverters produce a 'Modified Sine Wave'. It isn’t a smooth curve like utility power; it is blocky and harsh, like steps. <LINE> <LINE> Incandescent bulbs don’t care about the waveform. But if you plug a sensitive motor, a fridge pump, or medical gear into a square-wave inverter, the motor will hum loudly, overheat alarmingly, and the coils will burn out. For critical gear and motors, you must hunt down heavy-duty 'Pure Sine Wave' inverters.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Primitive Solar Power <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you are lucky enough to scavenge one of the rare and wildly expensive solar panels of this decade (early '90s), treat it like a sacred glass relic. They are heavy, incredibly fragile, and ridiculously inefficient if they get dirty. <LINE> <LINE> A thin layer of road dust or bird droppings can cut the panel's power generation in half. But the fatal mistake of solar power isn’t dirt; it’s a direct connection. <LINE> <LINE> Never hook a solar panel straight to a battery's terminals. A panel can put out up to 21 Volts on a sunny day. This excessive voltage will boil the acid in your 12-Volt battery until it cracks and sprays acid on the ceiling. The vital piece between the sun and the battery is called a Charge Controller. It’s the customs gate that dictates how much power can enter.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Radio and Vital Grounding <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the internet and telephone exchanges fall silent, the only bridge over the abyss will be shortwave ham radio. But operating powerful battery-driven radio transmitters requires an esoteric piece of care: RF Grounding. <LINE> <LINE> An antenna broadcasting heavy signals on the roof needs something to push against. It pushes against the earth. If your gear lacks a network of thick copper wires buried in the yard (radials), the transmitter's energy won't leave the antenna. <LINE> <LINE> Instead, the radio frequency will reflect back down the feedline, travel through the radio casing, fry the internal boards, and give you deep RF burns on your fingers when you squeeze the mic button to call for help. A radio without a ground is a miniature bomb.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Water Pumps and Capacitors <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Stagnant water kills in days. You need to pump water from the well. If you found a rugged industrial water pump, it’s probably three-phase (3 phases). But your gas generator or residential inverter only outputs a single phase (single-phase). <LINE> <LINE> Theoretically, the pump is useless to you. But there is an old, dangerous emergency trick: using Run Capacitors. <LINE> <LINE> By adding mathematically calculated heavy capacitors between the live hot line and the phantom leg of the three-phase motor, you create an artificial phase lag, tricking the motor into thinking it has a third phase. It will lose 30%% of its original strength and run hot as hell, but it will spin, and it will bring up the water your community needs to survive the week. Necessity ignores manufacturer manuals.
IGUI_BookElectrician5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Electricity and Hostile Weather <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the civilized world, we built climate-controlled shelters for gear. Now, you are storing batteries in freezing barns and inverters in boiling tin sheds. Weather destroys metal. <LINE> <LINE> Extreme cold paralyzes the chemical reactions inside a lead battery. On severe blizzard nights, an exposed battery can lose 60%% of its actual capacity to supply a load, and if it discharges too low, the water inside freezes and the plastic casing splits, spilling acid onto the floor. <LINE> <LINE> Summer heat does the exact opposite: it accelerates the chemistry to the point of boiling off the distilled water, dry-cooking the lead plates irreversibly in weeks. You must insulate your batteries in wooden boxes lined with styrofoam, keeping them at cool room temperature, or you'll be swapping parts all year round.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Better Gardening <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hello, neighbor! Welcome to the wonderful world of suburban gardening. If you bought this book at the Sunday market or your local bookstore, it is because you are tired of eating those tasteless supermarket tomatoes that look more like watery styrofoam balls. <LINE> <LINE> Gardening is not dirty work; it is therapy with your hands in the dirt. It is the miracle of placing a tiny seed in the ground and, weeks later, harvesting a fresh salad for your family. <LINE> <LINE> It does not matter if you have a huge backyard in Muldraugh or just a few window boxes in your apartment. Put on your straw hat, slip on your rubber gloves, and let us make the green magic happen!
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cabbages, the Plump Ones <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Planting cabbage is like adopting a slow-growing vegetable bowling ball. They are lovely leafy greens that love cold weather. Planting cabbage in the extreme summer heat only attracts clouds of chewing pests. <LINE> <LINE> The big secret to cabbage is space! When the seedling is small, it seems silly to leave almost three feet of distance between them. But trust me, those giant leaves will spread out like the wings of an eagle. <LINE> <LINE> If you plant them too close, they will fight for water and sun, and the heads will not form round and compact. Cabbage hates getting dehydrated; keep the soil consistently damp (but not flooded), and it will close up that crisp, delicious, and healthy little head.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Trash Can Potatoes <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You do not need a farm to grow potatoes; you just need a new, clean trash can! That is the wonder of potatoes. Poke holes in the bottom of the can for water to drain out. <LINE> <LINE> Put down a hand-span of soil, drop in your potato pieces with the 'eyes' (sprouts) facing up, and cover lightly. When the green plant grows a hand-span, throw more soil over it, leaving just the tips showing. <LINE> <LINE> Repeat this until the can fills to the top! The potato plant keeps creating more and more potatoes along the entire buried stem. When the plant up top turns yellow and dies in the autumn, you just flip the trash can upside down in the yard, and a magical mountain of clean potatoes will roll to your feet. It is a treasure hunt!
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Invaders: The Weeds <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your vegetable garden offers a free buffet of nutrients and water, and the neighborhood weeds know it. They are the rude party crashers of your gardening journey. They grow ten times faster than your vegetables and steal their water and sun. <LINE> <LINE> Weeding is not pulling the leaf with your hand and leaving the root down there to laugh at your face. The root will sprout again tomorrow. <LINE> <LINE> Use your trowel or a small hand-hoe, dig into the soil next to the unwanted plant, and pull the villain out whole, roots dangling. Remove weeds when they are still babies; do not wait for them to become small trees with roots gripping your precious tomatoes.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Bug Patrol <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Aphids! Those nasty little green things love to suck the sweet sap from your new plants. You do not need to use toxic industrial pesticides that will poison your family. Remember, we are friends of nature! <LINE> <LINE> Try the soap trick: mix a few spoonfuls of mild soap in a spray bottle with water and spray it directly onto the leaf-stripping bugs at the end of the day. The soap dries out their soft bodies and saves the garden. <LINE> <LINE> For the fat slugs that love to eat your cabbage at night, place shallow dishes of cheap beer buried rim-deep in the soil. Slugs love beer; they will crawl into the dish, drink, get dizzy, and happily drown in the barley trap.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Love Has Limits (Pruning) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Being a good plant parent sometimes requires discipline. When the lowest leaves of your plants start touching the soil, turning yellow, or showing old brown spots, grab a pair of sharp shears. <LINE> <LINE> Cut those diseased leaves away without mercy and throw them out! Dead or diseased leaves in contact with wet soil are open highways for fungi and mold to destroy your whole plant. <LINE> <LINE> You want the plant's energy directed upward, to create juicy fruits, not trying to keep old, dragging leaves alive. Pruning cleans the bed, brightens the look, and tells the plant: 'Focus on the tomatoes, my dear!'
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Joy of Harvest <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> And we have reached the best part! Knowing when to harvest is an instinct you develop. A ripe tomato yields gently to the soft squeeze of your thumb and snaps off the vine with a light 'crack'. Lettuce should be harvested before it flowers, early in the morning, when the leaves are full of water and crisp. <LINE> <LINE> Suburban gardening teaches patience. You cannot yell at a seed to make it grow faster. You have to water, watch, pull the weeds, and love the outdoor process. <LINE> <LINE> We wrap up our wonderful initiation here! You already know how to plant, tend, and get rid of rowdy slugs. But what if you want to stop playing around and start saving food for the winter? In Volume Two, 'Growing Food at Home', we will learn to plant to fill the pantries. Keep smiling, and until the next harvest!
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dirt vs. Soil <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first and biggest mistake of the novice gardener is thinking that all dirt is the same. 'Dirt' is what gets stuck to the sole of your shoe after it rains. 'Soil' is a living, breathing organism full of nutrients that your plants call home. <LINE> <LINE> If you dig up your backyard and the earth is hard, gray, or cracked, your tiny seeds will suffocate. The perfect soil is as dark as coffee grounds, loose, and smells like spring rain. <LINE> <LINE> Before planting anything, go to the garden center and buy a few bags of good topsoil and organic fertilizer. Mix it all into your garden bed. Think of the soil as your baby's crib; you would not put your baby to sleep on sharp rocks, would you?
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Seed Miracle <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A seed looks like a dead little pebble, but it is actually a tiny lunchbox! Inside that hard shell sits a sleeping baby plant and all the food it needs to make that first push out of the earth. <LINE> <LINE> The golden rule of depth: never bury the seed too deep! Most vegetable seeds should be planted at a depth that is only twice their own size. <LINE> <LINE> Radish and lettuce seeds sit almost on the surface, covered by just a dusting of earth. If you bury a tiny lettuce seed a hand-span deep, the poor thing will spend all its energy trying to climb, die of exhaustion in the dark, and never see the sun.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Water Magic <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Water is life, but first-timers love to drown their garden beds. Plants do not have gills; their roots need to breathe oxygen. If the earth turns into a muddy puddle, the roots rot and the plant dies yellow and sad. <LINE> <LINE> The foolproof Smart Watering technique: do the finger test! Poke your index finger into the soil up to the middle knuckle. If the tip of your finger feels moisture, do not water. If it comes out dry, it is time to give your green friends a drink. <LINE> <LINE> Always water early in the morning or late in the afternoon. If you splash cold water on the leaves in the midday sun, the droplets act like little magnifying glasses, and the Kentucky sun will burn your poor plant's foliage.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sun: The Healthy Fire <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Vegetables love to sunbathe, but each has its own tan preference. Tomatoes, peppers, and pumpkins are professional sunbathers; they require at least six to eight hours of direct, strong sunlight hitting their heads every day. <LINE> <LINE> But lettuce, spinach, and delicate greens prefer cool spring weather. If you plant lettuce in the scorching August sun, it will 'bolt' (quickly produce flowers to try to reproduce before dying) and the leaves will taste unbearably bitter. <LINE> <LINE> Plant your greens in the partial shade of your giant tomatoes. Gardening is like building a neighborhood where the tall neighbors protect the shorter ones from the harsh afternoon sun.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tools of the Trade <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You do not need to buy that expensive tractor featured in TV commercials. The backyard gardener needs only three things to be happy. <LINE> <LINE> The Trowel: an extension of your arm, perfect for digging the small cribs for seeds. The Watering Can with a rose nozzle: because a high-pressure hose will wash the soil away and blast your seeds onto your neighbor's wall. And your own Hands. <LINE> <LINE> Take off your gloves once in a while and feel the earth. Break up the clumps, feel the moisture. Modern gardening tries to pull us away from nature with shiny tools, but nothing replaces direct contact with the life pulsing in your garden bed.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Radishes (The First Victory) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Want to feel the glory of harvest in record time? Plant Radishes! They are the most eager and excited vegetable in the world. They grow so fast that you can almost see them stretching their leaves if you pull up a chair and watch. <LINE> <LINE> From the day you put the seed in the ground to the day the red, crisp, and peppery radish hits your salad, it takes only about 25 days! <LINE> <LINE> Plant a small row of seeds every week. That way, instead of harvesting two hundred radishes all at once and not knowing what to do with them, you will have fresh radishes every single weekend, continuous and perfect for Sunday dinner.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Carrot Struggle <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Everyone loves harvesting carrots, but they are picky roots. A carrot grows by pushing its tip down into the dark. If the earth in your garden bed is full of rocks, tree roots, or hard clay, the poor carrot will try to dodge the obstacles. <LINE> <LINE> The result? You will harvest carrots that look like twisted legs and mutant orange octopuses, instead of those straight supermarket carrots Bugs Bunny likes. <LINE> <LINE> The secret to a show-worthy carrot is turning the soil deeply. Loosen the earth down to about two hand-spans and sift out the rocks before sowing. Keep its bed as soft as a pillow, and it will grow perfectly straight in gratitude.
IGUI_BookFarming1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tomatoes: King of the Yard <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> No real vegetable garden is complete without a tomato plant. The tomato plant is not a quiet little thing; it is an aggressive, lanky vine that grows nonstop. If you leave it loose on the ground, it will crawl, the tomatoes will touch the damp earth and rot, and bugs will have a party. <LINE> <LINE> As soon as your plant is a hand-span tall, you need to stake the little creature. Drive a thick wooden stake next to it and tie the stem loosely with strips of old pantyhose or soft twine as it grows. <LINE> <LINE> By lifting the tomato plant upward, you improve air circulation through the leaves, prevent annoying fungi, and ensure your tomatoes turn red while swinging freely under the warm summer breeze.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Growing Food at Home <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first volume of this series taught you how to have fun in the dirt and harvest a few radishes for Sunday dinner. It was a lovely pastime. But today's economy is no joke. Supermarket prices rise every month, and feeding a family with factory-made canned food is not healthy, it is lazy. <LINE> <LINE> I wrote this second volume to transform your weekend hobby into a true home economy operation. We are going to stop planting what is 'cute' and start planting what sustains us. <LINE> <LINE> You will learn to maximize space, create your own fertilizer without spending a penny, harvest smartly, and fill your pantry with glass jars so your family has fresh food when winter snow covers the yard.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Seed Bank <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Buying pretty seed packets from garden shops every year means signing a dependency contract with corporations. Nature already gives you seeds for free at the end of each season. <LINE> <LINE> Select your best, reddest, and largest tomato of the summer. Do not eat it! Cut it in half, squeeze the seeds with that pulp into a cup with a little water, and let it ferment on the windowsill for three days (this destroys the protective gelatin coating). Then, rinse it in a sieve and let it dry on a paper towel for a week. <LINE> <LINE> Store these dry seeds in a dark paper envelope inside a glass jar in a cool place. Next year, you will plant tomatoes that are already genetically adapted to your yard's exact climate.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Mason Jar Magic <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> For tomatoes and fruits that do not last in the cellar, the only salvation for winter is Home Canning. Good old glass Mason jars with two-piece metal lids. <LINE> <LINE> The process is pure domestic science. You boil the food (like a thick tomato sauce) to kill bacteria. Fill the sterilized glass jar almost to the brim, place the flat metal lid on top, and screw the band on finger-tight. <LINE> <LINE> Then, you submerge the closed jars inside a large pot of boiling water (Water Bath). The heat forces air out of the jar. When you take the jar out of the water and it cools, the metal lid sucks down in the middle with a wonderful, sharp snap ('Pop!'). That snap means a vacuum has formed. That tomato sauce will be perfectly safe to eat for two years out of the fridge.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Water Bath vs. Pressure Canning <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Pay close attention here, or you will poison your family. The boiling water bath method taught on the previous page can ONLY be used for High-Acid foods, like tomatoes, fruit jams, or vinegared pickles. The acid, combined with the heat, prevents Botulism bacteria from reproducing. <LINE> <LINE> Common vegetables like canned carrots, green beans, corn, and meats are Low-Acid. If you try to preserve them in a regular pot of boiling water, the botulism bacteria will survive, multiply in the vacuum, and kill whoever opens the jar months later. <LINE> <LINE> For low-acid preserves, you are required to use a Pressure Canner. It reaches temperatures of 240 degrees Fahrenheit (well above the normal boiling point), the only heat capable of annihilating the deadly spores of botulinum bacteria.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Crop Rotation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Soil gets tired. If you plant cabbages in the same bed for three years in a row, the cabbages will suck all the nitrogen out of that square of earth and leave their specific diseases behind. By the fourth year, they will grow tiny and sickly. <LINE> <LINE> The organized homemaker uses Crop Rotation. Divide your garden into three parts. In bed A, plant greens and cabbages (heavy feeders). In bed B, plant roots like carrots (which break up the deep earth). And in bed C, plant beans and peas (which replenish lost nutrients). <LINE> <LINE> The following year, everyone switches places. Cabbage goes to C, roots go to A, and beans go to B. The soil regenerates on its own, bugs that slept in the dirt lose their favorite food upon waking, and the cycle of health stays strong.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Putting the Garden to Bed <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the heavy frosts of November arrive, the show is over. But you do not abandon your garden bed exposed to winter like an neglectful parent. Bare earth exposed to severe snow compacts and freezes vital microorganisms. <LINE> <LINE> You need to put the garden to bed. Pull up the old, dead tomato and cabbage plants and throw them into the compost bin. Next, cover all the bare earth in your bed with a four-inch layer of dry straw, fallen autumn leaves, and lawn clippings (Mulch). <LINE> <LINE> This organic blanket protects the earth from deep freezing and winter rains that wash away nutrients. The straw will slowly decay under the snow, and when spring returns, your soil will be loose, protected, and full of hungry new earthworms waiting for the new year's seeds.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Security of a Full Pantry <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the first winter storm howls outside and closes the town roads, you will not need to panic or run to the supermarket to fight over the last can of soup. <LINE> <LINE> You will go down to your cellar, look at the heavy shelves lined with dozens of Mason jars gleaming with red sauce and jams, and boxes of cured potatoes ready for the oven. A household's true wealth is not in its bank account, it is in the autonomy of its pantry. <LINE> <LINE> You have learned to sustain your family. But, if you decide you want to flee the city and live completely off the grid, you will need to scale up to a level of extreme sweat. This is where I say goodbye, leaving you with Volume Three: 'Subsistence Agriculture by Liam Keating'. A warm embrace and a bountiful harvest to all.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Black Gold (Composting) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you are buying bags of chemical fertilizer at the hardware store, you are literally throwing money into the trash. The best fertilizer in the world is created from the waste you already produce in your kitchen. <LINE> <LINE> Start a compost pile in the corner of the yard. What goes in? Eggshells, coffee grounds, raw vegetable scraps, potato peels, and dry leaves swept from the lawn. What does NOT go in? Meat, bones, dairy, or oil, unless you want to attract every rat and raccoon in the county. <LINE> <LINE> Turn the pile with a garden fork once a week. Earthworms and microorganisms will do the heavy lifting, turning your trash into a dark, rich, and sweet-smelling earth. This is the 'Black Gold' of home economy.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Succession Planting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The most frustrating mistake of a novice gardener is springtime excitement. You go out and plant all forty of your cabbage seeds on the exact same day. Three months later, you have forty cabbages ready at the same time. Your family cannot eat all that, and thirty of them rot in the yard. <LINE> <LINE> The smart homemaker uses Succession Planting. <LINE> <LINE> Plant only five cabbage seeds today. Wait two weeks and plant five more. Wait another two weeks and plant another five. This way, your harvest will be staggered. You will have a fresh salad and a pot of soup guaranteed for months on end, without food spoiling in the garden.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Strength of Roots <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Lettuce and tomatoes are delicious in the summer, but they are basically made of water. If the world faced a famine tomorrow, a garden full of lettuce would not keep anyone standing. <LINE> <LINE> If you want to feed your family, dedicate most of your garden bed to Root Crops and Tubers: Potatoes, Carrots, and Radishes. <LINE> <LINE> Roots are calorie-dense, rich in carbohydrates that give you energy to work, and most importantly, they last for months if stored properly, whereas a tomato spoils in five days on the kitchen counter. The potato is the backbone of any household that prides itself on not going hungry.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Companion Planting (The Three Sisters) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In nature, plants do not grow in solitary rows. You can save space and reduce water use by planting friends close to each other. This is the Companion Planting technique. <LINE> <LINE> Native Americans taught us the best companion planting in history: The Three Sisters. Corn, Beans, and Squash. The corn grows tall and strong, serving as a living 'pole' for the climbing beans to climb up. <LINE> <LINE> The beans, in turn, take nitrogen from the air and inject it into the earth, fertilizing the soil for free for the others. And the squash grows low along the ground, its giant leaves shading the earth, which prevents water from evaporating and chokes out weed growth. It is perfect efficiency.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rainwater Harvesting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The summer water bill can devour all the savings you made by growing your own food. Stop paying for what falls from the sky for free. <LINE> <LINE> Install one or two Rain Barrels beneath your home's roof gutters. A single summer storm can fill a fifty-gallon barrel in less than an hour. <LINE> <LINE> Besides being free, rainwater is infinitely better for your vegetables. Tap water comes full of chlorine and fluoride from the municipal treatment plant, minerals that dry out the soil and kill the good microorganisms in your compost. The sky sends perfectly distilled, oxygen-rich water.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Aromatic Defenders <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Buying expensive insecticides at the supermarket is, besides a financial waste, putting poison on your children's plates. You can repel most pests by using plants that smell strong and confuse bugs. <LINE> <LINE> Plant Marigolds around the entire edge of your vegetable garden. The roots of this flower release a compound into the soil that drives away the invisible root nematodes that kill tomato plants. <LINE> <LINE> Plant garlic and chives between your cabbage and carrot plants. The sharp sulfur smell masks the sweet scent of the vegetables, causing white butterflies and slugs to pass right by your house and go attack the garden of your neighbor who did not read this book.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Harvesting and Curing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The fate of your food is sealed the moment you pull it from the ground. If you dig up a potato and wash it under the tap to store in the pantry, it will rot quickly. Water on the skin wakes up fungi. <LINE> <LINE> Roots to be stocked for winter need to be 'Cured'. When digging up potatoes, onions, or garlic, do not wash off the dirt! Just brush away the excess with a dry cloth and leave them spread out on the garage or porch floor (in the shade, never under direct sun) in a well-ventilated spot for about one to two weeks. <LINE> <LINE> This curing process makes the outer skin dry out and harden like leather. It is this tough skin that will keep the potato from shriveling or rotting over the next four months inside your home.
IGUI_BookFarming2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Root Cellar <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Our grandparents did not have giant refrigerators powered by expensive electricity. They used the constant temperature of the earth itself to preserve food. <LINE> <LINE> If your house has an unheated basement (or if you can dig a wood-and-stone-lined pit in the yard), you have the Holy Grail of food storage. The cellar must be cool (but not freezing), pitch black, and slightly damp. <LINE> <LINE> Store your apples, potatoes, carrots, and squash down there in spaced wooden boxes. The darkness keeps the potatoes from sprouting, and the cold slows their metabolism down almost to a halt. But NEVER store apples and potatoes on the same shelf; apples release an invisible gas called ethylene that makes potatoes sprout and spoil prematurely.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Subsistence Agriculture <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I was paid by the publisher to write this third volume, and I confess I read the first two manuals before picking up the pen. I almost threw up. The 'gardener' from the first book thinks the earth is a playground. The housewife from the second thinks the world revolves around neat glass jars. <LINE> <LINE> I am Liam Keating. I do not plant to de-stress from an office job. I plant because if my harvest fails, my family starves in the winter. It is that simple. <LINE> <LINE> If trucks stopped supplying the city's supermarkets tomorrow, your lettuce garden would not keep you alive for a week. Subsistence farming is back pain, torn calluses, and war against the weather. If you have the stomach for it, keep reading.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Multiplying Without Seeds <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A real farmer does not cry when the packet seeds run out; he clones the plants. You do not need a potato seed to grow potatoes; we do not use potato seeds. <LINE> <LINE> Take an old, shriveled, forgotten potato that has started putting out those pale 'horns' (the sprouts). Cut the potato into three large pieces, ensuring each piece has at least one or two firm sprouts. <LINE> <LINE> Let the cut pieces dry in the open air for two days to seal the wound with a thick crust (if you bury a damp wound, it rots in the dirt). Once dry, bury each piece in the ground. From one old vegetable, you have just created three new giant potato plants.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cover Crops (Green Blood) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The land gets tired and dies. If you rip out all the crops in the autumn and leave the field bare and turned over, winter and icy rains will wash all the nitrogen away, leaving only dead sand for the next year. <LINE> <LINE> Before the first frost hits, toss cheap seeds of Winter Rye or Clover over the newly harvested field. <LINE> <LINE> These plants grow fast, withstand the ice, and cover the ground like a thick green carpet (Green Manure). They hold the soil so it does not blow away with the wind. In the spring, you do not harvest the rye; you run the hoe through and bury it alive back into the earth. The green mass rots down there and fills the field with fresh nutrients for your next carrot crop.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Seeds in the Dead Drawer <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you keep your bags of harvested seeds lying around on a hot kitchen shelf or in a stuffy, damp summer shed, they will be dead by the following year. <LINE> <LINE> Seeds are living fetuses breathing in extremely slow motion. If they feel moisture and heat, they try to wake up. If there is no soil, they spend all their vital energy inside the packet and suffocate. Heat destroys the germination rate. <LINE> <LINE> The perfect seed vault is as cold, dark, and dry as possible. Place the seeds in airtight glass jars with silica packets or raw rice at the bottom (to swallow moisture) and tuck the glass into the back of your cold cellar or the vegetable drawer of your fridge. That way, they will sleep for five years.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hidden Rot <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Cabbages are robust, but they harbor a dirty secret. The 'ball' shape of tightly packed cabbage leaves creates a thermal trap. If it rains heavily in the days leading up to harvest, water runs down into the middle of the closed leaves and cannot evaporate. <LINE> <LINE> This standing water in the warm core of the vegetable starts to rot the plant from the inside out. The cabbage will look huge, green, and perfect from the outside. <LINE> <LINE> But when you go to harvest it and slice through the middle, you will find a brown, foul, gelatinous puddle of bacterial rot right at the heart of your food. To avoid this, do not water over the top of cabbage leaves when they are forming their final head; pour water only onto the ground, straight to the roots.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Price of Failure <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The greatest lesson of subsistence farming is not technical, it is mental. Prepare for total failure, because it will happen. You will do everything right, fertilize, weed, and protect, and then a twenty-minute summer hail storm will turn your tomatoes into a shredded paste on the ground. <LINE> <LINE> A flock of crows will rip out your corn sprouts. A disease will wipe out your potatoes. If you count on a single crop, nature will murder you. <LINE> <LINE> The tough farmer's motto is: 'Plant three seeds in the hole. One for the birds, one for the disease, and one for me.' Always plant forty percent more than your family needs to survive the winter, because the weather toll is heavy and non-negotiable.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Woodsman's Farewell <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> My part ends here. I taught you to stop watering like an idiot, to recognize the white powder of Mildew before it consumes everything, to use tobacco as poison, and to understand that your own sweat is the gear that makes food grow. <LINE> <LINE> The earth does not care if you are tired, and the frost feels no pity for your rumbling stomach. Work with brutality and it will feed you in return. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Four, 'The Science of Crop Genetics and Yields', I step aside and hand over the floor to an agronomist in a lab coat from some fancy university. He will speak difficult words about nitrogen, crossbreeding genes, and soil pH that you will probably need a dictionary to understand. But their science makes potatoes bigger. Get your hands dirty, shut up, and keep hoeing.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Salad Myth <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Stop wasting your time and land planting thin leaves, peppery radishes, and pretty tomatoes. That does not fill a belly. A radish is a snack for rabbits; it has no energy. A tomato is just red water. <LINE> <LINE> You need fuel to chop wood and haul rocks. Fuel means Carbohydrates and Calories. If you are going to rely on the land to live, your absolute focus must be the farmer's sacred trinity: Potatoes, Giant Cabbages, and Dense Carrots. <LINE> <LINE> Potatoes are bricks of pure energy. You bury a dirty chunk in the ground and it hands you ten chunks back. A man can survive for months eating almost exclusively boiled potatoes and a little salt, if the situation demands it.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Nature's Wrath (Downy Mildew) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Nature is not your friend. It wants you to lose. The greatest enemy of a potato and tomato crop is not drought, it is persistent moisture. <LINE> <LINE> If it rains for days on end and your plants' leaves do not dry, you will notice a white, fuzzy powder covering the foliage. This is Mildew, a devastating fungal disease. It sucks the life out of the plant and destroys the harvest. <LINE> <LINE> If you see the white powder, grab a bottle of sour milk (or make a rustic milk-and-water spray) and mist it onto the sick leaves. The acid in the milk helps kill the fungus. If the plant is too covered, show no mercy: rip the entire plant out by the roots, burn it far from the garden, and save the rest of the bed. Compassion kills the crop.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Devil's Water Fungi <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Another nightmare born from moisture is what old farmers call the 'Devil's Water Fungi'. It mostly attacks cabbages and radishes when the soil turns into a stagnant swamp. <LINE> <LINE> Instead of white powder, the plant begins to wither mysteriously, and watery, brown spots appear on the leaves as if it were melting from the inside out. <LINE> <LINE> No milk spray will save this. Devil's Water Fungi rots the roots and the heads. When you see a cabbage melting into the wet ground, do not try to trim away the bad leaves to save the head. Rip the whole plant out and do not plant anything in that exact hole for the next two years. The fungus lives in the earth and will devour the next seed.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Manure Rule (Shit is Gold) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The previous book told you to make a pile of banana peels and coffee grounds. That is cute for a flower pot, but a half-acre field of potatoes demands real nutrients. You need animal manure. Cattle, horse, or chicken droppings. <LINE> <LINE> But pay attention: if you take fresh, smelly, steaming manure from a cow or chicken and throw it directly onto your plants' roots, the excess acidic nitrogen (ammonia) will 'burn' the roots and kill your entire harvest in two days. <LINE> <LINE> Manure needs to be aged (cured). You throw the shit into a pile under the sun for at least three months, until it stops smelling like feces and starts smelling only like wet earth. Only then is it safe to mix into your fields.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Water: The Balance of Life and Death <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Everyone knows that drought kills. The earth cracks, leaves turn yellow and crisp, and the plant dehydrates until it turns to straw. But the farmer's cruel irony is that overwatering is infinitely faster at killing. <LINE> <LINE> Carrots are the best example of vegetable pickiness. If they lack water, the root will not grow. But if you keep the carrot's soil constantly waterlogged, the carrot swells with water rapidly and explodes. Literally, the root cracks in half beneath the ground, attracting rot and maggots to the open wound. <LINE> <LINE> Never water the ground if it is already dark and sticking to your fingers. Puddled water drowns roots. Plants need to fight a little for water; lazy roots create weak vegetables.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Red Plague (Aphids) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Bugs are not visitors; they are looters. The worst are aphids. They are tiny vampires that stick to the underside of your cabbage or tomato leaves and suck the vital sap until the plant stunts and dies. <LINE> <LINE> As book one said, you can use a soap spray. But out in the fields, we make a brutal homemade poison: Nicotine Spray. <LINE> <LINE> Take handfuls of tobacco leaves (or gather dozens of old cigarette butts without the filter), soak them in a bucket of hot water for three days until the water turns dark brown and foul. Strain it and spray it on the pests. Nicotine is one of the most potent natural neurotoxins in the world. The bugs die instantly. (Warning: it is toxic; do not spray close to harvest time or you will poison yourself).
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Calluses, Tools, and Exhaustion <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forget shiny tractors with air conditioning. If the gasoline runs out tomorrow, your tractor becomes a three-ton paperweight. Real farming is done with heavy hoes, forged steel shovels, and your shoulders. <LINE> <LINE> Hoeing half an acre of land by hand under a hundred-degree sun will wreck your back and rip blood blisters onto your hands on the very first day. <LINE> <LINE> Do not stop. The blisters will burst, the flesh will thicken and turn into rigid, leather-like calluses. The back pain will fade once your muscles adapt to the daily torture of swinging the hoe. Manual labor filters out the weak. The land demands sweat as a daily tribute.
IGUI_BookFarming3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Terror of Furry Invaders <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You sweated blood to raise a row of perfect cabbages. You go to sleep. During the night, a family of deer, raccoons, or rabbits jumps your fence and devours three months of your work in half an hour. <LINE> <LINE> Do not make snare traps if you do not know what you are doing, or you will just injure the animals and leave them suffering. If you depend on this food to keep from starving, defend it like you would defend your life. <LINE> <LINE> A barbed wire fence buried a hand-span into the ground (to keep out armadillos and woodchucks) helps. But the best night repellent for wildlife is the scent of a predator. Gather cut human hair, urine, and spread it around the perimeter of the garden. Deer smell the human predator and keep their distance from the greens.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Science of Crop Genetics <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Mr. Keating, author of the previous volume, offered a picturesque, painful, and medieval view of agriculture. He believes that sweat and brute force convince the earth to produce. It is a romantic fallacy. Sweat does not alter the cellular metabolism of a tomato plant; what alters it is molecular biology and soil chemistry. <LINE> <LINE> I am Doctor Aris Thorne, professor of Agronomy. Modern agriculture is not a battle against nature, it is the mathematical manipulation of it. In this volume, we will abandon manure superstitions and enter the fields of selective genetics, macronutrient balance, root osmosis, and yield maximization. Strength fails; science does not.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fungal Pathogens (At a Cellular Level) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The 'Devil's Water Fungi' described by Keating is an ignorant designation for pathogens of the genus Phytophthora or Pythium. They are Oomycetes that possess flagellated spores that literally 'swim' in standing soil water. <LINE> <LINE> Treatment is not done with mysticism, but by altering the environment to suppress the replication of the pathogen's cellular DNA. Spaced ventilation reduces relative humidity in the rhizosphere. The use of lactic acid-based mixtures (present in sour milk) rapidly alters the leaf surface pH, destabilizing the chitin membrane of the spores and causing their cellular lysis (bursting).
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Integrated Pest Management (IPM) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Applying neurotoxins like nicotine (suggested in volume three) kills aphids but also eradicates their natural predators. In scientific agronomy, we apply Integrated Pest Management (IPM). <LINE> <LINE> Ladybugs and lacewings are apex predators of the foliar ecosystem. A single adult ladybug can devour fifty aphids a day. If you apply broad-spectrum insecticides, you kill the ladybug, and the aphid population, which reproduces asexually (parthenogenesis) at an absurd speed, will return ten times worse the following week, now free from their natural predators.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Spacing Mathematics <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A plant is a photosynthetic machine competing for solar radiation and soil volume. If planting density is too high, leaves overlap (mutual shading), energy conversion efficiency drops, and roots secrete allelopathic substances to inhibit the neighbor's growth. <LINE> <LINE> Crop yield obeys a parabolic response curve. Planting ten cabbage seeds cramped in one square meter does not yield ten medium cabbages; it yields ten stunted cabbages with a total biomass lower than that of three cabbages planted at the exact spacing determined by agronomic equations.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Hormones and Ethylene Gas <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The moment of harvest triggers irreversible chemical reactions. Ethylene is the gaseous phytohormone responsible for ripening and senescence (aging). <LINE> <LINE> Tomatoes and apples are climacteric fruits; they continue to ripen and emit ethylene gas after being removed from the parent plant. If you wish to ripen a green tomato quickly, lock it in a closed container with a ripe apple. The accumulated ethylene gas will force the tomato's enzymes to convert starch into sugars (fructose) and chlorophyll into lycopene (red) in a matter of days. Chemistry works for you.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Senescence and Post-Harvest Preservation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Just as important as growth is the interruption of post-harvest cellular respiration. A harvested carrot continues 'breathing', consuming its own stored carbohydrates. <LINE> <LINE> Storage in cold cellars (cited in volume two) works based on Biochemical Thermodynamics. For every 10 degrees Celsius that the ambient temperature decreases, the enzymatic respiration rate of the carrot drops by half. By reducing the temperature close to the 4-degree mark (39°F), we paralyze the root's biological clock, preventing the texture from becoming flaccid and woody due to loss of turgor pressure in the cells.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> From Science to Bureaucracy <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> My contribution ceases here. You entered this volume getting your hands dirty with soil and left understanding biological equations, cellular nutrient balance, ripening gas behavior, and the dangers of unstable genetics. <LINE> <LINE> Agriculture is not a gift or an art; it is organic chemistry applied on a field scale. Optimize your processes and your crop will reach the mathematical limit of plant physiology. <LINE> <LINE> In the fifth and final volume of this collection, 'USDA Guide to Agricultural Output Maximization', laboratory science will give way to cold, bureaucratic government statistics. The Department of Agriculture will show how to expand this science into long-term planning and massive food security. Empirical knowledge is now yours. Do not fail biology.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Potential of Hydrogen (pH) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Throwing fertilizers onto soil without knowing its pH is the equivalent of trying to feed a patient whose mouth is sewn shut. Soil pH (Potential of Hydrogen) measures the acidity or alkalinity of the earth on a logarithmic scale from 0 to 14. <LINE> <LINE> Most vegetables (like potatoes and carrots) require a slightly acidic pH, between 6.0 and 6.8. If your soil is too acidic (pH 5.0), essential minerals like phosphorus undergo chemical precipitation and become physically 'locked' in the soil. The plant can be swimming in nutrients and yet starve to death because it cannot absorb them. Liming (adding limestone) corrects acidity and unlocks the pantry.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The N-P-K Matrix <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Plants operate under the dictates of three primary macronutrients: Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), and Potassium (K). Any farmer who ignores this matrix is gambling with luck. <LINE> <LINE> Nitrogen is the architect of leaves; it composes chlorophyll molecules. Without it, the plant turns yellow (chlorosis). Phosphorus is the engineer of root development and flowers; without it, carrots stunt and tomatoes bear no fruit. Potassium is the immune system; it regulates stomatal opening and cellular water flow. A fertilizer labeled as '10-10-10' provides a balanced ratio of this trinity.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Biological Nitrogen Fixation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The air we breathe is 78%% nitrogen, but plants cannot absorb it in gaseous form. They need it in the soil, in nitrate form. Volume Two mentioned companion planting with beans, calling it 'magic'. There is no magic, there is cell-level bacterial symbiosis. <LINE> <LINE> Legumes (beans and peas) form nodules on their roots that house bacteria of the genus Rhizobium. These bacteria break the triple bond of atmospheric nitrogen and convert it into ammonia usable by the plant. When the legume dies and the roots rot, this synthesized nitrogen is released into the soil for the next crop. It is a fertilizer factory at a cellular level.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Genetics and Artificial Selection <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your agronomic goal is the highest possible yield for the lowest energetic effort. This begins with rigorous genetic selection of your seeds (Cultivars). <LINE> <LINE> If one tomato plant produced ten tiny tomatoes and another produced five colossal tomatoes, from which do you save the seeds? The novice saves from the one that produced ten. The scientist saves from the colossal ones. We are selecting for genes of cellular hypertrophy and pathogen resistance. You act as the vector of artificial selection. Select for traits of drought resistance, early maturation, and thick cell walls.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cross-Pollination and Hybrids <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Pollen travels through the wind or via insects. If you plant two different varieties of corn close to each other, the wind will cross their genetics (Cross-Pollination). <LINE> <LINE> The seeds generated from this corn will be Hybrids (F1). Hybrid vigor frequently generates giant, resilient plants in the first generation. But beware: if you save the seeds from this hybrid and plant them the following year (F2), Mendelian segregation will cause the plants to grow completely disfigured, unstable, and with dismal yields. Commercial hybrid seeds cannot be replanted the following year with success.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Root Osmosis (Suffocation) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The rustic author of volume three warned against waterlogging the earth but did not explain the physics. Roots absorb water through Osmosis, moving from a less concentrated medium to a more concentrated one. <LINE> <LINE> But roots also need to breathe oxygen (cellular respiration) to generate the ATP molecule, which provides the energy to pull nutrients. If the soil becomes saturated with water (flooded), the soil macropores lose oxygen and the root enters hypoxia. Without oxygen, osmosis ceases. The lethal irony of agronomy: in a completely flooded field, the plant physically dies of thirst.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Carbon Chemistry (Compost) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Composting is not tossing trash in a corner and waiting. It is a rigorous stoichiometric equation between Carbon (C) and Nitrogen (N). The ideal ratio for thermophilic microorganisms to operate at maximum efficiency is 30:1. <LINE> <LINE> Thirty parts Carbon (dry leaves, sawdust, straw — brown matter) to one part Nitrogen (freshly cut grass, fruit scraps — green matter). If there is too much nitrogen, the pile will undergo anaerobic decomposition, emitting hydrogen sulfide (rotten egg smell). If there is too much carbon, the bacteria will run out of energy and the pile will not heat up enough to kill pathogens.
IGUI_BookFarming4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Photoperiodism and Seasons <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Plants do not have eyes, but they measure the duration of the night with frightening precision using chemical photoreceptors called phytochromes. This is Photoperiodism. <LINE> <LINE> 'Short-day plants' (which actually need long nights) only flower as autumn approaches. If you plant a cultivar genetically programmed for long nights in the middle of a Kentucky summer, it will grow vegetative foliage indefinitely but refuse to bear fruit. Knowledge of the local solar cycle aligned with seed genetics is what separates a zero yield from a record harvest.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Official USDA Guide <LINE> Crop Maximization <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This document is an official publication of the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), approved for civil distribution. The purpose of this manual is not recreational gardening, but the standardization of protocols to transform residential soil into contingency production units. <LINE> <LINE> In scenarios of prolonged shortages or disruptions in federal logistical chains, national security depends on the citizen's ability to generate and stockpile caloric surpluses. Agricultural efficiency is not a hobby; it is a civil duty. Failure to comply with the storage guidelines described herein may result in nutritional collapse during winter.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Botulinum Danger and Canning <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> USDA public health safety directives require that low-acid vegetable preservation be treated as a biohazard operation. <LINE> <LINE> The toxin produced by *Clostridium botulinum* is lethal and odorless. Non-acidic vegetables (such as beans and carrots) must NEVER be canned using a simple water bath. The use of certified pressure canners is mandatory to reach the 116 degrees Celsius (240°F) required by the government manual for spore sterilization. Home cans displaying bulging must be buried deeply, away from water sources.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Strategic Seed Bank <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In times of instability, agricultural input supply chains can be interrupted. It is mandatory that every residential planting unit maintain its own Seed Bank. <LINE> <LINE> Separate 10%% of your best harvest, not for consumption, but for genetic extraction. Extracted seeds must be meticulously dried, labeled by species and harvest year, and stockpiled in moisture-proof containers in the coldest, darkest environment of the facility. Independence from external supplies is the pillar of state self-sufficiency.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Contingency Cultivation (Winter) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the extreme frosts of Knox County approach, outdoor operations will cease. Food continuity will require the construction of cold Greenhouses or plastic tunnel structures. <LINE> <LINE> Hardy crops, such as winter cabbages and carrots, can survive light soil freezing, provided they are protected from aerial frost and freezing winds. Internal irrigation water must be severely rationed during winter months, as plants enter a semi-dormant state and excess water will cause instant root rot.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Decline Diagnosis <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Citizens must learn to recognize structural failures in their plots. Stagnant foliar growth and a yellowish color do not indicate a lack of water, but a critical Nitrogen deficiency in the soil. <LINE> <LINE> If tomato leaves acquire a purple or purplish coloration on the underside, the plot suffers from severe Phosphorus deficiency, frequently caused by planting in cold soils. The application of properly matured manure is the solution recommended by the Department to reverse these nutritional failures in the absence of regulated chemical fertilizers.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Acoustic Isolation and Concealment <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> During declared periods of civil emergency, the security of your harvest transcends protection from wildlife. Odors attract pests and visual signals attract unsolicited attention. <LINE> <LINE> Compost piles must be kept aerated to avoid perceptible hydrogen sulfide gases at a distance. Furthermore, it is recommended that intensive planting plots be positioned in areas that offer visual barriers against the property's external perimeter. Your caloric survival production is a highly valuable strategic asset and must be safeguarded against unauthorized appropriation.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of Protocol <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The USDA concludes its guidelines here. The citizen who has absorbed the regulations of this volume and the technical knowledge of the four previous manuals possesses the necessary tools not to perish in a supply collapse. <LINE> <LINE> We have instructed on logical planning, the physics of water, the relentless control of fungal infections, the mathematical laws of modern botany, and the strict rules of state conservation. The success of your crop now depends solely on rigorous adherence to these standardized procedures. Preserve your equipment, study your yields, and fulfill your duty. The United States Government thanks you for your cooperation.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Caloric Density Directive <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> USDA policy for subsistence agriculture prioritizes 'Caloric Yield per Square Meter'. Dietary diversity is secondary to survival viability. <LINE> <LINE> High-water content crops, such as lettuce and radishes, are classified as 'Low-Return Supplements'. Citizens must allocate a minimum of 70%% of their planting area to 'Base Crops', strictly Tubers (Potatoes) and Dense Brassicas (Cabbages). The potato offers the highest carbohydrate conversion rate, being the standard strategic food recommended by the federal government for winter stockpiling.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Standardization of Plots <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Disordered cultivation reduces yields and hinders the application of defensive treatments. The Department recommends the 'Standard Grid System'. <LINE> <LINE> Every planting plot must be plowed in straight lines, with millimeter spacing calculated for the passage of standard hand tools without root disturbance. Cabbage seeds must be planted with a government safety distance that prevents adult leaves from touching. Foliar contact between healthy plants creates humid microclimates, violating state pest prevention protocols.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Federal Irrigation Protocol <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Water is a resource that may undergo civil rationing during periods of crisis. Waste due to excessive irrigation is a serious operational failure. <LINE> <LINE> The USDA strongly discourages overhead foliar watering. Water must be applied exclusively to the soil, preferably during hours of lowest solar evaporation rates (before 06:00 or after 18:00). Excessive soil saturation (visible puddles) is the primary cause of root suffocation and early loss of carrot and potato crops, reducing national yield.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Phytosanitary Quarantine <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fungal pathogens, such as Powdery Mildew and watery spots, are classified as Level 1 Crop Threats. They are not local issues; they are cross-contamination risks. <LINE> <LINE> USDA protocol demands Zero Tolerance. If a plant exhibits more than 15%% foliar contamination by fungi, the citizen must not attempt to save it. Federal directive requires immediate eradication. The plant must be uprooted, removed from the planting zone, and incinerated. The underlying soil must be left fallow or treated before replanting.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Insect Erradication <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Sucking and chewing insects are vectors of crop failure. In the absence of pesticides regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), contingency solutions must be applied aggressively. <LINE> <LINE> Population control of aphids and caterpillars must not wait until damage is visible. Visual inspections beneath leaves must occur every 48 hours. The application of soap-based solutions and alkaline extracts must be done preventively and systemically. Allowing pests to multiply is considered negligence toward plot security.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Maturation Indices <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Harvesting a subsistence crop prematurely results in an unacceptable loss of stored calories. Delayed harvesting results in cellular degradation and a dramatic reduction in shelf life. <LINE> <LINE> Potatoes should only be harvested after the above-ground leaves yellow and die completely. This indicates the plant has finalized starch transport to the tuber and the skin has undergone the hardening necessary to survive cellar storage. Cabbage must be inspected manually; the head should yield only millimeters to firm thumb pressure.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Mandatory Triennial Rotation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Soil exhaustion is the primary cause of long-term agricultural failure. The USDA stipulates a strict three-year Crop Rotation protocol. <LINE> <LINE> Plots of land must be divided. Potatoes and tomatoes (Solanaceae) must never be planted in the same plot in consecutive years to prevent pathogenic accumulation. After a heavy harvest, the land must obligatorily be rotated with nitrogen-fixing legumes or left fallow and fertilized. Violation of this cycle will guarantee 50%% smaller crops in the second year.
IGUI_BookFarming5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dark Storage Directives <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Producing food is useless without approved long-term conservation techniques. Root storage must occur under strict physical parameters. <LINE> <LINE> Carrots and potatoes must be stockpiled in dark, subterranean enclosures (cellars), maintained at temperatures fluctuating between 2 and 5 degrees Celsius (35-41°F), with relative humidity near 90%%. Exposure of tubers to light induces the synthesis of solanine (green coloration), a natural glycoalkaloid highly toxic for human consumption. Green potatoes are unfit for consumption.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: Time is Blood <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you’re reading this in a comfortable living room, great. If you opened this book while someone is screaming and bleeding on your rug, close it and call 911. You’ve already lost. <LINE> <LINE> I am a trauma surgeon. I spend my Friday nights fixing the holes that stupid people punch into each other. This manual won't turn you into a doctor. The goal of First Aid isn't to heal anyone; the goal is to keep the death clock from hitting zero before the patient reaches my operating table. <LINE> <LINE> The human body is a pressurized meat sack filled with fragile tubes and vital fluids. Your only job at the accident scene is to keep the red liquid on the inside and air on the outside flowing into the lungs. Take a deep breath, ignore the screaming, and let’s get to work.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Broken Bones (Closed Fractures) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A closed fracture is when the bone breaks, but the skin remains intact. It is incredibly painful, the area swells quickly and turns purple, and the patient usually cannot move the limb. <LINE> <LEFT> Your goal is not to set the bone like a mystical healer. Your goal is Immobilization. If the person is moved with the bone loose, the sharp edge of the fracture inside can cut vital blood vessels and nerves, immensely worsening the situation. <LINE> <LEFT> Grab rigid splints (pieces of flat wood, tightly rolled magazines, or thick cardboard), place them on each side of the broken limb, and wrap firmly. The golden rule of immobilization is: always immobilize the joint ABOVE and the joint BELOW the fracture. If they broke their shin, the splint must immobilize the knee and the ankle.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Visible Terror (Compound Fractures) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the force of impact is too violent, the broken bone tears through the muscles and pierces the skin from the inside out, remaining exposed to the open air. This is a compound fracture, and it is a terrifying sight. <LINE> <LEFT> Forget everything you know. Never, and I repeat, NEVER try to push the dirty bone back inside the victim's arm or leg. This will not only tear more vessels, but it will introduce all the dirt and bacteria from the environment directly into the deep bloodstream and bone marrow. <LINE> <LEFT> Cover the exposed bone and the wound with damp gauze (to prevent the bone from drying out in the open air), contain the bleeding with bulky dressings around the area, and immobilize the limb in the exact bizarre position you found it in. The operating room is the only place where that bone goes back inside.
