IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Brute Wound Cleaning <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you slipped on concrete or fell on asphalt and opened up a gash full of sand and small rocks in your arm, that dirt is a fast track to deadly sepsis if not cleaned on day one. <LINE> <LEFT> Wash your hands before touching someone else’s wound. Then, irrigate the wound with liters of clean running water and neutral soap. Don’t be gentle. Mechanical cleaning—scrubbing and removing stones and embedded dirt with boiled tweezers—will hurt like hell for the patient. <LINE> <LEFT> They will scream and curse you, but the pain of the scrubbing today saves the arm from gangrene tomorrow. Isopropyl alcohol is only meant to clean the INTACT edges around the wound or to sterilize tools. Dumping alcohol or pure iodine straight into a deep cut kills healthy living tissue and delays healing absurdly.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Symptoms of Infection <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You closed the bandage with pretty dressings and went to sleep. Three days later, the cut looks weird. The infection has set in. You need to recognize the four horsemen of cellular death. <LINE> <LEFT> 1. Heat: The wound site radiates abnormal heat, much warmer than the rest of the body. <LINE> 2. Redness: A strong, irritated redness spreads far beyond the edges of the cut. If you see red lines creeping up the arm's vein, the infection has hit the bloodstream. This is lethal. <LINE> 3. Edema: A hardened, throbbing, and tense swelling. <LINE> 4. Purulent Discharge: Pus. The war of defense cells forming that yellowish, stinking liquid. If you have these four signs in the camp, you don’t need more dressings; you need oral systemic antibiotics urgently.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cruel Triage <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In an accident with multiple victims, medicine abandons compassion and embraces cold math. This is Triage. You cannot save everyone, and a novice’s worst mistake is wasting their precious golden hour on the person screaming the loudest or crying desperately. <LINE> <LEFT> Anyone with the breath and strength to scream for help is breathing well and is not at immediate risk of death. Your target should be the silence. <LINE> <LEFT> Go first to the victims who are quiet, pale, unconscious, or have arterial bleeding gushing. We save lives by assessing who is seconds away from death and abandoning those who have already died. It is a merciless divine judgment, but if you cannot have the cold blood to prioritize the pulse and not the tear, you will let saveable people die.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Shift Report <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your first shift with me in the ER has ended. You learned not to be the movie hero who paralyzes a patient by dragging them, you understood the physics of direct pressure on bleeding, the dangers of the old-school tourniquet, and why butter on a burn is profound idiocy. <LINE> <LEFT> Keep the ABC rule, hypovolemic shock elevation, and the puritanical cleaning of embedded dirt in your head. Street medicine is violent, dirty, and ungrateful, but it follows rigid chemical logic. <LINE> <LEFT> In Volume Two, we will go deeper into anatomy. We’ll talk about hidden head trauma, poisoning, how to clear blocked airways, infectious bites, and how to sew up torn flesh with basic sutures when tape and bandages can no longer handle the heavy lifting. Wash the blood off your hands and come back tomorrow.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rule Zero: Do No Further Harm <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first rule of emergency medicine is the Hippocratic Oath: 'Primum non nocere' (First, do no harm). But on the street, that translates to: 'Don't be a stupid hero.' <LINE> <LINE> If you find someone injured inside a smoking car and try to rip them out by their arms like a ragdoll, you will likely shatter their spinal cord and leave them quadriplegic for the rest of their life. <LINE> <LINE> Unless the car is literally on fire or the person is about to drown, you DO NOT move a trauma victim. You stabilize them where they are. The impulsive Hollywood heroics of carrying people in your arms only serve to worsen hemorrhages and destroy fractured spines.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> External Hemorrhage (Direct Pressure) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> An adult human has about five liters of blood. If they lose two liters quickly, the engine shuts off. Bleeding is the fastest killer you will face. <LINE> <LINE> The solution for ninety percent of bleeding isn't magic, it’s pure physics: Direct Pressure. If there’s a hole leaking, plug the hole with force. Grab the cleanest gauze you have (or the cleanest shirt, if you have no choice), place it over the wound, and push down with your body weight. <LINE> <LINE> Don't keep lifting the cloth every ten seconds to 'see if it stopped bleeding.' Blood needs time and stagnation to coagulate and create a natural plug. If the blood soaks through the first cloth, don't remove it; place another cloth on top and press harder. Ripping off the old cloth destroys the clot the body was trying to form.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Torniquet Taboo <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If the main artery of the leg or arm is cut, blood won't ooze; it will spray in bright red rhythmic jets, synced with the heartbeat. Direct pressure won't hold that. <LINE> <LINE> This is where you use the Tourniquet. But pay attention: using a tourniquet is making the conscious decision to sacrifice the limb to save the life. If you tie a belt, rope, or strap three fingers above the wound and tighten it using a windlass bar until the blood stops, you have cut off 100%% of the circulation. <LINE> <LINE> The tissue below the tourniquet will start dying in a few hours from lack of oxygen. You use this for traumatic amputation or uncontrollable arterial bleeding. Put the tourniquet on? Write the exact time on the patient's forehead with a pen. The surgeon will need that info.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Silent Killer (Hypovolemic Shock) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You managed to stop the arm bleeding. The patient is no longer losing blood, but suddenly their skin goes pale as wax, lips turn blue, they start breaking out in a cold sweat, shivering, and their pulse is rapid and weak. <LINE> <LINE> The bleeding stopped, but they are dying right in front of you. This is Hypovolemic Shock. <LINE> <LINE> They lost too much blood and now the pump (heart) doesn’t have enough fluid to push oxygen to the brain. Lay them on the floor, elevate their legs about a foot (so gravity dumps the remaining blood from the legs to vital organs), and cover them with thick blankets. A body in shock loses the ability to regulate its own temperature. Warm the victim, or their heart will stop from internal cold.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The ABC Rule (Airway) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the emergency room, we don’t waste time on details before checking the holy trinity of life: A, B, and C. Airway, Breathing, and Circulation. <LINE> <LINE> If the victim is unconscious and lying on their back, their own tongue relaxes, falls back, and blocks the throat. They will suffocate on their own anatomy. Bring your ear close to their face and look at their chest. Do you hear air? Does the chest rise? <LINE> <LINE> If not, kneel beside them, place one hand on their forehead and two fingers of the other hand under their chin. Tilt their head back slightly and lift the chin. This stretches the trachea and lifts the tongue, opening the air passage. Often, this incredibly simple movement is enough for the patient to start breathing on their own again with a deep gasp.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Penetrating Wounds (The Cork Principle) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A bar fight gets out of hand or a carpentry accident happens, and you come across a man with a knife, a screwdriver, or a thick piece of glass stuck in his abdomen. Human instinct screams for you to rip the object out. NEVER do this. <LINE> <LINE> The blade or glass that tore the blood vessels inside is acting exactly like a cork in a wine bottle. As long as the object is there, it is blocking massive internal hemorrhaging. <LINE> <LINE> If you pull the knife, you remove the plug, and the patient will bleed to death inside their abdominal cavity in minutes. Your job is to grab bulky gauze, make a mound around the object to immobilize it, and secure everything with tape so the blade doesn’t move and cut anything else inside.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Thermal Burns (The Butter Myth) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Folk remedies have been driving me insane for decades. Every time someone arrives in the ER with a second-degree burn covered in butter, toothpaste, coffee grounds, or egg whites, I lose a year of my life. <LINE> <LINE> These filthy products seal the pores and trap the searing heat inside the flesh, cooking deep tissues, while guaranteeing a horrific infection the next day. <LINE> <LEFT> If there is a thermal burn from fire, hot metal, or boiling liquid, the only emergency treatment is water. Clean, running water at room temperature for at least fifteen to twenty minutes to dissipate the cellular heat. Never use ice, as the thermal shock from the ice causes frostbite that further destroys the already damaged cells. Water. Only water.
IGUI_BookFirstAid1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Curse of Blisters <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> After a second-degree burn, the skin will lift and form large blisters filled with a clear liquid (plasma). The temptation to grab a needle and pop the blister to 'relieve the pressure' is huge. Resist it. <LINE> <LEFT> That gross blister is a perfect, sterile dressing that your own body created to protect the raw, destroyed tissue underneath. The blister skin is an impenetrable barrier against airborne bacteria. <LINE> <LEFT> If you pop the blister, you expose wet, raw flesh to millions of pathogens. You’ve just turned a burn that would heal on its own in ten days into a purulent infection that will require heavy antibiotics. Cover the area loosely with dry, sterile gauze and let nature do its job.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: The Invisible Killer <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In Volume One, we dealt with obvious holes and blood on the floor. Any idiot notices when an arm is cut. The real test in trauma medicine isn't what you see bleeding on the sidewalk; it’s what’s bleeding in the dark, inside the patient’s body. <LINE> <LEFT> From now on, we will look for symptoms, not just wounds. The human body is a sealed engine. When the parts break inside, it doesn’t light up a red warning lamp on the dash. It gives you small neurological signs, color changes, and swelling before it shuts down forever. <LINE> <LEFT> We will cover head trauma, mechanical respiratory failure, poisoning, and the immense danger of sewing up a dirty wound. Put on your latex gloves. Class is about to begin.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Eye Injuries (Sympathetic Reflex) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A carpenter suffers an accident and a long nail or wood splinter flies and stabs his eyeball. The scene is grotesque. His first instinct is to try to rip it out. Tie his hands if necessary, but don’t let him touch the eye. <LINE> <LEFT> The vitreous liquid inside the eye leaks if the plug (the nail) is removed, and he will go blind instantly. Grab a paper or styrofoam cup, cut off the base, place it over the injured eye as a shield to protect the object, and tape it down. <LINE> <LEFT> Now, the golden rule few know: you MUST also bandage the healthy eye. Human eyes possess 'sympathetic movement.' If the healthy eye moves to look around, the stabbed eye will try to make the same movement automatically, tearing the retina against the nail and destroying vision permanently.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sutures (Stitching Flesh) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Pop culture glorified the idea of dumping whiskey into a dirty cut and stitching the skin however you like with fishing line and a straight sewing needle. Doing that is signing a warrant for amputation. <LINE> <LEFT> We stitch clean cuts, like those made by scalpels or recent clean glass. If the wound has crushed edges, happened in a dirty environment (like a fall in the mud), or is more than six hours old, IT SHOULD NOT BE STITCHED CLOSED. <LINE> <LEFT> If you close and stitch a dirty wound and seal the skin with tape and stitches, anaerobic bacteria will get trapped in a dark, warm environment without oxygen. In two days, the leg will swell to double its size, smelling of dead meat, taken over by deep gangrene. Clean it, pack it with damp sterile gauze, and leave the cut open.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Surgeon’s Knot (Simple Stitch) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If the cut is perfectly clean and you need to close it with an emergency surgical kit (which uses curved needles, not straight ones), you will apply the Simple Interrupted Stitch. <LINE> <LEFT> Hold the curved needle with fine pliers (needle holder). Enter with the needle about five millimeters from the edge of the cut at a ninety-degree angle, and exit five millimeters from the other edge. <LINE> <LEFT> Tension is the secret. You aren’t tying a tight shoelace. Pull the thread only until the two skin edges touch gently. If you tighten the knot until you strangle the skin and turn it white, blood won't reach the scar, dead skin will rip the stitches in two days, and the wound will open up much worse than before.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Crush Syndrome <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A mechanic drops an engine on their leg and gets trapped. They have no visible wounds or major bleeding. They lie there, leg crushed under six hundred pounds for three hours, conscious, until you manage to lift the part. <LINE> <LEFT> As soon as you move the engine and blood starts circulating in their leg again, ten minutes later, their heart suddenly stops and they die smiling. What killed them wasn't the impact; it was the Rescue. <LINE> <LEFT> Long-term pressure kills the leg muscle, which disintegrates and releases myoglobin and lethal levels of potassium into the stagnant blood pool of the limb. When you remove the weight suddenly, the dam of poison runs straight to the heart, causing immediate cardiac arrest. In long-term limb crushing, a prophylactic tourniquet BEFORE releasing the weight is essential.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Traumatic Amputation and Ice <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A chainsaw slips or a heavy plate falls. The patient just lost three fingers in the shop. After putting the tourniquet on the bleeding stump, you need to handle the severed parts if you want me to stitch them back on. <LINE> <LEFT> People usually throw severed fingers straight into a pot or plastic bag full of ice. Human flesh freezes, microscopic cells burst from ice expansion, and the tissue turns into a piece of dead ice useless for microsurgery. <LINE> <LEFT> The real protocol is: grab the clean fingers, wrap them in lightly damp gauze, place them inside a sealed plastic bag (no air and no direct contact with water), and place THIS closed plastic bag inside another container holding water and ice. You want the cold, not the water. You want to cool, not freeze.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of Shift <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your second shift has ended. If you paid attention, you realized that trauma medicine is a tense biological chess match. You learned not to underestimate the danger of the closed skull, how to break ribs to save the brain, how to disarm a pressure bomb inside the chest using a candy wrapper, and that sewing dirty flesh is indirect murder. <LINE> <LEFT> The body tries to keep you alive at all costs, but it isn’t very smart at doing it. In the ER, we guide this blind mechanism. <LINE> <LEFT> In Volume Three, we will abandon the clean environment of the city asphalt. We’ll talk about real, brutal medicine, isolated hunting camps, and the jungle. Severe hypothermia, compound fractures from trail accidents, infections caused by stagnant water, the hell of friction burns, and how to improvise everything when the ER is a three-day hike away. Wash the equipment and get some rest.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Lucid Interval (Head Trauma) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A guy in a bar fight takes a blow to the side of the head with a baseball bat. He falls, blacks out for a minute, then wakes up. He stands up, says he’s perfectly fine, refuses the hospital, and goes home to sleep. He dies in his own bed four hours later. <LINE> <LEFT> This is what we call an Epidural Hematoma, famous for the 'Lucid Interval.' The blow cracked the temporal bone and ruptured an artery beneath the skull. The brain is a closed box of rigid bone. There is nowhere for the blood to leak. <LINE> <LEFT> The blood starts accumulating slowly, pushing and crushing the brain tissue. The patient feels great until the pressure crushes the brain’s respiratory center. Never let someone who suffered strong head trauma go to sleep without rigorous medical observation.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Windows to the Brain (Pupils) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don’t have an X-ray machine in the middle of the street. To know if someone’s brain is being crushed by internal bleeding, you need to look into the victim’s eyes. Pupils are connected directly to the cranial nerves. <LINE> <LEFT> Take a small flashlight and shine the light into the patient’s eyes. Both pupils (the black balls) should shrink quickly and at the same time. <LINE> <LEFT> If one pupil is tiny and the other is huge and dilated, and doesn't react to light, the diagnosis is done: the brain is suffering from herniation. It is being pushed down by the blood. This patient’s life is now measured in minutes, not hours. Rush them to the hospital and prepare for the worst.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> CPR and Broken Ribs <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Television has been lying to you your whole life. In medical shows, actors perform CPR with the strength of someone petting a kitten, and the patient wakes up coughing. In real life, Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) is an act of brutal violence against the chest. <LINE> <LEFT> If the heart has stopped, the patient is already dead. You are acting as an external mechanical pump, crushing the heart between the chest bone and the spine to force blood up to the brain. <LINE> <LEFT> For an adult, you need to sink the chest at least five centimeters. One hundred to one hundred and twenty times per minute. It’s exhausting. And if you’re doing it right, you WILL hear and feel the patient’s ribs crack and break under your hands. Ignore the breaking bones. A broken rib heals; brain death does not.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Choking: The Silent Terror <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A real choking victim doesn't cough and doesn’t make noise. They grab their own throat with wide eyes, face turning red and then blue, in pure panic, while oxygen levels plummet. If they are coughing or speaking, the passage isn't totally blocked. Do not interfere; encourage the coughing. <LINE> <LEFT> If the blockage is total, apply the Heimlich Maneuver. Stand behind them, make a fist with one hand, place two fingers above the navel, grab the fist with the other hand, and deliver violent tugs INWARD and UPWARD, in a 'J' motion. <LINE> <LEFT> You are using the residual air left in the lungs like a syringe plunger, trying to expel the piece of meat wedged in the trachea by pure pneumatic pressure. Don’t play around with this, or you’ll rupture a friend’s internal organs.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Bites (Human Poison) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When dogs get loose and attack a child, people run to the hospital fearing rabies. But dogs, in most cases, have mouths cleaner than ours. The true infectious terror of the ER is the human bite. <LINE> <LEFT> In street fights, it’s common for someone to punch the other's mouth and cut their knuckles on the opponent’s teeth. The human mouth is a rotten swamp of deadly aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. <LINE> <LEFT> A human bite that breaks the skin has an almost guaranteed rate of infection and necrosis if it isn't opened, flushed with liters and liters of saline solution, and treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour. Never close a human bite with stitches. It must heal open, from the bottom up.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Sucking Chest Wound <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You found a man with a deep stab wound in his chest. He is breathing, but air isn’t entering only through his nose. You hear a terrifying 'sucking' noise and bloody foam bubbling directly from the hole in the chest with every breath. <LINE> <LEFT> This is an Open Pneumothorax. Lungs aren’t magic balloons; they inflate because the diaphragm creates a vacuum (negative pressure) in the chest. The knife wound breached the vacuum. Air now enters through the hole in the chest, crushing the lung until it shrivels like a raisin. <LINE> <LEFT> Don’t use standard gauze; air will pass through it. You need an occlusive dressing. Grab a piece of thick plastic (a bandage package or a credit card) and tape the hole to seal the vacuum and force air back to entering only through the mouth.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Three-Sided Valve <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Taping the chest hole with plastic is vital, but if the lung is punctured from within, air will leak from the lung into the thoracic cavity, accumulating pressure until it crushes the heart (Tension Pneumothorax). <LINE> <LEFT> To avoid this on the street, create a makeshift valve. Grab your square of thick plastic, place it over the chest hole, and tape it with adhesive tape on only THREE of the four sides. Leave the bottom part untaped. <LINE> <LEFT> This creates a one-way escape valve. When the patient inhales, the plastic is sucked against the skin, stopping outside air from entering. When they exhale, the internal pressure pushes the trapped air out through the loose edge, relieving the chest and allowing the lung to start working again.
IGUI_BookFirstAid2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Milk Myth (Poisoning) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> 1950s grandmothers have been trying to drive me crazy for decades. Every time someone arrives in the ER after swallowing poison or cleaning products, and you forced them to drink milk or stuck your finger down their throat to make them vomit—forget it, unless you want to face manslaughter charges. <LINE> <LEFT> If the child drank bleach, caustic soda, or battery acid, the product burned and destroyed the esophagus on the way down. If you force them to vomit, the acid will come back up and burn the entire tube a second time, causing irreversible internal hemorrhaging, plus the risk of them aspirating the vomit into the lungs and choking on acid. <LINE> <LEFT> For ingestion of corrosive chemicals, do not induce vomiting. Take the poison's label to the hospital immediately. For drug overdoses, the only real magic we have in the ER is pushing Activated Charcoal into the stomach, which absorbs toxins like a black sponge.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: The Savage Void <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first two volumes, we worked under the premise that the hospital exists. You stabilized the patient, put them in the back of a truck, and I took control in the operating room. But what happens when you’re at a hunting camp, three days' walk from the nearest highway? <LINE> <LEFT> Wilderness Medicine is a completely different beast. Here, you aren't the temporary paramedic; you are the entire hospital. And the environment around you is actively trying to murder your patient. <LINE> <LEFT> We will deal with absolute temperature extremes, trail accidents, severe infections, and the crushing truth about what isolation does to human fragility. Forget the clean floor. The ground is now mud, and the clock is running against you.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Tourniquet Clock <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first book, I taught you to note the time on the patient's forehead when applying a tourniquet. But in the city, the hospital is half an hour away. In the forest, it might be two days. <LINE> <LEFT> Science dictates that a strangled limb begins to suffer irreversible nerve and muscle damage at the four-to-six-hour mark without oxygen. <LINE> <LEFT> If you pass six hours of hiking, the leg tissues below the tourniquet will be completely dead and releasing acidic toxins. If you release the tourniquet at that moment thinking you’re helping, the poisoned blood will surge up and stop their heart instantly (Crush/Reperfusion Syndrome). Past six hours? The tourniquet stays tight until you reach me, and I will amputate the leg in the operating room. They survive.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Foul Wounds (Maggot Therapy) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Gross content alert, but you’re reading this to survive, not to feel good. You’re wounded, the bandage fell off three days ago, and the hole in your calf has turned black with gangrene and is putrid. The infection will climb into your blood and kill you of sepsis by tomorrow morning if the rotted tissue isn't removed. <LINE> <LEFT> If you don’t have a scalpel and don’t have the stomach to cut your own black flesh cold, nature has a gross surgeon. Blowflies (the green ones). <LINE> <LEFT> If they land on the gangrene, they will lay eggs. The maggots will hatch in a day. The biological magic? The maggots secrete enzymes that dissolve ONLY the rotted flesh and dangerous bacteria, leaving the pink, healthy tissue perfectly intact. Let them eat the dead tissue for two days, wash the wound brutally with water to remove the insects, and close the now-clean hole.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Death Jump (Pelvic Trauma) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A hunter falls from a tree, lands hard on their feet, and falls to the side howling in hip pain. The Pelvis is the thickest bone ring in your body. When it breaks, it opens like a book. And the great danger of pelvic fractures is the internal void they create. <LINE> <LEFT> Massive arteries run inside the pelvic bone. If the bone cracks and opens, these arteries rupture, and the pelvic cavity has enough room to swallow nearly three liters of blood without a single drop leaving the body. The patient will empty out from the inside and die on the spot. <LINE> <LEFT> You must act in the first minute. Grab a folded sheet or a wide belt, pass it around their hips (at the level of the large lateral bone, not the belly), and tighten it until it almost chokes them, like a mechanical bear hug, tying it tightly to close the pelvis back up. This stops the hidden bleeding.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The False Remedy (Alcohol) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> For the love of everything logical and sacred, if someone gets hurt or is freezing to death in the middle of nowhere, don’t give the wretch a bottle of whiskey. High-proof alcohol in camps is the worst drug you can use to 'relieve pain.' <LINE> <LEFT> First, alcohol is a vasodilator. It expands blood vessels on the skin surface, making the patient sweat and feel 'warm,' while they are actually releasing all the residual core heat into the cold atmosphere. It accelerates death by hypothermia. <LINE> <LEFT> Second, it thins the blood. If the patient has an invisible head concussion or a small internal cut bleeding slowly, alcohol will destroy natural clotting and force the wound to gush until it kills them. Drink after you are safe, not in the middle of the disaster.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Futility of CPR in Nature <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I taught you CPR in the last volume because I operated under the principle that the ambulance would arrive in twenty minutes and I would use an electric defibrillator (shock) and epinephrine on the patient. <LINE> <LEFT> Here is the cruelty of wilderness medicine. CPR doesn’t cure the heart; it only circulates a little temporary oxygen to buy time until the defibrillator arrives. <LINE> <LEFT> If a trail companion drops dead from a fulminant heart attack or total freezing, and you are a twelve-hour hike from the nearest road, CPR is useless. You will massage their chest for four hours in the middle of a blizzard, destroy your own body through physical exhaustion, they won’t come back, and then you will both die in the forest. Recognizing that rescue is geographically impossible and stopping the miracle attempt is the darkest, most necessary decision of extreme survival.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Jungle Shift End <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I didn’t mean to scare you, but I wanted to destroy your park-weekend illusions. Nature is apathetic to your screams, and the human body breaks fast when far from the asphalt. <LINE> <LEFT> Now you understand the brutal physics of hypothermia and why you shouldn’t suck on rattlesnake bites. You know what a real improvised stretcher is and learned to respect and even use the grossest biology (like maggot therapy) to beat rotted infections when the medicine cabinet goes empty. <LINE> <LEFT> In Volume Four, we will return to microscopic and biological war. You will abandon broken bones and bites to deal with severe diseases, brutal contamination, generalized infections (Sepsis), parasitism, asphyxia, and the over-the-counter pharmacology needed to keep a body functioning. Clean your canteen and see you in the next class.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cold Death (Hypothermia) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hypothermia isn't just 'feeling very cold.' It’s your biological core flipping off the power switches to protect the heart. When you fall into an icy river or get caught in a blizzard without gear, death comes in stages. <LINE> <LEFT> The first stage is uncontrollable shivering. It’s the body using muscles to generate friction and heat. The real danger starts at stage two: the patient stops shivering. If they are wet in the ice and suddenly say they 'stopped feeling cold' and the shaking has ceased, they haven't gotten better. Their body has simply given up. <LINE> <LEFT> Lethargy sets in, speech slurs like a drunk's, and they feel an uncontrollable urge to sleep. If they close their eyes in the snow, their heart will fibrillate in fifteen minutes. Keep them awake with kicks if you have to.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Human Cocoon <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you save someone in the severe stage of hypothermia? Packing them in cold blankets does nothing. A body in severe hypothermia has lost the ability to generate its own heat; placing a blanket over them is like putting a coat on a block of ice. The ice won’t warm up. <LINE> <LEFT> You need to transfer active external heat. Rip the wet clothes off the victim (they suck temperature twenty times faster than air). <LINE> <LEFT> Grab your thickest sleeping bag, get inside it naked, and pull the naked patient in with you. Hug them. Your body heat (skin-on-skin) is the furnace they need to reactivate their heart. Don’t have false modesty; social discomfort is preferable to burying a friend stiff as a board the next morning.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Internal Fire (Heatstroke) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The opposite of hypothermia is Heatstroke. If you force a march on a 105-degree day with extreme humidity and zero hydration, your thermostat breaks. <LINE> <LEFT> The body tries to cool itself by sweating. When the water runs out, the sweating stops. The fatal symptom of severe heatstroke is red, dry, boiling skin. If the patient is in the scorching sun, disoriented, and NOT sweating a drop, their brain is literally cooking inside their own skull. Neurological proteins begin to unravel. <LINE> <LEFT> Do not give ice water in large gulps, or they will vomit and choke. Get them immediately into the thickest shade, throw cool water on their armpits, groin, and neck (where the large arteries pass), and fan them frantically. The goal is to bring the core below 102 degrees before brain damage becomes permanent.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Road Rash <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You fall off your bike on a gravel road or roll down a hill in rocky terrain. Friction rips your skin off and injects thousands of tiny grains of sand, asphalt, and red dirt directly into your dermis, mixed with live blood. <LINE> <LEFT> This is severe abrasion. The pain is excruciating because hundreds of nerve endings have been sanded down and left exposed to the wind. <LINE> <LEFT> Treatment will require you to be cruel. If you don’t get every micro-piece of stone out of their flesh in the first few hours, the skin will heal over the asphalt, causing chronic infections and the famous 'Traumatic Tattoo.' You will need a sterile soft brush, neutral soap, and a lot of willpower to scrub the open-flesh wounds of your friend while they cry in pain.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dislocations (Dislocated Shoulder) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hunting accidents or tree falls often rip the humerus out of the shoulder socket. It’s a dislocation. The patient's arm hangs in an unnatural position and the pain locks their breathing. <LINE> <LEFT> Movies love to show a guy slamming their shoulder into a wall to 'pop it back in.' Doing that in real life will crush the axillary artery and nerves, paralyzing their arm forever. The secret to reduction isn't violence; it’s Muscle Exhaustion. <LINE> <LEFT> Lay the patient face down on a rock or high log, with the dislocated arm hanging into the void, loose downwards. Tie a ten-pound weight to their wrist and wait. It may take twenty minutes. The locked muscles around the shoulder will tire of holding the weight, they will relax involuntarily, and the bone head will slide smoothly back into the socket with a dull thud.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Snakebite Myth <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You step on a rattlesnake and it buries its fangs in your leg. Forget everything the Western movies taught you. <LINE> <LEFT> NEVER grab a knife to make an 'X' cut over the bite, and JAMAIS touch your mouth to the wound to try and 'suck the venom' out. Doing this only mixes the bacteria from your mouth with the snake’s hemotoxins, plus you’ll poison yourself if you have a cold sore or a cavity in your gums. And NEVER use an elastic tourniquet for the bite; concentrating the hemotoxic venom in a single spot will guarantee the leg amputates from necrosis. <LINE> <LEFT> What do you do? Keep the patient absolutely calm (a racing heart spreads venom faster), wash the wound, remove rings and boots (because the leg will swell like a balloon), and walk slowly to seek antivenom. Calmness wins hours.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Brutal Transport (Improvised Stretchers) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Carrying an unconscious 180-pound person on your shoulders for ten kilometers of rough trail is the fastest way to get two people to collapse. If the patient cannot walk, you need a stretcher. <LINE> <LEFT> A genius improvised stretcher requires only two thick wooden poles (about two meters long) and two or three heavy jackets (or heavy-duty trash bags). <LINE> <LEFT> Zip up the jackets, turn them inside out, thread the poles through the sleeves, and pull taut. The fabric will create a firm, safe bed in the middle. If you don’t have coats, wrap a thick rope from end to end on the poles like a tight spider web. If the victim has a suspected spine injury, ignore all of this: you tie their body to the hardest, straightest plank you can rip off an old cabin.
IGUI_BookFirstAid3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Water That Kills (Dysentery) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Isolation plays cruel tricks. A crystal-clear mountain stream looks safe, but if there’s a dead animal rotting two hundred yards upstream, you won’t see it. You drink the fresh water and, in two days, Giardia or Cholera takes control of your bowels. <LINE> <LEFT> Acute infectious diarrhea in the middle of the woods is lethal. You lose fluid and electrolytes so fast that you go into hypovolemic shock from dehydration within forty-eight hours. <LINE> <LEFT> If someone is expelling water non-stop, it’s useless to give them pure canteen water; it will go straight through. You need Oral Rehydration Salts. One liter of boiled water, a heaping handful (six teaspoons) of sugar, and a pinch (half a teaspoon) of salt. That’s what forces the intestinal wall to retain moisture and keeps the kidneys working.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: The Microscopic War <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you survived the first three manuals, it means you learned how to stitch your own skin, didn't freeze to death, and managed to stop a hemorrhage. But don’t celebrate yet. The bear or the axe that cut you yesterday was just the first wave of attack. <LINE> <LEFT> The real war begins the next day, and the enemy is invisible. Human skin is a castle wall. When you suffer a deep cut on a hunting trail, the wall falls, and millions of starving bacteria living in the dirt, under your nails, and in the air march into your bloodstream. <LINE> <LEFT> This volume is about enemy biology. Fulminant infections, water parasites, allergic shocks, and how to use the right medications without poisoning yourself. Welcome to the world of bacteria. They have much more patience than you.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Double-Edged Knife (Painkillers) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your over-the-counter medicine cabinet is Russian Roulette if you don't know the chemical difference between the little white plastic bottles. <LINE> <LEFT> Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) is a great painkiller and fever reducer, but it won't take away the inflammation of a sprained ankle. If you take several pills at once, it won't cure you faster; it will only melt your liver and you will die of acute liver failure, slowly, with yellow skin. <LINE> <LEFT> Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic Acid) relieves pain and lowers inflammation. But it has a serious side effect: it thins the blood (anti-platelet). If someone fell from a tree, suffered head trauma, or has any kind of deep bleeding, and you give them two aspirins to 'ease the fall pain,' you’ve just guaranteed their blood won’t clot, accelerating internal bleeding and death.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sterilization vs. Disinfection <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Words matter. Washing a surgical clamp with soap or tossing a bottle of alcohol on it is DISINFECTION. That reduces the number of bacteria to tolerable levels for daily life. But if you are going to sink that clamp into someone's flesh to pull out a splinter or bullet, it needs STERILIZATION. <LINE> <LEFT> Sterilization means total microscopic annihilation. No living cell survives. Common alcohol doesn't kill armored bacterial spores. <LINE> <LEFT> In a survival hunting camp, you have two options for hard metal tools: The first is Boiling, keeping the scissors rolling in the pot with boiling water for thirty minutes to kill almost everything. The second, and most absolute, is Flame. Run the tips of the pure steel tools directly through the blue fire of the torch or camp stove until the metal slightly changes color from the heat. Fire is purification. Let them cool in the air without touching anything before using.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Trench Foot (Moisture Rot) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don’t need to get shot to lose your leg in nature; you just need to be dumb enough to stay in boots soaked by rain for three days straight in the autumn chill. <LINE> <LEFT> This causes Trench Foot, a terror discovered in World War I. When skin is damp and occluded by socks for days while rubbing against the boot, and cold temperature constricts vessels, blood stops nourishing the tissue. The skin dies drowned in its own sweat and the icy rain water. <LINE> <LEFT> The foot turns completely white, wrinkled, numb, gives off a disgusting smell of maceration, and then starts to rot in black gangrene patches on the sole and toes. The amputator will be needed. Keeping boots waterproofed and swapping wet socks for dry ones every night (even if you have to sleep hugging the damp socks to dry them with your core heat) is a non-negotiable medical survival doctrine.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Activated Charcoal (The Eraser) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If someone swallowed a giant portion of poisonous wild mushrooms or a whole box of antidepressants in the camp tent, you should not provoke them to vomit if you don’t know exactly what went down. And in the middle of nowhere, there are no stomach-pump machines. <LINE> <LEFT> The only tool in your kit to fight a recent stomach overdose is medical Activated Charcoal powder. It’s not the coal from your brick grill; it’s lab-grade coal treated with high-temperature gas that makes it microscopically porous like a colossal sponge. <LINE> <LEFT> You mix dozens of grams of that hideous black powder with water and force the patient to swallow that sludge. The charcoal travels through the stomach and the microscopic pores suck up and trap the toxins and poisons before the intestine can absorb them into the blood. The poison is neutralized physically and exits the back door the next day.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Medicine Expiration (The Dirty Secret) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Society collapsed due to a massive flood, rescue hasn’t come in weeks, and the date printed on the camp medicine box expired two years ago. Do you throw it away and die of infection? Don’t be soft. <LINE> <LEFT> The US military proved that the vast, overwhelming majority of solid medicines (pills and dry capsules) stored in cool, sun-free, and moisture-free places retain 90%% of their original potency for five, sometimes fifteen years after the damned label date. The dates are, often, bureaucratic guarantees from the industry. <LINE> <LEFT> The old pill might take a little longer to kick in, but it still works. The ONLY major, vital exceptions to this rule are: Nitroglycerin, Epinephrine, liquid Insulin (hormones rot), and—mark this—TETRACYCLINE. Expired tetracycline-class antibiotics degrade and turn into a poison that will destroy your kidneys permanently. Throw expired tetracycline into the fire.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Last Frontier of Flesh <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We close the penultimate manual of your hellish residency. You are no longer the wimp who cries at a cut. You understood that bacteria are logical enemies and that pharmacy chemistry does not allow for foolish improvisation or grandma’s intuitions. You master chemistry and infection. <LINE> <LEFT> So far, we’ve treated the patient by stabilizing leaks or curing diseases with meds. But sometimes, tissue dies. Sometimes, metal gets in and won't come out. Sometimes, the only way to save the forest is by cutting and burning the rotted tree. <LINE> <LEFT> In the fifth and final Volume, you will learn to invade flesh. These will be lessons on extreme minor field surgery, improvised anesthesia, removing projectiles and foreign bodies deeply embedded, and the dark, irreversible decision of trauma amputations to save the rest of a life. Put away the pills, sharpen the pure carbon steel scalpels, and prepare your stomach for the sight of exposed flesh.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Red Line (Sepsis) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You got a silly cut on your arm while fixing a fence. You ignored it and didn't wash it. Three days later, the arm is hot and throbbing. And then, you notice a thin, irritated red line climbing up your skin, coming out of the cut toward your armpit or chest. <LINE> <LEFT> That is not an allergic irritation; that is Death taking the elevator. The bacteria defeated your local immune system, invaded the lymph vessels, and is now traveling straight into your central bloodstream and your heart. This is the onset of Sepsis. <LINE> <LEFT> When the infection hits the blood, it spreads to every organ at once. The patient will have an extremely high fever, violent shivering, and mental confusion. If you see the 'red line' climbing, you have less than twenty-four hours to load this person with potent intravenous antibiotics or they will die in agony.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Gas Gangrene (Dead Meat) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I said in the last manual that you should never suture and seal a deep, dirty wound. Here is the pathological explanation: the bacterium 'Clostridium perfringens'. <LINE> <LEFT> This bacterium loves places without oxygen (anaerobic). If you stitch a dirty cut and seal the flesh, you create paradise for it. It starts eating your living muscle from the inside and releases a highly toxic gas as bacterial feces. <LINE> <LEFT> The limb will swell terrifyingly, turn a bronze or black color, and when you press the skin, you will hear and feel a crackling sound of bubbles popping under your fingers (like bubble wrap). That is the gangrene gas trapped in the flesh. The smell is like an animal dead for a week in the sun. The only cure for established gangrene is the scalpel. We amputate before the rot climbs to the trunk.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Antibiotics Aren't Magic Bullets <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A layman’s biggest mistake with a first aid kit is thinking antibiotics cure anything. They are not magic pills. Antibiotics kill BACTERIA. They are absolutely useless against VIRUSES. <LINE> <LEFT> If you have a bad flu, a cold, or a stomach virus, swallowing Penicillin or Amoxicillin will only destroy your stomach’s healthy intestinal flora and give you colossal diarrhea, while the virus continues laughing at you. <LINE> <LEFT> And the golden rule: if you start a cycle of antibiotics for a real infection from a cut, you MUST take the pills until the whole box is gone, even if the wound looks healed on the third day. If you stop halfway because 'you feel better,' the strongest bacteria that survived will multiply and create a superinfection immune to that medicine. And then, my friend, you have no Plan B.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Nature’s Fury (Anaphylaxis) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A hunter is stung by a bee or eats a granola bar with peanuts. In five minutes, their face swells like a balloon, they start wheezing loudly, and their throat closes brutally. They grab their neck, cannot pull in a thread of air, and pass out. <LINE> <LEFT> This is Anaphylactic Shock. Their immune system got so confused by the venom (or food) protein that it fired a nuclear response against its own body, dilating all veins and locking the lungs shut. <LINE> <LEFT> Oral antihistamines take forty minutes to work. The guy will be dead in five. The only salvation is Epinephrine (Adrenaline) injected directly into the thigh muscle. Adrenaline forces the lungs to open and the heart to beat with fury. If you know someone has a severe allergy and you don’t carry an epinephrine auto-injector in your kit, you are useless.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fever: The Body's Furnace <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hysterical parents arrive in the ER crying because their child has a 100-degree fever. Fever isn’t the disease. Fever is your body’s weapon. <LINE> <LEFT> Bacteria love the comfortable 97.7 degrees of the human body. When the brain detects an invasion, it acts like a ruthless general: it raises the thermostat to 100 or 102 degrees in an attempt to literally bake the invaders alive, while accelerating white blood cell production. <LINE> <LEFT> If the fever is tolerable (up to 101-ish), don’t stuff yourself with meds to bring it down immediately. Let the fire burn the infection for a few hours, drink lots of water, and rest. The danger only becomes lethal if the fever exceeds 104 degrees Fahrenheit. At that point, the furnace is out of control and your own brain will begin to suffer structural damage to nerve proteins. That’s when you hit the ice.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Nail, the Dirt, and Tetanus <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> There’s an urban legend that rust causes Tetanus. Rust is just iron oxide; it doesn’t harm you. What causes Tetanus is a shielded bacterium that loves living in dirty soil, animal feces, and dust. The rusty barn nail is just an excellent 'taxi' that pierces your skin and injects this dirt deeply into your muscle. <LINE> <LEFT> When tetanic toxin hits your nerves, it causes violent, uncontrollable muscle contractions. It starts with 'Trismus' (the jaw locks shut with terrifying force). Then, the back arches backward, breaking the spine itself from muscle tension, until the chest locks and you die suffocated, perfectly conscious. <LINE> <LEFT> There is no magic cure when symptoms set in at a camp. The only treatment on the face of the Earth is washing the wound brutally and staying up to date with the tetanus shot. And vaccines expire every ten years.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Parasites (Water Invaders) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We talked about cholera in the last manual, but bacteria aren’t the only problem with wild water. Crystal-clear mountain streams, apparently pure, are full of microscopic bear and deer feces containing Giardia and Cryptosporidium. They are protozoa, parasites with armored shells. <LINE> <LEFT> Chemical water purification tablets based on iodine or chlorine kill common bacteria, but these armored parasite eggs just laugh at chlorine. They will hatch in your intestine and cause weeks of hellish cramps, sulfur burps, and chronic explosive diarrhea. <LINE> <LEFT> The only absolute, unquestionable guarantee to annihilate Giardia in wild water is thermal physics. You need to BOIL the water. 212 degrees Fahrenheit in vigorous boil (large bubbles rising) for a full minute. Boiled water never lies.
IGUI_BookFirstAid4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Intoxication vs. Botulism (Deadly Cans) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Eating undercooked meat ruins your day. Eating a can of bulging food ends your life. There is a brutal difference between common food poisoning and the nightmare of Botulism. <LINE> <LEFT> Common poisoning (Salmonella, E. coli) gives you fever, violent vomiting, and diarrhea. Your body detects the toxin and expels it out of every door violently. It’s exhausting, but you survive if you drink water. <LINE> <LEFT> Botulism, on the other hand, grows inside old canned foods, without oxygen and poorly processed (with cans dented at the seams or with lids bulging with gas). Botulinum toxin is the most potent biological poison known to man. It doesn’t cause diarrhea; it attacks your nerves. It starts with double vision, your speech slurs, your facial muscles sag, and, slowly, the toxin paralyzes your lungs. You stop breathing. Never open a can of beans that is swollen like a balloon.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: The Limit of Flesh <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the previous four volumes, you acted like a glorified paramedic. You stopped leaks, bandaged, and medicated. But there are traumas the body cannot solve on its own, even with ten rolls of gauze. <LINE> <LEFT> This is Volume Five. We cross the line from containment and enter the territory of invasion. We will open flesh, pull out metals that shouldn’t be there, stitch deep holes, and understand how the human biological engine rebuilds destroyed tissues itself. <LINE> <LEFT> From now on, the clean environment is gone. Prepare your surgical tools and your stomach. The survival butcher shop is officially open.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hunger of Healing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The human body is a 3D meat printer, but it doesn’t print blood and skin out of thin air. It demands raw matter. <LINE> <LEFT> If you are hurt, low on blood, and trying to heal holes in your body, starving is slow suicide. A thin, famished patient will take triple the time to close a cut and recover blood volume. <LINE> <LEFT> Accelerating recovery doesn't come from magic pills; it comes from being very Well Fed. Stuff your stomach with thick stews, heavy meats, and calories until you’re bursting full. A metabolically saturated body heals cuts and restores health and vigor in a fraction of the normal time.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Restorative Coma (Sleep) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Another tough-guy mistake: thinking you’ll recover from a heavy blow and blood loss while continuing to work, chop wood, or drive down roads for two days without catching a wink. <LINE> <LEFT> Adrenaline and effort block cellular healing mechanisms. True brute regeneration of muscles, bones, and blood tissues occurs exclusively during deep stages of uninterrupted sleep. <LINE> <LEFT> Sleep is the greatest anesthesia and the greatest medical clinic in the natural world. If you are near death and lost half your blood, eat a lot, find a perfectly safe place, and sleep for ten hours straight. You will wake up a new man.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sleeping Pills (Desperation) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Sometimes the pain of a fractured limb or the panic of an isolated situation leaves your mind racing at two hundred miles an hour. You know you need to sleep to heal, but you can’t close your eyes because of the pain and stress. <LINE> <LEFT> That’s what the blue bottles of Sleeping Tablets are for. They force your brain to power down and initiate repair, ignoring the pain. <LINE> <LEFT> BUT, and this is a massive 'but': never mix sleeping pills with alcohol. The chemical combination of depressants shuts down the airways of your autonomic nervous system. You lie on the floor feeling sleepy, and your brain forgets to tell the lungs to breathe. You never wake up.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Final Failure (Incurable Disease) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Part of real medicine is grief and acceptance. There will be moments when biology is against you and the wounds on the street won’t respond to common antibiotics or the alcohol you dumped into them. <LINE> <LEFT> You will know when the battle is lost. The patient’s fever will spike violently, their face will turn pale with necrotic spots, constant nausea will dominate their stomach, and their mind will begin to lose itself to delirium or unprovoked violence. <LINE> <LEFT> Some bites, deep infections, and rustic contagions alter who we are and shut the engine down undeniably. When this systematic, rapid decline begins and won't yield, your duty as a healer ends. Walk away. Lock the door. What happens next belongs to the inevitable.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Relentless Resilience <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The human body breaks, rots, and bleeds with pathetic ease. All it takes is a forgotten glass shard, an infected bite from a barroom idiot, or a poorly cured cold to send us into the dark. <LINE> <LEFT> But over these five volumes, I’ve also shown you the frightening resilience of our species. An open hole seals if kept clean. A broken bone that looks like ruins calcifies and turns into indestructible rock again. A drained body creates liters of red blood out of nowhere just because you had some soup and went to sleep. <LINE> <LEFT> The body wants to live more than you want to fight. It just needs you to create the sterile environment necessary for biological magic to act. The doctor doesn’t cure. They tidy the house so the body can repair itself.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Surgeon's Final Report <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This is the end of your theoretical training. You are no longer the cowardly citizen who faints at the sight of a compound fracture. You understand sutures, tourniquets, war disinfection, the dangers of ice, and the purifying virtues of boiling water. <LINE> <LEFT> In the ideal world the government tries to sell on American television today, you would just call us. But my emergency room might be dark tomorrow, the roads might close, and your life might depend on the cheap pliers sitting in the glove box of your dirty truck. <LINE> <LEFT> Respect infection, sleep hard when wounded, eat until you’re stuffed to regenerate, never underestimate the power of pain, and keep your needles boiled. My shift ends here, and from today on, life on the street is your responsibility. Stay alive.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Deep Wounds (The Trench) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A common scratch or laceration heals on its own under a bandage. But if the patient takes an accidental axe blow or falls onto a steel plate and opens a 'Deep Wound,' that’s a different story. <LINE> <LEFT> A deep wound is a trench opened down to the muscle. Skin cannot bridge the chasm to reconnect. If you just put a bandage over it, it will bleed slowly forever and never close. <LINE> <LEFT> The only solution for a deep wound is mechanical stitching. You absolutely need a Suture Needle and Thread. If you don’t have one, a sterilized common sewing needle and strong clothing thread will do the job in a pinch. Pull the edges together by force and stitch, or they will bleed until they pass out.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Glass Curse <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Human stupidity peaks when people decide to break windows with their own arms or jump through windows while shards are still stuck in the frame. <LINE> <LEFT> The result? The victim’s arm is riddled with glass shards lodged deep in the flesh. If you just put a bandage over the glass-filled arm, with every muscle movement, the glass blade inside will tear more tissue and generate excruciating pain. <LINE> <LEFT> You cannot stitch, and you cannot ignore. You MUST use metal Tweezers. Open the wound, grab the glass, and pull. The patient will howl in pain, and the hole will bleed much more once the glass cork comes out. Stop the blood immediately after.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Lodged Projectiles (The Lead) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hunting accidents or street fights end with lead in the flesh. A bullet lodged in the body is a lethal foreign object. The lead poisons, and the hot metal carries dirty clothing lint into the muscle. <LINE> <LEFT> Just like glass, the projectile prevents the wound from healing and guarantees a brutal infection. Extraction requires cold blood. With sterilized hands and Tweezers, you enter the bullet hole and pull it out. <LINE> <LEFT> Remember the logical sequence for a bullet or glass wound: First, use tweezers to remove the foreign object. Then, disinfect the blood pool. Next, use the suture needle to close the large hole left behind. Finally, apply a clean bandage. It’s the survival assembly line.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dirty Bandages (The Petri Dish) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You did everything right, applied sterile gauze, and stopped the blood. But the next day, the bandage is black, stiff, and soaked with old blood. <LINE> <LEFT> Dried blood in the heat of a human body is the perfect Petri dish for growing deadly bacteria. If you leave a dirty bandage tied to someone’s arm for days, infection will flourish rapidly under the fabric. <LINE> <LEFT> Change dressings constantly. And in the real world, where supplies run out, don’t throw the dirty (Ripped Sheets) strips in the trash. Get a pot of water on the stove and boil the bloodied rags with soap. Clean water turns dirty trash into reusable medical supplies.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Brute Disinfection (Alcohol) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The cotton-and-alcohol swab your mother rubbed on your scraped knee was kindness. In dirty trauma medicine, disinfection is a baptism by fire. <LINE> <LEFT> Bottles of hospital disinfectant are gold, but Isopropyl Alcohol, Alcohol Wipes, and even bottles of high-proof Bourbon whiskey work to purge the microscopic hell of a street scrape. <LINE> <LEFT> Pour the purifying liquid directly over open cuts before closing the bandage. The pain will be immediate, and the victim will grit their teeth, but the flammable liquid annihilates the infection rate, saving your last pack of antibiotics for problems alcohol can’t reach.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Paralyzing Effect of Pain <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I see tough guys arriving at the ER with dislocated shoulders, swearing they can go back to the street fight. They can’t. Pain isn't just a bad feeling; it’s a neurological anchor. <LINE> <LEFT> Severe pain causes shaking, kills your focus, drastically reduces the precision of your vision, and leaves you terribly slower to run or fight. You become a turtle with broken reflexes. <LINE> <LEFT> Using Painkillers isn't a luxury; it’s survival tactics. If you’re hurt and need to keep walking or fighting for your life, take the pills. Reducing the chemical agony in the brain returns your movement speed and arm strength to swing an axe or push an obstacle.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rustic Botany (Poultices) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I spent twelve years in medical school and learned to hate naturalistic healers, but as a man of science, I cannot deny the brutal chemistry of wild herbs when the pharmacy is reduced to ash. <LINE> <LEFT> If you master forest foraging, certain plants, when crushed with a mortar and pestle into a paste (Poultice), save lives. <LINE> <LEFT> Crushed Wild Garlic on a wound has absurd antibacterial properties, acting as a natural disinfectant against chronic infections. Raw, crushed Plantain leaves aggressively speed up cut healing times. And Comfrey applied over a fracture splint helps the broken bone calcify faster. Accept the earth’s help.
IGUI_BookFirstAid5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Broken Clock (Fractures) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you jump from the second floor of a house fleeing danger only to land hard on the cement, Newton’s laws will collect the bill. Your leg will break. <LINE> <LEFT> You don’t cure a broken bone with stitches or bandages. You align the leg straight, tie a branch or firm wooden board (Splint) around the fracture, and sit on the couch. <LINE> <LEFT> Fractures require absolute time. A splint allows you to move while limping with extreme slowness, but your mobility will be ruined for weeks. There is no tricking human physiology. You will walk slow, you will limp, and you will be useless weight for your group until the bone knits. Don't jump out of windows.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dean's Guide to a Good Fishing Trip <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hey there again. It's Dean. If you read my guide on twigs and stones, you already know I don't like nonsense. You are hungry, the canned food is gone, and the river water is running. <LINE> <LINE> Beneath that muddy water there is fresh meat, for free, waiting for anyone who has the patience to pull it out of there. Fishing isn't sitting in a chair drinking beer while waiting for a miracle. Fishing, in our world, is pure survival. <LINE> <LINE> In this first guide, I'm going to teach you the basics. No carbon fiber rods or electric sonars. We're going to talk about spears, worms, and how not to come home empty-handed.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hookset (The Tug) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The bobber went under. Your heart races. The number one amateur mistake is giving a violent yank backward, twisting your arms over your head like a lumberjack. <LINE> <LINE> If you do this with a weak line and a tied wooden rod, the line will snap, and the hook (with the bait and the fish) will stay in the river. The hookset must be a firm motion of the wrist. When tension hits, raise the rod tip quickly so the hook drives into the fish's mouth, and then reel in, keeping the line always taut. If the line goes slack, it spits the hook.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Loss of Gear (The Broken Line) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Get used to loss. Fish like Pike have teeth that look like tiny razors. They will slice through your cheap twine line in a second. <LINE> <LINE> Fighting a fish that is too heavy with light gear will invariably destroy your tackle. Always carry extra paper clips, nails, and spare rolls of line in your backpack. A fisherman with only one hook is a man one second away from losing his lunch.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading the Water (Where to Cast the Line) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Don't cast your hook into the middle of an empty river where the current is strongest and straightest. Fish are lazy; they don't like to swim against the current if they don't have to. <LINE> <LINE> Look at the river. Where is there a fallen tree in the water? Where does the bank curve and create a pool of still water? Where are there reeds and tall weeds coming out of the river? It is in these structures of protection and shade that fish hide to set up ambushes. Cast your bait near sunken wood and wait for the strike.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Old Trunk (Heavy Trash) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Water swallows many things. You won't always pull up a fresh fish. <LINE> <LINE> Don't get frustrated if you spend hours at the lake's edge and end up catching an old shoe, filthy socks, or even pieces of trash. The world before the fall was dirty, and Kentucky's rivers are full of junk. Just take the trash off the hook, check if the bait is still there, and cast again. Stubbornness feeds the survivor.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fillet Knife <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You caught the fish and dispatched it quickly. If you try to roast it whole with scales and guts on your campfire, the green bile from its liver will burst in the fire and poison the meat with a nasty taste. <LINE> <LINE> Use a Hunting Knife or a sharp Cleaver. Make a cut in the belly, scrape the guts out, and throw them back into the river to feed the other fish. Then, slide the blade from head to tail, close to the backbone, separating the bone-free fillet. A fillet fried in an iron skillet is the meal that rewards a cold day.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of the First Fishing Day <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> That's it. My part is done. You know how to improvise a spear, tie up a branch, find worms in the wet ground, and what hours of the day the water delivers food to you. <LINE> <LINE> Rustic survival is in your blood now. But fishing is an ancient art full of gentlemen who love finesse. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Two, 'Fly Fishing, with J.R. Hartley', I step out of the picture. An old British fellow in a suit and a felt hat will take over to teach a technique where the bait weighs less than a feather, and the line dances in the air like an elegant whip. Good luck with the cast.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fishing Spear (The Beginning) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don't have a fishing rod? Stop whining. Our ancestors pulled food from the river thousands of years before they invented the reel. You just need a Fishing Spear. <LINE> <LINE> Grab a long, straight branch. Use your knife (or that chipped stone I taught you to find) and sharpen the tip until it's lethal. The secret of the fishing spear isn't just making a point, it's making side barbs so the fish doesn't slip off the wood after you pierce it. With a sharpened stick, the riverbank is yours.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Spear Strike <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fishing with a spear isn't throwing a stick into the water like a madman. Water tricks the eyes because of light refraction. The fish is never exactly where you think it is; it is a little bit lower. <LINE> <LINE> Step into the shallow part of the river. Stand absolutely still. The cold water will numb your feet, but if you move, the vibration in the water scares everything away within a ten-meter radius. When the fish gets close to your boots, aim slightly below it and strike with sharp, quick force. If you miss, the fish vanishes in a second.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Wooden Rod <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Standing around in cold water gets tiring. If you want to fish from the top of a pier, you're going to need a rod. <LINE> <LINE> You don't need to loot a sporting goods store for this. Find a strong, flexible tree branch (Willow is excellent). You need three things: the branch, a sturdy line, and a paper clip or bent nail to serve as a hook. Tie the line firmly to the tip of the branch and ensure the hook knot won't come undone from a hard tug.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Bait (The Earth's Feast) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fish won't bite an empty metal hook. You have to offer a snack. The best bait in the world is hidden right under your feet. <LINE> <LINE> Remember the foraging lessons? Dig into the damp forest soil after a rain or flip over rocks and rotting logs. Fill your pockets with worms, grasshoppers, cockroaches, or small minnows if you have a net. The more the bait moves on the hook, the faster the predator will strike. A dead, white worm attracts far less fish than a fat, wiggly one.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Artificial Bait (Tackle) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Worms run out. Insects escape. If you find artificial plastic or metal lures abandoned by past fishermen, guard them as if they were gold. <LINE> <LINE> These small, colorful tools mimic injured fish by flashing under the sunlight. They never rot and don't need to be dug out of the ground. But the risk is high: if your line snaps, the lure will sink with the fish and you will lose it forever in the river depths.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Magic Hours (Dawn and Dusk) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Trying to fish at midday, with the sun frying your head, is a fool's errand. The water heats up, oxygen levels drop, and the big fish sink to the dark, cool holes of the river where they don't eat. <LINE> <LINE> The smart fisherman knows that fish feed during two magic hours: dawn (when the sun is starting to paint the sky) and dusk (when shadows begin to cover the water). In these twilight periods, fish rise to the surface to hunt fallen insects. It's when the water boils with life.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Blessing of Rain <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Most people run indoors when it starts to rain. A real fisherman runs to the river. <LINE> <LINE> Rain breaking the water's surface does two fantastic things. First, it oxygenates the water, making the fish active and hungry. Second, the sound and impact of the drops hide your movement on the bank and your shadow, making the fish much less skittish. Cast your bait during a warm storm and you will pull in dinner twice as often.
IGUI_BookFishing1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Curse of Winter <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In summer, fishing is a feast. When November arrives and frost covers Kentucky, the water in rivers and lakes will get stupidly cold. <LINE> <LINE> The metabolism of fish plummets. They don't waste energy hunting; they stay still at the bottom, conserving calories. Your chances of catching anything in winter (even using the best bait) drop to almost zero. If you depend solely on the river to survive, the ice will starve you to death. Fish in the summer and freeze the fillets for the low months.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fly Fishing <LINE> With J.R. Hartley <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hello, dear reader. Mr. Dean, in his admirable rusticity, taught you to spear fish with wooden lances and get dirt under your fingernails digging for worms. While effective for raw survival, these methods lack poetry. <LINE> <LINE> Fishing shouldn't be a barbaric act of desperation; it is a ballet between man, water, and the mind of the trout. Fly Fishing is the supreme art of elegant deception. We do not feed the fish; we delude it with feathers. Adjust your hat, wipe the mud from your hands, and allow me to introduce you to true class.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Stealthy Presentation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fly Fishing is done in shallow rivers with crystal clear waters. This means that just as you can see the fish, the fish can see you perfectly. <LINE> <LINE> Walking heavy on the bank, wearing loudly colored clothes, or letting your long shadow project over the pool where the fish is will ruin your afternoon. Approach crouched down, crawl through the bushes if you must. The first cast is always the most lethal; if the fish wasn't spooked, the first kiss of the fly on the water almost always draws a furious strike.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fine Hookset (The Master Touch) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fly hooks are microscopic, sometimes no larger than your pinky fingernail. The leader (the transparent line at the tip) is thin as a hair. <LINE> <LINE> If you give a brutal yank (like Mr. Dean recommended for bottom fish), you will rip the hook out of the trout's mouth or, worse, snap your delicate leader with a pop. The hookset with a fly is a sharp, elegant wrist movement, lifting the rod just enough for the small steel point to pierce the soft lip of the fish.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Taming the Salmonid <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A trout hooked on ultralight gear is an electric demon. It will jump out of the water and run to tangle itself in tree roots. <LINE> <LINE> Do not try to winch it in like a crane. Keep the rod raised at 45 degrees so the flexibility of the whole rod acts as a shock absorber against the furious headshakes of the fish. If it runs fast, let it take line, braking with the pressure of your own fingers against the spool. It is a war of attrition. You tire it out slowly, with British patience.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Respect for Running Water <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> It is very common to walk inside the river (Wading) to reach the golden fishing spots. The sound of gravel beneath your boots and the cold current at knee height bring a deep peace. <LINE> <LINE> In the midst of the cold water, focused on the tiny bait floating between the rocks, the outside world goes silent. The anguish of society's collapse disappears. Fly fishing is the survivor's yoga. It demands so much mental focus that your brain has no room to suffer over other things.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Ethics of the Return and Hunger <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In civilized times, a gentleman practices 'Catch and Release'. We fished for the thrill of the puzzle, removed the hook, and returned the beautiful spotted creature to the river. <LINE> <LINE> Unfortunately, things have changed. We are hungry. If you need to dispatch the fish, do so mercifully and quickly with a blow to the head. Do not let it suffocate on dry land slowly. A noble fisherman honors the prey that sustains his life and never takes more from the river than he can eat in a night.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> A Gentleman's Farewell <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> And with that, I reel in my line. The mist is falling and the yellow fly box needs to be closed. I hope I have instilled in you the value of patience and respect for the fluidity of water and the behavior of insects. <LINE> <LINE> But there is more than trout in crystal streams. The aquatic world is vast, going from deep, dark lakes to the salty infinity of the ocean where true monsters swim. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Three, 'Freshwater and Saltwater Fishing', we will abandon subtlety and enter the realm of variety and deep waters. Keep your hooks sharp, my dears.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Philosophy of the Fly <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In traditional fishing, you throw a heavy sinker with a piece of meat bait into the water and wait. The fish catches the scent and bites out of hunger. <LINE> <LINE> In Fly Fishing, our bait is made of a tiny hook, tied with silk threads, animal fur, and feathers. It has no smell and weighs nothing. Our mission is to make that tangle of feathers land on the water in a way so incredibly natural that the trout will swear, on its own life, that it is a real insect that just dropped there. We catch fish by their hunting instinct, not their sense of smell.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Physics of the Cast <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you cast a bait that weighs less than a blade of grass fifteen meters away? The secret of fly fishing lies in the inverted gear. <LINE> <LINE> In common fishing, the heavy bait pulls the thin line. In fly fishing, the bait weighs nothing. It is the LINE that is thick and heavy. The fly rod, long and absurdly flexible, functions like a graceful whip. You don't cast the bait; you cast the weight of the thick line forward, and the light fly just hitches a ride on the tip.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Gentleman's Clock (The Technique) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Casting the fly doesn't use the brute strength of the shoulder. The elbow must remain tucked against the rib. Imagine you are holding the handle of a light sword, facing an imaginary giant clock. <LINE> <LINE> You raise the rod in a swift, continuous motion to the 10 o'clock position.
