Stop abruptly (to let the line unroll behind you in the air). Then, drive forward to the 2 o'clock position and stop abruptly again. The line will unroll through the air in a perfect loop. The movement is 'Pull, Pause, Push, Pause'.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dry Fly vs. Wet Fly (Nymph) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> There are two major theaters of illusion. The 'Dry Fly' floats on the water's surface, mimicking an adult insect with wings that just landed. You see the exact moment the trout rises to strike, swallowing the bait in an explosion of water. <LINE> <LINE> The 'Wet Fly' or Nymph, on the other hand, sinks slightly. It mimics the larval stage of river insects that live underwater. Fish eat nymphs 90%% of the time, but the fishing is harder because you don't see the strike; you must 'feel' the subtle hesitation of the line.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading the Current <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A wise trout does not swim against the current all day; it would tire itself to death. It looks for the 'Seams' of the river. <LINE> <LINE> A seam is the dividing line where a fast current meets calm water (usually behind a large submerged rock). The fish stays stationary in the calm water, just turning its face toward the fast water, waiting for the river to act as a food conveyor belt, bringing insects straight to its mouth. That is exactly where your fly must land.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Dead Drift <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you place a fake insect in the water, but it gets pulled by your line dragging sideways faster than the current, the fish will know it's a trap and flee in terror. Dead insects don't swim sideways like speedboats. <LINE> <LINE> The presentation of the bait demands a 'Dead Drift'. Your artificial fly must float at the EXACT speed of the current, without your line exerting any tension that pulls it unnaturally. You must master the technique of releasing extra line into the air to create slack before the water drags it away.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Dance of the Hatch <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before wetting the line, the gentleman sits on the bank and observes. What is flying today? Are they tiny black midges? Are they yellow mayflies with white wings rising from the water? <LINE> <LINE> The phenomenon of insects hatching and flying from the river is called a 'Hatch'. During a hatch, trout become selective; they only eat what is hatching that day and ignore everything else. You must open your fly box and choose the one that most closely matches the size and color of the insect nature is offering today.
IGUI_BookFishing2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fly Tying <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If civilization collapsed and the fancy shops vanished, a gentleman will tie his own flies. You need a bare hook and a lot of creativity. <LINE> <LINE> Scraps of deer hair harvested in the forest float beautifully due to their hollow fiber. Partridge feathers make exceptional wings. Wool threads unraveled from an old sweater form the colorful body of a nymph. Tying flies with sewing thread under the light of a lantern is a meditative hobby during long winter nights.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Freshwater and Saltwater Fishing <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The fellow from the previous book tried to teach you how to fish for tiny trout with light feathers. Pretty, but it doesn't fill a family's belly. My name is Captain Ahab, or what's left of him, and I fish for monsters. <LINE> <LINE> Water isn't all the same. A stream is kindergarten; a large deep lake or the open ocean is the battlefield. In this volume, we're leaving finesse in the drawer. We're talking heavy sinkers, bloody bait, tides, and the creatures that break rods in half. If you're afraid of the dark deep, close this book.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Trolling Technique <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you are lucky enough to find a motorboat that still works, deep water fishing uses Trolling. <LINE> <LINE> You deploy large artificial lures that mimic squids or fleeing fish and leave the line trailing far behind the boat. The boat sails slowly, dragging the lures through the surface or mid-water. The action of the lure ripping through the water mimics panicked prey, provoking the killing instinct of apex predatory fish.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Ohio River Monster <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We are in Kentucky and the sea is far. But don't think you are safe from heavy gear. The Ohio River hides creatures that would put sea fish to shame. <LINE> <LINE> Massive sturgeon and mutant catfish live down there. To pull them from the deep river currents, you apply the rules of the sea: large chunks of dead fish, half-kilogram sinkers to pierce the strong current, and a line thick as rope. Freshwater doesn't just mean small fish.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Invisible Water <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The sea and large rivers don't play around. A rip current on the beach will pull an adult man to the ocean floor in seconds. <LINE> <LINE> At the mouths of large rivers or on beaches, if the water looks calm in a narrow lane but rough on the sides, NEVER enter. That calm is the current ripping backward. A good fisherman is one who reads the water for the hunt, but also knows how to read the water so as not to drown. Never turn your back on waves or currents.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Improvising Weight <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Original fishing sinkers run out fast. If civilization collapsed, you need to keep your line on the bottom against water movement anyway you can. <LINE> <LINE> Heavy steel nuts, old car bearings, or even round stones well-tied and secured to the line work perfectly as makeshift sinkers. The fish doesn't care if you're using imported polished lead gear or a rusty gear stolen from a dead factory, as long as the bait reaches the bottom.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Salt Preservation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You caught ten kilograms of meat in a large lake using heavy gear. Eat one fillet today. But what to do with the other nine kilograms if the electricity is gone? <LINE> <LINE> Salt is the answer. Cut the fish into thick slabs, remove the blood, and cover them with mountains of coarse salt. Let it dry on a makeshift clothesline (if insects allow). Dried salt cod saved sailors from hunger across oceans for centuries. Deep-water fishing is about mass harvest, and mass harvest demands mastery over salt.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The End of the Captain's Manual <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We reel in the line for today. You learned about thermoclines, tamed invisible tides, and now know that to hunt large demons in rough waters, you use the smell of death, steel on the tip, and lead weights. <LINE> <LINE> The simple rod did its job, but humanity invented greedier ways to plunder rivers than using just a solitary lone hook. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Four, 'Latest Rod and Net Techniques', we'll leave classic patience behind to explore modern brutality: how to set up submerged traps and the use of nets and traps, which fish all day long for you, even while you sleep at your base.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Salty Destruction (The Salt) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first thing you need to understand if you reach the ocean shore: salt devours everything. <LINE> <LINE> Saltwater is an acid bath for cheap metal gear. If you use the same reel you used in your town's little pond to fish on the beach and don't wash it with freshwater immediately afterward, the bearings will lock up in rust in three days. The sea demands respect and marine grease. Freshwater gear fails miserably in saltwater.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Freshwater: The Lake Thermocline <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you are at a large freshwater lake in the height of summer, don't cast your bait into the warm shallows. Big fish hate the heat. <LINE> <LINE> They dive for the 'Thermocline', an invisible layer beneath the surface where the warm water from above meets the freezing, oxygen-depleted water of the bottom. It is a perfect comfort zone. The secret of deep lake fishing is using sinkers calibrated to make your bait sink exactly to this middle layer and park there. It's where the predators sleep.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Hunting Catfish <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The biggest freshwater monsters, like the giant Catfish, don't hunt with their eyes. They hunt with their whiskers, scavenging the dark, muddy bottom of rivers like carnivorous vacuum cleaners. <LINE> <LINE> You don't use plastic bait for a catfish. You use stink. Pieces of rotted chicken liver, chunks of old hot dogs, or bloody cut bait. Cast a heavy sinker, let the bait sink into the muck, and wait for the smell to travel through the water. The catfish comes by the trail of carrion.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Black Bass (The Brush Fighter) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Unlike the catfish, the Largemouth Bass hunts by visual ambush. He loves structures: submerged logs, old bridge pillars, or thick weed beds. <LINE> <LINE> If you cast your line into open, clean waters, the Bass won't be there. You need to throw your bait (like a rubber frog or an artificial worm) right into the middle of the densest, ugliest vegetation in the lake, risking a snag. The big fish is always in the hardest place to reach.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Dictate of the Tide <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you finally reach the ocean, forget clocks. At sea, the Moon rules time. <LINE> <LINE> Fishing in the open sea or on the beach depends brutally on the Tide. Still water is dead water. You want to fish when water is in motion, meaning during 'running tides' (flood or ebb). The movement of the water stirs up small crabs, marine worms, and disoriented baitfish, triggering the feeding frenzy of larger fish. Fishing at slack tide (when it stops totally) is casting a line into a desert.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Beach Fishing 'Surfcasting' <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Standing on the beach sand trying to hurl a hook behind giant waves requires ignorant gear. 'Surfcasting' rods are three to four meters long. <LINE> <LINE> The technique is reading the beach. Look for where waves don't break aggressively; this indicates a 'Channel' or deep hole. It's through channels that big predators come and go close to the sand. You need to use an anchor-shaped sinker (Pyramid) that digs into the sand beneath the waves and keeps your piece of squid or fish on the bottom.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Saltwater Bait (Blood and Oil) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The sea is gigantic and dilutes smells quickly. If your bait is timid, it will go unnoticed. <LINE> <LINE> The best sea baits are incredibly oily and bloody. Sardines, mackerel, or chunks of squid. The oil leaking from these baits creates a slick in the water ('Chum') that attracts fish from miles away. At sea, the more your bait stinks and shines, the greater your chances of pulling in a giant.
IGUI_BookFishing3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Steel Leader (Wire Leader) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Most freshwater fish have small teeth. At sea, and in large rivers like the Ohio, monsters have saws in their mouths. Barracudas, sharks, or gar cut nylon lines as if they were sewing threads. <LINE> <LINE> You never tie the hook straight to nylon line if you're targeting sharp-toothed fish. The last twenty centimeters of your line must be a 'Wire Leader'. It's a flexible metal cable. The fish swallows the bait, bites the metal with razor teeth, and can't cut through.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Latest Rod and Net Techniques <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The previous volumes taught the poetry of fishing. Standing at the river's edge, feeling the breeze, waiting for a fish to bite. That's beautiful for a vacation weekend. <LINE> <LINE> But in the real world of survival, time is life. You can't afford to waste six hours holding a stick when you need to barricade windows and chop firewood for the winter. <LINE> <LINE> In this manual, I'm going to teach you Passive Fishing. We are going to abandon hope and adopt mathematics. With the use of traps and nets, you will make the river work for you while you sleep. Brutal efficiency enters the scene.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Trotline <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you don't have a net, use the strength of numbers. The Trotline is a massive technique. Instead of using a line with a hook, you stretch a thick, heavy rope from one bank of the river to the other. <LINE> <LINE> Along this main rope, you tie thirty or forty smaller lines ('drops'), each with a baited hook. Instead of fishing with one hook, you are fishing with forty, covering the entire riverbed at once. Leave it stretched out at night and harvest the crop in the morning.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hidden Danger of the Trotline <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Extreme caution: checking a heavily baited trotline from inside a boat or with water hitting your waist is dangerous. <LINE> <LINE> If a huge fish is hooked on one of the hooks and begins to thrash wildly while you pull the main rope, the other thirty sharp hooks will be flying through the air or whipping underwater. It is very easy for one of these flying hooks to drive into your hand or leg, and the big fish will drag you along. Always use thick leather gloves and have an emergency knife on your waist to cut the line if you get hooked.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Checking Frequency <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Passive Fishing is wonderful, but it has a strict clock. If you set the trap or net at night, you must absolutely go fetch it early in the morning. <LINE> <LINE> If you leave fish trapped there for two days, they will suffocate or die of exhaustion, and the meat will rot quickly in the water. Worse still: the smell of trapped fish will attract turtles that break traps, and alligators that will shred your entire gillnet to steal the free catch. A forgotten trap is a lost trap.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Nylon Thread Maintenance <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Nets tear. They get caught on submerged branches or are cut by the teeth of predators. <LINE> <LINE> A net with a giant hole in the middle stops being a wall and becomes an open door for the school to escape. The smart survivor carries a 'Netting Needle' made of flat wood or bone, and a roll of nylon thread. At the end of every day, sit near the campfire and sew up the holes in the torn mesh. The fishing net is your asset, take care of it better than you take care of your clothes.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Overfishing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A serious warning. Gillnets and traps do not select prey. They kill big fish, microscopic fry, frogs, and anything that swims there. <LINE> <LINE> If you leave a heavy net in the same small tributary for a consecutive month, you will completely decimate the fish and fry population of that stretch of the river. 'Overfishing' destroys your long-term food base. Alternate trap locations and release fish that are too small to eat, otherwise the river will become sterile next summer.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Meat Factory <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Our journey through large-scale harvesting ends here. You gave up a little rod with a hook to dominate the water with barricades, nets, and dozens of traps. The river is no longer a hobby; it is a constant protein factory working under your command 24 hours a day. <LINE> <LINE> But applying all this mechanics, whether with the spear, the fly, or the net, requires knowledge of the territory. You are in Kentucky, after all. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Five and last, 'The Authoritative Guide to Kentucky Fishing', the local master reveals absolute regional secrets. What species are in our waters, what bait works in the Ohio River, and where the true trophies of our state are. Tie your hooks.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Calorie Math <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Active fishing (rod and line) requires you to burn hundreds of calories swinging your arm and waiting in the sun, to maybe catch a fish that will return those calories to you. It's a risky bet. <LINE> <LINE> The fishing trap flips the game. You spend ten minutes setting up the gear, leave to do other useful things, and return twelve hours later to collect dozens of trapped fish. You maximize caloric gain by reducing physical effort to almost zero. The one who survives isn't the best fisherman, it's the laziest and smartest fisherman.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fish Trap <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The oldest and most efficient trap in the world is the Fish Trap (Covo). It is essentially a cylinder or box made of wire, bamboo, or cut plastic bottles. <LINE> <LINE> The secret of the trap is the Inverted Funnel. The entrance is a cone that narrows inward. The small fish follows the bait's scent, enters through the large hole of the cone, and falls into the main chamber. When it tries to leave, its tiny brain can't find the small central hole of the funnel amidst wire walls. It enters easily, but never leaves again.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Baiting the Trap <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> An empty trap at the bottom of the river attracts nothing. You must bait the inner chamber. And the trap bait doesn't need to be fancy. <LINE> <LINE> Pieces of stale and old bread, flour dough with water, or rotted meat you wouldn't eat work perfectly. Place the bait inside an old pair of pantyhose or a piece of cloth with holes and tie it in the middle of the trap. This prevents the small fish from eating all the bait and escaping; they will stay swimming around the stinky cloth until you return to get them.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Trap Placement <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don't throw a trap into the middle of the river where the water is fast and clean; the current will drag your trap to the ocean. <LINE> <LINE> Traps must be tied to a firm tree root on the bank and sunk in shallow waters where there is thick vegetation or large rocks (structures where small fish hide from predators). The trap for small fish will provide not only quick food for soups, but the perfect, bloody bait to fish for the true monsters of the deep.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Gillnet <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Gillnet is the invisible wall of death. It is a rectangular net, made of very fine, transparent nylon thread. <LINE> <LINE> You stretch it transversely across a slow part of the river. The mesh is calculated for the head size of the target fish. The fish tries to swim through the invisible net, its head passes through the hole, but its thick body jams. When it tries to back out, the nylon threads catch on its gills. It gets stuck there, suffocating slowly in the water itself.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Static Net Structure <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> For the net to function as a perfect wall under the water, it needs to be tensioned in two opposite directions. <LINE> <LINE> On the bottom line (the lower rope of the net), you tie lead weights or heavy stones along its entire length. On the upper line, you tie plastic, cork, or styrofoam floats. The lead pulls the bottom of the net into the mud, and the styrofoam pulls the top toward the sky. The result is a straight underwater fence that doesn't forgive anything swimming down that corridor.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Cast Net <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you don't want to wait hours, there is a lethal active hunting net: The Cast Net. <LINE> <LINE> It doesn't look like a wall; it looks like a parachute. It is a giant circular net, with heavy weights tied around its entire lower edge. You observe from the bank until you spot a school of silvery fish flashing near the water's surface. It's an aerial ambush technique. You throw the net over them.
IGUI_BookFishing4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Throwing the Cast Net <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Throwing the cast net requires swing and centrifugal force, otherwise it falls into the water tangled like a wet rag. <LINE> <LINE> You wind part of the net in your right hand, place a sinker between your teeth (if you are old school), and throw the mass of net spinning through the air like a frisbee. In the air, centrifugal force makes the edge weights open the net into a perfect circle. When the cast net falls over the water, the sinkers sink instantly, creating a dome that imprisons the whole school at once.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Authoritative Guide to Kentucky Fishing <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You learned to use spears, tie artificial flies, face saltwater monsters, and set up lethal nets. But universal tactics are useless if you don't know the backyard you are stepping into. <LINE> <LINE> Welcome to Kentucky, specifically the Knox County Basin. This isn't the ocean and these aren't the frozen northern mountains. We have our own waters, our own species, and our own dirty rules. <LINE> <LINE> This final volume is the definitive census of our scales. I am going to show you what swims in the Ohio River, what hides in the ponds of Muldraugh, and what bait works in our mud.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Kentucky's Bipolar Weather <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To fish in Knox Country, you must master our brutal weather. Summer boils the water, forcing the big fish to the bottom in search of oxygen (fish at dawn or weighted to the bottom). <LINE> <LINE> But in winter, from December to February, the small lakes freeze at the edges and water temperatures drop to the point of lethargy. Cold-blooded fish don't eat in the winter with the same aggressiveness. Fishing in the Kentucky winter is a game of millimeters: use tiny lures, retrieve almost in slow motion, and keep the bait static right in front of the fish's face until you annoy it enough to bite.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Baiting with Local Nature <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If your gear runs out, the county forest has everything. The riverbanks here are packed with frogs in the spring and crickets in the summer. <LINE> <LINE> But our secret weapon for local bait is the little creek minnow. If you tie a fish trap to the bank with a piece of bread and collect dozens of these shiny minnows, your lunch is guaranteed. Every predator in Kentucky, from Bass to Catfish, throws instinct out the window when they see a silvery minnow thrashing on a hook.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Biological Waste and Safety <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The world ended, I know. And that means dead things tend to fall into the river. Rotten zombies float down the waters of the Ohio constantly. <LINE> <LINE> The fish themselves aren't poisoned by the dead flesh in the river, but their scaly skin can carry the infection. Never eat raw fish (like sushi) in this new era, no matter how pure the water looks. Clean the fish far from your camp, wash the fillet well, and cook it until the white meat turns opaque and the flakes separate easily with a fork. Fire cleans the river.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Night Trotline <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Want to dominate the Ohio River without spending energy? Set up a Trotline. <LINE> <LINE> Tie a thick rope from a fallen log on the bank to a deep rock. Hang ten hooks baited with pieces of old meat along the line, all touching the dark mud at the bottom. Go to sleep. During the night, the catfish will patrol the mud and swallow everything. In the morning, you'll just need muscle in your arms to pull fifty kilograms of fish onto dry land.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Golden Rule of the River <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Never turn your back on the Ohio River, and never underestimate the silence of the bank. <LINE> <LINE> Fishing is an act of patience and focus. You look at the water, not behind you. This makes the fisherman the easiest target for any pack of infected wandering through the forest. Never fish with your ears covered, clear the area around dense trees so you don't get ambushed, and if your line gets snagged, don't enter the dark water to untie it. It's better to lose the line than your life.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Master Fisherman <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Our aquatic journey ends here, my friend. You started out making wooden points with Dean, learned the aerial dance of J.R. Hartley, embraced the Captain's marine brutality, multiplied your time with nets, and now you know the native secrets of Knox County. <LINE> <LINE> The rod and line are now extensions of your arm. The water has stopped being a wet obstacle and has become your infinite refrigerator. <LINE> <LINE> Knowledge flows from you like the waters of the Ohio. Close the book. Bring your tackle box, pick your curve of the river, and sit on the damp earth. The feast never ends for those who know how to pull the line.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Waters of Knox Country <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Knox territory is cut by two very distinct types of water, and you must fish them differently. <LINE> <LINE> First, we have the Small Forest Lakes (like those scattered around Muldraugh and isolated campgrounds). These are still waters, rich in vegetation and dead logs, perfect for visual ambush fish. <LINE> <LINE> Second, we have the veins of the world: the Salt River and the monstrous Ohio River to the north in West Point and Riverside. The Ohio is a dark, muddy, and deep current machine, home to gigantic predators that hunt by scent in the depths.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sunfish <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Sunfish is the bread and butter of the Kentucky survivor. It's small, shaped like a plate, and brightly colored. <LINE> <LINE> It is the easiest fish to catch in the state. It bites almost anything that drops in the water, especially worms and small insects. If you are starving and need quick protein, go to any still pond and cast a small hook with live bait. They swim in schools, so where there is one, you will pull in ten in less than an hour.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Crappie (Paper Mouth) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Another abundant panfish is the Crappie. Its meat is the whitest, sweetest, and most delicious in all of Kentucky's waters, flaking perfectly in the pan. <LINE> <LINE> The Crappie's nickname is 'Paper Mouth'. Its lips are thin and fragile like wet parchment. If you give it that violent hookset (like they taught you in Volume Three), you will tear the fish's mouth and bring back only an empty hook. The Crappie demands the delicate touch of fly fishing or light rods. Tiny shiny lures or live minnows are its weak spot.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The King of the Lake: Bass <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Largemouth Bass is the undisputed king of Kentucky's lakes. He is a greenish tank of war, pure muscle, with a mouth big enough to swallow a whole duckling. <LINE> <LINE> The Bass hates clean water in the middle of the lake. He stays hidden in thick weeds, under dock pillars, and beneath lily pads. If you want to pull in a Bass, you have to cast plastic lures right into the middle of the heavy cover. When he bites, pull hard, because the first thing he'll do is try to wrap your line around submerged branches to snap it.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ohio River Monsters (Blue Catfish) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Change your gear. If you head down to West Point or Valley Station and face the brown waters of the Ohio River, you're going to need thick line. The Ohio houses Blue Catfish and Channel Catfish. <LINE> <LINE> Some of these demons weigh more than a full-grown dog. Since the river water is very murky, they are completely blind; evolution gave them whiskers that work like carrion radars. They are bottom predators.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Catfish Feast (Cutbait) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don't fish for a twenty-kilogram Blue Catfish with a grasshopper or a clean plastic lure. You need something nasty. <LINE> <LINE> The supreme Kentucky technique is 'Cutbait'. Take a small, worthless fish, chop it into bloody pieces, and leave it in the sun for an hour until it starts to smell bad. Stinky baits, old livers, or dead frogs secured on a heavy circle hook with a strong sinker. Sink that into the darkest trench of the river current and wait for your rod to double over.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Pike <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Pike is the lone wolf of our waters. A long fish, shaped like a camouflaged torpedo, full of teeth sharp as razors. He hunts by cutting smaller fish in half. <LINE> <LINE> If you go fishing for Pike in the winter or early spring in clear waters, you MUST use the Wire Leader you learned about in the sea manual, or he will slice your line in the first second of the fight. He reacts to fast movement, so use your metallic lures that mimic fleeing fish and retrieve quickly.
IGUI_BookFishing5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Netting on the Salt River <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Passive techniques work wonderfully in Kentucky's tributaries. The Salt River, which cuts across the county's landscape, has perfect medium currents for Gillnets. <LINE> <LINE> Stretch your net between two roots crossing a narrow channel of the Salt River. The steady current will force whole schools of Sunfish and small Bass against your invisible wall of nylon. Just remember the rule: check the net in the morning. The Salt River has large snapping turtles that will destroy your net if they catch the scent of rotting fish.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Flint Knapping 101 <LINE> Introduction to Lithic Art <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You don't know what 'Knapping' is, do you? You probably think it's just a fancy name for smashing two rocks together like a primate. <LINE> <LINE> The truth is that Flint Knapping is humanity's oldest and most enduring technology. It is the art of shaping rocks by intentionally breaking them to create edges sharper than modern surgical steel. With the collapse of civilization and knife factories fallen silent, whoever knows how to break stone dictates the rules. Grab a piece of leather to protect your lap and get ready to bleed your hands.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Bifacial Thinning <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your Spall has one flat face and one fat face. We need to make it a 'Biface' (cutting on both sides, like a tree leaf). <LINE> <LINE> Abandon the heavy round stone. Grab your Billet (the heavy piece of deer antler). The antler is soft enough to 'catch' the edge of the flint when it strikes, and heavy enough to send the shockwave. Striking with the antler on the edges will remove very wide, shallow flakes that travel across the face of the stone, leaving it perfectly thin without reducing its width.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading the Ridge of the Stone <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A good knapper does not look only at where they are striking; they look at where the flake will travel. The wave of force travels through the mass of the stone. <LINE> <LINE> If there is a hole, an internal flaw, or an abrupt step on the back of your flint, the shockwave will hit it and break your entire blade in half (an error called a 'Hinge' or 'Step Fracture'). You must plan each antler strike like a game of chess, always striking the highest ridges to progressively flatten the stone.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Pressure Flaking <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your stone is now thin and leaf-shaped, but the edges are still zigzagged and do not cut. Enter the Pressure Flaker. <LINE> <LINE> Stop striking. Sit down, place the stone flat over the tight leather on your thigh. Take the bone or copper-tipped tool, place the tip exactly on the edge of the flint, and push with the force of your entire shoulder 'in and down'. A small 'click' will sound, and a tiny flake will fall off. You are literally carving the serrated teeth of your blade using only static muscle pressure.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Scraper (The First Instrument) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Do not try to make a symmetrical dragon spearhead on your first day; you will get frustrated and give up. Your first tool should be the Scraper. <LINE> <LINE> Take any fat flake. Use pressure solely to align and sharpen a SINGLE edge, leaving the back thick for you to hold with your hand. The primitive Scraper is the essential tool for cleaning fat and muscle from the inside of a hunted animal's hide. A survivor with a good scraper has leather clothes and ropes; without it, they have only rotting peles.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Accepting Frustration and Blood <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The stone has a mind of its own. You will spend three hours thinning the perfect knife and, on the last touch of the antler, the angle will be wrong and the stone will snap in half in your hands. <LINE> <LINE> Do not scream. Breathe. Use both broken halves as arrowheads. <LINE> <LINE> And you will bleed. Even with gloves and leather, microscopic glass splinters will lodge in your fingers. Small cuts that sting and take time to heal are the knapper's baptism. Your blood will stain the flint, and that will only make you a true master.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Rebirth of the Stone Age <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Metallurgy was a luxury. Steel rusts. Broken flint stays sharp in the soil for ten thousand years waiting for someone to pick it up. <LINE> <LINE> Now you know the sound of antler against volcanic glass, understand the exact angle to extract a flat flake, and can already wrench a rudimentary scraper out of a gray rock you found in the brush. You no longer depend on manufactured knives. <LINE> <LINE> But to knap the perfect rock, you need to know where our soil hides the best nodules. In Volume Two, 'Kentucky Geology Guide', we will open the map and understand what the earth beneath our boots holds.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Conchoidal Fracture <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You cannot just grab any round garden stone and make a knife. Common rocks crumble or break into ugly blocks. Knapping relies on a specific physics: the Conchoidal Fracture. <LINE> <LINE> Rocks like Flint, Chert, or Obsidian have an amorphous molecular structure (like glass). When you strike them, the impact force travels through the stone in a cone shape (like waves in a puddle of water), causing a smooth, curved, shell-shaped flake to detach. If the stone doesn't break like glass, it is garbage to us.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Search for the Right Stone <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Where to find the raw material? At the bottom of rivers, near ravines, or in areas rich in limestone. You are looking for Flint (a gray or black, shiny, and hard stone) or Chert. <LINE> <LINE> If you are lucky, you can find thick glass or the bases of old bottles in the city; glass behaves exactly like the finest volcanic obsidian. A thick piece of porcelain from a destroyed toilet can also be knapped into a lethal arrowhead if you know what you are doing.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Stonebreaker's Kit <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To begin, you need three simple tools. You don't need to buy them; you can find them in the woods. <LINE> <LINE> 1. The Hard Percussor (Hammerstone): A round, solid stone, about the size of a large egg, that won't crumble. <LINE> 2. The Soft Percussor (Billet): A heavy piece of deer antler or extremely hard wood. <LINE> 3. The Pressure Flaker: A thick stick with a sharp piece of bone or a thick copper nail bound to the tip. This is what you'll use to make the teeth of your blade.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Protection (Eye Safety) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Pay close attention: when you strike flint, stone flakes shoot through the air at bullet speed. They are sharper than shaving razors. <LINE> <LINE> If one of these flakes hits your eye, you will go blind on one side instantly. At the end of the world, one-eyed men die fast. Before delivering the first hammer blow, put on safety glasses. If you don't have glasses, improvise any barrier of clear plastic or glass. And always, always place a thick piece of leather (Leather Pad) over your leg when supporting the stone.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Direct Percussion (The First Blow) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The process begins with Direct Percussion using your Hard Percussor. You have taken a raw piece of flint (the Nodule) and want to remove the dirty, useless outer crust (the Cortex). <LINE> <LINE> Hold the stone loose in your left hand (protected by leather). With the round stone in your right hand, deliver precise blows to the edge of the nodule to tear off large chunks. You are not trying to cut the stone in half; you are trying to 'peel' it to reveal the smooth, shiny material inside.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Angle of Attack <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The beginner's biggest frustration is striking the stone until crushing it, but failing to remove any flakes. This happens out of ignorance of the Angle. <LINE> <LINE> You never strike the stone directly from top to bottom (at 90 degrees), otherwise it just cracks into square blocks. You must strike the edge of the stone at an angle smaller than 90 degrees (as if scraping the tip), and the blow must go 'in and down'. This force vector is what makes the shockwave travel beneath the surface and detach the thin flake.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Preparing the Platform <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before each blow, you must prepare the 'Percussion Platform'. The force needs a flat place to enter the stone. <LINE> <LINE> If the edge where you want to strike is too thin and crumbly, your blow will only crush powder and no flake will come out. You need to take another smaller stone and gently grind the edge (Abrading) to remove weak parts, creating a solid, dull, and reliable platform to receive the impact of your stone hammer. Without preparation, there is no clean knapping.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Extracting the Spall (The Blank) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> After cleaning the nodule, your goal is to detach a 'Spall'. The Spall is a giant, large, and flat flake that falls from the core rock. This giant flake is NOT the waste; it is what will turn into your knife. <LINE> <LINE> The round piece left in your hand can be thrown away (or kept to make small points). Take that flat flake that fell off. It is your Blank. Now, our job becomes reducing, thinning, and sharpening it on both sides.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Kentucky Geology Guide <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first volume, we understood the basic mechanics of knapping: the physics of conchoidal fracture and the use of percussors. But knowing how to strike a stone is useless if you are striking the wrong material. <LINE> <LINE> Kentucky's soil is not just grass and mud; it is an immense mineral archive holding the best secrets of the Stone Age. <LINE> <LINE> This second volume is your geological survival map. We are going to analyze the rock structure of our state, the limestone outcrops, and the riverbeds where the best nodules of Chert and Flint are hidden. Learn to read the earth to arm your arsenal.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Karst Topography and Caves <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Kentucky possesses one of the vastest karst topographies in the world, full of sinkholes, swallow holes, and complex underground cave systems. <LINE> <LINE> The ceilings and walls of these caves are made of ancient limestone that has never seen sunlight or suffered from the extreme weather of the surface. <LINE> <LINE> If you have the courage to explore small grottoes or geological depressions in Knox Country's dense forests, use a flashlight to inspect low walls. Cave Chert is usually in a perfect state of conservation, retaining the rock's natural moisture (Quarry Sap), which makes knapping incredibly smooth and predictable.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Quartz and Fossil Inclusions <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When cracking open a rustic Chert nodule in the middle of the woods, inspect the core before loading the weight into your backpack. Many Kentucky rocks contain 'Inclusions'. <LINE> <LINE> These are small trapped marine fossils (like crinoids or ancient shells) or cavities filled with glittering quartz crystals (Geodes). <LINE> <LINE> Though beautiful, fossils and crystals interrupt conchoidal fracture. When your strike's wave hits a hard fossil or a crystal void, the force ricochets and destroys the flake's alignment, ruining the blade. Good material must be smooth and uniform, without surprises inside.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wedge Extraction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You found a perfect St. Louis nodule in a limestone hillside wall in Muldraugh, but it is firmly embedded in the bedrock. Trying to strike it directly with a percussor will crush the edge of the useful stone. <LINE> <LINE> Use rustic mining techniques. <LINE> <LINE> Find natural crevices in the limestone around the nodule using a hard branch or an iron bar. Hammer dry wooden wedges into these crevices and pour water on them. The wood will absorb moisture, swelling with immense force inside the rock, breaking the surrounding limestone and freeing the Chert nodule intact and free of impact damage.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Urban Geology (Industrial Glass) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you are trapped on the asphalt of Muldraugh or West Point and the forest is too dangerous, shift your geological focus to industrial scrap. The city is a repository of artificial silicon. <LINE> <LINE> Look for remnants of commercial buildings that used heavy Plate Glass, such as shop display windows or thick mirrors. <LINE> <LINE> Glass over one centimeter thick behaves exactly like the purest obsidian in the world. It has no impurities, possesses no internal fossils, and breaks in surgical conchoidal fashion. You can knap commercial window glass chunks until turning them into translucent, lethal arrowheads.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Frost Effect on Soil <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Kentucky's winter alters the dynamic of lithic gathering. When temperatures drop below freezing, water trapped in microscopic fissures of exposed rocks freezes and expands. <LINE> <LINE> This process (Frost Wedging) cracks surface nodules on its own during the cold season. <LINE> <LINE> Collecting stones from the ground in the dead of winter is a risk; almost all will be 'doomed' by internal frost. If you need stone in the winter, dig a few inches into the forest dirt to reach rocks that were below the soil's frost line, where earth temperature remains stable.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mineral Map Complete <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You have completed reading the geological map. Now, when you walk Muldraugh's roads or West Point's gravel shores, you don't just see gray stones and dirt. You perceive St. Louis limestone, Fort Payne nodules, and industrial glass from dead storefronts. <LINE> <LINE> Your hands know where to find the foundation for cutting tools. The lithic arsenal is mapped in your mind. <LINE> <LINE> But finding the right rock is only half the journey. The raw shape needs to turn into fine engineering. In Volume Three, 'Lithic Technology Manual 1993', we will enter the design lab. We will learn the exact geometry of flakes, ridge control, and the creation of symmetrical bifacial tools. Keep your safety glasses close.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Pennyroyal Plateau <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The central and western region of Kentucky is dominated by a geological formation known as the Pennyroyal Plateau (or Mississippian Plateau). To a knapper, this place is the promised land. <LINE> <LINE> This entire area rests upon massive layers of ancient carbonate rocks, deposited millions of years ago by prehistoric oceans. <LINE> <LINE> Where there is ancient limestone, there is Chert. As acidic rainwater penetrated the rock throughout the eras, it dissolved the calcium and deposited pure nodules of concentrated silica. If you are in this region, your search for high-quality stones will be ten times easier.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Muldraugh Chert (The Outcrop) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We are in Knox County, and our biggest geographical feature is the Muldraugh escarpment (Muldraugh Hill). This immense rustic ridge cuts through the landscape and is a lithic goldmine. <LINE> <LINE> Erosion caused by wind and rain on the hillsides constantly exposes the deep layers of rock. <LINE> <LINE> Walk along the bases of Muldraugh's steep slopes or explore paths cleared by excavators on dirt roads. You will notice rounded nodules, dark gray or yellowish in color, projecting directly out of the soft limestone walls. This is Muldraugh Chert, the foundation of your local survival.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> St. Louis Limestone <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you want the purest material in the state, you must learn to identify the St. Louis Limestone formation. It is a dense, gray rock layer that outcrops in various parts of Kentucky. <LINE> <LINE> The Chert extracted from this specific formation is famous for its incredibly smooth texture, almost like wax or frosted glass. <LINE> <LINE> It varies from a bluish gray to a deep black. When you break open a fresh St. Louis nodule, the resulting blade is so homogeneous that it allows high-precision pressure flaking, ideal for making long knives and perfect spearheads.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> River Gravels <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you don't have heavy tools to pry nodules out of Muldraugh's stone walls, let nature itself do the hard work for you. Go to the rivers. <LINE> <LINE> The Ohio River to the north and the Salt River are gigantic natural rock sorters. <LINE> <LINE> Strong currents drag rock pieces down mountains for thousands of years. This rolling process breaks weak, soft stones (like sandstone and shale), leaving only the hardest, most resistant rocks intact on gravel banks. Walking along the gravel shores at low tide in Riverside or West Point will reveal hundreds of ready blanks.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Geological Sound Test <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When you are scouring a gravel bank along the edge of the Ohio River, you will see thousands of similar stones. How to know which one is high-quality Chert and which is just a useless piece of limestone? Use your ears. <LINE> <LINE> Take the suspect stone and tap it lightly with a small hard percussor of quartz. <LINE> <LINE> If the resulting sound is a dull pop, like a dry dirt 'thud', the stone is full of internal fractures or is soft limestone; throw it away. If the sound is a sharp, clean, almost metallic ring, like a bell or glass clinking, the molecular structure is intact and pure. Take it back to base.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fort Payne Chert <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Moving a bit further south in the state, you will cross into the Fort Payne formation. Fort Payne Chert is abundant, rustic, and thick. <LINE> <LINE> It usually has a light gray color, sometimes with white mottling or coarse textures resembling chalk. <LINE> <LINE> It is not a pretty or sophisticated material like St. Louis, and requires a lot more arm power using a hard stone percussor to extract the initial flakes. But Fort Payne has a crucial advantage: it is extremely tough and does not easily break on impact, making it the perfect rock for making heavy axes and wedges for splitting wood.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Harrison County Chert <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Just beyond our northern border, crossing the Ohio River into Indiana, lies the famous Harrison County Chert (also known as Indiana Flint). Due to ancient trade and river transport, it is easily found on the northern shores of West Point. <LINE> <LINE> This material is the crown jewel of local lithic geology. It possesses a shiny dark blue color and a glass-like texture. <LINE> <LINE> It knaps with frightening ease, producing long, clean conchoidal waves with minimal effort from the deer antler. If you spot a bluish rock gleaming in the river gravel, pick it up immediately.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Weathering <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Not every good stone in nature stays good forever. Rocks exposed to the scorching summer sun and freezing winter ice for centuries suffer from Weathering. <LINE> <LINE> Sunlight and abrupt temperature changes expand and contract the stone microscopically, creating an invisible network of internal flaws. <LINE> <LINE> If you collect a Chert nodule that spent years exposed on top of a dry hill, it will explode into useless little pieces as soon as it receives the first strike from your antler billet. Always look for stones that were protected beneath the dirt, in the dense shade of the forest, or buried in the damp mud of a riverbed.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Lithic Technology Manual 1993 <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Previous volumes dealt with brute force and basic geology. From now on, we abandon rustic empiricism and enter the realm of geometry and planning. <LINE> <LINE> Flint Knapping is not a game of luck; it is applied physics. This 1993 technical manual focuses on 'Bifacial Reduction', platform control, and shockwave propagation. If you want to stop making ugly pointed rocks and start sculpting blades that rival metallic scalpels, study these pages with anatomical attention.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Heat Treatment (Stone Alchemy) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If your local chert is too hard, porous, and stubborn to knap cleanly, you can use the ancestral technique of Heat Treatment. <LINE> <LINE> Bury your chert blanks under four inches of clean sand in the ground. Build a large campfire on top of the sand and let it burn for 24 hours, then let it cool very slowly for another 24 hours. The heat bakes the silica, closing microscopic pores and fusing the crystalline structure. The stone will emerge shiny, buttery, and incredibly easier to knap (though more fragile).
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Transition to Pressure <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When your piece (the Preform) is thin and nearly the size of a knife, percussion strikes become too dangerous. The force of an impact can snap it in half. <LINE> <LINE> The manual dictates an immediate transition to 'Pressure Flaking'. Grab your copper or bone Pressure Flaker. Now, there is no swing. Platform alignment, abrading, and ridges remain the rule, but energy is applied by extreme isometric tension using your own body weight.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Notching for Hafting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You have a perfect sharp blade, but it needs to be secured to a spear or an axe handle (Hafting). Binding a smooth stone to a stick ensures it will slip and fly into your face. <LINE> <LINE> You need to make Notches. Using a thin pressure flaker or the edge of a tiny flake, apply force to the side bases of your blade in a 'C' shape, removing small successive flakes until creating two deep necks at the base. This is where cords and resins will lock the stone to the wooden handle forever.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Serration <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A smooth, sharp obsidian edge cuts skin with surgical perfection, but dulls quickly upon hitting bones or cutting branches. <LINE> <LINE> For brutal survival tasks, you want a Serrated edge. Use a sharp flaker to press deep flakes out of the edge at regular millimetric intervals, leaving 'teeth' projecting between the hollows. A serrated chert knife tears meat, hide, and wood with terrifying aggressiveness, acting as a stone-age handsaw.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Symmetry and Balance <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The difference between a novice and a master in the year 1993 is symmetry. If you place your knife flat on the table and one side is fat while the other is thin, the center of gravity will be misaligned. <LINE> <LINE> If you throw an unbalanced spear, it will veer in the air. If you use an asymmetrical knife, it will force your wrist into a crooked angle, wearing out your ligaments. Bifacial reduction demands that you work both sides of the piece equally, flipping the stone in your hand every minute to ensure the profile is a perfect lens.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> From Geometry to Evaluation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Lithic technology holds no more mysteries for you. Your mind does not just see rock; it sees platforms, ridges, conchoidal fractures, and correct impact angles. Manual engineering has been mastered and you can already haft weapons that will never rust in the rain. <LINE> <LINE> However, there are rocks in the world that defy common knapping, stones that can withstand the heaviest impacts without yielding. How do we test the ultimate durability of material the earth hands us? <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Four, 'Schmidt Rock Hardness Testing Techniques', we will advance to the metrics of pain. We'll explore density tests, the rebound hammer, and how to guarantee your axe isn't destroyed on the first zombie bone it hits. Keep safety glasses nearby.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Flake Anatomy <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before designing a tool, you must understand the flake you remove from the rock. Every flake has a specific anatomy. <LINE> <LINE> The spot where your percussor strikes the stone is the 'Platform'. Just below the impact, the 'Bulb of Percussion' forms, a swelling where energy concentrated before spreading out. The sides are cutting edges, and the end of the flake is the 'Termination'. The ability to read the bulb and termination of flakes falling to the ground will tell you exactly if your force and angle are correct or if they are destroying the core.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mass Rule (Ridges) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The shockwave traveling through stone has a universal rule: energy always follows the path of greatest mass. <LINE> <LINE> If your stone's face is perfectly flat, a flake will spread directionless and die fast. To take a long, perfect flake that traverses the stone's entire face, you must strike exactly on top of a Ridge — an elevated line left by previous flakes. The crest of this ridge functions like a train track, guiding energy straight to the other side.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Centerline <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Most beginners destroy their pieces because they try to knap above the Centerline. <LINE> <LINE> Imagine your stone lying on its side. The imaginary line dividing it exactly in horizontal half is the 'Centerline'. You must NEVER strike a platform that is above this line. If you do, your percussor will crush the edge instead of slicing the stone. Your strike's target (the prepared platform) must always be located BELOW the centerline so the flake successfully 'peels' the lower portion of the piece.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Platform Isolation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You found the ridge and the angle is below the centerline. Is it time to strike? Not yet. You need to 'Isolate' the platform. <LINE> <LINE> Using a small percussor or stone file, remove material from the sides of the exact spot you will strike, leaving the platform slightly projecting (like a small nipple on the stone's edge). Isolation ensures that when the deer antler hits, all energy goes into that exact point instead of dissipating across irrelevant edges.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Abrading <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The final step before the blow is abrading. If your projecting platform is sharp, your antler percussor will only snap it like glass, failing to generate the shockwave. <LINE> <LINE> Vigorously rub an abrasive stone (like sandstone) over the platform until it is rounded, dull, and strong. An abraded platform withstands the percussor's massive impact for a fraction of a second longer, time enough for the bulb of percussion to form and strip away a long flake instead of shattering the edge.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Swing and Follow-Through <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Using a soft percussor (antler Billet or hardwood) requires arc technique. Do not strike the stone and pull your hand straight back. <LINE> <LINE> The strike must be a fluid, circular motion slicing through the air. When the Billet hits the platform, your hand must continue moving down and away from the stone, as if trying to pull the flake to the ground. This Follow-Through drags the energy wave through the piece, ensuring feather-thin terminations instead of abrupt fractures.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fault Diagnosis: Step Fracture <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The knapper's terror is a 'Step Fracture'. The flake begins traveling well, but suddenly stops abruptly, leaving a thick, square step in the middle of your blade. <LINE> <LINE> This happens for three reasons: a blow without enough force, striking above the centerline, or trying to remove a flake across a dip/hollow in the stone's face. This step will form an impassable barrier for subsequent flakes, ruining the piece's reduction if not fixed quickly.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Curing the Step <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You caused a Step Fracture. If you try to strike it directly again, you will only crush it and make the situation worse. <LINE> <LINE> The cure demands geometry. You must flip the stone, go to the opposite edge, and prepare a platform aligning a new ridge coming from behind the step. By firing a strong flake from the other side, the energy wave will travel 'under' the step, undermining its base and ripping the entire flaw off the stone's face. It's high-risk lithic surgery.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Schmidt Rock Hardness Testing Techniques <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your stone axe looks beautiful. Symmetrical, sharp, and perfectly hafted. You raise your arms, strike the first skull or first oak trunk and... your blade shatters into a thousand useless pieces. <LINE> <LINE> Beauty does not mean durability. This 1993 engineering manual, focused on the principles of the Schmidt Hammer, teaches stone metrology. You will learn to test the strength, density, and shock limit of material before spending days knapping a rock that will betray you at the crucial moment.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Detecting Microfratures (Stone Disease) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You have a flint stone with perfect grain and Mohs 7, but it may be secretly 'sick'. Weathering microfractures (freezing in winter) create fault lines invisible to the naked eye inside the block. <LINE> <LINE> How to find them? Moisten the stone nodule with water and place it in the sun. The surface will dry quickly, but water will remain trapped and seeping along the invisible capillary fractures. If you see dark, wet lines forming a spiderweb on the dry flint, throw it away. The block is doomed and will break during knapping.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Edge Crush Test <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You finished the knife and want to make sure the edge will hold up to work before putting it in its sheath. Perform the Crush Test. <LINE> <LINE> Knap a small side edge of the same core rock. Take a hard piece of dry wood (like oak) or a cylindrical piece of old bone. Press the bone hard directly against the edge of the stone blade, pushing and rubbing sideways. It is a brutal and cruel test.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading the Crush <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If your knife's edge sheds dust, crumbles like flour, or the tiny serrations snap off leaving a flat, dull line, the material does not withstand lateral pressure; it is too brittle for bones and joints. <LINE> <LINE> However, if the edge of your stone knife bites into the bone, carving white calcium shavings from the wood or femur without losing a single flint tooth, your blade is approved. It will slice meat joints and won't break when bumping a bone during slaughter.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Weight and Water (Porosity Test) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Dense rock cannot have empty space inside it. Porosity ruins tool strength, making it an inefficient shock sponge. <LINE> <LINE> Take a block of raw stone and weigh it in your hands. Submerge it in a bucket of water for half an hour. Remove it, dry the surface with a cloth, and weigh it again. If the stone is noticeably heavier, it has hundreds of thousands of microscopic pores that absorbed water. It failed. The perfect stone does not absorb a milligram of liquid.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Engineering Applied to the Arsenal <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With an understanding of Schmidt, Mohs, and Microfracture tests, you are no longer knapping stones blindly and praying they don't break. <LINE> <LINE> You test nodules before the first hammer blow. The survival arsenal requires quality control. A hafted spear that shatters upon hitting an enemy's ribs leaves you unarmed in the next second of the fight. Stone metrology guarantees the weapon will finish the battle whole.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Pinnacle of Lithic Geometry <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You found the raw material and proved through engineering that it is indestructible. Now all that's left is to sculpt it into the definitive shape of human lethality. <LINE> <LINE> The Stone Age reached its technological peak in North America long before steel existed. A point so perfect and devastating that it was responsible for hunting mammoths: The Clovis Point. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Five and last, 'Technological Morphometrics of Clovis Artifacts', we will reach master level. You will learn fluted knapping (Fluting) and build the most advanced ballistic weapon bare hands can forge. Sharpen your percussors.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Schmidt Principle (The Rebound) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Civil engineers used the Schmidt Hammer to test concrete hardness on bridges. The tool fires a steel mass against the surface and measures how high that mass 'bounces' back (the Rebound). <LINE> <LINE> At the end of the world, we don't have a Schmidt machine, but we use its physics. The rule is unalterable: hard, elastic, and dense rocks return impact energy. Soft, porous, or fractured rocks absorb energy and the impact dies. Survival demands materials that strike back.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Drop Test <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How to apply the Schmidt principle in the forest? Use the Drop Test. <LINE> <LINE> Find a flat piece of solid steel (like a large tractor nut or a heavy bearing) or a round pebble of pure quartz. Hold the sphere exactly twelve inches high over the flat face of the flint nodule you want to evaluate and drop it. <LINE> <LINE> Don't blink. Pay attention to the height of the bounce and the sound the impact produces.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading the Stone's Rebound <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If the steel sphere hits the nodule, makes a dull 'thud' sound, and barely jumps an inch back, throw the stone away. It is soft, chalky, or full of internal voids. It will crumble in your hand. <LINE> <LINE> If the sphere hits, producing a sharp, bright, metallic ring ('Ping!'), and bounces back almost to your hand, you found a geological monster. This rock has an incredibly dense and connected silica matrix. It will withstand the impact of splitting firewood without collapsing.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mohs Scale Test <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Rebound measures elasticity, but you also need to measure scratch resistance: the Mohs Scale. Talc is level 1, diamond is 10. <LINE> <LINE> Good flint for cutting tools should be at level 7 (Quartz Hardness). How to measure this without lab equipment? Use a piece of industrial glass from a broken window. Glass has a hardness of 5.5. Take the tip of your raw rock and try to scratch the glass hard.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Scratch of Survival <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If the rock slides across the glass, leaving only a trail of powder from the stone itself, the rock is weaker than glass (below 5.5). It will not hold a cutting edge; the blade will dull cutting a simple piece of leather. <LINE> <LINE> If the rock tears the glass surface with a horrible screech, leaving a deep white scratch, congratulations. Your stone is in the level 7 range. It is hard enough to cut meat, bone, and wood and maintain a razor edge through days of constant use.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Toughness vs. Hardness <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Understand this law of materials engineering: Hardness is not the same thing as Toughness. <LINE> <LINE> Common glass and volcanic obsidian are incredibly 'hard' (they scratch other things), but have zero 'toughness' (they shatter under impact). A pumice stone has low hardness but high toughness (it dents instead of shattering). For a thin arrowhead meant to slice arteries, you want extreme hardness. For a heavy axe that will strike doors and zombie bones, you need toughness. The material cannot be brittle.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Grain Size Analysis <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You can predict a rock's toughness using sight. Break off a small piece of the nodule and look at the fresh surface against the sunlight. <LINE> <LINE> If the surface is smooth, shiny, and glassy like porcelain (Fine Grain), the stone will cut like a scalpel but will be brittle (low toughness). If the surface is slightly rough, dull, and looks like very fine sandpaper (Medium/Coarse Grain), the blade won't be as surgical, but internal grains will stop cracks from spreading. Medium Grain is the supreme material for heavy-duty work.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Spark Test (Steel and Stone) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A truly hard rock has a secret chemical property: it can melt steel under friction. <LINE> <LINE> Take the spine of a carbon steel knife or an iron file. Hold your stone in hand and strike the edge of the stone against the steel corner in a scraping downward stroke. Pure flint is so hard that upon striking, it shaves off microscopic flakes of steel. Instant friction ignites this steel in the air, creating a shower of orange sparks. If the stone generates fire, it is worthy of your effort.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Technological Morphometrics of Clovis Artifacts <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You learned to skin stone, read geology, and test nodule resistance. Your knives cut and your axes split firewood. <LINE> <LINE> But raw survival is not the human limit. The human limit was reached thirteen thousand years ago on the plains of North America, when Ice Age hunters forged a weapon so devastatingly perfect that it allowed them to hunt mammoths to extinction: The Clovis Point. <LINE> <LINE> This is Master level. Prepare for lethal geometry.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Split-Shaft Hafting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Clovis design was made for a specific type of hafting. Take your sturdy wooden shaft and make a deep slit in its tip (Split-Shaft). <LINE> <LINE> Slide the fluted base of the Clovis Point into this slit. The two halves of the shaft wood will fit PERFECTLY inside the grooves (flutes) you made on both sides of the stone. The stone and wood now have a perfectly smooth, continuous profile, reducing aerodynamic drag and flesh penetration friction to nearly zero.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sinew <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> No plant cord holds a Clovis Point under the impact of heavy hunting. You need animal Sinew. <LINE> <LINE> Take the tendons from the back or legs of hunted deer, dry them, and beat them until they turn into thin threads. Sinew is magic: when you chew or wet it, it softens. Bind the stone point to the wood using wet sinew wrapped very tightly. When the sinew dries, it will shrink brutally, creating a vacuum grip as strong as steel clamps.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Pine Pitch <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To seal the sinew and lock the stone's micro-movement, you will make ancient glue: Pine Pitch Glue. <LINE> <LINE> Collect sticky sap from pine trees. Melt it over the fire (careful, it is highly flammable). Mix with very fine charcoal powder (to give molecular structure) and dried, ground herbivore dung (to prevent the resin from breaking like glass when it cools). Pour the hot, black glue over the bound sinew and shape it with a stick. When it cools, you will have an indestructible prehistoric epoxy.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Atlatl Dart <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Clovis Point was rarely used on hand spears for melee thrusts; it was a flight projectile. It crowned Darts thrown by an Atlatl (Spear Thrower). <LINE> <LINE> The Atlatl is a piece of wood with a hook at the end that fits into the bottom of the dart. It acts as an extension of your arm, adding brutal leverage to the throw. A dart with a Clovis Point thrown by an Atlatl travels at over 150 km/h, ripping through thick hide and bone before you hear the impact.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Lithic Terminal Ballistics <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Steel pushes flesh aside upon penetrating. A Clovis Point of flaked flint cuts flesh at a cellular level. <LINE> <LINE> The bleeding caused by a sharp lithic point under Atlatl leverage is hemorrhagic and catastrophic. The long, slender Clovis shape meets no resistance in tissue, while the smooth, flush wooden shaft follows the channel without drag. It is the ultimate union of geometric intelligence with volcanic brutality. You are no longer playing at survival; you are the apex predator.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Silence of the Cold Forge <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The books are finished. We walked the path of dust to the ultimate weapon. <LINE> <LINE> You understood conchoidal fracture, mined the right rocks in the entrails of Kentucky, read flint ridges, tested density through metallic pain, and sculpted the slender, bloody perfection of the Clovis Point. <LINE> <LINE> The city may crumble, steel may turn into red rust powder, and gunpowder may run out. But stone is eternal. Collect your Atlatl and your newly glued dart. The top of the food chain belongs to you again.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Clovis Geometry <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A Clovis Point is not a simple triangular spearhead. It is a piece of aerodynamic engineering. <LINE> <LINE> It possesses a lanceolate shape (like a long, slender willow leaf), with perfectly sharp, bifacial edges. But what separates it from all other stones in the world is not the tip; it is the base. The Clovis base is slightly concave, designed with a mathematical precision that allows the stone to integrate with the wooden shaft as if they were a single organism.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fluting <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The absolute secret of Clovis technology is 'Fluting'. <LINE> <LINE> A flute is a long, hollow, shallow channel that rises through the center of the stone point's base toward the middle of the blade, looking like a groove sculpted into both sides of the rock face. <LINE> <LINE> Stripping away this perfect central flake is the most dangerous and difficult move in all of flint knapping. A one-millimeter error in angle or a gram too much force, and the entire point you spent hours thinning snaps in half in your hands.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Flute Physics <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Why did the ancients risk breaking the weapon at the last second just to make this channel in the center? The answer is Shock Absorption and Ballistics. <LINE> <LINE> When the spear hits a hard target, impact energy travels back to the point. The flute thins the center of the base, making it slightly flexible. It acts as a shock absorber. Additionally, the grooves on both sides serve as massive bleeding channels (Fullers), preventing the wound from closing around the spear shaft.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Nipple Platform <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To create the flute, you cannot simply strike the straight base. You need to sculpt a sacrificial platform. <LINE> <LINE> Using very careful pressure flaking, you isolate exactly the center of your point's concave base, leaving a small prominent peak of stone there. This peak is called a 'Nipple'. It is the hyper-focused target. You will grind this nipple until it is dull, so it can receive the biggest blow of its life without crumbling instantly.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Indirect Percussion (The Punch) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You are not going to strike the Nipple by swinging your antler Billet loose in the air; it is impossible to guarantee the perfect angle with a free swing. <LINE> <LINE> You will use 'Indirect Percussion'. Place your spearpoint vertically, secured firmly to the ground or between your leather knees. Take a punch (a long, straight piece of hard bone or copper) and place its tip exactly over the Nipple. You do not strike the stone; you strike the top of the punch with your hard percussor, transferring energy in a straight line.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fluting Strike <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Breathe. Hold the punch at the exact angle (slightly tilted toward the base of the nipple). <LINE> <LINE> Deliver a sharp, heavy, and incredibly fast blow to the top of the punch. If the physics are right and the rock face's ridges are perfectly aligned, you will hear a crystal snap. A long, straight, beautiful flake will detach from the stone's center and fall to the ground. You have just fluted the first side of your Clovis Point. Now, pray and repeat the process on the opposite side.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Outrepássé (The Maximum Risk) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before fluting, Clovis artisans used an insane technique to thin the blade called 'Overshot Flaking' (Outrepássé). <LINE> <LINE> Instead of striking the edge to remove a flake that goes to the stone's center, they prepared the platform at such an aggressive angle that the shockwave traveled across the entire face of the stone and CUT the edge on the other side, taking a chunk of the opposite margin along. This thins the stone brutally and leaves it perfectly flat, but a minimal error cuts the spear in half.
IGUI_BookFlintKnapping5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Edge Grinding <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You finished knapping and the fluting is perfect. The point is razor-sharp from top to bottom. If you bind this to wood right now, the sharp edges of the base themselves will cut your cords when the weapon suffers impact. <LINE> <LINE> The master's final touch is 'Edge Grinding'. Take an abrasive stone and aggressively rub only the lower side edges of the point's base and the inside of the cavity (where wood and cord will touch) until they are completely dull and polished.
IGUI_BookForaging1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> A Feast in the Forest <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Supermarkets have turned modern humans into spoiled and blind animals. We walk through a forest and see only useless weeds and dry leaves. But for our ancestors, the forest was the largest supermarket on the planet. <LINE> <LINE> This first volume will cure your green blindness. Learn to read the colors, shapes, and scents that the earth offers us. From today on, you will never feel hungry near a damp woodland again.
