Taking the piece out of the Glory Hole and touching it to the cold metal of the table can cause it to shatter instantly. The annealing oven (Annealer) must lower the temperature over forty-eight consecutive hours. One degree less at the wrong time, and your work turns to dust.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Cold Shop <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The piece has cooled. It is heavy, has an oily shine, and emits a high-pitched musical tone, like a bell, if you flick it with your fingernail (the hallmark of lead). But Carlow's work hasn't begun yet. <LINE> <LINE> We enter the Cold Shop. You will need abrasive wheels. You can use grinding wheels meant for sharpening steel tools (carborundum stone). Attach this stone disk to a motor (if you have power) or a belt-driven foot-pedal lathe. Crystal is not blown for beauty; it is carved.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Geometric Roughing Out <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The stone wheel is spinning. A constant drip of water MUST fall onto the wheel. Without water, friction will melt the glass locally, breaking the piece, and raise deadly clouds of silica and lead dust (Silicosis). <LINE> <LINE> Hold your heavy crystal vessel with both hands and press it firmly against the edge of the spinning stone wheel. The wheel will devour the glass, tearing deep grooves into the thick wall of your piece. This is where you create the classic diamond and crisscross star patterns.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Venetian Glass <LINE> An Electron Microprobe Analysis <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Lead gave us weight and strength in volume four. But now, we look at absurd lightness. This is the mountaintop. <LINE> <LINE> Before the world stopped, a chemical archaeology team used an Electron Microprobe to bombard ancient fragments from Murano Island (Venice) and discover how, in the 15th century, they created glass so thin and colorful it seemed like magic. <LINE> <LINE> We have the translation of that data. We will abandon the dark utilitarianism of survival and revive impossible art. We will color the fire.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Latticino and Reticello <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Once cooled, the long colored canes are cut into pencil-sized pieces and aligned side by side on a ceramic plate. <LINE> <LINE> They are heated until they melt into each other, forming a flat striped mat. The glassmaker rolls a hot glass core over this mat, gathering the stripes. By blowing and twisting, the stripes swirl into the classic spiral pattern (Latticino). If you cross two bubbles twisted in opposite directions, it forms a network of diamonds with a micro air bubble trapped at each intersection (Reticello).
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Millefiori (A Field of a Thousand Flowers) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The pinnacle of glass geometry is Millefiori. Instead of a single color in the center, the glassmaker layers glass of different colors (e.g., red, white, blue), molding the mass into a star shape using jacks before stretching it into a long cane. <LINE> <LINE> When this long glass cane is cut into cold slices, each small glass disk shows a perfect pattern of a flower with a red core, white petals, and blue borders. These slices are then fused onto a bubble of colorless glass, creating a vessel that looks entirely made of suspended flowers.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Diamond Shears and the Hot Dance <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Venetian fragility demands precise tools. Unlike common glass, a Murano artisan used 'Diamond Shears' — tongs that snip away excess hot glass with the precision of a surgeon cutting thread. <LINE> <LINE> The detailing of swan wings, dragons, or wavy goblet stems is done by pinching hot glass in the air, stretching and bending it in three or four seconds before it freezes. The margin of error is zero.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fire of Multiple Pots <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the apocalypse, making flat glass required a single crucible. To achieve Murano levels at your base, you will need to rebuild your furnace. <LINE> <LINE> A Murano kiln demands arched openings and multiple small crucibles heating simultaneously in the same furnace. One pot for clear, one for cobalt blue, one for white Lattimo. Managing the flames and oxygen levels of three pools of volatile chemistry while stretching filigree lines is the absolute peak of low-tech human engineering.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Art Above Survival <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Someone in camp will ask you: Why burn firewood, risk lead poisoning, and spend hours taming heat just to create a blue-striped wine goblet in a land destroyed by the dead? <LINE> <LINE> The answer does not lie in calories or shelter. The answer is the soul. Surviving is the physical act of keeping blood circulating; Art is proof that humanity is still alive. A Reticello goblet gleaming under the campfire light is a silent cry against the savagery of our new world.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Last Breath <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> And with this, the furnace cools. The Glass journey is over. <LINE> <LINE> We walked from lightning striking sand and ancient Egyptian core-formed jars, through the hollow pipe revolution, forging crude utility jars, mastering cold cuts of Irish crystal with lead and powder, all the way to the ethereal ballet of gold and cobalt threads of Murano Island. <LINE> <LINE> You no longer look at river sand as dust; you perceive it as raw material for rainbows, waiting for your lab's heat. Close the furnace door. Your base shines now.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Electron Readings <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The microprobe revealed Venice's greatest secret: they did not use ordinary sand. The masters of Murano crushed incredibly pure quartz pebbles harvested from rivers. <LINE> <LINE> This pure silica, mixed with ashes from marine plants (rich in sodium), created a glass that did not harden quickly upon leaving the kiln. This extended Long Working Time is what allowed the artisan to stretch and twist glass into rods as thin as hairs without them breaking. The secret of Venetian art was time.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Glassmaker's Soap (Manganese) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Even with clean quartz, iron impurities still tinted glass a pale, sickly green. The probe detected the chemical antidote in Renaissance goblets: Manganese Oxide. <LINE> <LINE> The Venetians called it 'Glassmaker's Soap'. When you throw a pinch of manganese into the boiling crucible, it reacts with iron, chemically oxidizing it, neutralizing the green color and leaving the glass clear as the purest water. But too much manganese turns the glass into a deep, somber purple.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Lattimo (Milky Glass) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> One of the greatest achievements was 'Lattimo', a completely opaque, white glass that imitated Chinese porcelain (an unattainable luxury at the time). <LINE> <LINE> How does a survivor make white? Chemistry reveals: Bone Ash. Take old animal bones, burn them in the fire until they turn into calcified ash, and add it to the frit. Phosphorus and calcium from the bone do not dissolve in liquid glass; they remain suspended as microcrystals. The result is a thick, milky glass, the base for all filigree decorations.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Color Chemistry (Blue and Green) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Making colorless glass is science; coloring glass is metallic sorcery. If you rummage through urban trash and find old, oxidized (green) copper wires, you found your painting palette. <LINE> <LINE> A handful of Copper Oxide in the crucible yields a vibrant emerald-green glass. If you add elemental Cobalt salts (extremely rare nowadays, sometimes found in heavy machinery batteries or old paints), the glass will take on a Sapphire Blue so deep it swallows surrounding light.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Murano's Blood (Rubino Oro) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Red was always the most fickle and impossible color to forge. Common attempts result in dirty brown. The Venetians created 'Rubino Oro' (Ruby Red). <LINE> <LINE> The shocking secret of the microprobe: perfect red demands pure Gold. Dissolving a minuscule amount of gold chloride into the vitreous mass creates microscopic colloidal particles that absorb all light colors, reflecting only a dazzling, bloody red. In the apocalypse, melting a wedding band in the furnace is the price to pay for ruby beauty.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chalcedony (Imitating Rock) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Venetian vanity knew no bounds. They created 'Chalcedony' glass to mimic natural veins of marble, agate, and semi-precious stones. <LINE> <LINE> This required mastering multiple pots. Glass of various dark and milky colors is melted in different crucibles. Then, the artisan gathers the different glass masses, layering them at the tip of the pipe, and twists them furiously. When blown, the colors do not blend completely; they form swirling veins and streaks that perfectly mimic earth's geology.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Avventurina (Star Dust) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> 'Avventurina' is a type of translucent brown glass that looks full of gold dust glittering inside. The name comes from 'avventura' (chance), as it was diabolically hard to make without failing. <LINE> <LINE> It is made by supersaturating molten glass with massive amounts of copper powder and then cooling the furnace absurdly slowly. In this slow cooling, pure copper crystallizes and separates from the glass, forming microscopic metallic triangles that glint against light like a trapped galaxy.
IGUI_BookGlassmaking5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Birth of Filigree (Cane Work) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The spiral stripes of ancient Murano goblets were not painted; the color was inside the glass itself. This is the Cane Work technique. <LINE> <LINE> The artisan creates a thick cylinder of clear glass. He dips this cylinder into white Lattimo glass, and then coats everything with more clear glass. Two men connect metal rods to both ends of this hot mass and run in opposite directions across the factory, pulling the glass like chewing gum until it stretches into a thin cane dozens of meters long, with the color trapped perfectly in the center.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> A Tale of St. Francis <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Saint Francis of Assisi called the birds his brothers and the wolves his friends. He understood something that modern man, locked away in his concrete cities, has forgotten: we are not the masters of the earth, we are its caretakers. <LINE> <LINE> This short manual was written for those who wish to bring animal life back to their backyards and farms. Caring for an animal is not like fixing a tractor or harvesting a potato. You are dealing with a soul that breathes, feels pain, fears the unknown, and depends entirely on you. <LINE> <LINE> Before we talk about feed, pens, and medicine, we need to talk about your soul. If you lack patience and compassion, close this book. Animals do not need bosses; they need guides.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Food Bridge (Treats) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you take in a skittish or traumatized animal, the way to its heart is not through force, it is through its stomach. Food is the ultimate bridge to breaking down distrust. <LINE> <LINE> But do not just throw the food on the ground and walk away. Use food to build your positive image. Bring small treats that they love (apple slices for pigs, sweet carrot chunks for sheep). <LINE> <LINE> Sit on a bucket in the middle of the pasture with the food in your hand and remain silent. Do not call them. Let curiosity and greed conquer their fear. When they eat from your open palm, the pact of friendship has been sealed. Never raise a hand to strike an animal that has just eaten from it.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Clean Water: The Universal Right <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> It is a terrible crime to see animals drinking green water, full of rotting algae and mud, in waterers that haven't been washed in months. If you wouldn't drink that water, do not force your creatures to drink it. <LINE> <LINE> Dirty water is the primary vector for intestinal parasites and severe diseases in livestock. Water must be changed and troughs scrubbed with a brush and mild soap regularly. <LINE> <LINE> In the suffocating heat of a Kentucky summer, cows and pigs can consume dozens of liters a day. Dry up the water sources, and their kidneys will fail in less than forty-eight hours. Abundant fresh water is the most basic demonstration of your love for the herd.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hierarchy (The Alpha Animal) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When you place several animals in a pen, they do not form a democracy; they create a brutal monarchy. There will always be an 'Alpha' animal (be it the oldest cow or the strongest pig) that will dictate the rules. <LINE> <LINE> The Alpha will eat first and push the weaker ones and the young away from the trough. If you are not observant, your strongest animal will become obese while the weakest will waste away into malnutrition, even if you put plenty of food in the pen. <LINE> <LINE> Your duty is to spread the food across several troughs placed far apart from one another. The Alpha cannot be in three places at once. Protect the weak by ensuring they have a dish far from the eyes of the king of the pen.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Silent Suffering <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the wild, if a wolf notices a sheep limping, that is the one it will hunt. Because of this terrible instinct, prey have learned to hide their own pain until the last possible moment. <LINE> <LINE> By the time a pasture animal lies on the ground, groans, and refuses to stand up to eat, the sickness is already in a very grave, often fatal stage. It has struggled to hide its pain from you for days. <LINE> <LINE> You must observe the herd daily, looking for early signs: an animal standing isolated in a corner, drooped ears, dull eyes, a dry cough, or one that fails to join the others at feeding time. Early detection is the only medicine that works on a farm.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Weight of Life <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I need to be very honest with you before we finish. Owning animals means losing your right to time off. Livestock do not understand Sundays, holidays, or blizzards. <LINE> <LINE> If you have the flu, burning with fever, and a sub-zero blizzard is raging outside, the animals will still be there, penned up, waiting for you to break the ice in their waterer and bring them hay. They cannot open the refrigerator door. They depend on you to breathe tomorrow morning. <LINE> <LINE> It is a daily burden that tires the arms and weighs on the soul. But the reward of walking into a barn and being greeted by small bleats of joy and wet noses nudging you affectionately... that heals the ache.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Journey Begins <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Saint Francis believed that respect for all creatures made us better humans. You have reached the end of your first lesson. You have understood that you do not dominate nature through force, but through constancy, patience, and empathy. <LINE> <LINE> If you master the lessons in this tale, your animals will not try to break the fence to flee from you; they will stay near the gate waiting for you to return. <LINE> <LINE> But affection does not fix broken bones or nutritional deficiencies. In Volume Two, 'Basic Animal Welfare', we will abandon philosophy and dive into manual labor: proper pens, caloric nutrition, and primary veterinary health. Treat your beasts with honor, and I will see you in the next reading.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Pact of Domestication <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Thousands of years ago, humanity made a silent pact with the herds. We took cows, sheep, and pigs out of the wild. We stripped them of their ability to flee from predators and to migrate in search of green pastures. <LINE> <LINE> In return, we promised them safety, shelter, and abundant food. When you place a fence around a pasture and lock the gate, you assume a sacred debt. <LINE> <LINE> If you forget to water your garden, the plants die in silence. If you forget to feed your animals or leave them without water in the summer sun, you are committing an unforgivable cruelty against creatures that trusted you with their very lives.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Language of Silence <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your dog might bark when it wants to play, but the vast majority of farm animals live in a world of dense silence. A sheep will not scream to let you know it is in pain; a calf will not cry because it is afraid of you. <LINE> <LINE> They speak through body language. The movement of their ears, the tension in their neck muscles, the stamping of a hoof on the ground, or the nervous twitch of a tail. <LINE> <LINE> A good caretaker learns to read this silent language. If you walk into the barn and the horse's ears are pinned back flat against its head and the whites of its eyes are showing, it is terrified or furious. Back away. Approach only when the ears are relaxed and turned forward, showing curiosity.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Understanding the Prey Mind <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To care for pasture animals (cows, sheep, goats, and chickens), you must understand a fundamental biological fact: they were born to be someone's dinner. They are Prey. <LINE> <LINE> A prey's mind is governed by the constant fear of being devoured. Their eyes are on the sides of their head so they can see nearly 360 degrees around them, searching for wolves in the grass. <LINE> <LINE> If you run toward a sheep waving your arms and shouting, its primate instinct won't see an owner bringing food; it will see a predator attacking. Its response will be blind panic. To work with prey, you must abandon your predator stance.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Art of Approach <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you approach an animal that is afraid of you? With the slowness of a cloud in the sky. Never walk in a harsh, straight line directly toward a timid animal's face, staring intently into its eyes (staring is what wolves do before they spring). <LINE> <LINE> Walk in a casual zigzag pattern, looking away to the sides. Keep your arms relaxed at your sides. Show it that you have no intention of hunting it. <LINE> <LINE> Once you are close, do not reach your hand out over its head. Movements coming from above simulate birds of prey or predators pouncing from trees. Reach your hand out from below, at muzzle height, and let the animal take the final step to sniff you. Scent is their handshake.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Melody of the Human Voice <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Animals do not understand English vocabulary, but they are experts at interpreting tones of voice. If you shout, curse, or speak in a high-pitched, rapid manner, you will transmit stress and chaos to the entire herd. <LINE> <LINE> Talk to your animals. Sing to them. When you enter the dark barn in the morning, do not flip the lights on all at once and do not clatter the buckets. Murmur a soft song or speak in a low, deep, rhythmic tone of voice. <LINE> <LINE> 'Good morning, big girl. Steady, I'm here.' The constancy of your voice soothes the nerves of prey. They associate that gentle, low hum with the arrival of fresh hay and clean water.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Power of Touch <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When an animal finally allows you to touch it, you have been accepted into its circle of trust. Do not waste that by being rough. <LINE> <LINE> Avoid touching the face, ears, or hind legs of unaccustomed animals. These are areas of extreme vulnerability. The safest and most comforting place to stroke a herbivore is the base of the neck or the shoulders. <LINE> <LINE> Do not pat them with quick, light taps; this irritates the skin like landing flies. Use your entire palm and apply firm, long, slow pressure, like a massage. This is how their mothers licked them when they were young. A firm touch says: 'I am touching you, and you are safe.'
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Magic of Routine <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The natural world is chaotic, full of storms and dangers. What domesticated animals crave above all things is predictability. They love routine more than they love sweet apples. <LINE> <LINE> Establish a strict schedule and do not deviate from it. If you feed the pigs and cows at six in the morning and five in the afternoon, do it rain or shine. If you are two hours late, they will become anxious, stressed, and will begin walking in circles and fighting among themselves. <LINE> <LINE> Routine creates peace in the barn. When they know exactly what is going to happen, who is walking through the door, and when the food will drop into the trough, their biological fear vanishes.
IGUI_BookHusbandry1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Barn: A Sanctuary <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Many people build pens thinking they are merely assembling wooden prisons so that the food doesn't escape. But to the herd, the barn is their safe cave. It is their refuge from the darkness of the night. <LINE> <LINE> Their sanctuary must be kept clean. An animal does not willingly defecate where it sleeps; they only become filthy if you fail to give them enough space. <LINE> <LINE> Lay down fresh, golden straw on the floor for them to sleep on. A clean straw floor in the winter is a warm bed that insulates against the cold of the concrete and prevents the animals' joints from falling ill. Sweep out the manure daily. Respect their roof and they will grow strong.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Animal Welfare <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first volume, we talked about the philosophy of care and the importance of looking at animals with empathy. Now, it is time to roll up our sleeves. Animal welfare is not an abstract or sentimental concept; in farm practice, it is measured in kilograms of feed, square meters of clean area, and the absence of disease. <LINE> <LINE> If an animal lives under constant stress, hungry, cold, or surrounded by filth, its body reacts in the only way biology allows: it wastes away. Stressed cows dry up their milk, sheep lose the quality of their wool, chickens stop laying eggs, and pigs lose weight rapidly. <LINE> <LINE> Caring for the welfare of your herd is what separates a successful breeder from a negligent hoarder. Let's learn the basic rules of infrastructure, hygiene, and nutrition to keep your creatures healthy and productive.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Hoof Care <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The nails of farm animals are hooves made of keratin. In the wild, they walk miles over rocky terrain, which wears the hoof down naturally. In a soft pen or on barn straw, the hoof grows continuously, curls downward, and accumulates dirty mud inside. <LINE> <LINE> This causes Foot Rot, a horrendous bacterial infection that rots the sole of the hoof and leaves the animal limping in intense pain, refusing to walk to eat. <LINE> <LINE> You must inspect the herd's hooves regularly. Use a hoof knife or trimmers to pare away the excess overgrown keratin, cleaning out all the caked mud and manure from the sole. If there is an infection, wash it with copper sulfate or an appropriate disinfectant and keep the animal in a perfectly dry pen until it heals.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> External Parasites <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Flies, ticks, and lice are more than an annoying nuisance; they are blood-suckers and vectors for severe anemia and skin infections. Hundreds of flies disturbing a cow prevent her from resting or eating properly, destroying her productivity. <LINE> <LINE> If you notice animals scratching frantically against fence posts or losing tufts of hair, inspect their skin beneath the coat. <LINE> <LINE> Use antiparasitic wash solutions or sprays on the bodies of affected animals to eliminate the parasites. Keeping the barn straw clean and dry reduces fly breeding in the environment by 80%%. Pest control on the animal's skin directly reflects in the tranquility and weight gain of the herd.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Milk Harvest <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The daily milking of a cow or goat is the direct fruit of your work with her welfare. But milk is a sensitive biological fluid that spoils quickly if harvested in a filthy manner. <LINE> <LINE> Before beginning, wash your hands thoroughly. Next, clean the teats of the animal's udder with warm water and a clean cloth to remove any remnants of dirt or manure stuck to the skin. <LINE> <LINE> Use a clean metal bucket scalded with boiling water. The first squirts of milk from each teat should be discarded onto the ground, as they contain the bacteria living in the external canal. Milk with firm, smooth, and continuous movements from top to bottom. When finished, apply a protective sealant to the teats to prevent infections (Mastitis) from entering while the canal closes.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sheep Shearing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Sheep produce wool continuously to protect themselves from the cold. But if you fail to shear the animal in early spring, the excess heavy wool in the summer will cause heat stress, as well as accumulating dirt and moisture that rot the skin beneath the coat. <LINE> <LINE> You will need sharp, clean manual Shearing Shears. Restrain the sheep by sitting it on its rump on the ground, keeping its legs unsupported so that it remains calm and does not struggle. <LINE> <LINE> Begin cutting the wool close to the skin, starting from the neck toward the belly and sides. Work with the blade parallel to the animal's body. If you tilt the shears downward in a hurry, you will tear the sheep's skin, creating deep wounds that will attract flies and severe infections. Patience yields a clean fleece of wool and a grateful sheep.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Quarantine Protocol <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You went to the neighboring farm or found a lost animal on the road and decided to add it to your healthy herd. If you open the gate and throw it straight into the midst of your clean cows, you are playing Russian roulette with your livelihood. <LINE> <LINE> The new animal may look perfectly healthy on the outside, but it could be incubating bacterial pneumonia, severe worm infestations, or resistant parasites. <LINE> <LINE> Create an isolated Quarantine Pen, at least thirty meters away from the main barn. Keep any newly arrived animal, or one that begins to cough and show signs of weakness, locked in there for at least two weeks. Observe its behavior, treat sicknesses in isolation, and protect the collective of your herd from devastating epidemics.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Foundation Is Solid <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We have concluded our lessons on the foundations of welfare. You have learned the crucial importance of vital space in pens, learned to clean the stable and line the bed with protective straw, understood the caloric need for hay and grains to raise livestock quality, and know how to harvest milk and wool without harming your creatures. <LINE> <LINE> Your barn is now clean, the waterers are free of ice, and the animals trust the sound of your footsteps when you walk through the gate in the morning. <LINE> <LINE> But to become a true master of livestock, you must go beyond physical care. You need to understand the deep psychology of each species. In Volume Three, 'How Animals Think: A Helpful Guide', we will unlock the mysteries of the animal mind: herd patterns, leadership instincts, mating behavior, and how to predict the reactions of each beast before you even touch them. Keep the troughs full, and until then.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Vital Space <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Crowding ten sheep into a wooden pen designed for two is not space optimization; it is cruelty and logistical foolishness. Overcrowding is the primary trigger for chaos in any animal livestock operation. <LINE> <LINE> When animals are deprived of space to walk, lie down, and get away from each other, the herd's stress levels explode. Animals begin to compete violently for basic resources, the strongest will injure the weakest, and diseases will spread through the pen like wildfire through dry straw. <LINE> <LINE> When planning your pens or stables, calculate a generous area for each head of livestock. Animals need room to exercise and keep their muscles active. A confined, motionless animal is a sick animal in the short term.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Stable Hygiene <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The barn is the herd's refuge, but if you fail to clean the floor, it turns into a cesspool of contamination. Animals defecate and urinate daily, and the accumulation of manure mixed with moisture creates the perfect environment for the proliferation of bacteria and blowflies. <LINE> <LINE> Cleaning the stable must be a daily doctrine. Grab a hoe and a shovel, remove all the heavy manure, and discard it far from the barn (in your compost pile, as you learned in the farming book). <LINE> <LINE> After cleaning the floor, never leave the concrete or bare dirt exposed. Spread a generous layer of dry, clean straw. Straw absorbs residual moisture, keeps the animals' hooves dry, and provides vital thermal insulation against the frost that rises from the ground during cold Kentucky nights.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Basic Nutrition (Hay) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forcing livestock to live solely on meager pasture grass all year round is a common beginner's mistake. In the summer, grass is plentiful, but in the autumn and winter, the pasture dries up, loses its nutrients, and freezes beneath the snow. Your herd will starve if they depend entirely on the ground. <LINE> <LINE> You must produce and store high-quality Hay. Hay is grass mowed at the right moment of maturation and dried in the sun to preserve its fibers and proteins. <LINE> <LINE> Replenish the barn's feed troughs regularly. Cows and sheep have complex stomachs (ruminants) that require the constant chewing of long fibers to keep the digestive system functioning without fatal colic. Keep hay stocks dry inside the shed; moldy, damp hay is poison to livestock stomachs.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Advanced Nutrition (Grains) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If your goal is not just to keep the animals alive, but to increase the herd's quality, boost milk production, and ensure healthy weight gain for the pigs, you need to introduce Grains and Concentrated Feed into their diet. <LINE> <LINE> Ground corn, oats, and barley are massive sources of carbohydrates and pure energy. Adding a daily portion of grain to the troughs accelerates the development of the young and drastically improves overall animal quality. <LINE> <LINE> But use common sense: pigs eat almost any vegetable food scraps from your kitchen, but cows and sheep are strict herbivores. Giving processed or spoiled food to ruminants will cause bloat (a lethal accumulation of gas in the stomach). Treat feed as an energy supplement, never as a replacement for hay.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Hydration and the Danger of Ice <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A large animal can survive a few days without food by consuming its own fat reserves, but a lack of water kills within forty-eight to eighty hours. Waterers must always be full, clean, and accessible. <LINE> <LINE> The breeder's greatest challenge in Kentucky occurs during the harsh winter months. When the temperature drops below freezing, the surface of the water in outdoor troughs freezes over, creating a hard crust of ice. <LINE> <LINE> The animals go to the trough, bump their muzzles against the ice, and cannot drink, dying of dehydration right next to the water. Every winter morning, grab a sledgehammer or a heavy piece of iron, go to the waterers, and smash the entire layer of ice, removing the frozen blocks so the livestock can drink the liquid water underneath.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Protection against the Elements <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Domestic animals possess natural coats of hair or wool, but they have physical limits. A cold autumn rainstorm combined with strong winds can plunge the body temperature of a shorn sheep or a newborn calf into lethal hypothermia in a matter of hours. <LINE> <LINE> The barn must have sturdy walls and a leak-free roof. During severe storms or blizzards, lock the entire herd inside. <LINE> <LINE> Do not leave animals penned in the open pasture under extreme weather conditions. The cold wind steals the caloric energy that the animal should be using to produce milk or meat, forcing its body to burn vital reserves just to keep from freezing. Dry shelter is the best preventive medicine on the farm.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Stress Factor <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Frightened animals are unproductive animals. If you have dogs barking and chasing around the pen all day, or if you shout and assault the cows during handling, their endocrine system releases a massive amount of cortisol and adrenaline into the blood. <LINE> <LINE> Prolonged stress directly weakens the animals' immune system. They become vulnerable to any opportunistic bacteria in the environment. <LINE> <LINE> Furthermore, stress blocks the release of oxytocin, the hormone responsible for milk let-down during milking. Make your handling a calm, quiet, and predictable process. Move the herd by walking slowly behind them, using calm gestures and visual physical barriers, never violence or loud, piercing noises.
IGUI_BookHusbandry2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Safe Handling (Avoiding Kicks) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To examine an animal's health, apply medication, or perform milking, you will need to restrain it. A kick from a five-hundred-kilogram cow or a headbutt from a mature ram can break your legs or ribs in a fraction of a second. <LINE> <LINE> Never approach a large animal from behind by surprise. The blind spot in their lateral vision is located exactly behind their tail. If you touch a cow's rear without her seeing you approach, her defensive instinct will be to fire a violent kick backward. <LINE> <LINE> Approach from the side, at shoulder height, speaking softly so she knows exactly where you are. Use wooden squeeze chutes or sturdy ropes to immobilize the animal's head before attempting to handle the hind legs.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> How Animals Think <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the previous volume, we dealt with the body: straw, water, hay, and cleanliness. But the body is merely a machine driven by an invisible engine: the mind. To raise animals without driving them mad (or getting yourself hurt), you must understand how they perceive the world. <LINE> <LINE> Animals do not think in words; they think in images, scents, and raw emotions. Fear, curiosity, hunger, and safety are the pillars of barn psychology. <LINE> <LINE> When you try to force an animal to act like a human, you fail. When you learn to think like it, you no longer need to push it; it decides to go where you want on its own. Welcome to the herd mind.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Intact Males (Bulls and Rams) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Breeding males that have not been castrated live under the command of pure testosterone. A dominant bull or ram does not see the caretaker as a friend; he frequently sees him as a rival in his territory. <LINE> <LINE> The golden rule on the farm is: Never turn your back on an intact male. Even if the ram has seemed calm and docile since he was a lamb, one day his biological instinct will take over, and he will attempt to establish dominance by ramming the back of your knees. <LINE> <LINE> A charge from an eight-hundred-kilogram bull that has decided the pen belongs solely to him will end your story in this world. Keep your eyes on them. If they begin pawing the ground, lowering their head, or making rigid sideways movements, step away from the fence immediately.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The World of Olfaction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> While we humans rely almost exclusively on our vision, animals experience reality through incredibly rich maps of odors. Their noses see entire stories that we ignore. <LINE> <LINE> When you buy a new bucket, or bring clean clothes smelling of synthetic detergent into the pen, the harsh alien scent frightens them. <LINE> <LINE> Furthermore, cows and sheep reject pastures that have been defecated on by other animals, because their noses detect microscopic parasites in old feces even if the grass looks clean to your human eyes. Trust their muzzle. If an animal refuses to sniff or eat something on the ground, it is because the air there warns of rot.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Curve of Curiosity <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The mind of a herbivore is split between two opposing forces: a phobia of the new and extreme curiosity. <LINE> <LINE> If you want to investigate a pen of young cows that are afraid of you, do not walk up to them. Sit on the ground in the middle of the pasture and look away, pretending to ignore them. <LINE> <LINE> The lack of eye contact removes the threat. Within a few minutes, their innate curiosity will conquer their fear. They will begin to approach slowly, stretching their necks until they begin licking your boots and sniffing your hair. Let their curiosity do the work of breaking the ice. Voluntary approach is the bedrock of trust.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Silenced Pain <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I must repeat this concept for the love of animals: a predator howls when it breaks its paw; a prey attempts to walk normally until it collapses. <LINE> <LINE> Showing weakness in a herd's mind is an invitation to wolves and an invitation to be expelled from the group itself (other animals will often bully or push away the sick individual so as not to attract predators to the rest of the flock). <LINE> <LINE> To detect pain, look at the fine details. A sheep grinding its teeth softly, a pig whose tail used to be curled now hanging loose and straight, or a cow spending too much time persistently licking her own hind paw. They are telling you that agony has set in. You must be the detective of silence.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Memory of an Elephant <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Livestock and pigs have excellent memories, especially for trauma. If you hit a cow with a yellow plastic pipe to make her walk down a narrow alleyway, she will never forget the pain, your face, and, surprisingly, the color yellow. <LINE> <LINE> The next time you approach holding any yellow object, or try to lead her down that same alleyway, she will go into a paralyzing panic before you even touch her. <LINE> <LINE> Building trust takes months of gentle interactions, buckets of food, and peaceful routines. Destroying that trust takes only three seconds of blind fury on your part. Control your temper. Aggression is not a tool on the farm; it is proof of your incompetence.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Functional Empathy <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We have reached the end of our psychological immersion. Now you understand that the Flight Zone replaces physical force. You know that boredom creates monsters in the pigsty and that one should never trust the love of an uncastrated bull, no matter how docile he seems. <LINE> <LINE> The true skill of husbandry lies not in your muscles, but in your ability to read fear and appease it with safety and routine. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Four, 'The Wants and Needs of Diverse Fauna', we will get specific. I will teach you how to set up the perfect diet and environment for each separate species: what swine require that ruminants hate, the minerals sheep need, and the precise schedules for them to flourish. Treat them with kindness and let them rest.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Lens of Fear <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Humans walk through the world with the confidence of an apex predator. Our eyes are on the front of our face to focus on the hunt. Cows, sheep, and chickens, however, have their eyes on the sides of their head. They are the prey. <LINE> <LINE> Their peripheral vision encompasses nearly the entire surrounding environment, but their depth perception is horrible. To a sheep, a dark shadow swaying on the ground isn't just a tree; it's a wolf ready to pounce. <LINE> <LINE> If an animal balks at the barn door and refuses to enter, do not beat it. Look at the ground. Almost always, there will be a discarded coat, an unfamiliar bucket, or a contrasting shadow that, to the prey's brain, looks like an abyss. Remove the scary object and the animal will walk through peacefully.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Flight Zone (The Force Field) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Every pasture animal carries an invisible 'force field' around itself called the Flight Zone. The size of this bubble depends on how tame it is. <LINE> <LINE> If you take a step inside this invisible bubble, the animal will move to get away from you. If you take a step back, it stops. This is the most powerful steering tool in existence. <LINE> <LINE> You do not need to push cows with your hands. Walk calmly toward the cow's side, penetrating just one step into her Flight Zone. She will take two steps forward to maintain her distance. By mastering visual pressure, you move an entire herd without touching a single hair.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Point of Balance <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In addition to the Flight Zone, animals have an invisible 'steering wheel' located exactly at their shoulders. This is the Point of Balance. <LINE> <LINE> If you want the animal to walk FORWARD, position your body behind its shoulder line and apply visual pressure. The animal will move forward to escape you. <LINE> <LINE> If you cross the shoulder line and walk toward its head, it will instantly stop, turn around, and try to go BACKWARD. Many novices stand right in front of a sheep's face, waving their arms and shouting 'Let's go!', and do not understand why the animal desperately tries to run backward. You are blocking its mental exit.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Herd Instinct (The Lone Curse) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> For a human, isolation can be peaceful. For a sheep or a cow, being alone is a death sentence. In the wild, predators hunt the isolated individual. <LINE> <LINE> If you lock a single sheep away from the rest of the group, its brain will collapse. It will bleat incessantly, run against the fence until it injures itself, and stress will accelerate its heart to dangerous levels. It believes it is going to die at any second. <LINE> <LINE> Never isolate an animal from its flock unless it is for emergency medical treatment, and even then, place it in a pen where it can still see and hear the others. Their calm comes from the unity of the group.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Blind Leadership of Sheep <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Sheep possess the strongest following instinct on the farm. If the lead sheep runs into an abyss, the ones behind will jump right after it. They do not question leadership. <LINE> <LINE> The trick to moving a large flock of sheep is to ignore the sheep at the back. Focusing on pushing the stragglers only creates panic. <LINE> <LINE> Your focus should be on convincing the two or three lead sheep at the front to start walking slowly in the desired direction (using the Flight Zone or a bucket of food). Once the leaders begin to move calmly, the rest of the flock will be drawn behind them like water draining down a pipe.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mind of the Pig (Intelligence and Boredom) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Treating a pig as if it were a stupid sheep is a grave mistake. Pigs are, neurologically, as intelligent as dogs. They solve problems, recognize faces, feel complex emotions, and suffer from a very human affliction: boredom. <LINE> <LINE> If you lock a pig in an empty concrete sty with nothing to do, it will go mad. Boredom breeds stress and aggression. They will begin biting the iron bars, chewing on other pigs' tails, or destroying the waterer. <LINE> <LINE> Pigs need to root. Provide loose hay, deep dirt, safe pieces of wood, or heavy balls for them to push around. A pig with a busy mind and a full belly is the most peaceful creature on earth.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Emotional Contagion <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The herd operates as a single shared mind (Hive Mind). Fear is transmitted not by words, but by pheromones and body language. <LINE> <LINE> If a single cow in the pen gets startled by a slamming door and begins running and panting, the brains of the other cows will smell the panic sweat and see the agitation. Within ten seconds, every cow in the pen will be terrified, even without knowing what triggered the panic. <LINE> <LINE> This is why you never work with animals when YOU are angry or in a hurry. If your heart rate is high and your movements are abrupt, they will sense your aggression as a biological alarm. The caretaker's calm dictates the herd's peace.
IGUI_BookHusbandry3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Defensive Motherhood <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The cow that always allowed you to stroke her face and brush her coat is not the same creature after giving birth. Progesterone and oxytocin transform the docile prey into a defensive predator. <LINE> <LINE> Never, under any circumstances, walk between a mother and her newborn offspring, or you will be crushed. If the calf is at the back of the barn and you enter, the mother will block the path with her own body. <LINE> <LINE> Speak to her softly from a distance. Let her sniff you before you even attempt to look at the newborn. Maternal instinct overrides the fear of death. She will leap onto your shotgun if she thinks you are a threat to her young.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Wants and Needs of Diverse Fauna <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The greatest arrogance we can commit on the farm is treating all animals as if they were identical machines running on the same gasoline. They are not. What strengthens a horse can poison a sheep; what refreshes a dog can kill a pig. <LINE> <LINE> In this fourth volume, we will honor the diversity of creation. Understanding the specific needs of each species is the true demonstration of respect for them. <LINE> <LINE> We will get down to details. We will talk about multi-compartment stomachs, mud baths, the ingestion of stones, and the dangerous chemistry that differentiates your herd. Open your mind and pay attention, because mixing the wrong food in the trough doesn't just cause heartburn; it causes death.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Miracle of Mineral Salt <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Grass and water never provide all the minerals that the bone structure and nervous system of a giant creature need (Selenium, Sodium, Iodine). In the wild, deer walk miles looking for rocky outcrops of salt in the earth to lick. <LINE> <LINE> In captivity, you are the one who must bring the stone to them. Every barn MUST have a 'Salt Block' (Salt Lick) attached to the wall or in the trough. <LINE> <LINE> Animals are incredibly smart when it comes to nutritional deficiencies. They will lick the salty block with their rough tongue just enough to replenish their own blood chemistry and then stop on their own. Just make sure, as I warned, to use the copper-free block for sheep.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Backyard Toxicity (The Green Poison) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We think animals instinctively know what they shouldn't eat. The truth is, if they are bored or starving in a short pasture, they will eat death. <LINE> <LINE> Many decorative plants common in backyards are highly toxic. Oleander, Foxglove, and especially wilted leaves from Apple or Cherry trees. <LINE> <LINE> When a cherry or plum branch breaks in a storm and the leaf wilts on the ground, a chemical reaction inside generates Cyanide. If a cow or sheep eats a handful of those fallen leaves, it will suffocate from the inside out within twenty minutes, and there is no cure. Patrol your pen after heavy winds and remove leaves and branches of ornamental trees.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Shelter Requirements (Winds vs. Cold) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Cold weather rarely kills a well-fed adult animal. Their coats are phenomenal insulators. What kills a calf or a chicken is a cold draft. <LINE> <LINE> A barn does not need to be hermetically sealed to retain heat. In fact, closing everything off prevents the escape of urine vapor (ammonia), which causes fatal pneumonia. The barn MUST have ventilation in the roof for stale air to exit. <LINE> <LINE> What you must eliminate are holes in the walls at ground level, which allow freezing wind to cut horizontally across the enclosure and hit the animals' legs and lungs while they try to sleep. Roof ventilation is health; a floor-level draft is death.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Multi-Species Dynamics <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you place sheep, cows, pigs, and chickens all together in the same confined space like Noah's Ark, you will have serious coexistence issues. <LINE> <LINE> Cows and sheep can graze together in large fields (the cow eats the tall grass, the sheep eats the grass close to the ground), but never put pigs in the mix. Pigs are territorial, heavy, and can, in a moment of aggression, attack and seriously injure smaller sheep or try to devour chickens that enter their sty. <LINE> <LINE> Furthermore, chicken feces, if they fall into cow feed, can transmit severe infections. Separate poultry and swine from ruminants with sturdy fences. Create good neighbors, not cellmates.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Love Smells Foul <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To close, a note on porcine hygiene. People complain about the smell of the pigsty, but the fault is not the animal's. The pig is the only farm animal that, of its own free will, will designate an exact, distant corner of the pen solely to drop its feces (Bathroom), and will keep its sleeping area perfectly clean. <LINE> <LINE> The smell of a pigsty comes exclusively from the laziness of the handler who refuses to sweep the manure from that corner, or who crowds so many animals into a tiny pen that they are forced to sleep on top of their own waste against their natural desires. Give them space and they will keep their own home in order.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Final Species Portrait <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We have finished our classification. You have learned to respect the complex stomachs of ruminantes, the rustic gizzard of poultry, and the vital mud puddles for swine. You understood that copper saves the ox but murders the sheep, and that a wilted cherry leaf hides death in autumn. <LINE> <LINE> Your herd now has the correct salt blocks, and your barn roof protects against the cutting ground draft. <LINE> <LINE> What are we missing? We have learned the day-to-day. But what about when the fierce, basic instincts of birth, critical illnesses, and the cycle of life happen? In Volume Five and last, 'Wilds Tamed: An In-Depth Comparative', we will speak of births, the silenced predatory instinct in domesticated beasts, and how to accept victories and grief. Take care on the land, neighbor.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Ruminants (Cows and Sheep) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Cows and sheep possess a digestive system that is a miracle of biology. They are 'Ruminants.' They have massive stomachs divided into four chambers (the Rumen being the largest), which function as fermentation vats. <LINE> <LINE> Their bodies do not digest the grass; the billions of microorganisms inside their stomach digest the grass, and the cow absorbs the byproducts of this fermentation. <LINE> <LINE> Because of this, they NEED long fibers (like tall grass and dry hay). If you feed them solely fine grains (corn and bran), their fermentation chamber becomes excessively acidic, the microorganisms die, and the stomach inflates with gas until it suffocates the animal. Grain is a supplement; grass is life.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Copper Poison (Sheep) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Here is one of the most lethal lessons you can learn: Sheep are extremely sensitive to the mineral Copper. Their liver accumulates it until it reaches fulminant toxic levels. <LINE> <LINE> Commercial feed manufactured for pigs, horses, or cows generally receives extra copper supplementation, which is great for them. But if you use the same cow or pig feed to feed your sheep (or use the same mineral salt block for all of them), you will murder your ovine flock. <LINE> <LINE> The sheep will become jaundiced (yellow eyes), its urine will turn dark like coffee, and it will die in agony. Sheep require salt and feed strictly formulated WITHOUT added copper. Watch what you share in the barn.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Nature of the Pig (Monogastrics) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Unlike cows, pigs have a simple stomach (monogastric), just like yours and mine. They cannot live solely by chewing grass. They need diets rich in concentrated energy and protein. <LINE> <LINE> In the wild, pigs are omnivorous forest hunters. They root up the ground searching for roots, tubers, fallen fruit, insects, and even small rodents. They devour almost anything. <LINE> <LINE> On your farm, they will be the destination for most of the organic scraps from your garden: old potatoes, bruised apples, and broken carrots. But they need a base grain feed to gain the weight that will give them strength and health for the winter.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Myth of Sweat (The Mud Bath) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> 'Sweating like a pig' is the most incorrect saying in our language. Pigs practically have no functional sweat glands. They do not sweat. <LINE> <LINE> In the height of summer, when the midday sun beats down on the animal's back, the pig has no way to cool its own body, and heat stroke is a common cause of death in overly clean sties. <LINE> <LINE> They do not roll in the mud because they are dirty. They roll in the mud because the water cools their skin, and the crust of dirt that dries on top serves as a perfect sunscreen, preventing burns and insect bites. The ideal pigsty must have a dry area covered with clean straw for sleeping, but it MUST have a puddle of muddy water in the shade for vital cooling.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Poultry (Chickens and Stones) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Chickens are the most active creatures on the farm and are descended from dinosaurs. But look closely at their beak: chickens have no teeth. How do they grind hard kernels of corn if they cannot chew? <LINE> <LINE> They possess a powerful internal organ called the Gizzard. For the gizzard to function like a stone mill, the chicken deliberately swallows small stones and coarse sand (Grit). The stones remain trapped in the gizzard, and muscles crush the food against them. <LINE> <LINE> If you raise chickens locked on a clean concrete or wooden floor, and give them only hard grains, they will die of malnutrition with a full crop, because they cannot digest the food. Always leave a pile of coarse sand and gravel available to them.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Magic of Calcium and Light <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Egg production is a brutal physical sacrifice for a chicken. To form an eggshell every day, the chicken consumes a massive amount of calcium. If calcium is lacking in the diet, her own body will leach calcium from her own bones until she becomes rickety, or the eggs will come out with shells soft like a rubber balloon. <LINE> <LINE> Crush old eggshells, toast them in the oven, and mix them into the feed, or provide crushed oyster shells. <LINE> <LINE> Furthermore, the hormonal gland that tells the chicken to lay eggs is activated by Sunlight. In the middle of winter, when days become short and dark, chickens stop laying eggs naturally. Respect their rest in winter; do not force them to lay eggs all year round, or they will die of exhaustion within three years.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Goats: The Escape Masters <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Many people confuse the needs of sheep with those of goats, which is a huge mistake. Sheep look down; they are grazers. Goats look up; they are browsers. <LINE> <LINE> A goat prefers to eat the leaves of shrubs, bitter weeds, thin branches, and tree bark over eating your perfectly green grass from the ground. They clear out overgrown vacant lots full of coarse brush. <LINE> <LINE> And because they are agile, hyper-intelligent explorers, they are escape artists. If there is a ten-centimeter gap in your wooden fence, a stone leaned against a post, or a loose latch, the goat will find it within a day and will be on the roof of your barn the next morning. Goat fences must be foolproof.
IGUI_BookHusbandry4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Diet Transitions (The Shock) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Regardless of the species, every domesticated animal stomach has an inviolable rule: Never make abrupt changes. <LINE> <LINE> If your animals have eaten only poor-quality dry hay for months of winter, and in the first week of spring you turn them loose all at once into a pasture of lush, damp green grass and clover, the shock to the stomach will cause severe acute diarrhea, and the gases from the new fermentation will kill cows from bloat. <LINE> <LINE> Any change in feed, brand, or the introduction of green pasture must be done over two weeks. On the first day, give 90%% old hay and 10%% green. Keep mixing until their gastric system adapts. The owner's haste drowns the animal's life.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wilds Tamed <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the four previous volumes, we treated animals as domesticated creatures that depend entirely on our hands to eat, drink, and survive. This is true most of the time. <LINE> <LINE> But domestication is only a thin layer of paint over millions of years of evolution. When pain strikes, when the scent of blood rises into the air, or when the miracle of birth approaches, that layer of paint peels away. Docile cattle remember the wild aurochs; the pig remembers the wild boar. <LINE> <LINE> In this final volume, we will compare barn life with the instincts of the forest. We will talk about the cycle of life: birth, rejection, predators, and death. Take a deep breath. The work is now with the soul of nature.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Donkey: The Rustic Protector <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you do not have trained dogs, nature offers you the Donkey. Unlike a horse, which flees blindly from danger, the donkey has a visceral, ancestral, and biological hatred of canines (wolves, coyotes, and stray dogs). <LINE> <LINE> If you place a single adult donkey in a pasture alongside cows or sheep, it will adopt the pasture as its kingdom. If a coyote or wild dog leaps the fence, the donkey does not run; it attacks with a demonic fury. <LINE> <LINE> It will bray, trample, and use its front hooves to crush the predator to death without mercy. The donkey is the poor man's silent, rustic security guard, working in exchange only for water and grass.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Inevitable End <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Caring for animals means, inevitably, living with death. Incurable illnesses happen. Limbs break irreparably in frozen mud. Births go wrong and entrails rupture. <LINE> <LINE> This is where the caretaker cannot be a coward. Leaving an animal to agonize for days at the back of the barn because you lack the emotional courage to end its suffering is not compassion; it is pure cruelty and selfishness. <LINE> <LINE> You tamed nature to keep it safe, and now you must be nature to spare it from torture. Compassionate sacrifice (Euthanasia) must be performed swiftly, cleanly, and with honor. Use your firearm with precision to the brain or fast field methods. Do not leave them waiting in the dark.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Carcass Management <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Grief ends at the time of slaughter, and sanitary science begins. A five-hundred-kilogram carcass rotting in the backyard is not just a visual disrespect; it is a biological bomb for the rest of your herd and for your water table. <LINE> <LINE> The body will attract flies, vultures, and every desperate predator in the county. Bury the animal as far away as possible from wells and rivers. The pit must be deep enough to have at least one meter of heavy dirt over the body, otherwise wild animals will scent and unearth the remains during the night. Hygiene protects the living.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Final Agreement of Meat <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you raise pigs, beef cattle, or meat chickens, the day of harvest will arrive. Many novices feel guilt when consuming the creatures they raised and fed every day. <LINE> <LINE> Remember our pact from the first page of the first volume. If they were in the wild, they would die torn apart by a bear's teeth after months of starving in winter. In your hands, they lived with a full belly, slept on warm golden straw, were stroked and protected from pain. <LINE> <LINE> Death on the farm, when done with dignity and speed, is infinitely kinder than a wild fate. Their life sustains yours; your strength maintained theirs. It is the honest cycle of the earth.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Transfer of Wisdom <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You picked up the first book as a big-city novice who was afraid of taking a kick. You learned not to look at prey as if you were a wolf. You lined the stables, broke the ice in the waterers at dawn, and separated the sheep's diet so as not to poison them. <LINE> <LINE> You studied their stomach chemistry, dealt with aphids without industrial poison, learned to ward off starving dogs, helped exhausted sheep give birth in the dark, and had the courage to sacrifice those that could not be cured. <LINE> <LINE> Your barn is no longer just a pile of wood and dirty animals. It is an ecosystem. It is an ancient pact functioning in perfect harmony.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Farewell of St. Francis <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I conclude my writings here. I have put everything life taught me about the animal soul into these pages. The rest—the calluses on your hands and the tears from inevitable losses—the earth itself will take care of teaching you. <LINE> <LINE> Field work never ends, and livestock will always be hungry at the end of the day. But on winter nights, when you slide the latch on the barn gate, hear the animals chewing calmly in the dark, and feel their live warmth contrasting with the snow outside, you will know you did the right thing. <LINE> <LINE> You are no longer their owner. You have become the Caretaker. Go now, neighbor. The herd is calling and the day has already dawned.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Birth Isolation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the wild, the smell of amniotic fluid and birthing blood is a dinner bell for every wolf within a ten-kilometer radius. Therefore, wild herbivores hide their young. <LINE> <LINE> In your safe pasture, a pregnant sheep or cow will do the exact same thing. Days before giving birth, she will become skittish, separate herself from the herd, and seek out the darkest, most isolated, and protected corner of the barn or brush. <LINE> <LINE> Do not try to force her back into the middle of the group, and do not stand in her face with a flashlight wanting to 'help.' The stress of your predator presence can cause her body to halt contractions, killing the offspring by suffocation inside. Observe from afar. Nature has known what it's doing for eons.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Sow's Nest (Wild Boar Instinct) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Pigs do not just lie in the grass and let their young drop the way cows do. A pregnant sow reassumes the exact instinct of wild boar matriarchs. Twenty-four hours before farrowing, she enters a building frenzy. <LINE> <LINE> She will bite, tear, and carry straw, branches, and dirt to create a deep, circular nest. It is her biology demanding thermal insulation for the hairless piglets that are about to be born. <LINE> <LINE> Your only job is to provide mountains of clean straw in the sty and get out of the way. If you do not give her material to build her nest, she will become so frustrated and blinded by stress that she may end up crushing or even devouring her own piglets when they are born due to post-partum psychosis.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mechanics of Birth <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the water bag breaks, the countdown begins. The natural and safe position for the birth of calves and lambs is the 'diving position': the two front hooves appear first, pointed downward, with the muzzle resting right on top of them. <LINE> <LINE> If you see only one paw, or if you see the tail (inverted breech birth), the newborn is stuck. This is where the caretaker intervenes. <LINE> <LINE> With arms washed thoroughly with soap, you must push the newborn slightly back inside during the intervals between contractions, correct the position of the legs, and pull the hooves out in sync with the mother's straining. It is a viscous, exhausting job that requires absolute calm.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The First Breath of Life <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> As soon as the newborn drops to the ground, the mother must turn around immediately and begin licking it vigorously. This licking is not just a mother's kiss; her rough tongue clears the mucus from the nostrils and the violent friction against the ribs delivers a 'shock' to the newborn's nervous system, forcing the lungs to inflate and breathe for the first time. <LINE> <LINE> If the mother is too exhausted or confused and fails to lick, you must act instantly. Grab dry straw or a clean cloth and rub the newborn's chest vigorously until it coughs and draws air. Remove any membrane blocking its nose. Oxygen is king in the first minute.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Miracle of Colostrum <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Human babies receive antibodies through the mother's blood before birth. Calves, lambs, and foals receive nothing. They are born with a completely blank immune system. If bacteria enter them now, they die. <LINE> <LINE> The only way they receive immunity is by drinking Colostrum, the first thick, yellowish milk produced by the mother, within the first twelve hours of life. The newborn's gut can only absorb these massive antibodies during this short window of time. <LINE> <LINE> If the newborn is too weak to nurse, you must milk the colostrum from the mother and bottle-feed it by force. If the twelve-hour window closes and it hasn't drunk colostrum, it will succumb to the first infection in the pen.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Tragedy of Rejection <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Sometimes, instinct fails. A first-time mother, terrified by the pain, may look at her offspring and fail to recognize it, refusing to let it nurse, kicking it away, or even attacking it. <LINE> <LINE> It is sad, but common. Scent is the glue of maternal love. If you rub your hand with soap on the newborn right after it is born, the mother will smell your predator scent, not the newborn's, and will abandon it instantly. Never wash a newborn animal. <LINE> <LINE> If the rejection is permanent, the weight of life falls upon you. The newborn becomes an orphan and you become the mother, bottle-feeding it every few hours, day and night, keeping it warm under lamps or blankets. It is an unbreakable but exhausting bond.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Domestic Dogs and Cold Blood <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We love farm dogs. But man's best friend still shares more than ninety-nine percent of its DNA with the Gray Wolf. And when food runs out, the wolf awakens. <LINE> <LINE> If domestic dogs are left hungry and form packs, the dormant hunting instinct returns with a terrifying ferocity. They will not hunt to satisfy hunger in the same clean way a wolf does; they will kill dozens of sheep or chickens merely for the chaotic thrill of the instinct triggered by the smell of barn panic. <LINE> <LINE> Never allow your pet dog into maternity pens. Always keep your dogs very well-fed and disciplined. Hunger voids a thousand years of domestication.
IGUI_BookHusbandry5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Livestock Guardian Dogs <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <LINE> <SIZE:medium> To combat nocturnal predators (coyotes, foxes, or wild dogs), domestication has given us a marvelous shield: Livestock Guardian Dogs (such as the Great Pyrenees or the Maremma Sheepdog). <LINE> <LINE> Unlike herding dogs (which mimic predators to move livestock), guardians are raised INSIDE the pen along with the sheep from the moment they open their eyes. The dog doesn't think it owns the herd; it thinks the sheep are its canine family. <LINE> <LINE> At night, while the livestock sleep blindly, the guardian patrols the fences in silence. They will not hesitate to fight to the death against anything that tries to cross the fence and harm their adopted family of wool.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cool Swords! <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Man, swords are so cool! Who hasn't watched a samurai or medieval knight movie and wanted to go around slicing everything? But the truth is, picking up a real sword for the first time is terrifying. It's heavy, dangerous, and if you mess up, you'll end up cutting your own leg. <LINE> <LINE> This book is for you, who just found a cool sword and wants to know how to swing this giant piece of metal without looking like an idiot and without getting hurt.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Personal Space (Footwork) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The biggest advantage of a Long Blade is, well, that it's long! You don't need to hug the enemy to hit him. <LINE> <LINE> Use your feet. Step forward when you cut, and retreat right after. The tip of the sword travels faster and hits harder than the part near your hands. You want to hit the target with the final third of the blade (the Sweet Spot). Keep your distance. If the enemy gets in close on you, your long sword becomes a useless weight.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Thrust <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Know what's faster than a big cinematic cut swinging the sword? Pointing and pushing. <LINE> <LINE> The thrust (driving the point in) is a direct, fast strike and uses very little energy. Furthermore, a deep thrust into the chest or head solves the problem on the spot. When you thrust, don't just use your arms. Aim, brace the point, and take an explosive step forward, putting all your body weight behind the blade. It's a brutal piercing strike.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Quick Maintenance (Oil and Rag) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Awesome swords rust. Blood is full of water and salt. If you store your sword dirty today, tomorrow morning it will be stained with red rust. <LINE> <LINE> Understand this: long blades require cleaning. Wipe the steel with a dry cloth as soon as the fight is over. Then, apply a thin layer of oil to it (clean motor oil, gun oil, WD-40, whatever you find). The oil creates a barrier that stops moisture in the air from eating your weapon.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Watch the Scabbard <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A sword is not magical; it loses its edge quickly. If you have a wooden or metal scabbard (that sword cover), pay double attention when drawing the weapon. <LINE> <LINE> Don't rub the sword's edge against the borders of the scabbard when drawing or sheathing it. Drawing the sword while dragging the sharp side along the cover will dull the blade incredibly fast. Slide it so that only the back of the sword (the thick spine) touches the scabbard. A ninja's quick draw is useless if the sword comes out completely dull.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Avoid Walls and Ceilings <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The long sword is phenomenal out there on the asphalt or in the field. But if you go inside a cramped house with narrow hallways and a low ceiling, it becomes a nightmare. <LINE> <LINE> You raise the sword to cut the undead in the kitchen, the blade hits the ceiling fan, and you're done for. You swing to the side, hit the fridge, the sword bounces off, and the enemy bites you. In tight spaces, rely only on forward thrusts or grab a short knife. Giant swords need clear airspace.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of the Basics <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> That's it! You're no longer a sucker swinging an iron bar. You know how to hold the handle, you know you need to pull the cut, and you know how to keep the edge aligned so you don't ruin your awesome weapon. <LINE> <LINE> But that was just the beginning, the garage tips. To truly fight like a pro, you need to understand how the warriors of the past did it in real wars. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Two, 'Swordsmanship: A History', we'll leave the teenage excitement aside and understand where these techniques came from and how the art of the long blade shaped the military history of the world. Until then, keep the edge clean!
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Movies vs. Reality <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forget everything you saw on TV. Real swords don't weigh twenty kilograms (in fact, most weigh between one and two kilograms). And they definitely don't slice through steel pipes like butter. <LINE> <LINE> If you take your katana or greatsword and smash it with all your strength against a metal pole, the blade won't cut the pole; it will chip, bend, or shatter in your face. Swords were made to cut flesh, thick clothes, and bones, not to knock down walls. Treat your new toy with respect.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sword Anatomy (The Basics) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before you go spinning your awesome sword around, you need to know the names of the parts so you don't hold it by the wrong end. The part that cuts is the Edge. The back part, if it doesn't have an edge, is the Spine. <LINE> <LINE> The whole thing is the blade. The metal bar protecting your hand is the Guard, the place where you hold it is the Handle (Grip), and that round or square weight at the end of the grip is the Pommel. Yes, the pommel is also meant for bashing people's heads in.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fuller <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Many swords have a long, sunken groove running down the middle of the blade. In movies, people call this a 'Blood Groove' and say it serves to let blood drain or to stop the sword from creating a vacuum in the enemy's stomach. <LINE> <LINE> That's a lie! The technical name is 'Fuller'. This groove serves only to make the sword lighter without losing stiffness, just like structural steel I-beams. If your sword has a fuller, it's way more agile than you think.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Grip <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you hold this long thing? If it's a two-handed sword, your dominant hand (the right, if you're right-handed) goes at the top of the handle, right against the guard. Your left hand goes way down, near or even holding the pommel. <LINE> <LINE> Don't hold the sword like a baseball bat with your hands glued together in the middle of the handle. Having your hands separated acts as leverage. The top hand is the pivot and the bottom hand pushes and pulls to guide the strike with speed.
IGUI_BookLongBlade1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Hold (Don't Crush the Handle) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A beginner's mistake is squeezing the sword handle so hard that your knuckles turn white. This is terrible. <LINE> <LINE> If you lock your arms and squeeze too much, the sword becomes slow and your muscles tire out in thirty seconds. You should hold the handle firmly enough that the sword doesn't fly out of your hand, but loose enough for your wrists to rotate. You only squeeze the handle with maximum force at the exact moment of impact. It's like holding a small bird: don't let it escape, but don't crush it.
