IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Kinetic Chain <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The lay operator believes that hitting with an axe or swinging a sledgehammer is arm work. That is a recipe for tendinitis and for splitting wooden handles. <LINE> <LINE> The human body works through the 'Kinetic Chain'. True power isn't born in the biceps, it's born in the ground. Power rises through your feet, passes through the legs, rotates in the hips, climbs up the torso, and only then is thrown like a whip through the arms to the tool. Using only your arms to strike doesn't generate enough kinetic energy, forcing the tool to do work it doesn't have the mass for.
IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Death Grip Problem <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Observe an amateur woodworker using a hammer. He squeezes the handle so hard his knuckles turn white. He thinks this guarantees control. <LINE> <LINE> In biomechanics, the 'Death Grip' locks the wrist ligaments. When the hammer hits the nail, the shock vibration (Recoil) has nowhere to go. Because your wrist is locked, the energy stays trapped in the handle, causing instant microfractures in the wood or fiberglass. The professional holds the hammer firmly, but the wrists are loose enough to absorb the vibration, saving the gear.
IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Muscle Fatigue (The Hidden Enemy) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Why do workplace accidents with chainsaws and heavy sledgehammers almost always occur at the end of a shift, near five in the evening? <LINE> <LINE> The answer is Exhaustion (Fatigue). When your muscles are depleted of oxygen and your stamina runs out, your posture collapses. You stop using your legs and start throwing your body weight forward in a sloppy manner. Striking under extreme exhaustion means you no longer have precision. You will mess up the angle. And a bad angle breaks tools in seconds.
IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Glancing Blow Effect <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When you are tired, your alignment fails and you begin delivering 'Glancing Blows'. Your axe head doesn't strike at 90 degrees to the wood; it hits sideways, at 45 degrees, sliding off. <LINE> <LINE> A glancing blow is the greatest cause of structural degradation. It applies torsional leverage to the shaft, bending the steel head and grinding down the handle fibers. Furthermore, the energy that didn't go into the tree's wood travels back into your elbows, injuring your joint. If you are exhausted, put the tool down. Resting is doing maintenance.
IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Breathing and Oxygenation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This sounds like yoga class, but professional Canadian lumberjacks train their breathing as much as they train their arms. <LINE> <LINE> The rule is the same as in weightlifting or boxing: you exhale violently at the moment of impact. Holding your breath while working with sledgehammers or axes increases blood pressure and locks your diaphragm, stiffening the chest and preventing the follow-through. Expelled air loosens the muscles, and the tool strikes smoothly, transferring the shock correctly.
IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Calluses: Body Diagnosis <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your body warns you when your technique is destroying the tool. Look at the palms of your hands. <LINE> <LINE> If you are getting blisters or severe calluses on only one edge of your hand, like the base of your thumb, it indicates disproportionate friction. The tool is dancing in your grip because your biomechanics are misaligned. Exaggerated friction doesn't just burn your skin; it signals that shock energy is escaping through the handle. Correct your posture until the handle rests quietly in the hand.
IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Weight and the Pendulum Effect <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Long tools, like pickaxes and scythes, are Third-Class levers. The power doesn't come from pushing the heavy head; it comes from guiding it. <LINE> <LINE> The bottom hand acts as a fulcrum, the top hand pulls the handle toward you. You don't 'throw' the pickaxe into the ground, you let gravity and the pendulum do the heavy lifting, using your hands only to direct the sharp tip. Anyone fighting gravity to force the tool down faster causes reverse stress on the wood.
IGUI_BookMaintenance5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Axis of Absorption <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> There is a clear difference between a blade and a blunt weapon regarding recoil. <LINE> <LINE> If the gear was built to cut (Axe), it penetrates and is 'caught' by the target. The abrupt stop happens inside. If the gear was built to smash (Sledgehammer, Bat), the impact is a hard shock that bounces back. The operator must be prepared for the kickback. Letting the tool bounce back slightly absorbs the wave and saves tool condition. If you hold the tool rigidly, the energy will snap the shaft.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> A Bricklayer's Life <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I spent thirty years getting my hands dirty with cement under the Kentucky sun. I built houses, walls, and fireplaces that will still be standing long after I go into a coffin. <LINE> <LINE> This book is not for tie-wearing academics. It's the real life of a bricklayer. If you want to learn to build masonry walls, get ready to feel your back ache and the skin on your hands crack. Construction is made of sweat, basic math, and a lot of respect for gravity.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Level and Plumb <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The bubble Level ensures the wall is lying straight horizontally. The lead Plumb Bob ensures it stands straight vertically. <LINE> <LINE> Gravity is the only constant in the world. If the lead weight of the plumb bob is scraping hard against the brick, the wall is leaning forward. If it's too far away, it's leaning backward. The plumb bob should kiss the face of the brick without swinging. Trust gravity; never trust your own tired eyes.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Secret of the Line <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A pro doesn't measure every single brick with a level; that would take a year. You build up the corners of the wall first (the lead pillars). They need to be surgically perfect. <LINE> <LINE> Then, you stretch a tight, bright yellow nylon line from one corner to the other. This string becomes your absolute guide. All you do in between is fill the gap, laying bricks quickly until they lightly touch the taut line. The line speeds up the job by hours.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Jointing (The Finish) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the gray mix begins to 'pull' (dry and set), it's the sacred time for jointing. <LINE> <LINE> You take a smooth piece of old hose or a curved metal jointer and run it over the fresh joints between the bricks. This pushes the mortar in, compacting it against the weather and leaving that nice, clean concave design. A poorly jointed gap sucks in rain, turns to moss, and crumbles over the years. The job doesn't end with the mud; it ends with the seal.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Weather Factor <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fresh cement hates extremes. If you try to lay bricks in a 40-degree summer with the sun beating down, the hot brick will suck the water out of the mix instantly, killing the chemical reaction (curing). <LINE> <LINE> If you work in a harsh Kentucky winter below freezing, the water in the mortar freezes before drying and ruins the strength of the structural bond. Work in the shade when you can and keep plastic tarps handy to cover everything if rain hits by surprise.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wetting the Brick <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fired clay bricks are like thirsty sponges in the sun. <LINE> <LINE> A valuable secret from old masons: on a very dry summer day, give your stack of bricks a light spray of water with the hose before laying them. If they are bone-dry, they will suck all the moisture out of your mortar before the cement can fuse. A slightly damp brick marries the mix in harmony and dries right along with it, creating a solid rock.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of the Shift <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> At five in the evening the steel trowel is washed, the wheelbarrow is scraped down, and the entire body aches. But when you look back, there is a sturdy wall where there was nothing this morning. That's the pride: creating civilization block by block. <LINE> <LINE> You now understand the back pain, the sweet spot of the mud, and the law of the plumb bob to erect walls. But keeping your boots in raw mud is no way for a proper house to stand. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Two, 'Floors: Do It Yourself', we will look at the ground. We will talk about paving, rustic stones, and how to ensure a clean floor that won't give way during the first storm of the year.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Price of the Craft <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first thing you learn on the job site is that bricks are heavy. A single brick in your hand feels like nothing, but carry a thousand of them in an afternoon and your spine will beg for mercy. <LINE> <LINE> It's not just about stacking blocks. If it were, any kid could do the job. It's about rhythm, saving your movement, and not destroying your body before you're forty. The golden rule of the site: learn to bend your knees, not your lower back.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Three Tools <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A mason only needs three extensions of his own body to build an empire: <LINE> <LINE> The Trowel, the Bubble Level, and the Plumb Bob. The trowel is your open hand, the level is your horizon, and the plumb bob is your sense of gravity. If you don't take good care of these three pieces in your toolbox, you're not a builder, you're just a guy trying to throw mud at a wall.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Magic of Mortar <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The brick is the bone; the mortar is the cartilage. Making the mix is an art. The classic blend is cement, lime, sand, and water. <LINE> <LINE> Lime is what provides the bond, the smoothness that makes the mix stick to the trowel like soft butter. Mortar that is too dry crumbles before curing. A mix that is too wet slips, sinks under the weight of the brick, and messes up the whole wall. The exact sweet spot has the sheen and texture of thick ice cream.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Right Sand <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Don't even think about grabbing dirty sand from the backyard, full of dirt and roots. Organic matter rots and creates invisible, rotten voids in your cement joint. <LINE> <LINE> You need clean, fine river sand. The quality of the sand dictates the lifespan of the wall. If the sand has stones that are too large, you will never manage to make a millimetric joint between the bricks. A wire sieve is a mason's helper's best friend.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Human Mixer <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before I could buy a motorized cement mixer, I mixed a lot of mud in a wheelbarrow using nothing but a hoe. <LINE> <LINE> Pulling wet mortar back and forth tears shoulder muscles. The secret is to mix the powders (cement, lime, and sand) dry first. Let the color become entirely gray and uniform. Only then do you hollow out a hole in the middle and pour the water in slowly, pulling the dry earth into the central pool. Haste makes the mix lump up and ruins the bond.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The First Course <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Everything you need to know about the success of a wall is decided on the 'First Course' (the initial line of bricks that goes straight on the ground). <LINE> <LINE> If the base is one millimeter crooked, by the time the wall reaches three meters high, that millimeter will have turned into five centimeters and the wall will come down heavy on your head. Spend all the time in the world leveling the first bed of mortar. The rest of the wall just follows the leader.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Buttering <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Scooping up the mortar with the trowel and spreading it on the side of the brick is called 'Buttering'. <LINE> <LINE> A good mason does this with a quick flick of the wrist. You scrape a thick slab of mortar from the trough, throw it onto the edge of the brick, and trim the edges in a single motion so it doesn't fall to the ground. The goal is to create a full layer free of air bubbles. Air pockets trap rainwater in the winter, and that water freezes and cracks the wall from the inside out.
IGUI_BookMasonry1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Laying and the Tap <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When you place a raw brick onto the cement mortar, it never sits at the perfect level right away. <LINE> <LINE> You lay the block and give light taps on top with the wooden handle of your trowel. 'TAP, TAP'. This squeezes the excess mortar out and adjusts the piece's height. Pay attention: always use the wooden HANDLE of the tool; never strike with the metal part of the trowel, or you will snap the clay brick right in half.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Floors: Do It Yourself <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Add value to your property and transform your backyard into a true suburban oasis! Welcome to the 'Do It Yourself' guide for paving and patios. <LINE> <LINE> Hiring contractors costs an arm and a leg, but with a sunny weekend, a willingness to sweat, and the right instructions, you can build a masonry floor yourself that will leave the neighbors dying of envy. Put on your old clothes and let's turn this mud into art.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Rubber Mallet <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> As you lay the pieces, some bricks might sit one or two millimeters higher than the others. Don't use the brute force of your feet. <LINE> <LINE> Grab your White Rubber Mallet (black rubber leaves ugly scuff marks on decorative brick). Give light, sharp taps on top of the rebellious piece, gently bedding it into the sand until it sits perfectly flush with the others. If you hit too hard and the brick sinks, you'll have to pry it up with a putty knife and reset the sand.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cuts and Fittings <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Inevitably, you will reach the edge of the patio and will need brick halves to close the gaps in the design. <LINE> <LINE> For the weekend warrior, renting a Masonry Saw from the tool store is the best option, as it guarantees perfect cuts. If you're going old-school, you'll need a wide brick chisel and a hammer. Score the cut line all the way around the brick by tapping the chisel lightly, then give a sharp, heavy blow in the center to snap the piece.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Polymeric Sand (Final Interlocking) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The floor is laid, but the bricks are still loose. Now we apply the magic of locking: Polymeric Sand. <LINE> <LINE> Dump bags of this superfine sand over the entire dry patio. Use a push broom to vigorously sweep the sand, filling every joint and crack between the bricks. The sand functions as a giant wedge spread across the whole floor. Without sand in the joints, the bricks would click and wobble under your feet.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Water and Curing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Modern Polymeric Sand has a hidden trick: it contains dry polymers that react with moisture. <LINE> <LINE> After sweeping all the sand into the joints, use a leaf blower to clear the excess off the top of the bricks. Next, take your garden hose on the 'mist' setting and dampen the patio lightly. This water will activate the polymer in the fine sand, hardening it almost like a flexible cement grout, locking the floor for good.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Patio Maintenance <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your new masonry floor will last decades, but it requires a little annual care. <LINE> <LINE> Weeds love to sprout in the sand joints where the wind brings seeds. Spray weed killer or pull them out manually before roots displace the stones. If green moss appears in damp areas, a good wash with a pressure washer in the summer will solve the problem. Just remember to replace a little joint sand if the power washer blasts too much of it out.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Victorious Weekend <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Congratulations! You started with a dirty lawn and now you have a magazine-worthy brick patio. You mastered the gravel, leveled the sand, created the perfect slope, and locked the system with polymers. Flat geometry is mastered. <LINE> <LINE> But a true builder doesn't just stay on the ground. We need to go up. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Three, 'Dibnah's Book of Bricks', we will dive into history and industrial firing. We'll leave the garden behind and build marvels that reach the clouds: thermal monuments, kilns, and colossal chimneys.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Weekend Warrior's Kit <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Put the wet mortar aside for now. To lay paving bricks (Pavers), you will work with dry bases. <LINE> <LINE> Your arsenal will consist of: spade shovels for excavating, a garden rake, nylon lines, wooden stakes, a long bubble level, a straight piece of timber (2x4), and, most importantly, a Rubber Mallet. Oh, and do your knees a favor: buy a good pair of thick rubber kneepads at the hardware store. Your cartilage will thank you on Monday.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Soft Dirt Mistake <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The number one mistake of the rushed homeowner is simply throwing bricks on top of the grass or the packed dirt of the yard. <LINE> <LINE> Organic soil is alive. It expands when it rains, shrinks in the sun, and harbors worms and roots. If you lay blocks straight onto the dirt, your perfect patio will look like a bumpy roller coaster after the first winter. The golden rule of a perfect floor is Excavation. You must remove at least 15 centimeters of organic soil before you even dream of placing the first brick.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Gravel Base (Sub-Base) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With the hole dug, it's time to build the foundation. Pour in a thick layer of crushed stone or gravel. <LINE> <LINE> Gravel is angular, so the stones lock into each other, creating a rigid floor that still allows rainwater to drain into the earth below. The gravel base should be about 10 centimeters thick. Use a manual steel plate hand tamper to pound the gravel until it's as hard as the asphalt concrete on the street.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Sand Bed and the Screed <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> On top of the hard gravel, you add the 'Bed'. It's a layer of about 3 centimeters of coarse sand. <LINE> <LINE> To get the sand perfectly flat, we use the screeding technique. Place two parallel PVC pipes over the gravel to serve as rails. Pour the sand over them and pull a straight wooden timber across the pipes, leveling the sand as if you were scraping icing off a cake. Once the sand is smooth, NEVER step on it.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Water Nightmare (Slope) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Attention, builders! You aren't building a swimming pool; you're building a patio. <LINE> <LINE> Rainwater needs somewhere to go, or it will pool against your house's foundation and flood your basement. Every pavement must have a Slope. The safety math is a drop of 1 centimeter for every 1 meter of floor, always sloping away from the house toward the lawn. Use the bubble level on the gravel line to ensure this invisible tilt.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Pattern Geometry <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You have a canvas of smooth sand. What pattern will your bricks form? <LINE> <LINE> The 'Running Bond' pattern is the easiest, aligning bricks just like a traditional wall. The 'Basketweave' forms double squares, ideal for barbecue patios. But if you're building a driveway, you MUST use the 'Herringbone' pattern. Blocks locked in a 'V' shape at 45 degrees disperse the pressure from two-ton tires, stopping the bricks from sliding out.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Rigid Border <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Imagine your new brick patio as a shoebox full of wooden blocks. If you take away the sides of the box, the blocks spill out, right? <LINE> <LINE> The same thing happens to bricks on the ground. Before laying them, you must secure Edge Restraints around the perimeter of your patio. These can be heavy-duty plastic strips spiked into the gravel with steel pins or a narrow trough of invisible cement beneath the dirt. Without a rigid border, your beautiful floor will separate in months.
IGUI_BookMasonry2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Click-and-Drop Laying <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The fun time has arrived! Start from the straightest corner and work your way down the bricks one by one. <LINE> <LINE> A pro's secret is: never drag the brick across the sand. Dragging creates microscopic ridges of sand that will make the brick uneven. The correct motion is to butt the new brick against the side of the brick already on the ground, let it slide straight down flush against its neighbor, and drop it gently onto the sand bed. 'Click and Drop'. Maintain a two-millimeter gap between them.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dibnah's Book of Bricks <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Modernity has ruined building. Today, they erect glass and steel boxes that have no soul. In my days, we built the world with fired clay, steam, and sweat. <LINE> <LINE> This book is a tribute to the industrial age. If you have a passion for chimneys that scratch the sky, blazing kilns, and red bricks covered in soot, pull up a stool and light your pipe. We are going to learn how the old-timers made clay last five hundred years.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Smoke Shelf <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Just above the firebox, before the chimney goes straight up, a true master builder crafts a 'Smoke Shelf'. <LINE> <LINE> It's a recessed brick step right behind the damper. When cold wind beats outside and rushes down the chimney, it hits this hidden shelf and is deflected back upward, instead of blowing soot into your face in the living room. Without a smoke shelf, your fireplace will spit embers across the whole house on windy nights.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Flue Liner <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the old days, the inside of chimneys was pargeted with mortar. But wood smoke generates creosote, a flammable tar that sticks to bricks and can cause catastrophic chimney fires. <LINE> <LINE> Modern chimneys require a Flue Liner. These are large, smooth ceramic (or stainless steel) square pipes. They are inserted inside the brick tower. Creosote doesn't stick well to smooth ceramic, making annual cleaning easier and ensuring fire doesn't escape through any gaps.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Sacrificial Chimney Crown <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The absolute top of the chimney, exposed to the open sky, suffers more than any other part of the build. The sun bakes it and frost shatters it. <LINE> <LINE> You don't leave the last brick exposed. You build a 'Crown', a thick cap of sloped concrete that covers the top bricks and has an edge (drip edge) to shed rainwater away from the masonry. This crown should be checked every five years. If it cracks, water leaks down the entire inside of the chimney and rots the monument from the inside out.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Men of the Heights (Steeplejacks) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the old industrial days, when a 60-meter chimney started cracking near the top, the factories called in the 'Steeplejacks'. <LINE> <LINE> They didn't use cranes or helicopters. These madmen lashed wooden ladders to one another, climbing up the outside of the chimney using hooks driven into the old mortar, hammering and patching bricks in an insane balancing act up high, smoking cigars in the middle of the smog. They were the true heroes of the brick.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Art of Felling <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Everything that goes up must one day come down. The old method for demolishing a giant chimney without explosives is pure science. <LINE> <LINE> The feller chops a wide hole at the base of the tower, propping it up with thick logs of solid timber. Next, he fills the hole around the logs with tar, firewood, and oil. When the fire is lit, the feller runs. The fire consumes the logs. Suddenly, the base gives way and thousands of tons of brick topple in a perfect straight line, falling exactly where he planned.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The End of Steam <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The factories closed, the coal vanished, and the great chimneys were brought down. But the brick technique doesn't die. <LINE> <LINE> You learned the difference between dried mud and the strength of fire. You understood the power of the English and Flemish Bonds and know the physics that draw smoke out of a safe house. The spirit of Dibnah is now in your rustic tools. <LINE> <LINE> But construction evolution didn't stop in the last century. In Volume Four, 'Secrets of a Master Mason', we will advance to the ultimate tricks of heavy building, structural arches, and true waterproofing.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Respect for the Clay <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A brick isn't just a piece of dried mud. It is earth forged in fire. <LINE> <LINE> Common bricks are great for house walls, but they are porous. If you're going to build heavy-duty structures, you need 'Engineering Bricks'. They are baked at temperatures so extreme that the silica partially melts, vitrifying the piece. They are dense, incredibly heavy, and nearly waterproof. When you tap them together, they don't make a dull dirt thud; they ring like crystal glasses.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Firebricks <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you try to build a heavy fireplace or a smelting furnace using normal bricks, they will shatter like grenades in the first week of fire. <LINE> <LINE> You must use Firebricks for the interior. They are made with special alumina and silica, and baked slowly until they can withstand volcanic temperatures of 1500 degrees Celsius without melting or cracking. They are a pale yellow and do not handle external weather well; they are creatures born to live in the dark and the fire.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Mortar for the Fire <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Another beginner's mistake is building a kiln out of firebricks and sticking them together with common cement. Common cement explodes when the fire hits 400 degrees. <LINE> <SIZE:medium> A furnace demands refractory mortar, a mix of pure fireclay and water. The joints between firebricks must be as thin as possible, barely two millimeters thick. It's a near-perfect fit of block against block. When the first fire lights, this clay bakes and fuses the entire furnace into a single piece of immortal ceramic.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Crime of the Stacked Wall <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Stop building walls by stacking bricks perfectly on top of one another, with all the vertical joints aligned. In England, we call that a 'Stack Bond'. It's the weakest wall ever conceived by man. <LINE> <LINE> If the ground shifts a single centimeter, the crack will tear the entire wall from top to bottom right down that straight line of mortar. The strength of masonry comes from interrupting that line. That's why Bond Patterns exist.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Stretchers and Headers <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before you learn the bonds, learn the language. <LINE> <LINE> When you lay a brick sideways, showing its longest face to you, we call it a 'Stretcher'. When you turn the brick, pointing its short end toward you (going into the middle of the wall), we call it a 'Header'. The strength of a thick wall comes from crossing Stretchers to provide length, and Headers to lock the front of the wall to the back of it.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The English Bond <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The most brutal and strong of all structural bonds is the English Bond. It was used to build cotton mills, railways, and military fortifications. <LINE> <LINE> It works like this: you lay an entire course using only Stretchers (long bricks). In the course above, you lay a whole line using only Headers (short bricks pointing inward). The third course goes back to Stretchers. It's the heaviest interlocking system in the world, impossible to be brought down by winds or industrial vibrations.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Flemish Bond <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Flemish Bond requires more skill from the mason, and it is the most beautiful to look at. It's used in government buildings and luxury estates. <LINE> <LINE> Instead of separate courses, you alternate within the same line: one Stretcher, one Header, one Stretcher, one Header. In the course above, you center the Stretcher exactly over the Header below. It creates a gorgeous cross-shaped pattern across the whole wall. It is incredibly solid but requires cutting dozens of bricks in half to close the edges, which takes a lot of time.
IGUI_BookMasonry3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Black Heart: The Chimney <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Building a chimney isn't just making a tube of bricks on top of a fireplace. A chimney is the suction engine of a house. <LINE> <LINE> Hot air is lighter and wants to rise. The size of the fireplace opening must be in exact proportion to the size of the flue. If the tube is too wide, the hot air cools before escaping and smoke backs up into the room. If it's too narrow, it chokes. The chimney must be tall enough to clear the peak of the roof, or the wind will blow smoke right back down.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Secrets of a Professional Mason <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Any man with two strong arms can stack bricks in a yard. But erecting a structure capable of holding a three-ton roof, resisting hurricanes, and keeping moisture out of a house for a century requires the secrets of a master builder. <LINE> <LINE> This manual pushes amateurs aside. Here, we tackle the anatomy of heavy construction. You will learn about double walls, the miracle of arches over windows, temperature control, and the absolute defense against water.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Retaining Walls <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A house wall only holds up a roof. A Retaining Wall holds back thousands of tons of earth in a yard. It is a completely different beast. <LINE> <LINE> If you erect a straight brick wall to hold back a slope, rain will soak the dirt, multiplying the weight by ten, and the wall will burst like paper. Retaining walls must be built with a backward lean toward the hill, and must be packed with drainage pipes at the back to relieve groundwater pressure.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Expansion Joints <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> An eighty-meter-long wall bakes and expands in the July sun. Bricks grow by centimeters. <LINE> <LINE> If it's a solid, continuous block, thermal expansion will cause the wall to blow out its own ends or crack violently in the middle. Professional construction uses Expansion Joints: every ten or twelve meters, we leave a vertical gap in the wall and fill it with expandable rubber or polyurethane. The wall has room to 'breathe' and stretch in the summer without destroying its own bones.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Toothing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You built a formidable workshop, but you want the option to build an extension in the future without tearing down what you already did. <LINE> <LINE> The professional technique is called 'Toothing'. At the end corner of the wall, instead of making a straight, flat line, you leave one brick projecting and the one above recessed, creating a sawtooth pattern along the edge. When the time comes to build the extension, the new courses of mortar simply slot in and lock perfectly into the teeth of the original building.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Concrete Block <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Red brick is beautiful, but the Concrete Block (CMU) is the modern workhorse. It is giant, fast to lay, and has hollow cores in the middle. <LINE> <LINE> A block shed goes up three times faster. And the industrial secret: to make a bunker resistant to gunfire or vehicles, the builder threads steel rebar through the hollow cores and pours liquid concrete all the way to the top. You transform a hollow wall into a reinforced monolith impossible to bring down without dynamite.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Master's Repair <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With fifty years of acid rain, the external mortar between bricks rots and falls out. But the brick itself is perfect. What does the master do? He doesn't demolish. He does Repointing. <LINE> <LINE> Using a grinder or chisel, we scrape three centimeters of all the old dead mortar out of the wall. Then, we inject a fresh, rich, new mortar into the void and joint it again. It's a face-lift for buildings. The house becomes structurally new for another half century.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Legacy of Cement <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Here rest the secrets. The weep hole, the curved arch, the steel lintel, the wall that breathes, and the expansion gaps. You no longer build blind walls; you raise living machines made of clay that drain, hold back mountains, and survive hurricanes without blinking. <LINE> <LINE> But what is the real limit of these structures? How much pressure would your reinforced block fortress withstand if tested to the extreme? <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Five, 'Statistical Analysis of Historical Buildings', raw engineering takes over. We'll set the trowel aside and calculate the weight of catastrophe.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Frost Line <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A house never begins at ground level. The earth freezes in winter. When water in the soil turns to ice, it expands violently upward. <LINE> <LINE> If your wall's foundation is shallow, the frost will heave it, snapping the entire house in half. A Kentucky master builder knows they must dig foundation footings well below the 'Frost Line' (about 80 centimeters in our state). The foundation must anchor where the earth stays warm all year round.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Cavity Wall <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Look at a modern brick house. You think it's a single, solid wall? Wrong. It's a structural illusion. <LINE> <LINE> Good houses are built with 'Cavity Walls'. These are two parallel walls, one inner and one outer, with a 5-centimeter empty space (an air cushion) between them. If heavy rain manages to penetrate the first barrier of bricks, the water slides down the void and never reaches your house's inner plaster. The air in the middle also serves as thermal insulation.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wall Ties <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> But if they are two thin, separate walls, wouldn't the wind blow the outer layer over? Not thanks to Wall Ties. <LINE> <LINE> The professional mason inserts galvanized steel ties every few bricks, connecting the back wall to the front wall across the air gap. These little steel anchors make the two walls act as a single solid block against the force of winds, while maintaining thermal and moisture separation. It's invisible engineering.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Weep Holes <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If rainwater enters and runs down the air cushion of the double wall, where does it go in the end? If it pools at the bottom, the house becomes a swamp. <LINE> <LINE> That's why you leave 'Weep Holes'. In the lowest course of bricks, at external ground level, the mason leaves several vertical joints completely free of mortar. It is through these empty gaps that the wall "weeps," expelling blocked water back to the yard and saving your living room.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Door Opening and Arch Magic <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you raise two pillars for a door and simply place bricks straight across the top, the weight of the ceiling will break the middle bricks and crush the door. Bricks have no tensile strength. <LINE> <LINE> The Romans solved this: The Arch. Building a brick arch over a window or door takes all the weight from above and, thanks to curved geometry, redirects the force to the sides (to the sturdy pillars). The 'Keystone' at the center of the arch locks the whole system. It's indestructible.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Lightweight Lintels <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Building perfect arches takes time and money. The modern professional method for making window openings in a solid wall is using a Lintel. <LINE> <LINE> A Lintel is a thick beam of steel or reinforced concrete that you lay across the opening before continuing to lay bricks upward. Steel has incredibly high tensile strength and supports the wall above without sagging, allowing you to create perfect square openings to fit glass frames without fear of the roof falling on your head.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Flashing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Where the wooden roof meets the brick chimney, there is a continuous war. Materials shift with the weather, and gaps open up. Water will get in there. <LINE> <LINE> Master sealing requires Flashing – bent sheets of lead or copper. The mason makes a shallow cut in the brick and inserts the metal sheet inside the wall, bending it to cover the roof. This overlapping seal prevents the most violent storm from seeping into the house's joints. Trusting only silicone is rookie work.
IGUI_BookMasonry4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The White Disease (Efflorescence) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Have you ever seen a brand-new brick wall that, months later, is covered in stains and a ghostly white powder? That's called Efflorescence. <LINE> <LINE> This happens when the mortar used was full of soluble salts or when the wall absorbed excessive water from the ground due to a lack of waterproofing. Water travels inside the brick, dissolves the salts, and when it evaporates in the sun, leaves the white crust behind. It's a visual defect and a clear sign that water is invading your structure.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Statistical Analysis of Historical Masonry Constructions <LINE> Technical Abstract <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This treatise compiles data from mechanical testing conducted by the Institute of Civil Engineering (1989). The objective is to quantify the structural response of unreinforced masonry systems under extreme conditions of thermodynamic stress, static load, and dynamic trauma. <LINE> <LINE> This is strictly academic literature, intended for structural engineers. Understanding the force vectors described here separates an impassable barrier from a structure on the verge of systemic collapse.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Historical Mortar Paradox <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Why are Roman walls still standing, while modern cement walls crack within 50 years? Chemical analysis points to the Hardness Paradox. <LINE> <LINE> Modern Portland-based cements are too rigid. When a building settles, the hard cement does not yield, forcing the brick to shatter. Historical mortars based on pure hydraulic lime were extremely soft and flexible, allowing the structure to 'breathe' and move millimeters under pressure, accommodating kinetic trauma without breaking the vital blocks.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Thermodynamics and Hydric Degradation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The most lethal destructive test for masonry is the Freeze-Thaw cycle. <LINE> <LINE> Bricks absorb up to 15%% of their weight in water. When temperatures plummet in winter, this water freezes in the internal capillaries and undergoes a volumetric expansion of 9%%. This microscopic internal expansion force reaches up to 14 Megapascals, tearing the clay brick into powder from the inside out in a few seasons. A wall not sealed with water repellents is statistically useless long-term in cold climates.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Blast Overpressure <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Cold War structural test records measured the impact of overpressure waves on residential masonry. <LINE> <LINE> When a massive pressure front hits an unreinforced surface, the immediate vacuum that follows pulls the wall outward, fracturing the grout joints. The survival of brick bunkers requires circular geometry to dissipate the shockwave around the structure, rather than offering a flat resistive face that will inevitably fail under pressures exceeding 5 psi.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Transition to Reinforced Hybrids <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The final conclusion of the 20th century is inevitable: pure masonry has unbreakable mathematical limits in the face of modern dynamic trauma. <LINE> <LINE> Ultimate resistance is only achieved with 'Confinement'. Filling the hollow cores of perforated blocks with deformed carbon-steel rebar and fluid concrete creates a hybrid composite. The brick provides compressive resistance and thermal barrier; the steel core provides elastic tensile resistance. A confined structure is statistically invulnerable to lateral forces.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Conclusive Report <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> For the structural engineer, a wall is a graph of forces. They do not see the wall; they see the invisible shear, the crushing of joints, the pressure of frozen moisture, and ballistic absorption. <LINE> <LINE> If you designed with the correct slenderness ratio, locked the bond in double English block, utilized buttresses and efficient drainage, the mathematical probability of failure is negligible. Your monument will not fall by the action of the elements or physical chaos.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Immortality of Clay <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We close the analytical treatise. You now see the world through the mechanics of solids. <LINE> <LINE> From the first drop of sweat mixing lime on the Kentucky floor (Volume I), to the moment you calculated the fatigue limit against impact masses at the tip of your pencil, you have become the Master of Masonry. The world of wood can burn or rot, the world of steel can rust in the rain. But the walls you raise from this day forward will stand for eternity.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Limited Compressive Strength <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Masonry is an anisotropic material characterized by its formidable Compressive Strength. Laboratory tests on 19th-century fired clay blocks demonstrate the capacity to withstand axial loads exceeding 30 Megapascals (MPa). <LINE> <LINE> In practice, this means vertical weight is never the primary failure vector of a well-executed wall. A pillar of solid bricks can support the static weight of dozens of tons of roofing or steel beams without suffering crushing at a cellular level.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Tensile Deficit <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If compression is masonry's virtue, Tension is its fatal flaw. The tensile strength (the capacity to be stretched or bent without breaking) of a brick wall is statistically close to zero. <LINE> <LINE> When a severe horizontal force strikes the center of a wall, the impact side is compressed, but the opposite side is tensioned. Since mortar lacks the elasticity to hold blocks together under bending, the joint fails almost immediately, generating a step-like crack that compromises the monolith.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Shear Stress <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Shear Stress occurs when coplanar forces push sections of the wall in opposite directions (such as tectonic movement during an earthquake or differential soil settlement). <LINE> <LINE> Statistical failure analysis reveals that shear does not break the brick itself, but obliterates the brick-mortar interface. The mortar acts as the slip plane. Static friction is overcome, and the wall splits into giant blocks that slide past one another, resulting in catastrophic 'X'-shaped collapse.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Lateral Mass Pressure <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A peculiar case study involves 'Crowded Live Load'. When a dense biological mass (such as panicked crowds fleeing through narrow corridors) presses continuously against an unreinforced masonry wall, the distributed lateral force can exceed 3 kN/m². <LINE> <LINE> Single-brick thick walls invariably buckle and collapse under this level of continuous pressure. A statistically viable defense against crowd crushing requires interlocking English Bond in triple-thickness walls.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Slenderness Ratio <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Slenderness Ratio is the equation that dictates the stability of an isolated structure. It is the ratio of a wall's height to its effective geometric thickness. <LINE> <LINE> Computer models prove that any freestanding masonry wall with a Slenderness Ratio exceeding 20 is mathematically doomed to topple under moderate lateral loads (such as 100 km/h storm winds). To transform a tall wall into an unshakeable fortification, engineering demands the introduction of buttress pilasters every four meters.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Concentrated Blunt Trauma <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Pendulum impact tests with heavy steel masses (simulating destruction by demolition tools like the Sledgehammer) show that masonry suffers conical fragmentation. <LINE> <LINE> The initial blow crushes the face of the impacted brick, but the shockwave travels in a cone shape toward the rear face of the wall, ejecting a much larger piece of material from the other side. Destroying a masonry wall by brute force requires methodical strikes at specific tension points, never random blows on the flat surface.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cyclic Load Fatigue <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The concept of Material Fatigue does not apply only to metals. Masonry structures suffer fatigue when exposed to continuous low-amplitude vibrations, such as heavy train traffic or the constant slamming of heavy objects against the surface. <LINE> <LINE> Vibration degrades silicate crystals in the mortar's microstructure over the years, reducing adhesion. A statistically 'safe' wall can collapse under a trivial impact if it has spent the last decade absorbing undocumented cyclic micro-shocks.
IGUI_BookMasonry5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Parabolic Distribution in Arches <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Analysis of historical masonry arches reveals the genius of the 'Inverted Catenary Curve'. <LINE> <LINE> When a perfect curved arch is subjected to a load, the geometric vector converts all vertical tensile force (destructive) into lateral compressive force (safe), pushing the bricks against one another. The strength of a brick arch is limited only by the crushing strength of the material itself, making it theoretically capable of supporting direct impacts or colossal roof loads without steel reinforcement.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: Welcome to the Grease <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you paid a guy in a clean jumpsuit at a dealership last week to change your oil or top off your windshield washer fluid, you are the reason the automotive industry makes billions. They love people who are afraid to open the hood. <LINE> <LINE> A car isn't black magic. It’s just a heavy piece of metal, controlled explosions, and basic physics in motion. This manual was written to take away your fear of getting your hands dirty. <LINE> <LINE> We'll start with the basics. If you don’t know the difference between a flathead and a Phillips screwdriver, or if you think the engine runs on fairy dust, pay close attention. As of today, your relationship with your vehicle changes. Buy some good degreasing hand soap, because you're going to need it.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Art of Changing a Flat <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you get a flat on the highway, for the love of God, don't stop on the lane. Destroy the wheel driving slowly on the shoulder, but don’t get run over. <LINE> <LINE> The novice mistake is trying to loosen the wheel lugs AFTER lifting the car on the jack. The wheel will spin in the air and you won't be able to apply leverage. With the car still firm on the ground, use the lug wrench to break the initial torque of all the nuts. Just loosen them a bit; don't take them off. <LINE> <LINE> Lift the car, remove the loose nuts, change the wheel, put the nuts on, and tighten them lightly by hand. Lower the car to the ground, and only then apply the final, forceful tightening using the wrench. And always tighten in a cross pattern (star), never in a circle, so the wheel doesn't sit crooked on the axle.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Squeal of the Belt <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You start the car in the morning and it lets out a sharp, ear-piercing squeal that wakes up the neighbors. Don’t panic, the engine isn’t broken; that’s just a worn belt crying for help. <LINE> <LINE> The engine pulley spins rubber belts that drive the alternator, power steering pump, and air conditioning compressor. If the belt gets old, it dries out, slips on the metal pulley, and gives that hideous shriek of a spinning tire. <LINE> <LINE> Cars from the '80s used several thin 'V' belts. Newer cars from this decade use the Serpentine Belt, a single wide band that runs everything. If it breaks in the middle of the road, your steering will become hard as stone, the A/C will shut off, and the car will stop charging the battery. Learn to tension it or buy a can of belt dressing spray to delay the inevitable.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Coolant (Ice and Fire) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fuel exploding thousands of times per minute creates a heat inferno under the hood. Without the cooling system, the engine block would melt into itself. Water mixed with additive liquid travels through the engine galleries, steals the heat, and throws it to the radiator at the front of the car, where the wind cools everything down. <LINE> <LINE> Never, and this isn't a suggestion, NEVER open the metal radiator cap with the engine hot and the car overheating. <LINE> <LINE> The system works under immense pressure. If you unlatch the cap, a geyser of green or pink water boiling at over 120 degrees Celsius will explode violently and melt the skin off your face in seconds. Wait for the car to cool completely before topping off the water.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wipers and Visibility <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> It’s ironic to think that a vehicle that costs tens of thousands of dollars and weighs two tons becomes completely useless if two five-dollar rubber strips fail during a night rain. <LINE> <LINE> Windshield wiper blades dry out in the hot summer sun. When the autumn rain hits, they will shudder on the glass, smear the mud, and blind you completely at the moment you most need to see the road. It’s the most ignored maintenance in the world. <LINE> <LINE> And for your own sake, mix a proper cleaning fluid into the wiper water reservoir. If you use only tap water and a giant insect smashes onto your windshield on the highway, plain water will only spread its grease, turning your windshield into an opaque blur.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Engine's Pulse (Spark Plugs) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We talked about the 'Spark' at the beginning of this book. The little ones responsible for taking that torture are the Spark Plugs. They are screwed into the engine head, entering directly into the infernal combustion chamber. <LINE> <LINE> Every rotation, the coil sends tens of thousands of Volts through the cable that end at the tip of the plug, forcing a spark to jump the gap and explode the gasoline. Over time, this metal tip wears down, melts, and the spark fails. <LINE> <LINE> When a cylinder fails to fire, the car shakes like a tractor, loses power, and the exhaust smells strongly of unburned fuel. Changing the plugs is simple, but requires a long tool (spark plug socket). Never tighten the new plug as if you were the Hulk; the head is aluminum, and if you strip the threads, you’ll need to have the engine machined.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of the Beginning <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Congratulations. If you read this manual to the end and kept something in your head, you are no longer the perfect prey for dealerships and dishonest mechanics. You know how a car breathes, what it drinks, and the basic maintenance to keep it from dying before its time in your garage. <LINE> <LINE> Remember: mechanics isn't guessing, it’s cold deduction. Follow the car's symptoms, respect the weight of the steel parts, and don’t be stubborn enough to use the wrong tool for the job. <LINE> <LINE> The basics are mastered. But your car is more than filters and bolts. In Volume Two, we will go deeper into the brutality of the chassis. We’ll talk about the suspension, the disc brake system, how to bleed lethal fluids, and the transmission system that makes this metallic marvel actually move forward. Close the hood, wipe off the grease, and see you then.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Holy Trinity of the Engine <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before you go tightening random bolts, you need to understand what makes that hunk of cast iron rumble. Internal combustion engines, from your grandfather’s clunker to your modern V8 pickup, need three absolute things to run. <LINE> <LINE> 1. Fuel: Vaporized gasoline that feeds the beast. <LINE> 2. Spark: The fire that ignites the mixture, provided by the spark plug. <LINE> 3. Compression: Air being brutally crushed inside the cylinder before the explosion. <LINE> <LINE> If your car won't start in the morning, it has lost one of these three elements. It’s that simple. A real mechanic's job isn't swapping parts until the car runs by luck; it’s investigating which of these three ingredients has fled the engine.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Safety: The Killer Jack <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We lose good men every year to sheer stupidity under cars. Every car comes with a small metal scissor jack hidden in the trunk. In the shops, we call that the 'Widow Maker.' <LINE> <LINE> That fragile jack is meant ONLY and exclusively for changing a flat tire on the shoulder of the road. You never, ever, under any circumstance in the universe, should you crawl your body under a car held up only by a hydraulic or scissor jack. <LINE> <LINE> If you are going under two tons of American steel, you lift the car and support it firmly on steel Jack Stands on flat concrete, and you still throw the tire you just took off under the chassis for safety. A falling car won't give you time to scream.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Curse of the 10mm Socket <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the old days, American cars were built entirely with Imperial (standard) bolts. Today, because of that global mix-up in the '90s, cars mix metric and Imperial parts. <LINE> <LINE> Buy a decent, high-quality socket and ratchet set. Don't buy cheap tools at the supermarket, or they will strip the bolt head and turn a ten-minute job into a three-day nightmare using drills to extract destroyed metal. <LINE> <LINE> And an ancient workshop warning: buy three extra 10mm sockets. It is the most used size on any modern engine, and it possesses the magical, inexplicable ability to fall on the floor and vanish forever into another dimension. You will always lose the 10mm socket. Accept it.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Engine's Blood (Oil) <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The engine is full of sharp metal parts rubbing against each other at thousands of revolutions per minute. Without lubrication, they would melt and fuse into a useless block of metal in thirty seconds. Motor oil is the vehicle's blood. <LINE> <LINE> If you run with oil that’s too old, it loses viscosity and turns into a thick black sludge that clogs lubrication channels, killing the engine with a heart attack. Check the dipstick weekly with the engine cold and the car on level ground. The mark should be between the two holes. <LINE> <LINE> Changing the oil at home is the easiest thing in the world. Loosen the drain plug under the car, let it drain into an old pan, change the filter by hand (never tighten the new filter with tools, only hand-tight), and pour in the new oil. There, you just saved twenty bucks.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Air Filter: The Lungs <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The engine runs by burning gasoline and air. In fact, it pulls in way more air than fuel. If you drive on dirt roads or dusty environments, the air outside is fine sandpaper that will destroy your cylinder walls if it gets into the engine. <LINE> <LINE> The Air Filter is a pleated paper barrier that sits inside that big black box on top of or to the side of the engine. If it gets clogged with dirt, insects, and dead leaves, the car will 'choke,' lose power, cough on hills, and waste a fortune in gas. <LINE> <LINE> You don't need tools for this. Undo the metal clips, take out the dirty old filter, and put in the fresh white one. It’s literally easier than toasting bread, and mechanics still charge you to do it for you.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Battery: The Spark of Life <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> It’s Monday morning, you turn the key, and hear only an agonizing 'click-click-click' without the car starting. Welcome to the world of dead batteries. <LINE> <LINE> Car batteries are heavy, dangerous boxes full of lead plates submerged in sulfuric acid. They serve to provide that massive punch of energy to the starter motor so the car wakes up. After the engine turns over, the battery does nothing; the Alternator takes over the energy supply. <LINE> <LINE> If the lead terminals (the battery posts) are covered in white or greenish dust, that’s corrosion. It blocks the current. Disconnect the cables (always the black Negative first!), pour hot water with baking soda to clean it, scrub with steel wool, and put them back. Watch out for the acid on your hands.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Magic of 'Jump Starting' <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If the battery died because you left the headlights on, you’ll need jumper cables and a donor car that’s running. Doing this wrong can fry the entire electrical system of both vehicles. <LINE> <LINE> The order is an irrevocable law. First, connect the RED clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the dead battery. Then, connect the other RED clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the good car's battery. <LINE> <LINE> Now, connect the BLACK clamp to the negative (-) terminal of the good car. Here’s the kicker: DO NOT connect the last black clamp to the dead battery's negative terminal. Connect it to a clean metal part of the bad car's engine block, away from the battery. This prevents a spark from igniting the invisible hydrogen gas that a dead battery exhales and blowing acid in your face.
IGUI_BookMechanic1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tires and the Penny Test <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You might have a four-hundred-horsepower V8 under the hood and Italian racing brakes, but the only four pieces of your car that actually touch the asphalt and keep you alive in a rain-slicked turn are the size of your palm. The tires. <LINE> <LINE> If the tread is bald, rainwater has nowhere to drain, forming a film of water between the rubber and the asphalt (hydroplaning). The car becomes an uncontrollable steel sled. <LINE> <LINE> The old test never fails: take a penny with Abraham Lincoln’s head and place it upside down into the tire groove. If you can see the top of the president's entire head, your tires are dangerously bald and you are gambling with death.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: The Iron Underworld <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In the first volume, we opened the hood. You played with filters, changed the oil, and felt like a real automotive engineer. Wipe that smile off your face. The hood is the clean, polite part of the car. <LINE> <LINE> Now we’re going to crawl under the chassis. It’s down here that real American engineering happens. A car’s underworld is a cruel desert of dried mud, petrified grease, bolts fused by rust, and forged steel parts that weigh more than you do. <LINE> <LINE> Here, brute force meets unforgiving physics. If you mess up the engine, the car won't start. If you mess up the suspension or brakes, the car starts, drives, and throws you off a cliff at sixty miles an hour on your next vacation trip. Pay attention.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Automatic Transmission (ATF Fluid) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> I hate automatic cars. They replaced the pure trust of steel gears with a magic cauldron full of cardboard discs, microscopic valves, and complex hydraulic pumps under the floor. But today’s market demands this laziness. <LINE> <LINE> The blood of the automatic transmission is ATF fluid. It should be perfectly red, shiny, and smell like factory chemicals. If your automatic gear is hitting with violent jolts when shifting, pull the transmission dipstick and smell the oil. <LINE> <LINE> If the fluid is black or dark brown and smells exactly like burnt toast, the internal friction discs have disintegrated into the oil. Changing the oil now won’t save the transmission; it’s already dead. Prepare to take thousands of dollars out of your pocket.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> CV Joints (The Click) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In modern front-wheel-drive cars, engine power needs to reach the front wheels, which are constantly turning left and right as you steer. A straight steel bar would snap. <LINE> <LINE> The invention that solves this is the Constant Velocity (CV) Joint. It’s a complex metal globe, full of steel balls bathed in heavy grease, covered by a rubber accordion (boot), allowing the axle to bend without stopping its spin. <LINE> <LINE> If the rubber tears, the grease flies out and street grit gets into the balls. If you turn the steering wheel all the way to the left to take a corner at the intersection and the tire starts clicking loudly and repeatedly ('click-click-click-click'), your CV joint has been destroyed by grit and is about to snap, leaving you with no traction in the middle of the intersection.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Pickup Driveshaft <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In real pickups, with the engine in the front and traction on the heavy rear wheels, the power travels underneath the entire cabin through a very long, balanced, hollow ballistic steel tube called a Driveshaft. <LINE> <LINE> This shaft is pinned at the ends by small cross-shaped pieces called Universal Joints (U-joints). These U-joints need grease often. If the internal rollers dry out under farm dust, they will develop play. <LINE> <LINE> The symptom is clear: you shift into 'Drive,' step on the gas, and hear a heavy metallic clunk ('CLANK') coming directly from under your seat, even before the pickup moves. That’s the worn U-joint play. Ignore it, and the driveshaft will detach on the highway, fall onto the asphalt, and catapult the rear of your car into the air.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wheel Bearings (The Airplane) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A heavy wheel spinning thousands of times while holding a thousand pounds of weight needs to roll smoothly and perfectly. It does this by spinning on top of the Wheel Bearing, a double ring full of polished steel balls or cylindrical rollers behind the brake drum. <LINE> <LINE> Over the years, hitting deep potholes creates tiny chips and craters in the bearing's polished steel. It starts to hum imperceptibly. <LINE> <LINE> But when you hit the highway at 50 mph, the hum turns into a deep, constant buzz that sounds exactly like a large turboprop airplane flying right next to your door, changing pitch when you take long curves. The bearing is ground-up inside. The friction will weld the wheel to the axle at high speed if you keep driving like that.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The War Against Rust <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Every chassis mechanic smells rust and hates it. Water and salt in the winter turn the car's original black bolts into round, reddish iron-oxide tumors. <LINE> <LINE> The amateur's biggest mistake is grabbing a massive breaker bar and yanking a very rusty suspension bolt all at once. The bolt body twists and snaps in half, leaving the threads stuck forever inside the part. <LINE> <LINE> When you find a bolt locked by aggressive rust, don’t be a gorilla. Use science. Drown the bolt in aerosol penetrating oil (WD-40 is okay, but specific oils are better) and let it work for ten minutes. If the wrench won't turn with moderate force, grab a gas torch, heat the nut until it almost glows hot. Heat expands the nut ring, breaking the ancient seal of rust.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Raising the Stakes <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You survived the under-chassis inspection and now know why your car rattles, clicks, and screams every time you ignore a pothole. Understand: the suspension and brakes don't make the car look pretty, they make the car obedient and keep you away from walls. <LINE> <LINE> With the lessons from Volume One and the brutality absorbed in this Volume Two, you dominate seventy percent of what breaks day-to-day on the forgotten roads of the American interior. <LINE> <LINE> But our journey isn't over. The tin is strong and the chassis is greased, but in Volume Three, we’re going to open the beast's heart and take off the lids. We’ll talk about the complexities of the engine head, the dreaded timing belt, bent valves, rotary distributor failures, and the dangers of a blown head gasket that mixes water into the oil of your cylinder block. Prep the torque wrench, and see you then.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Coiled Death (Springs) <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your car's suspension is what keeps your teeth from falling out at every pothole on the road. The heart of it is the Coil Springs. They are thick steel bars wound under absurdly violent pressure, designed to handle the weight of a two-ton vehicle hitting a pothole. <LINE> <LINE> Never, in your entire miserable life, try to remove a suspension spring from the car by unscrewing the control arms without using a heavy carbon-steel Spring Compressor. <LINE> <LINE> When a suspension spring is released without being locked down, it doesn't just jump. It detonates with the kinetic force of a cannon shot, punching through your garage wall and taking your jaw or left arm with it in the process. Respect the stored potential energy.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Bounce Test (Shocks) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Springs absorb the hit, but if the car had only springs, it would keep bouncing down the road like an iron basketball until you lost control. That’s what Shock Absorbers are for. <LINE> <LINE> The shock is a tube filled with thick oil and tiny valves. It brakes the spring's movement and forces the tire to stay glued to the asphalt. If your shocks leak oil and die, the tire will spend more time floating in the air than touching the street, doubling the distance you need to stop the car. <LINE> <LINE> To test their health, go to the corner of your car, push the fender down with the full weight of your body, and let go. The car should rise, go down once, and lock motionless. If it keeps bouncing like a boat on the sea, your shocks have turned to garbage.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Disc Brakes: The Pliers <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your grandfather stopped his car using drum brakes on all four wheels, which would heat up and fail if it rained. Today, any decent pickup uses disc brakes in the front. The engineering is so simple and brilliant it’s stupid. <LINE> <LINE> Behind your tire, there’s a massive steel disc spinning with the wheel. Hugging this disc is a heavy iron claw called a Brake Caliper. When you push the pedal, hydraulic fluid pushes a piston inside the caliper, which crushes the disc with the pads, turning motion energy into extreme heat. <LINE> <LINE> Every time you brake the car to avoid hitting traffic, your discs reach a few hundred degrees Celsius. It’s raw friction. If your brakes are shaking the steering wheel when you step on the pedal, it means the heat warped the steel disc like an old frying pan.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Squeal of the Pad <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The friction material of brake pads is made of resins and metals that slowly break down over time into black dust (that’s the horrible dirt that sticks to your wheels). <LINE> <LINE> Dishonest mechanics love to say you need to replace your pads 'now' to overcharge you. But your car talks to you. Almost every brake pad manufactured has a tiny flexible metal hook on the end, called a Wear Indicator. <LINE> <LINE> When the pad material is gone and it gets dangerously thin, this metal hook starts touching the steel disc while you drive, producing a continuous sharp squeal that sounds like a knife scratching a plate. When you hear that whistle on the street, the car isn't broken; it’s politely warning you that you have two weeks to buy new pads.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Brake Fluid (Killer Acid) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The system that crushes the calipers doesn't use water or motor oil; it uses DOT 3 or DOT 4 Brake Fluid. Pay close attention to what I’m about to say: this liquid is one of the nastiest and most troublesome chemicals in your car. <LINE> <LINE> First: It dissolves automotive paint as if it were remover. If you spill a drop of brake fluid on the hood and don't wash it off with water within thirty seconds, your car's paint will peel right down to the bare steel sheet. <LINE> <LINE> Second: It is extremely hygroscopic. This means it has a nasty habit of sucking moisture and water right out of the air itself. Over the years, old fluid gets full of diluted water. When you hit the brakes on a long mountain descent, the heat will boil that water in the calipers, creating vapor bubbles that leave you with a mushy pedal and no brakes.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Bleeding the Brakes <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Physics dictates that liquids cannot be compressed, but gas can. If there is a single bubble of air inside your brake line, when you step on the pedal, the force of your foot will only crush that bubble like a balloon, and the caliper won't exert any force against the wheel. The pedal goes to the floor and the car doesn't stop. <LINE> <LINE> After messing with the lines, you need to 'Bleed' the system. You will need a friend. They sit in the car and 'pump' the brake pedal several times until it gets hard, and hold it tight. <LINE> <LINE> You go under the car with an open-end wrench and open the tiny bleeder screw behind the wheel for a second. The fluid will squirt out along with air bubbles (and your friend's pedal will sink again). Close the screw. Repeat this until only pure liquid comes out without foaming. Air is the enemy.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Manual Transmission <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your car engine likes to spin fast. Car wheels need to spin slowly to start moving. The Transmission (Gearbox) is the mechanical wonder full of steel gears that multiplies the engine’s force for the wheels. <LINE> <LINE> A manual box from the good old days is indestructible if it has gear oil (Valvoline) inside. It’s a box full of toothed discs. <LINE> <LINE> The biggest mistake modern drivers make is resting their hand on top of the shift lever while driving. The weak weight of your arm pushes the internal selector fork against gears that are spinning at thousands of revolutions. You don't feel it, but you are slowly burning and sanding down the small internal synchronization pieces (synchros) inside the gearbox until second gear starts 'grinding' to go in.
IGUI_BookMechanic2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Burnt Clutch <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you disconnect the engine from the gearbox so you can shift gears without blowing up the gears? With the clutch disc. It’s basically a giant brake pad in the shape of a round disc that’s crushed between the engine and the gearbox. <LINE> <LINE> When you step on the left pedal, you move that disc away, releasing the engine's power. The horrible smell of 'burnt clutch' (which smells like sulfur and hot tire) happens when the novice driver revs the car too high and releases the pedal too slowly. <LINE> <LINE> The disc ends up rubbing against the engine flywheel loosely, sliding without locking. The friction burns the disc material. Don’t be the kind of idiot who holds the car stopped on a hill using only the clutch instead of the handbrake. You’re frying a part that requires half the car to be disassembled to be replaced.
IGUI_BookMechanic3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chapter 1: The Heart of the Beast <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You’ve changed the oil, you haven't been crushed by the suspension, and your wheels haven't fallen off on the road. Congratulations, you’ve mastered the exterior. But now the games are over. We’re going to pop the lid off the pressure cooker. <LINE> <LINE> Welcome to the guts of the internal combustion engine. Here, you don’t use brute force; you use mathematical precision. If you overtighten a lug nut, you just break the bolt. If you overtighten an engine bolt with the wrong force, you warp the metal, crush the valves, and destroy a three-thousand-dollar cast-iron block. <LINE> <LINE> Clean your workbench. Wash your hands. The inside of an engine demands the respect of an operating room. If a single grain of coarse grit gets into the wrong place now, your car will be nothing but a very heavy anchor.
IGUI_BookMechanic3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Timing Light <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Gasoline explosion isn't instantaneous; it takes a tiny fraction of a second to expand. If the spark jumps exactly when the piston reaches the top, the explosion will arrive too late. The spark needs to happen a little BEFORE the piston reaches the top. This is 'Ignition Advance.' <LINE> <LINE> To regulate this, we use a Stroboscopic Timing Light. You point the light at the timing marks on the engine pulley while it’s spinning. Every spark, the light flashes. Since it flashes at the exact speed of the engine, the pulley looks like it’s stopped in mid-air, frozen by an optical illusion. <LINE> <LINE> You loosen the base of the distributor with a wrench and turn it slightly by hand left or right, advancing or retarding the firing until the pulley mark aligns with the factory chart mark. Your engine will stop coughing and gain the aggressive roar it deserves.
IGUI_BookMechanic3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Carburetor (Pure Engineering) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you open the hood of a car today and see a mess of wires and fuel injectors firing under the command of a computer chip, mourn. When the chip burns out in the middle of nowhere, you’re stranded. I prefer brute engineering: The Carburetor. <LINE> <LEFT> The carburetor is an aluminum piece full of mechanical butterflies and holes where air is swallowed, sucking gasoline out of the bowl by pure vacuum force, like a straw in a glass of soda. No wires, no chips. Pure atmospheric pressure physics. <LINE> <LEFT> The problem is that carburetors get out of tune and clog if the car sits for months. Old gas turns into a stinking yellow jelly that plugs the tiny bronze holes (jets). A good mechanic cleans, replaces the gaskets, and adjusts the air-fuel mixture screws by guiding themselves only by the sound of the idle and the smell of the exhaust.
IGUI_BookMechanic3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Cold-Start Choke <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Fuel condenses on the cold iron walls of the block and the engine refuses to start on a harsh winter day. The carburetor compensates for this with the Choke. <LINE> <LEFT> It’s a metal butterfly at the top of the carburetor that closes almost completely when you pull a lever on the dashboard. By closing the air intake, the engine goes into a panic and starts sucking an absurdly rich amount of raw gasoline into the cylinders, forcing the explosion to happen in the cold. <LINE> <LEFT> As soon as the engine wakes up and coughs, you need to start opening the choke butterfly slowly.
