IGUI_BookMetalWelding5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Fishmouth Fit <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you join the tip of a round tube against the side of another round tube to form a vehicle's skeleton without leaving holes? <LINE> <LINE> The straight cut of a saw will leave immense gaps in the curved sides of the piping. The required industrial cut is the fishmouth shape. Using the thick grinder, you hollow out the tip of the first tube into a deep concave shape, so that it perfectly hugs the curve of the second tube. Without gaps to fill with extra material, the fire fuses the metal structurally continuously.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ancient Pottery <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Long before steel, bronze, or writing, man mastered mud. Pottery is the oldest of human industries. Our ancestors realized that the wet earth beneath their feet was not just dirt; it was a plastic medium waiting for a purpose. <LINE> <LINE> This book explores the primordial methods of pottery. Before electric wheels or gas kilns existed, there were only hands, the riverbank, and the open fire.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Chemical Transformation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> What happens inside that fire? The extreme heat drives off the 'Chemically Bound Water' that is attached to the clay molecules at an atomic level. <LINE> <LINE> When the piece reaches around 600°C, it undergoes an irreversible transformation. It stops being mud that melts in the rain and becomes 'Terracotta' (Baked Earth). From that moment on, no matter how much water you pour on it, it will never return to malleable clay. The vessel is born.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Slow Cooling <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Haste is the enemy of pottery. When the campfire finally dies out, the pieces inside are glowing red with heat. <LINE> <LINE> If you are impatient and pull away the ashes, exposing the terracotta vessel to the cold wind or room temperature, the thermal shock will shatter the piece with the loud crack of a revolver. You must let the firing cool naturally beneath the ashes, sometimes for a whole day, until you can pick up the vessel with your bare hands.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Limitation of Porous Terracotta <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You made a beautiful ancient 'Pit Fired' jar and filled it with fresh water. But the next day, the water is gone and the table is wet. <LINE> <LINE> Pottery fired at low temperatures (like terracotta plant pots) is extremely porous. It 'sweats'. Water seeps through the microscopic walls. In ancient times, this was useful because evaporation kept the water cold, but for long-term liquid storage, it was a terrible disaster.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Primitive Sealants <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To bypass this porosity, before the invention of glass glaze, the ancients turned to resin. <LINE> <LINE> They harvested pine sap, heated it, and poured it inside the vessel while it was fresh out of the fire and still hot. They rolled the sap around inside, creating a natural varnish layer that penetrated and sealed the open pores of the clay. It was a temporary fix that made the vessel watertight (capable of holding liquids without leaking), but the resin left a taste in the water and degraded over time.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Burnishing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Another brilliant technique to close pores even before firing is 'Burnishing'. <LINE> <LINE> When the pot is at the leather-hard stage, you take a very smooth and perfectly polished river stone and spend hours rubbing it vigorously against the vessel wall. This friction squashes the clay particles, closing the surface and creating a beautiful natural sheen without needing any chemical paint. It drastically reduces terracotta leakage.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Change of an Era <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Pinch Pot and Pit Firing brought humanity out of the cave age, allowing us to cook and store seeds for the winter. You now possess the basic knowledge to survive if dropped naked in the woods. <LINE> <LINE> But evolution demands perfection. Open fires waste too much wood and never reach high enough temperatures to turn earth into absolute rock. We need to trap the heat. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Two, 'Build Your Own Kiln', we will leave the pits behind and enter the era of thermal engineering. Let's build the dragon's chamber.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Search for Clay <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> True clay is not found on the surface of your garden. Topsoil is full of organic material and is useless for anything other than planting. <LINE> <LINE> To find clay, the ancients dug deeper, or looked in river cuts and dry creek beds. Raw clay is dense, sticky, and heavy. If you take a handful of wet dirt, roll it into a 'worm' and try to bend it in half, common dirt snaps. High-quality clay bends without cracking. This is 'plasticity'.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Purification (Levigation) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You cannot just take clay straight from the river and make a pot. Wild clay is full of pebbles, twigs, and coarse sand. If a small stone gets baked inside the wall of your pot, it will expand in the fire and explode the entire piece. <LINE> <LINE> Ancient peoples used the technique of Levigation. They mixed the clay with plenty of water until it turned into a thin soup (Slip). Stones and heavy impurities sank to the bottom of the bucket, and the pure, fine clay remained suspended in the water. Afterward, they transferred only the water with the good clay to dry in the sun.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wedging <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With clean clay in hand, there is one final enemy before shaping: air. <LINE> <LINE> If there are air bubbles trapped inside your clay block, guess what? Air expands violently when heated. Your pot will turn into a fragmentation grenade inside the fire. 'Wedging' is the vigorous technique of kneading the clay on a hard surface, exactly like kneading bread dough, pushing all the air out and aligning the clay's microscopic particles.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Pinch Technique <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The most primitive and instinctive way to make a vessel is the Pinch Pot. <LINE> <LINE> Take an apple-sized ball of clay. Press your thumb right into the center of the ball, hollowing it out. Then, using your thumb on the inside and fingers on the outside, pinch and squeeze the wall while rotating the ball in your other hand. Gradually, the walls rise and thin out. This is how humanity's first bowls were made to gather water and grains.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Coiling Technique <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Pinch Pot has a size limit. To make large amphorae or tall storage jars, the ancients used the Coiling technique. <LINE> <LINE> They took clay and rolled it on the ground until it formed long, finger-thick 'snakes'. Next, they made a flat base and began stacking these snakes in a spiral, one on top of the other, building up the vessel wall. With their fingers or a piece of wood (rib tool), they smoothed the inside and outside to fuse the coils and erase the lines.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The 'Leather-Hard' Stage <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A common mistake is trying to add handles or carve designs while the clay is too wet. It will sag and collapse under its own weight. <LINE> <LINE> You must let the piece dry in the shade for a while until it reaches the 'Leather-Hard' stage. At this point, the clay has lost moisture, no longer smudges your fingers, and is rigid, yet it can still be cut and joined. It is the perfect moment to attach handles or scrape the walls with a knife to make them symmetrical.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Drying <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before reaching the fire, the piece needs to dry completely, until it becomes what we call Bone-Dry. <LINE> <LINE> Never place your raw piece in strong sunlight or under a hot, intense wind. The outside will dry much faster than the inside, and the clay will split in half before even seeing the campfire. Drying must be slow and gradual in a sheltered environment.
IGUI_BookPottery1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Pit Firing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Ancient tribes did not have closed brick kilns. The first way to turn mud into pottery was 'Pit Firing'. <LINE> <LINE> They dug a shallow hole in the ground, lined it with dry leaves, straw, and twigs, placed the completely dry clay pieces in the middle, and covered everything with piles of dry herbivore dung and thick wood. The pit was lit and burned slowly for hours, reaching temperatures around 180°C, enough to bake primitive clay.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Build Your Own Kiln <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you want to take pottery seriously and step out of the stone age of backyard campfires, you need to trap the heat. To that end, this month's DIY hobbyist magazine brings you this project: The Pottery Kiln. <LINE> <LINE> Building your own kiln isn't just a fun weekend project; it is your gateway to indestructible pottery. This guide will teach you to erect a classic wood-fired updraft kiln that would make your local neighborhood association pull their hair out.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Bisque Firing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With the kiln ready, we conduct our first heavy firing: The Bisque Firing. <LINE> <LINE> This stage transforms fragile raw clay (which would melt if you put water on it) into rigid, permanently solid ceramic. In Bisque firing, we aim for a temperature between 900 and 180°C (Cone 06 to 04 in professional jargon). The pot comes out of the kiln pink or pale, very hard, yet still incredibly porous.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Boiling Water <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The biggest killer of pots is rushing at the start of the firing. <LINE> <LINE> Even a 'Bone-Dry' pot still contains chemical water. In the first two hours of the kiln, you must keep the fire at a 'light smoke' level, keeping the chamber below 180°C to allow residual water to gentle evaporate. If you throw on heavy wood right off the bat and the kiln sharply shoots past 180°C, the water will boil, turning into steam inside the clay walls and exploding your pieces.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> How to Measure 180°C Without Gadgets? <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If we don't have digital pyrometers or fancy thermocouples at home, how on earth does the rustic potter know the temperature inside? <LINE> <LINE> Through something ingenious called 'Pyrometric Cones'. They are small ceramic pyramids manufactured to melt and bend at a very specific temperature. You place the cones on the shelf alongside the pots, near a 'Peep Hole' in the brick wall. When cone number 04 bends like melting butter, you know you've hit 180°C.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reading the Fire's Color <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Older potters don't even need the cones; they read the color through the peep hole. Steel and clay emit universal thermal light. <LINE> <LINE> Dark Red is around 650°C. Cherry Red indicates you've crossed the line of chemical transformation (180°C - 900°C). If the inside of the kiln is glowing an Intense Orange that hurts your eyes, you've reached the perfect Bisque Firing (close to 1050°C). Brilliant white is lethal high temperature (1300°C) where your common clay will start melting into a glassy puddle.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Art of Cooling <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hit 180°C? Great. Stop adding wood. But what now? <LINE> <LINE> Shutting down the draft and letting it cool requires monastic discipline. You must not, under any circumstances, open the kiln door while it is still glowing red. The rush of cold ambient air will cause immediate thermal shock to the ceramic pieces inside, and everything will crack in a chorus of horrible pops. Seal the air intakes, close the ceiling damper, and go to sleep. You will only open the door the next day.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ready for the Next Level <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You built your kiln and baked your first perfect batch of 'Bisque' pottery. <LINE> <LINE> The pieces are now hard as stone, emit a high ring when tapped with a pencil, and will last for decades. But there is a catch: as we saw in primitive firing, bisque pottery still absorbs water and will slowly leak if used as a jar. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Three, 'Glazing Pottery at Home', we will return to hobby magazines to solve porosity for good. We will learn the magic of melting glass over clay to create the ultimate waterproof ceramic.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Fire Pit vs. Kiln <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Why build a brick box? An open campfire radiates 180%% of its heat into the atmosphere. It is an enormous waste of energy and wood. <LINE> <LINE> A Kiln is a thermal confinement. The heat from the fire is forced to circulate within a tiny space, reflecting off the inner walls and baking the clay from all sides with a brutal, stable temperature that open fire could never achieve. We are talking about crossing the magical barrier of 180°C.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Materials List <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If you try to build a kiln using the common red bricks left over from your barbecue grill, it will melt and collapse during the first heavy firing. <LINE> <LINE> For the inner lining (the 'Hot Face'), you must buy Firebricks, made of clay with a high percentage of alumina, capable of resisting industrial temperatures. To bond these bricks, you will use special refractory mortar, not common cement. The outer structure can be made of concrete blocks or common bricks for support.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Updraft Flow <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The design we are going to build is the Updraft Kiln. It is the simplest and cheapest for a garage hobbyist. <LINE> <LINE> The basic physics are: the fire sits at ground level (in the firebox), the hot air rises naturally, passes through the chamber where the pots are stacked, and escapes through a small hole in the top lid of the kiln. It is basically a controlled chimney where you place your vessels right in the path of the scorching smoke.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Firebox <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The foundation of everything is the Firebox. It is the lower brick chamber where you stoke the wood (or position a gas torch, if you are fancy). <LINE> <LINE> The Firebox needs a front opening to feed the fuel and, crucially, adjustable air intakes (Draft Holes). Fire feeds on oxygen. If you close the primary air intake, the fire smothers. Controlling the temperature of the entire kiln depends on your ability to open and close the air intakes at the base.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Grated Floor <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How does heat rise from the Firebox to the pottery chamber without ashes destroying your pieces? <LINE> <LINE> You will build a suspended floor using firebrick pillars and support shelves. The floor must have open gaps (like a grate) or a wide slit around the shelf edges. This allows the flames and extreme heat to rise to the second floor of the kiln without the wood physically touching the raw clay.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Loading Chamber <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Above the grated floor lies the Main Chamber, the heart of the kiln. <LINE> <LINE> This is where you stack your bone-dry pieces. The secret to an even firing is spacing. Never pile raw clay pots right up against one another. The hot air, which can exceed 900°C, needs to flow freely between every piece like an invisible river. If the vessels are tightly crammed, the heat won't circulate, and some pots will remain raw.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Ceiling 'Damper' Control <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A kiln without a ceiling is useless. We will make a brick dome with an exhaust hole at the top. <LINE> <LINE> Over this exhaust hole, you will place the 'Damper', which is nothing more than a thick sheet of refractory metal or a flat brick that can slide. Opening the damper draws air and builds up the fire below (increasing the draft). Closing the damper traps hot air inside the chamber. Piloting the damper and the air intakes below is like driving your car's engine.
IGUI_BookPottery2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Additional Thermal Insulation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Even when using firebricks, a good designer adds insulation. <LINE> <LINE> If you are going to build your kiln as a permanent installation in the yard, mix fine dirt, straw, and sand to make a thick, rustic plaster (Cob) and apply it all over the outside of the kiln. This plaster acts as a heavy blanket, retaining a monstrous amount of thermal energy inside and saving hours of wood consumption during the firing.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Glazing Pottery at Home <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Your pot survived the kiln and turned into a beautiful piece of 'Bisque'. The problem is, if you pour hot soup into it, the clay will sweat and leak through the bottom in a matter of minutes. Low-fired pottery is a microscopic sieve. <LINE> <LINE> To transform pots into functional kitchen utensils, we enter the world of household chemistry: Glaze. Get ready to fuse glass on top of earth and make your pieces completely waterproof and ready for daily use.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Application (Dipping vs. Brushing) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> There are two domestic ways to apply glaze. If you made gallons of the mix in a large bucket, grab the piece with tongs and give it a quick three-second 'Dip'. The porosity of the bisque sucks up the water and leaves a perfect, even layer of chemical powder on the surface. <LINE> <LINE> If you are going to use a Brush (buying ready-made glazes in small jars), apply three thick coats, always crossing the direction of the brushstrokes. Glaze does not spread like wall paint; if applied too thin, it ends up rough and scratchy.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Glaze Firing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The glazed piece is dry to the touch (it looks like it's covered in flour). It's time to put it back in the kiln for the second firing: The Glaze Firing. <LINE> <LINE> The kiln will now need to be much hotter than during the Bisque firing. You must pilot the air intakes to drive the chamber up around 1150 to 1180°C (Cone 5 or 6). The intense heat will be responsible for activating the chemistry, creating the magic of fusion between silica and clay.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Shock of Crazing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You cooled the kiln, opened the door, and your vessel is beautiful and shiny. But then you hear a tiny sound: 'Tink... Tink'. <LINE> <LINE> Suddenly, a network of fine cracks appears across the entire glass layer. The name for this is 'Crazing'. This happens because the glaze's glass shrunk much faster than the jar's clay while the kiln was cooling. Aesthetically it can be charming, but functionally it is terrible: these microfissures collect food bacteria over time.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Lemon Test (Food Safety) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Made a nice mug in the garage but don't know if the glaze is safe to drink coffee from? Run the Lemon Test. <LINE> <LINE> Squeeze a lemon (or white vinegar) inside the mug and leave it there overnight. The next day, wash it and look at it against the light. If the color of the glaze changed where the juice sat, or if the mug's shine turned dull, the glaze is unstable. Acid is corroding poorly melted chemicals. This piece is for holding flowers, not food.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Functional Daily Sealing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> But when the formula is correct, the pots emerge perfectly glossy and vitrified. <LINE> <LINE> You have just created a hygienic household object. A glazed storage pot keeps air moisture away from corn grain, keeping pests out. Sealed jars hold olive oil and rainwater indefinitely without leaking a single drop, and can be cleaned with boiling water and soap, eliminating pathogens. You have mastered storage.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> On the Way to Mastery <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Now indeed. Your pieces are hard as steel due to the kiln firing (Volume II) and waterproof as glass thanks to the Glaze formulation from Volume III. You have mastered 90s garage chemistry. <LINE> <LINE> However, your work is still crude. The manual coil method is slow and rustic. If you want speed, symmetry, and grandeur, we need to look to the East. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Four, 'Ming Chinese Masterpieces', we will abandon pinching and climb onto the definitive equipment: The Potter's Wheel.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> What is Glaze? <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Many people think that glazing pottery is just painting it with colorful paint. That is a glaring mistake. Paint burns up and turns to ash in the kiln. <LINE> <LINE> Ceramic glaze is, fundamentally, a layer of liquid glass mixed with ground minerals that melt in the fire and coat the piece. When the kiln cools, this glass hardens and fuses with the pores of the clay, sealing the vessel forever. Glaze is the clear (or colored) shield of your pottery.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Danger of Lead (Attention!) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Before we mix chemical powders in the garage, a vital warning: READ THE LABEL! <LINE> <LINE> For decades, vibrant red and orange glazes contained lead oxide. If you use a lead glaze on a plate that will hold food or acidic drink (like orange juice), the acid leaches the lead into the food and slowly poisons your family. Nowadays, only buy and formulate 'Food Safe', lead-free glazes. Lead belongs in car batteries, not the kitchen.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Formula Trinity <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Every functional glaze in the world is composed of just three basic elements, balanced mathematically: <LINE> <LINE> 1. The Glass Former (Silica). <LINE> 2. The Flux. <LINE> 3. The Stabilizer (Alumina). <LINE> <LINE> Without silica, there is no glass. Without flux, silica won't melt. Without alumina, the glass runs and ruins the kiln. Let's understand the magic of each one.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Silica (The Glass Builder) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Silica (Silicon Dioxide) is simply finely ground quartz or pure white sand. It is the substance that transforms into glass. <LINE> <LINE> The problem with silica is that it only melts at an incredible 180°C. Our backyard brick kiln barely reaches 1150°C. If you put only silica powder on your jar, it will come out of the kiln looking exactly the same: as a dry, useless white powder. We need a helper to lower that melting point.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Flux (The Accelerator) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This is where the Flux comes in. It acts as a chemical catalyst that forces the silica to melt at much lower temperatures. <LINE> <LINE> Calcium Carbonate, Sodium, Potassium, or Boron are common fluxes. Mixed with the flux, the silica powder gives up its resistance and happily melts at 1100°C in your wood-fired kiln. But now we have a new problem: molten glass is very runny. It will stream down the vessel walls and form a puddle stuck to the kiln floor.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Alumina (The Brake) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To stop the glaze from running like water, we add the Stabilizer: Alumina (or Aluminum Oxide, generally sourced from pure clay). <LINE> <LINE> Alumina is the skeleton of the glaze. It thickens the mixture in its molten state, giving it the viscosity of hot honey instead of water. With alumina, the glass melts shiny, but holds onto the side of the jar and stays there, sealing the piece evenly without dripping onto the floor.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Preparing the Pot (Sponge Bath) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You have your liquid glaze in a bucket. Don't dip the piece yet! <LINE> <LINE> Your 'bisque' pots have been gathering dust on the garage shelf. If you try to glaze dusty ceramic, the dust will repel the water in the glaze and create bald spots (Crawling) where the glass doesn't stick. Always take a clean, damp sponge and wipe down the whole vessel before glazing. A clean pot drinks up the mixture perfectly.
IGUI_BookPottery3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Wax Resist <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The number one Fatal Error of the beginner: Glazing the bottom (the foot) of the pot. <LINE> <LINE> If there is glaze on the bottom of your piece and you put it in the kiln, at 1100°C the glaze will turn into liquid glue and fuse to the brick shelf. When the kiln cools, the vessel will be permanently welded to the brick, and you'll have to destroy it with a hammer to get it out. To avoid this, paint the bottom of the pot with liquid wax. Where there is wax, glaze doesn't stick.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ming Chinese Masterworks <LINE> A Guide <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The West played with clay for millennia, but the true ceramic revolution happened in the East. During the Ming Dynasty, pottery ceased to be just a rustic means of survival and became pure high technology and symmetrical art. <LINE> <LINE> This museum catalog is not just for admiring untouchable vases. It reveals the mechanical secrets of how the Chinese achieved production speed, absolute control of symmetry, and the invention of the precision potter's wheel.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> High-Capacity Vessels <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> And what about giant pots with a fifty-liter capacity? Not even the best master can pull fifty kilograms of clay in a single go on the wheel. <LINE> <LINE> The technique was 'Sectional Throwing'. They threw the base of the vase (which looked like a giant bowl). Then they threw the top part separately (a cone). When both parts reached the leather-hard stage, they painted slip on the edges, stuck one half on top of the other on the wheel, and smoothed the seam. It's modular engineering.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Cobalt Blue (Underglaze) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The famous Ming dynasty vases with blue and white paintings did not use ordinary paint. They used Cobalt Oxide. <LINE> <LINE> This black powder was painted directly onto the raw, dry porcelain. Then, a transparent glaze was dipped over everything, and the piece went for the final firing (High temperature). The extreme fire fused the glaze, and the cobalt oxide exploded into a deep sapphire color, trapped and protected forever under the layer of clear glass (Underglaze Technique).
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Reduction Atmosphere <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Asian kilns utilized a dangerous chemistry called 'Reduction Atmosphere'. <LINE> <LINE> Instead of letting the oxygen burn clean in the kiln, the kiln master strangled the air output of the chimney. The fire, desperate for oxygen, began stealing oxygen atoms from inside the chemical compounds of the clay and glazes themselves (such as from copper or iron oxide). This chemical asphyxiation drastically changed the pottery's color. A glaze that would come out green in a normal kiln turned a brilliant blood red in reduction.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Production Muscle Memory <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Ming dynasty was humanity's first great factory. There was a division of labor. <LINE> <LINE> One man only ground the kaolin. Another just sat at the wheel and pulled the same bowl a thousand times a day. When a potter repeats a pull a thousand times, their muscle memory crystallizes. They no longer look at the clay; they just pull, and all the bowls come out exactly the same size and weight, without molds. Repetition transforms shaping into biology.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Wheel's Impact on Survival <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Reading this museum guide, you learned the practical value of speed. The patience of coiled pottery is beautiful, but inefficient for rural scale. <LINE> <LINE> If you are going to build dozens of storage jars for harvests, clay water cisterns, and tiles to shelter equipment, the principle of the wheel and modular shaping are your salvation. Mastery of centrifugal force allows you to raise a water base in days, rather than weeks.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Far Beyond Art <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Ming relics combine the precision of the motorized wheel, mastery of porosity through kaolin, and the fury of Dragon Kilns. We have ceased to be hobbyists kneading mud and risen to the peak of mass fabrication control. <LINE> <LINE> However, the true behavior of molecules at these infernal temperatures still feels like magic. It is time to strip away the magic. <LINE> <LINE> In the Fifth and final Volume, 'Pyrometamorphic Process of Ceramic Materials', the art ends. We will treat ceramics through the lens of modern thermodynamic engineering, understanding industrial crucibles and resistance to lethal impact.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Wheel Revolution <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Making pots by stacking clay coils takes hours and results in thick, irregular vessels. The Potter's Wheel changes the rules of time. <LINE> <LINE> By utilizing rotational momentum, a heavy platter spinning at high speed allows centrifugal force to do the heavy lifting. What used to take a whole afternoon to shape by hand can now be raised from scratch into a perfect vase in less than five minutes. The wheel is the ancient assembly line.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Battle of Centering <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Anyone sitting at a wheel for the first time will be humbled by the clay. The first and most critical stage is 'Centering'. <LINE> <LINE> If you drop the clay onto the spinning wheel and try to shape it without the block being millimetrically on the central axis, centrifugal force will cause the vase to wobble, rip, and fly across the room. The potter braces their elbows firmly against their own thighs, locking their body like a human mechanical lathe, and pushes the wet clay into the center until it spins so perfectly it looks stationary.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Opening and Pulling <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With the clay cone centered, you pierce the middle with your thumbs (Opening). Next comes the 'Pulling'. <LINE> <LINE> The classic Ming movement is using one hand on the inside and the other on the outside of the clay wall, gently squeezing the mass and raising your arms in a straight line while the wheel spins. This squeeze displaces the clay from the bottom upward, growing the vase wall into a tall, symmetrical tube. Lubrication with water is constant; if your hand dries out, the clay twists and the piece collapses.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rhythmic Speed <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Modern electric lathes or traditional kickwheels demand different rhythms. <LINE> <LINE> The master's secret lies in the foot. To center a thick lump of clay, the wheel needs to spin at maximum speed. But as soon as the walls start to rise and the piece becomes tall, hollow, and thin, high speed would destroy the structure. The potter brakes the wheel progressively, shaping the final neck at a very slow and majestic speed. It is a dance of acceleration.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The White Gold: Porcelain <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The Ming dynasty is synonymous with Porcelain. Unlike terracotta (which is iron-rich, porous earth), porcelain is made from a highly rare primary clay called 'Kaolin', mixed with Feldspar. <LINE> <LINE> Kaolin is not plastic. It does not bend easily and resists wheel throwing. But the advantage is that it withstands incredibly brutal kiln temperatures (up to 1400°C). At these temperatures, the feldspar melts completely inside the piece's wall, transforming the entire vessel into a solid block of white glass.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dragon Kilns <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To reach 1400°C in the Middle Ages, the Chinese did not use square backyard kilns. They built Dragon Kilns. <LINE> <LINE> They were gigantic tube-shaped kilns that climbed up hillsides, sometimes stretching for dozens of meters. The fire was lit at the base of the mountain, and the hot air rushed up the giant tube, creating an infernal thermal draft vortex. This natural pressure sucked in so much oxygen that temperatures inside the chamber melted volcanic rocks.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Ming Translucency <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The hallmark of fine porcelain is its translucency. A high-quality piece is thrown so thin and vitrified so completely that if you place a lit candle inside the cup, you can see the light glowing right through the white stone wall. <LINE> <LINE> Only the masters achieved this. Pulling kaolin on the wheel until it was the thickness of an eggshell, without the wall collapsing wet, was the pinnacle of human motor control and tactile sensitivity.
IGUI_BookPottery4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Trimming <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A vase on the Chinese wheel is never finished purely with wet hands. When the vase rises, the bottom always stays thick. <LINE> <LINE> The master lets the pot dry to the 'Leather-Hard' stage. Then, he inverts the pot, sticks the top upside down on the spinning wheel, and uses loop-shaped steel tools (Trim Tools) to slice away clay ribbons from the bottom with the wheel spinning fast, sculpting the perfect Foot Ring of the fine piece.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Pyrometamorphic Process of Ceramic Materials <LINE> Technical Abstract <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> This treatise departs from aesthetic pottery to address materials mechanics. Ceramics, from the engineering standpoint of 1993, is not art; it is the process of human 'Pyrometamorphism'. It is the controlled thermodynamic application to force the geological alteration of room-temperature minerals into new synthetic compounds. <LINE> <LINE> The operator who understands molecular vitrification doesn't just make pots; he builds industrial crucibles capable of containing liquid steel.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Silicon Carbide <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In modern kiln engineering, old clay shelves have been replaced by Silicon Carbide (SiC). <LINE> <LINE> This synthetic compound has an incredibly low rate of thermal expansion and is almost as hard as a diamond. Kiln shelves made of SiC do not warp under extreme weight at 1300°C and withstand aggressive cycles of cold and heat that would obliterate traditional kaolin ceramics. It is the ultimate refractory material of the late 20th century.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Heat Work <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The glaring mistake of the amateur is thinking that ceramic firing is dictated solely by the maximum temperature achieved. The engineer understands 'Heat Work'. <LINE> <LINE> The pyrometric cone does not measure absolute temperature; it measures heat absorption over time. A piece exposed to 1000°C for ten hours reacts (and melts glazes) identically to a piece brought rapidly to 1100°C. Time saturates the crystalline matrix. Haste demands higher temperature peaks; patience saves the clay's limit.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Acoustic Resonance for Diagnosis <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How to inspect whether an industrial ceramic tube suffered internal flaws after cooling without using X-rays? The acoustic test. <LINE> <LINE> The inspector suspends the piece by a neutral point and taps the surface with a light wooden stick. A perfectly vitrified and intact ceramic propagates sound waves in crystal, sustained rings (like a long bell). If there is a structural microfracture imperceptible to the human eye, the crack interrupts the sound wave, resulting in a hollow, dead, and muffled sound. Discard it.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Molecular-Level Glaze Defects <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The phenomenon of 'Crawling' (The glaze moving away and creating bald spots) is not black magic; it is surface tension physics. <LINE> <LINE> When glaze dries too thick over the piece and is then heated, it shrinks and cracks. When vitreous fusion begins, the cracked islands melt. Due to the high surface tension of liquid glass, it forms chubby droplets on itself, refusing to cover the opened hole. The correction requires adding Ball Clay to the liquid glaze to increase raw binding strength.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Survivor's Final Forge <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The pyrometamorphic theory in this book guarantees your ability to advance to the Iron Age. <LINE> <LINE> Your pottery is now directed toward foundry molds, grog-coated bellows blowpipes, and thermal shielding for industrial furnaces. You understand Quartz Inversion, the mechanical braking of Grog, and how Thermal Shock tears the ignorant apart. Mastery of heat is no longer just for storing water.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Pinnacle of Earth and Fire <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The journey that began on muddy riverbanks searching for clay (Volume I), passed through kiln construction (Volume II), chemical glass control (Volume III), and the relentless speed of the wheel (Volume IV), reaches its scientific limit here. <LINE> <LINE> Geological material obeys your will. Ceramics is proof that human intelligence can alter stone itself and crystallize it against time. The fire has died. The kiln has cooled. Your work is now perpetual rock.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Quartz Inversion <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Clay contains free silica (quartz). When the kiln reaches exactly 573°C, a critical phenomenon called 'Quartz Inversion' occurs. <LINE> <LINE> Alpha-type silica crystals suddenly change their atomic structure to Beta, causing an immediate physical expansion of 1%% to 2%% in the piece's volume. If the kiln temperature rises too quickly when passing through this exact window of 573°C, the asymmetrical expansion shatters the entire structure. Thermodynamic control demands heating deceleration at this mark.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Sintering and Vitrification <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Above 1000°C, particle physics dominates. Individual clay particles begin fusing at the edges without completely melting the core. This is 'Sintering'. <LINE> <LINE> As the temperature advances to 1200°C, fluxes melt impurities, creating the vitreous liquid that fills the pores (Vitrification). Simultaneously, 'Mullite' crystals form as long microscopic needles that interlace through the piece's body. Mullite is the titanium skeleton of high-temperature ceramics.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Thermal Shock Effect <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The lethal fragility of common ceramics is Failure by Thermal Shock. <LINE> <LINE> If a dense ceramic material is at 200°C and receives the impact of cold water, the external surface contracts instantly while the internal core remains expanded by heat. The tensile stress on the surface exceeds the material's modulus of rupture, causing a catastrophic failure (the pot explodes). To withstand sudden changes, the material's thermal conductivity must be chemically adjusted.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Crucible Engineering <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To melt metals like copper or bronze in forges, you need a Crucible: a vessel that withstands 1300°C without melting along with the metal. <LINE> <LINE> Common river clay is useless here. Crucibles require massive refractory alumina or graphite mixtures. Furthermore, the crucible wall must be thick enough to retain mechanical structural integrity when lifted with iron tongs, supporting dozens of kilograms of glowing liquid metal.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Use of Grog <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The secret to stopping thick ceramics (like kiln bricks or crucibles) from splitting under thermal stress is Grog. <LINE> <LINE> Grog is made of already fired ceramic, crushed into a coarse sand powder, and added to raw clay. Because grog has already been through the fire, it no longer shrinks. It acts as a microscopic brake system. When a crack tries to spread through the shrunken clay matrix, it hits an inert piece of grog and the failure propagation is halted.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tension versus Compression <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Just as in civil construction (masonry), pyrometamorphic ceramics possess astonishing compressive strength, but deplorable tensile strength. <LINE> <LINE> You can support a car on a compact block of vitrified ceramic and it will not yield. But if you try to bend the same block or give it a lateral blow (shear/tensile force), it will shatter. Understanding this is vital when designing refractory tools: they must always operate under compressive weight, never as levers.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Slag Erosion <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A crucible fails in metallurgy by Chemical Erosion, not just by melting. <LINE> <LINE> When iron or copper is melted, impurities float and form 'Slag'. This liquid slag is highly reactive. If your crucible is made of basic clay, the acidic slag will act as a solvent, eating away the internal ceramic walls from the inside out with each firing, until the bottom of the vessel thins and molten metal leaks straight to the kiln floor.
IGUI_BookPottery5_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Refractoriness Index (PCE) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How does the laboratory measure whether a brick will withstand industrial fire? Through the PCE (Pyrometric Cone Equivalent) Test. <LINE> <LINE> Pure ceramic material is shaped into a standardized cone and subjected to electric arc furnaces until it collapses. A common brick reaches structural collapse (Cone 02) at 1120°C. A super duty alumina refractory only yields above Cone 33 (1743°C). This classification separates decorative ceramics from boiler linings.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Basic Reloading <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Forget Hollywood action movies. In real life, your firearm doesn't have infinite ammo. When the lead runs out, a thousand-dollar piece of steel turns into a useless paperweight. <LINE> <LINE> Welcome to Volume One. This civilian instruction manual was written to build your foundations. We are going to talk about the mechanics of a magazine, the importance of muscle memory, and how to keep your weapon fed without taking your eyes off the threat.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Finger Indexing <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> How do you grab a spare magazine from your belt without looking? Using your index finger. <LINE> <LINE> When you pull a fresh magazine from your pocket or pouch, your index finger should be extended and resting flat against the tip (the nose) of the first round in the magazine. The human brain has an innate ability to point at things. Wherever your index points inside the magwell, the magazine will follow it perfectly.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Don't Look at the Gun <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The moment you look down at the gun on your chest to find the magwell, you lose peripheral vision of your environment. The target shifted, the threat changed. <LINE> <LINE> Military reloading is done in the 'Workspace' — at chin height, with your eyes focused on the threat ahead, visualizing the gun only as a blur in the lower part of your vision. This requires dozens of hours of practice in the dark.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Retention vs. Speed <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> If your gun goes completely dry in the middle of a desperate firefight, you hit the button and let the empty magazine drop straight to the concrete floor (Speed Reload). Time is your life. <LINE> <LINE> But, if the gunfight pauses and you still have a few rounds left, you swap the magazine, but store the partially full magazine in your back pocket. This is 'Reload with Retention'. In a long term survival scenario where supplies are gone, your empty steel magazines are as precious as gold.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Counting Trap <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> 'Did you fire five shots or was it six?' Movies teach you to count your shots. In practice, under the adrenaline explosion of an attack, the blast of firearms is deafening and your mind blanks out. <LINE> <LINE> Nobody counts shots in the real world. We shoot until the slide locks open, the weight of the gun suddenly changes in your hands, and the trigger goes dead. That's when the muscle memory of the reload must take over your body on autopilot.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dry Fire Training <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Mastery is not forged by shooting expensive ammo at the firing range. Reloading mastery is forged in your living room with an empty gun. <LINE> <LINE> Grab empty magazines, face the wall, and practice the motion of drawing the magazine from your belt, indexing your finger, inserting it into the gun, and cycling the slide a thousand times. Do this until the metal flakes off its paint, until your thumbs form calluses and the movement requires no more conscious thought.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> End of the Basics <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Now you understand the tactical weight of springs, the importance of the 'Push-Pull', and why the gun should stay high in your line of sight. Reloading in perfect conditions is mastered. <LINE> <LINE> But a perfect world doesn't exist. What if the gun suddenly jams, with the barrel choked on twisted metal and the threat running toward you? <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Two, 'The Dead Man's Click', we will enter the hell of equipment failures and learn to resurrect a jammed gun in less than two seconds.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Magazine Anatomy <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Most civilians call it a 'clip', but the correct term is Magazine. It is the heart of your pistol or rifle. <LINE> <LINE> It is composed of four parts: The Tube (Body), the Spring, the Follower (the plastic piece that pushes the ammo up), and the Base Plate. Believe it or not, 90%% of feed failures in semi-automatic weapons occur because the shooter bought terrible quality magazines or dropped them in the mud.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Respect the Feed Lips <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The top of the magazine, where the bullet is held before moving into the chamber, is called the 'Feed Lips'. <LINE> <LINE> They are the most sensitive part of the equipment. If you drop a magazine on hard concrete and bend the steel of the lips by even a millimeter, the bullet will enter the barrel at the wrong angle, jamming the gun instantly. Treat your empty magazines as if they were made of glass during reload training on hard ground.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Loading Correctly <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Loading loose bullets into a magazine hurts your thumbs, especially on the last three rounds when the spring is under maximum tension. <LINE> <LINE> The correct motion is not forcing the cartridge straight down; it's pressing the base of the previous cartridge down with your thumb and, simultaneously, sliding the new cartridge backward, under the feed lips. Use the edge of the ammo box or a plastic speedloader to save your fingernails if you are going to shoot all day.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Spring Fatigue Myth <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A common garage myth: 'Don't leave your magazine fully loaded for months, or the spring will weaken.' False. <LINE> <LINE> The physics of steel springs prove that they wear out from cycles (the repetitive act of compressing and decompressing thousands of times). A spring compressed and stored statically in a drawer for five years will retain its strength perfectly. You can leave your home defense weapon fully loaded on the nightstand without fear.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Seating (Push-Pull) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You shoved the full magazine into the grip of the pistol. You heard the 'click'. It's ready to fire, right? Maybe not. <LINE> <LINE> The most dangerous beginner mistake is the false lock. The catch button made the noise, but the magazine didn't seat high enough. On the first shot, the vibration will make the magazine drop straight to the ground. The professional technique is the 'Push-Pull': Insert the magazine with force and, immediately, give it a firm tug downward. If it doesn't come out, it is properly locked.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Closing Blow (Slingshot) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> When the gun runs empty, the slide locks back. You insert a new magazine. How do you chamber the first round? <LINE> <LINE> There are two schools of thought. The first is pulling the slide fully backward with your free hand and letting it go, like a slingshot. Never ride the slide back with your hand; let the raw force of the recoil spring slam the piece forward on its own, ensuring the extractor bites the casing with maximum force.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Release Button (Slide Stop) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The second school for closing the gun is using your thumb to press the slide stop lever down, releasing the piece instantly. <LINE> <LINE> It is a fraction of a second faster than the slingshot technique. However, under extreme stress (when your heart rate goes over 150 bpm), you lose fine motor coordination. Trying to find a tiny metal button with sweaty hands can fail. Pulling the entire slide with a full hand grip is a gross motor movement and is foolproof.
IGUI_BookReloading1_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Administrative Reload <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> An 'Administrative Reload' is the one done in the safety of your bedroom before leaving the house. There is no rush, no danger. <LINE> <LINE> You insert a full magazine, pull the slide to chamber a round. Now the gun is ready, but the magazine is missing a round. The doctrine demands that you remove the magazine, load one more loose round into it to return to maximum capacity, and lock it back into the gun. Known as the 'Plus One' (+1).
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Dead Man's Click <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The loudest sound in the world isn't the blast of a .45 caliber shot. The loudest sound in the world is a faint 'click' when you expected a bang. <LINE> <LINE> Volume Two of this tactical survival manual deals with malfunctions. Your weapon will fail. Factory ammo comes defective, the extractor gathers carbon, the magazine spring catches. When the trigger locks with the threat five meters away, you have two seconds to clear the malfunction, or the next sound you hear will be your own end.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Type 3 Malfunction: The Nightmare (Double Feed) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A Type 3 Malfunction is known as a Double Feed. It is the ultimate tactical nightmare. <LINE> <LINE> It occurs when the extractor fails to pull the spent casing from the chamber, but the slide recycles and tries to shove a fresh live round in there anyway. The gun tries to occupy the same space with two solid metal objects. Everything locks up violently. The trigger goes mushy and the slide stays partially open, wedged against the live round stuck halfway.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The False Tap-Rack <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Since the shooter doesn't look at the gun in combat, he will instinctively perform a 'Tap-Rack' when the gun fails. <LINE> <LINE> In a Type 3 Malfunction, when attempting to Rack, the slide won't move cleanly. It will feel like it's clogged with sand. This tactile sensation in the dark is your body warning you: 'You have a Double Feed. Tap-Rack won't work.' The time to clear a Type 3 isn't one second; it's a terrifying five seconds.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Locking the Slide <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> To clear a Type 3, the first step is to seek cover. You are temporarily out of the fight. <LINE> <LINE> You can't just drop the magazine out, because the pressure of the slide and the crushed rounds pin it inside like a vise grip. First, you must push the slide stop lever up and pull the slide back to Lock it Open. This relieves the crushing of the rounds in the ejection port.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rip the Magazine <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With the slide locked back, the tension has decreased, but the magazine still won't drop on its own. The half-fed round is still gripping it. <LINE> <LINE> You need to press the magazine release and Rip the magazine from the gun with brute force, as if you were tearing the equipment apart. If the magazine spring is still good, you can retain it (tuck it in your fingers), otherwise, let it drop to the floor with the mess of loose rounds falling out of the gun.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Rack, Rack, Rack <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> With the gun stripped of its magazine, the chamber is still compromised by the initial spent casing that caused it all. <LINE> <LINE> You must tilt the gun slightly toward the ejection port side and give three hard, full pulls on the slide ('Rack, Rack, Rack'). This aggressive movement forces the extractor to finally grab the dead casing and throw it out with the help of gravity. After the third pull, the gun is clear and empty.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Back in the Fight <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The gun is now functional, but empty. Grab a spare magazine, insert it firmly, and close the slide. You just resurrected a dead block of steel. <LINE> <LINE> Understanding the tactile difference between a clean jam and a Type 3 Malfunction is the mark of a trained operator. When dirt gets into steel, methodical brutality beats delicacy. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Three, 'Jungle Style Reloading', we will leave malfunctions behind to talk about field modifications. The use of tape to join magazines, Vietnam veteran tactics, and how to optimize your combat vest for dark times.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Freeze Effect <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The psychology of 'The Dead Man's Click' is brutal. The inexperienced shooter pulls the trigger, the gun doesn't fire, and his brain short-circuits. <LINE> <LINE> He lowers the weapon, frowns, looks into the ejection port as if trying to solve a math puzzle, and starts pulling the trigger repeatedly in a panic. This leads to death. When the gun fails, you shouldn't think about why. You must act with your lizard brain, using raw muscle memory to clear the weapon blindly.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Trinity of Chaos <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In modern tactical doctrine, we divide all pistol and rifle malfunctions into three main categories, based on gravity level and resolution time: <LINE> <LINE> Type 1: Failure to Fire <LINE> Type 2: Failure to Eject / 'Stovepipe' <LINE> Type 3: Double Feed <LINE> <LINE> Knowing each monster is the first step to destroying it in the heat of combat.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Type 1 Malfunction: Failure to Fire <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A Type 1 Malfunction is the most common. The slide is fully closed, you pull the trigger, hear the click, but nothing comes out. <LINE> <LINE> This usually means two things: either the round in the chamber has a defective primer (factory flaw or moisture), or the chamber is completely empty because your magazine wasn't seated and the gun didn't pick up the bullet. Either way, don't waste time inspecting. You need to immediately execute the Immediate Action.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tap-Rack-Bang <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The universal response to a Type 1 Malfunction is the maneuver known in every police academy as 'Tap-Rack-Bang'. <LINE> <LINE> It is a fluid, three-count movement that takes less than a second in the hands of a pro. It resolves 90%% of combat stoppages without you even having to take your eyes off the target. Let's deconstruct this life-saving maneuver.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The 'Tap' <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The first movement (Tap) attacks the root of the loose magazine problem. <LINE> <LINE> Without lowering the weapon, you bring up the palm of your support hand and deliver a violent blow from the bottom up on the base of the magazine. Strike it with anger. The goal is to ensure that if the magazine is loose by even a millimeter and preventing feeding, this raw strike will lock it back onto the gun's catch with an affirmative click.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The 'Rack' <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The second movement (Rack) attacks the bad bullet. <LINE> <LINE> Immediately after the blow to the bottom, your support hand moves up, grabs the back of the slide, and pulls it backward to its maximum limit with violence, releasing it immediately (like a slingshot). This movement ejects the defective round (or the nothing) that was in the chamber, and the slide spring fires forward, chambering a fresh, new round.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Type 2 Malfunction: The Stovepipe <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You fired, but the slide stopped halfway. Looking at the weapon, you see the empty brass casing caught in the ejection port, pointing straight up like a chimney flue. <LINE> <LINE> A Stovepipe occurs when the gun doesn't have enough pressure (weak ammo) or when the shooter has a 'Limp Wrist', absorbing the recoil energy that should have ejected the casing. The slide slams back into the empty casing before it can jump out.
IGUI_BookReloading2_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Clearing the Stovepipe <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Some instructors teach to 'wipe' the stovepipe with the side of your hand, sweeping the trapped casing away like dirt. <LINE> <LINE> Forget that under stress. Modern doctrine teaches that the response to Type 2 is exactly the same as Type 1: Tap-Rack. You tap the magazine and rack the slide vigorously. The act of pulling the slide back gives room for the trapped casing to fall free to the side, while loading a new round.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Jungle Style Reloading <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The smell of wet brush, the deafening noise of a sudden contact, and the absolute need to keep shooting. War doesn't happen on a clean, well-lit firing range. <LINE> <LINE> This Volume Three was written with the blood of veterans. When your life depends on putting another 30 rounds into your rifle in less than a second, you don't trust your vest pouch. You trust 'Jungle Style'. We are going to learn the art of field modifications and how duct tape can save your life.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Weight Mathematics <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Every tactical advantage demands a price. The price here is gravity and balance. <LINE> <LINE> Sixty 5.56mm rounds plus the steel of two magazines weigh over a kilogram hanging from the center of your weapon. The rifle will become terribly unbalanced, pulling to one side. With the day's fatigue, keeping your weapon aimed becomes a fight against your own shoulders. Precision sharpshooters don't use Jungle Style; that's for infantry ambushes.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Snag Hazard <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A dual magazine bundle is wide and clumsy. If you are patrolling dense vegetation, vines and branches will snag on the exposed magazine. <LINE> <LINE> The same goes for your rifle's sling. The tape adds friction, catching the strap fabric at the worst possible time. Jungle Style demands that you adapt how you carry your weapon against your chest to keep the protrusion from banging into your tactical vest.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Industrial Mag Clamps <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The 80s commercial market listened to veterans. Today, you can buy 'Mag Clamps' made of phosphated steel or polymer. <LINE> <LINE> These metallic clamps secure the two magazines parallel and tight, creating the perfect spacing without the messy glue of melted duct tape. They are much more structurally reliable, but old-fashioned duct tape still reigns in garages where military supplies have run dry.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The ALICE Pouch Failure <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Where do you store this dual duct-tape monster? Answer: you don't. <LINE> <LINE> Standard military belt pouches (like the ALICE system) were made for individual magazines. A dual bundle won't fit anywhere. Jungle Style is strictly a configuration to be INSIDE THE GUN at the moment of your first patrol. It is your 'Glass-Breaker' for initial contact with the threat.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Post-Contact <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You fired magazine A and swapped to B. The firefight cooled down. Now what? <LINE> <LINE> Now you have a heavy, useless anchor on your gun, composed of 30 dead rounds and a few remaining. As soon as you have cover, perform a tactical reload: remove the entire Jungle Style bundle, throw it inside your jacket or dump pouch, and insert a fresh, single magazine from your waist. Restore your gun's balance for the rest of the patrol.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Rustic Combatant <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Jungle Style isn't pretty. It's dirty, focuses on immediate survival, and sacrifices comfort for speed in the first seconds of life or death. It is the pinnacle of field adaptation for modern box-magazine fed armaments. <LINE> <LINE> But what happens if your gear isn't a modern assault rifle? What if all you have is an old police revolver or your grandfather's hunting rifle? <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Four, 'Clips, Speedloaders, and Bolt Action', we will leave plastic behind. We will learn to reload classic weapons with the fury and precision of the old masters.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Jungle Style Concept <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> What is the fastest reload in the world? It's the one where the new ammo is already taped to your weapon. <LINE> <LINE> 'Jungle Style' is the practice of joining two rifle magazines side by side using duct tape. When the first magazine runs dry, you don't have to reach down to your waist. You just release the empty magazine from the gun, move your hand a few inches to the side, and shove in the full magazine that's already right there, glued to the empty one.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Born Out of Necessity <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Engineers didn't design weapons for this. Soldiers invented it. <LINE> <LINE> We saw it with Thompson submachine guns in WWII and, later, with M16 rifles in Vietnam. Back then, the original magazines only held 20 rounds. In a close-range ambush, 20 rounds disappear in three seconds. Taping two magazines together guaranteed 40 rounds of almost uninterrupted suppressive fire to break the initial ambush.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Rookie Error: The Spacer <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> An eager recruit grabs a roll of tape, glues the two magazines flat against each other, and heads into the jungle. When he tries to insert it into the weapon, the extra magazine hits the side of the receiver and won't go in. <LINE> <LINE> A magazine needs clearance to slide into the weapon's well. The master's secret is the 'Spacer'. Before wrapping the tape, you place a piece of wood, a roll of paracord, or even a few spent casings between the two magazines to create a one-centimeter gap between them.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Up/Up vs. Up/Down <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Hollywood loves taping magazines inverted (Up/Down), where one sits upside down. It looks cool in the movies, but it's tactical suicide. <LINE> <LINE> If you crawl in the mud or hit your gun on the ground, the magazine facing down will fill with dirt. When you flip it to reload, you'll inject mud straight into the heart of your rifle, causing a catastrophic jam. The pro uses the Up/Up configuration, with both feeds pointing to the sky.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Up/Up Geometry <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> But if both are pointing up, won't the extra magazine block the gun's empty casing ejection port? <LINE> <LINE> Yes, unless you offset them. In the Up/Up method, the spare magazine (the one on the outside) is fixed two centimeters lower than the primary magazine. This way, it stays clear of the ejection port and doesn't interfere with your weapon's slide controls. It's an asymmetrical staircase of ammo.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> 100 Mile An Hour Tape <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Don't use stationary masking tape, nor electrical wire tape. The weapon's heat melts the glue and moisture rots the material. <LINE> <LINE> You need military-grade tape or classic heavy-duty Silver Tape (Duct Tape). Wrap the bundle with violent pressure at the base and in the middle. Remember: the bundle will suffer recoil shock with every shot, impacts against trees, and the double weight of bouncing ammo.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mechanics of Movement <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Combat broke out. The slide locks back. The gun is empty. <LINE> <LINE> Your support hand moves down to the base of the taped bundle. Your index finger presses the gun's release button. With the heavy bundle free, you drop your wrist slightly, shift your hand to the side, align the full magazine, and push it up (Push-Pull). A slap to the slide release and you're back in the fight. Total time: 1.2 seconds.
IGUI_BookReloading3_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Advantage of Inate Retention <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> In Volume Two, we talked about the time lost storing an empty magazine in your pocket (Reload with Retention). <LINE> <LINE> Jungle Style cancels out this problem on the first reload. The empty magazine doesn't need to be stored or thrown to the ground; it stays right there, hanging along with the new full magazine inside the weapon. You keep your steel gear with you without wasting milliseconds to sheath it.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Strippers, Speedloaders, and Bolt Action <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The world isn't just made of black assault rifles and 30-round polymer magazines. If modern supplies dry up, you're going to have to open your grandfather's closet. <LINE> <LINE> This Volume Four honors walnut wood and forged steel. We are going to learn how to feed old police revolvers, pump-action shotguns, and bolt-action rifles. They are weapons that are slow to load by nature, which means your technique needs to be flawless for you to survive the intervals.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Bolt Action <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A bolt-action rifle requires you to extract the spent casing and chamber a new round manually after each shot. The weapon's speed is exactly the speed of your hands. <LINE> <LINE> The Sunday hunter lowers the rifle, takes it off his shoulder, looks at the bolt, pulls it with his whole hand, looks at the port, and pushes it back. This takes three seconds per shot. In a gunfight, this is unacceptable. You aren't hunting relaxed deer; you are fighting for survival.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Mad Minute <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> During the Great Wars, trained soldiers fired bolt-action rifles at a speed that the enemy thought were machine guns. The secret is cheek retention. <LINE> <LINE> You NEVER take your cheek off the rifle stock and NEVER take your eyes off the sights. You shoot, and while the recoil throws the barrel slightly upward, the palm of your right hand slaps the bolt up and back with violence, and the same second it hits the limit, pushes it back into the chamber. The rifle moves around you, but your eyes stay locked.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg12: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Two-Finger Operation <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The ultimate speed tactic (popularized with the British Lee-Enfield rifle) is using only your thumb and index finger to grip the bolt's steel knob. <LINE> <LINE> While the index and thumb cycle the action frantically, your middle finger (the third finger) is the one pulling the trigger. You can keep the bolt flying forward and backward with your first two fingers and shoot as soon as it closes with your middle finger. The rate of fire reaches 30 rounds per minute on a manual gun.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg13: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Bolt Bite <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Old ammo or poorly cleaned military rifles can end up with an expanded casing stuck inside the chamber after shooting. The bolt refuses to open by pulling with your hand. <LINE> <LINE> Never try to pull it by slamming the stock on the ground with the barrel pointed at your chin (you might blow your own head off). The tactical clearing technique involves sitting down, positioning the stock on your knee with the barrel pointed to the open air, and using your stiff boot sole to stomp the bolt handle with controlled force. The raw leverage will break the friction.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg14: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Vintage Metal Advantage <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Heavy steel and manual action may be old-fashioned, but they are immune to gas problems that plague modern rifles. Your tube shotgun will feed ammo with rain, sand, or blood in the gears. Your revolver doesn't care about magazine dirt, because it doesn't have one. Mechanical simplicity is the guarantee that the 'bang' will happen.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg15: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Manual Training <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> We finished the classic era. You learned the gravity of the cylinder, the infinite hunger of 12-gauge tubes, the fury of stripper clips dropping into the rifle, and the speed of the bolt's 'Mad Minute'. The weapon is old, but death is the same. <LINE> <LINE> Now that you've mastered 19th and late 20th-century manual weapon mechanics, we need to bind everything into a definitive neuro-muscular format. <LINE> <LINE> In Volume Five and last, 'The Ultimate Encyclopedia of Reloading Techniques', we will leave primary notions behind to understand total tactical ergonomics, combat timing, and how to integrate reloading into the movement of your whole squad.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg2: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Broken Clock (The Revolver) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A revolver never jams, but the price of that reliability is a reloading nightmare. When the cylinder spins empty, you have six empty chambers and a hand full of lead. <LINE> <LINE> The movement begins in your support hand. Your left hand passes through the open frame, pushing the cylinder out with your fingers and holding the gun steady by the middle. The barrel must point directly to the SKY. Why? Gravity. When you hit the ejector rod with your right hand, the spent brass casings need to fall free to the earth.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg3: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Speedloaders <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Inserting loose bullets one by one in a gunfight is begging to die. Modern police use a Speedloader: a plastic cylinder that holds six rounds in the exact geometry of the cylinder. <LINE> <LINE> With the gun empty and the barrel pointed to the GROUND, you grab the speedloader, align the tips of the six bullets with the six chambers, and push. Some models require you to twist a knob clockwise to release the ammo (HKS model), others drop the bullets automatically when the plastic body hits the steel (Safariland).
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg4: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Speed Strips <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Speedloaders are round and hard to carry in a pants pocket without looking like you have an apple in your leg. The alternative is the 'Speed Strip'. <LINE> <LINE> It's a flat rubber strip that aligns six rounds in single file. The tactic is to insert two bullets into the cylinder at once and, with a sharp snapping motion of your wrist to the side, release them from the rubber. You spin the cylinder with your thumb and repeat for the next two. It's slower, but the flat profile is ideal for concealed survival.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg5: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Tube Hunger (Shotguns) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A 12-gauge pump-action shotgun is the queen of close-quarters combat, but it has a fixed tubular magazine that empties terrifyingly fast. <LINE> <LINE> The golden rule of the shotgun is: 'The beast is always hungry.' If you fired twice, and there's a three-second pause in combat, don't stand there staring. Grab two shells and feed the tube immediately. Shoot one, load one. Your shotgun's tube should never reach zero unless the fight is over.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg6: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Emergency Reload (Port Load) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> But what if the tube empties out and the gun clicks right in front of the threat? <LINE> <LINE> Don't load the shell into the bottom tube. The barrel is empty! You must do a 'Port Load'. Pull the pump slide fully backward to open the ejection port. Grab a single shell from your belt and drop it directly from above, into the open window. Push the slide forward with violence. You just chambered a live round and the gun is ready to fire in a second. Once you shoot, feed the lower tube.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg7: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Don't Pity the Pump <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The worst mistake someone can make with a pump-action shotgun is being gentle when cycling the weapon. <LINE> <LINE> The mechanism is made of raw steel and loose tolerances. If you pull the slide back slowly for fear of making noise or hurting the gun, the spent casing won't be thrown out with force, creating a massive stovepipe. Work the action like you're angry. Pull back hard, push forward hard. The loud rack scares, but it guarantees feeding.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg8: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Stripper Clips <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Vintage rifles (like the Chinese SKS, German Mauser, or Springfield) don't use removable box magazines. The magazine is internal. To load it quickly, you use a 'Stripper Clip'. <LINE> <LINE> It's a small strip of metal that holds 5 to 10 rounds by their base. You lock the rifle's slide open, fit the clip into a small metal guide rail right above the opening, and use your hand to squeeze the entire set of bullets down into the weapon's well, 'stripping' them from the clip.
IGUI_BookReloading4_Pg9: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Thumb Technique (Clip) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> The rookie tries to push the 10 bullets off the Stripper Clip by pressing the middle of them. Brass friction locks everything up, and the bullets slice open the guy's finger. <LINE> <LINE> The professional movement requires you to place your right thumb as close as possible to the BASE of the bullet (near the metal clip). You raise your elbow pointing it to the stars and push straight down with a single stiff, brutal movement of your entire arm, not just your finger. The 10 rounds slide into the gun's void like water down a drain.
IGUI_BookReloading5_Pg1: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> The Ultimate Encyclopedia of Reloading Techniques <LINE> Introduction <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> You are no longer a scared civilian on a firing range. You absorbed equipment failures, the tactical brutality of the jungle, and the precision of vintage steel. Now, we enter the realm of Special Operations. <LINE> <LINE> This Fifth Volume is the advanced biomechanics manual. We will deal with fractions of a second, absolute darkness, combat injuries, and the total elimination of conscious thought. Here, your body becomes the machine.
IGUI_BookReloading5_Pg10: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Kneeling in the Fatal Funnel <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> A doorway and a narrow hallway are known as a 'Fatal Funnel', as they channel all the enemy's defensive fire. <LINE> <LINE> If you are the front man (Point) clearing a hallway, and your gun dries up, you cannot retreat and you cannot stand there reloading (blocking your squad's view behind you). Doctrine demands that you immediately drop to your knees where you stand. This keeps the line of fire clear over your head for your rear partner to annihilate the threat while you reload crouched.
IGUI_BookReloading5_Pg11: <RGB:0,0,0> <CENTRE> <SIZE:large> Subconscious Tracking (Weight) <LINE> <LINE> <LEFT> <SIZE:medium> Counting shots is movie lore.
